Amid flydubai crash scare, a look at 4 other times things went wrong inside a cockpit
The flydubai episode has highlighted how developments inside a cockpit can sometimes prove as dangerous as problems outside the aircraft.
flydubai's Flight FZ1073 was travelling from Dubai to Tel Aviv with 174 passengers on Wednesday when a fight between the two pilots escalated into a life-threatening emergency. The aircraft plunged about 16,000 feet, dropping from 33,000 feet to 17,000 feet in roughly a minute. As an investigation is underway to determine the sequence of events that led to the incident, the episode has highlighted how developments inside a cockpit can sometimes prove as dangerous as problems outside the aircraft.
As the flydubai incident gains focus, here are four unusual incidents inside flight cockpits that led to safety lapses in recent years. Track flydubai incident LIVE.
2023: SpiceJet pilots' Holi celebration inside cockpit
In 2023, a photograph went viral showing a glass of coffee and a gujiya (an Indian sweet) placed on the flight deck console. The incident triggered sharp reactions online, following which SpiceJet took the two pilots off duty.
Deep Dive
Aviation experts also criticised the incident, saying a sudden movement of the aircraft could cause the liquid to spill over critical electronic systems, potentially affecting flight operations.
The airline's spokesperson later issued a clarification, saying, “SpiceJet has a strict policy for consumption of food inside the cockpit, which is adhered to by all flight crew. Appropriate disciplinary action will be taken upon completion of the investigation."
2018: Jet Airways pilots' mid-air fight
In another incident, two Jet Airways pilots were grounded after an alleged altercation broke out aboard a London-Mumbai flight in January 2018.
According to an HT report, the argument allegedly became violent, following which the female pilot left the cockpit crying. Following this, the male pilot also left the cockpit, leaving the operations to the cabin crew, which violates flight safety norms.
The incident took place while the aircraft was flying over Iran-Pakistan airspace and was about 2.45 hours from Mumbai, according to an airline source cited by PTI.
2013: Air India pilot locked out of cockpit
In 2013, an Air India flight was diverted after its commander was unable to re-enter the cockpit following a toilet break because the door had jammed.
According to a BBC report at the time, Flight AI 403 was travelling from Delhi to Bangalore when the incident occurred. The co-pilot reportedly tried to open the door from inside but was unsuccessful.
"The commander of the flight had left the cockpit for a short while to visit the toilet, and on returning to the cockpit found the door locked. The door had jammed, and all efforts to open the door, even from inside by the co-pilot, failed," Air India said in a statement at the time.
The co-pilot subsequently sought permission from ground control and diverted the aircraft to Bhopal.
2013: Air India pilots nap, leave cockpit unattended
Another Air India incident reported in April 2013 involved allegations that two pilots left the cockpit of a Bangkok-Delhi flight while the aircraft was on autopilot.
The Telegraph reported at the time that the pilots had allegedly moved to the business class section for a nap while two air hostesses remained in the cockpit. The flight was carrying 166 passengers.
Air India denied that the pilots had left the cockpit. However, it said the flight attendants “were in the cockpit for a prolonged period” and acknowledged that “due to distraction, the co-pilot had touched the autopilot disconnect button momentarily.”
The airline suspended all four crew members with immediate effect.

Renee Good: Family of US woman killed by ICE agent sues Trump officials
- Published
The family of a woman who was killed by an immigration agent in Minneapolis in January has announced two lawsuits against the US government and members of the Trump administration.
Renee Good was killed by an Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officer during a sweep of the city targeting immigrants and criminals that was called Operation Metro Surge.
One of the suits blames the government for her death, claiming the operation created "an unprecedented environment for state-sponsored violence", a lawyer for the family, Antonio Romanucci, said during a news conference on Thursday.
The White House and Department of Homeland Security (DHS) have not yet commented on the lawsuits.
After another Minneapolis resident, Alex Pretti, was killed by immigration agents weeks later, hundreds of federal agents were withdrawn from the Minnesota city.
The lawsuits were filed by Good's partner, Becca Good, and her brother Brent Ganger.
In one, they accuse the government of "battery, assault, false imprisonment, intentional infliction of emotional distress and negligence that caused Renee's death".
It cites the Federal Tort Claims Act, which allows citizens to sue the government for personal injury, death, or property damage caused by the negligence of federal employees.
The second lawsuit targets ICE officer Jonathan Ross, who shot Good, as well as White House Deputy Chief of Staff Stephen Miller, former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem, White House border chief Tom Homan and others, alleging a "conspiracy to interfere with civil rights by senior federal officials, federal immigration enforcement agents, and private actors".
Good was a 37-year-old mother of three who had just moved to the city. She was shot on 7 January in a traffic stop, which immigration authorities said occurred after she made "an attempt to kill or cause bodily harm to agents" in "an act of domestic terrorism".
Family members and witnesses disputed that she was attempting to attack officers when she was killed inside her car.
Her death sparked nationwide protests, which intensified after Pretti was also shot to death by immigration agents on 24 January.
On Tuesday, Good's mother and brother testified to Congress.
"She should still be alive. I will say it again, my daughter should still be alive," Donna Ganger, Good's mother, told lawmakers.
"I am a registered Republican. I voted for President Trump under the impression that these agents were here to protect the citizens of the United States," Ganger continued.
"But far more than being a Republican, I am a Christian. Jesus teaches us to forgive and I have, but what we are asking for is accountability."

Greetings from Syria, where time seems to melt as a glassmaker braves scorching temps
Our world as journalists can move fast; every day there's breaking news from all corners of the world, and we scramble to stay on top of multiple threads of information each day.
That is why I loved watching this glassmaker just outside the historic Old City in Damascus. In 100 degree summer heat, he patiently shaped cup after glass cup in the blistering furnace in front of him, seemingly impervious to the temperature.
Time seemed to matter less than the process of melting and stretching the hot, melted glass. He made cups and oil jars and decorative lamps in a variety of jewel colors, using techniques and styles that have not changed for decades. Watching his craft reminded me to slow down and enjoy the moment, too.
Even though his shop was right on the edge of the Old City of Damascus, it was largely empty. Syria's nearly 14-year civil war has ended, but the economy is still struggling, while inflation has ratcheted up the cost of living in the last year. Even a glass can be a luxury for some.

Most implants like pacemakers and insulin pumps work in isolation. To help them coordinate with each other, a team of Georgia Tech researchers built a networking system that sends signals through body tissue instead of antennas and radio waves.
Radio problems
Implants that communicate today mostly rely on radio protocols like Bluetooth Low Energy or near-field communication (NFC). Both are a poor fit for in-body data transfer, says Alex Abramson, a Georgia Tech engineer and co-author of the new study.
The first problem is power. “If you want an implant to remain in an active state such that it can respond within milliseconds, it’s very difficult to do that with the Bluetooth system,” Abramson said. According to the paper, Bluetooth components, when they’re activated, can cut an implant’s battery life by up to 90 percent.
The second problem is that radio waves don’t travel well through the body. “Bluetooth and near-field communication are attenuated quite a lot in the tissue,” Abramson said. He said that implant-to-implant radio communication systems run into attenuation issues if the signal has to travel more than one centimeter through the tissue. Then there’s size. Radio needs antennas, and commercial Bluetooth components require a device at least five millimeters wide. Implants thinner than three millimeters can be injected with a syringe at an outpatient clinic; bigger ones usually need surgery.
The fix Abramson’s team came up is called SWANS (Smart Wireless Autonomous Networking System) and was inspired by the way body’s own internal communication networks. “The nervous system can take a lot of inputs from all over the body, harvest all that data, and make a specific decision. And our system mimics that,” Abramson said. SWANS relies on ionic conduction just like neurons, which communicate by shuttling sodium and potassium ions through their membranes, creating voltage differences. “But instead of using nerves, we use normal body tissue to send those signals,” Abramson said.

Cornell Jane Doe's attorney says she told police in 2024: 'I was raped'
The woman who alleges she was gang raped by fellow Cornell University students in 2024 clearly stated in her statement to police two years ago that she was sexually assaulted.
That's according to her attorney, Thomas Giuffra, who confirmed to NPR that his client told investigators, "I can say with 100% percent confidence I was raped," citing transcripts from Jane Doe's sworn statement in 2024.
NPR asked Giuffra to specifically confirm on the record to NPR that his client made this exact quoted statement regarding her assault. His response by text: "Yes she did."
This is in contrast to statements from the local prosecutor who claimed on Monday that Doe never stated she was raped. Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten told NPR local station WSKG Wednesday that he had not read the full account of her detailed statements to investigators where she repeatedly described being assaulted.
NPR asked Cornell if campus police provided the DA with all of the information from their investigation, including her repeated statements about being assaulted. The university did not respond to the request for comment.
CBS News New York reported Wednesday on a transcript of an interview between the Cornell University Police Department investigator and the alleged victim. NPR has not been able to obtain a copy of these transcripts.
Van Houten said in Monday's statement that in the 2024 statement taken by Cornell University police Doe "did not allege that she was drugged against her will or gang raped. On the contrary, Jane Doe's statement described her participation in drug use and sexual conduct as voluntary, conscious, and consensual."
No criminal charges were ever filed against the seven men Doe alleges drugged and assaulted her for several hours in October 2024.
Van Houten told NPR member station WSKG Wednesday evening that he was in the process of getting the interview transcript from Cornell. He told the station over email he doesn't know when he will get the transcript from the university "or if Cornell will resist turning it over."
"If it's factual, we absolutely should have been informed about what Jane Doe said to police that was not in her six-page statement," he told WSKG.
Van Houten said earlier this week that his office is reexamining the case.
He added that particular transcript is part of the confidential Title IX investigation Cornell launched into the alleged assault.
Earlier this month, Doe filed a lawsuit against the seven men who she alleges assaulted her two years ago. Cornell was also named in the lawsuit.
Following the onslaught of public backlash against Cornell and the local prosecutor, the school said Wednesday night that it will bring in an outside counsel to conduct an independent probe into the handling of the case.

Sixty-three per cent of the 3,253 Water Supply Schemes (WSS) taken up under the Jal Jeevan Mission (JJM) in Jammu and Kashmir are non-operational despite expenditure of around Rs 7,000 crore, a House Committee of the Jammu and Kashmir Legislative Assembly has found, raising serious questions over planning, execution, procurement, quality control and monitoring of the flagship rural drinking-water programme.
The findings are contained in the voluminous 1253-page report of the House Committee constituted to examine alleged irregularities in the implementation of JJM in the Union Territory. The report was laid before the Legislative Assembly on September 21 by committee chairman Justice (Retd) Hasnain Masoodi. The committee was constituted on April 9, 2025, to examine alleged irregularities in implementation of the Mission.
“The result is that 63 per cent of 3253 WSS involving an expenditure of Rs. 7000.00 crore are non-operational,” the report states. It adds that even the 37 percent of schemes claimed by the Jal Shakti Department to be functional were “not fully operational”.
The committee said the institutional mechanism established to oversee JJM had failed to discharge its responsibilities effectively, resulting in inadequate planning, supervision and monitoring.
“The House Committee is of the considered view that there has been complete abdication of authority,” the report said, referring to the Apex Level Committee, Executive Committee and District Level Committees.
The panel attributed the failure to achieve the Mission’s objectives within the stipulated timeframe to what it described as “gross negligence” on the part of these committees and the officers who manned them.
According to the report, 37 per cent of schemes claimed by the Jal Shakti Department to be functional were also “not fully operational” in several cases.
The committee also questioned official figures relating to Functional Household Tap Connections (FHTCs), saying discrepancies emerged between departmental records and ground conditions during field inspections.
The panel said records supplied to it contained what it described as “false claims” regarding the number of FHTCs provided in habitations and the number of habitations covered.
“On spot visits, the House Committee came to know that far less than the number of FHTC indicated in the record, have actually been provided benefit of the Safe and Adequate Drinking Water of the prescribed quality,” the report said.
The committee also questioned the department’s claim that 81 per cent of rural households in J&K had tap-water connections as of March 2025, saying the figures required physical verification.
The House Committee was headed by Justice (Retd) Hasnain Masoodi. Its 13 members were Mohammad Yousuf Tarigami, Ali Mohammad Dar, Altaf Ahmad Wani, Aijaz Ahmad Jan, Rajiv Jasrotia, Ranbir Singh Pathania, Tanvir Sadiq, Javaid Riyaz Bedar, Muzaffar Iqbal Khan, Rafiq Ahmad Naik, Arjun Singh Raju and Iftikar Ahmad.
The committee subsequently undertook field inspections to assess the implementation of JJM works. It inspected schemes in Rajouri and Poonch, among other areas, before finalising its findings.
One of the major concerns highlighted by the committee was the failure to establish the sustainability and adequacy of water sources before executing schemes.
The panel found instances where expenditure had been incurred on pumping systems, storage facilities, transmission networks and distribution infrastructure without adequately establishing the viability of the underlying water source.
In WSS Shirpora Bangil, the committee found high sulphur and iron content in the source and said this had rendered the scheme useless. It termed the expenditure “unfruitful” and directed fresh testing of the source.
“Providing of FHTC is immaterial in absence of safe and viable source,” the committee observed.
The report also cited schemes affected by land and source disputes. These included WSS Dachnipora in Pahalgam, WSS Lelhara, WSS Syed Mantaqi Khrew and WSS Greenland Wuyan. In WSS Bugam Dooniwari, the committee said Rs 10 crore had been spent without benefiting the targeted population because of a source dispute.
The committee has also scrutinised the decision to shift from GI pipes to HDPE pipes during JJM implementation.
It noted that the Jal Shakti Department, Jammu, authorised Executive Engineers in April 2023 to use HDPE pipes instead of GI pipes depending on site feasibility. However, an earlier technical committee had recommended modification of DPRs before the change.
The panel said the national-level communications cited in support of the shift did not mandate compulsory replacement of GI pipes with HDPE pipes and questioned why the decision was taken several years after the Mission’s launch.
It said the decision had significant financial and operational implications and “ought to have been taken by the Apex Level Committee”.
The report also records allegations made by retired IAS officer Ashok Parmar concerning procurement orders and changes in pipe specifications. Parmar alleged that procurement orders worth Rs 4,000 crore were placed without approval and that HDPE pipes were ordered in violation of approved DPRs. The committee recorded these as allegations and evidence presented before it, rather than independently establishing every allegation.
The committee separately examined tube-well projects and raised concerns over tendering, technical qualifications, quality assurance and functionality.
It said some tube wells had failed to meet desired standards and noted submissions that water from certain sources was unsuitable for human consumption. The committee observed that quality-assurance mechanisms appeared to have been inadequately enforced.
The panel also questioned the effectiveness of third-party monitoring agencies hired for audit and inspection of JJM works. It said field observations regarding faulty execution indicated that such agencies had failed to discharge their obligations adequately despite being paid for monitoring and audit work.
The committee has recommended constitution of a High-Level Committee to conduct a comprehensive audit of JJM and retrofitting schemes, including procurement of DI, GI and HDPE pipes and execution of civil works.
It has recommended identifying officers and engineers responsible for irregularities and initiating action against those found responsible under applicable rules.
The panel has also called for scrutiny of officers who served on the Apex Level, Executive and District Level Committees from their constitution until March 31, 2025, with their actions and omissions examined against the respective terms of reference.
A comprehensive technical, financial and administrative review of tube-well projects has also been recommended, covering functionality, water quality, payments released, pending liabilities and possible additional expenditure.
The committee said the problems identified were not confined to isolated technical failures but indicated “possible systemic deficiencies in planning, procurement, quality control, contract administration and project oversight”.
Its central finding is that the success of JJM cannot be measured merely through construction figures or tap connections recorded in official databases. The ultimate test, the committee said, is whether households are actually receiving safe and adequate drinking water.

Researchers have documented the first confirmed snakebite envenomation and subsequent human deaths in India caused by the venomous Caspian cobra (Naja oxiana), which have never previously been reported in the country, according to a case report published in Epidemiology International, a peer-reviewed journal.
The study titled ‘First Report of Deadly Bites by Caspian Cobra (Naja oxiana) From India’ by Bharti O.K., Menon J.C., Phull A., Joy S., Sharma V. and Malhotra A. details two fatalities and two survivals from bites by the species, also called the Central Asian cobra, in Himachal Pradesh’s Chamba’s Pir Panjal mountain range.
“Envenomation and subsequent deaths from the Caspian Cobra (Naja oxiana) have never previously been reported from India. While collecting data for the Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR) project on snakebites, we came across two deaths due to the bite of N. oxiana,” said Omesh Kumar Bharti of Himachal Pradesh’s Directorate of Health Services, who led the study.
“Deaths due to N. oxiana have never been previously reported from India. Naja oxiana is primarily found in Central Asia, with high human mortality resulting from envenoming. This species has been reported from Pakistan and Kashmir and was recorded in 2019 from Tissa block of Chamba district, Himachal Pradesh. Naja oxiana has been shown to have rapidly expanded its range from Iran towards the northeast and it has been observed to be slowly expanding its range in Chamba towards lower elevations as reported by local rescuers,” noted the study.
The first death occurred in July 2020 in Ullansa village, when a 40-year-old man was bitten twice on the leg while spraying an apple orchard. He was taken to a nearby faith healer. However, his condition continued to worsen and on the third day after the bite, he was taken to the Civil Hospital Bharmour, where he was seen by the doctor and was found to lack a detectable pulse. A second victim, a 62-year-old man from Bhanjraru village, was bitten in July 2021 while walking to work and collapsed within half an hour. He died before reaching Civil Hospital Tissa; a post-mortem attributed the death to the venom’s neurotoxic effects, the study said.
Snakebite envenoming (SBE) remains a major cause of preventable mortality in rural India. The big four species, namely the spectacled cobra (Naja naja), Russell’s viper (Daboia russelii), common krait (Bungarus caeruleus) and saw-scaled viper (Echis carinatus), are responsible for the majority of snakebite envenomation and deaths in the country. The commercially available anti-snake venom (ASV) correspondingly covers these species only, it said. The study also noted that the available anti-snake venom (ASV), designed to counter the ‘big four’ species responsible for most snakebite deaths nationally, does not effectively neutralise the venom components of N. oxiana.
The researchers said that there is a need to create greater community awareness about the danger of this species of snake in affected areas and educate them about ways to reduce the risk of being bitten.

Engineering education needs to move beyond writing code and equip students to understand how entire software systems work, according to speakers at Inc42’s inaugural ‘The CTO Summit 2026’. Speaking during the panel ‘The Great Engineering Reset: Teams, Talent & Leadership After AI’, the participants called for greater emphasis on logical thinking, philosophy, and systems design to prepare engineers for work increasingly shaped by AI. Moderated by Accel VP Anagh Prasad, the panel featured Naukri.com CTO Arvind Heda, Acko cofounder and CPTO Vishwanath Ramarao, and IDfy CEO Ashok Hariharan. The discussion examined how AI is changing engineering roles and team structures, with automation taking over more routine coding and quality assurance work. Hariharan said this shift raises a longer-term question: how will engineers develop the expertise to design and manage complex systems if they spend less time building them? Drawing on his “old-school engineering background”, he recalled how earlier generations of engineers had to grapple with problems such as memory management. Over time, tools and software layers made those underlying processes less visible to developers. “There's a lot of crap code that gets written,” he said, warning that AI-assisted development could amplify existing quality problems if engineers assume the tools can do everything for them. The concern extends beyond the code being produced today to the capabilities engineers will develop over the coming years. Hariharan joked that engineers can advance into leadership roles before fully understanding the responsibilities of a lead or manager, eventually becoming VPs. “I think we are in danger of the same kind of thing now,” he said. Hariharan said engineering teams have fewer mid-level engineers, leaving a skills gap between senior architects and junior developers. This raises a question about how junior engineers will learn to design systems. “How do you teach systems design when they don't necessarily code on a daily basis?” he asked. The growing demands of testing also surfaced in a separate discussion at the CTO Summit on how AI is changing coding and review. Cashfree Payments CTO Ramkumar Venkatesan said the company’s spending on virtual environments for testing now exceeds its spending on AI tools. For Hariharan, the shift towards AI-generated code increases the need for architects who understand deployment, security, and scaling. Automating routine implementation work does not remove the responsibility to ensure that the resulting systems are reliable and secure. “I think there’s a huge number of security flaws that are going to be exposed. I am pretty sure that’s a fear every CTO has,” he said.

On July 19, as Sahida Fakir stepped out of her Navi Mumbai home to buy dinner, she was allegedly picked up and detained by Mumbai police’s Chembur crime branch. Four days later, her husband Jumman Fakir learnt that she was forcibly pushed across the border into Bangladesh on suspicion being an illegal immigrant.
Even as Sahida remains steeped in uncertainty, away from her family in Bangladesh to this day, a writ petition filed in the Supreme Court was heard by a Bench comprising Chief Justice Surya Kant, Justice Joymalya Bagchi and Justice V Mohana on September 17. The court sought a response from the Centre within four weeks.
A native of Gobindapur village, Swarupnagar block in West Bengal’s North 24 Parganas district, Sahida was not given any opportunity to established her Indian citizenship before being detained, her husband alleged.
Alt News spoke to Sahida Fakir, who narrated to us the harrowing experience of being pushed into no-man’s land at midnight and wading through a marsh to reach the Bangladesh side. According to her, she was picked up by the Mumbai police and kept in a detention centre for four days before being pushed out of India. In this duration, the police didn’t produce her before a magistrate.
“When I was pleading with Mumbai police officials to let me go, they just sneered at me and said we need to fill up the empty seats of the deportation airplane,” she alleged, asking, “How can they be so inhumane? What is my fault? Being a Muslim who speaks Bengali?”
Jumman told Alt News that he reached Chembur crime branch office on July 19 and attempted to prove his wife’s citizenship by furnishing her documents. “The police said that they would need few days to verify her documents and, if necessary, would ask for additional documents. I went to the office again on July 22 with more papers, but the next day, they informed me that she had been pushed into Bangladesh. When I asked how they could do such a thing without giving us any opportunity to prove our citizenship, I was thrown out of the office,” he claimed.
According to Jumman, after almost a week, Sahida called from Bangladesh to inform him that she had allegedly been expelled from India through either the Assam or the Northeast border, and that she was currently living with a family from Satkhira that provided her shelter. “She called me from an unknown number and was crying inconsolably. A family from Bhadiyali village in Kalaroa Upazila of Satkhira was sheltering her, and the Bangladesh police posted two armed guards for her protection outside the residence,” he said. “I get to speak to her occasionally by calling the Bangladeshi family’s number. She is a thyroid patient. Local journalists had arranged some food, clothes and medicines for her, however, that stock is fast depleting.”
The couple has lived in Mumbai for the last 20 years — Jumman works as a car cleaner while Sahida worked as a domestic help. Their elder son Sahin Fakir lives in their native village in Bengal’s North 24 parganas district while 13-year-old Samim Fakir lived with his parents in Mumbai. After Sahida’s pushback, Jumman and Samim left Mumbai and returned to Swarupnagar.

What The Documents Say
According to Sahida’s citizenship documents, including her birth certificate, her Aadhar card, voter card, PAN card, accessed by Alt News, she was born in November 1988. On October 19, 1995, the Bithari-Hakimpur Gram Panchayat, under the Swarupnagar Block, issued her birth certificate (serial number 6382).
Sahida’s father, Aminuddin Gazi, is listed in the 2002 SIR electoral roll (Part 89, Serial 514, Swarupnagar assembly); her grandfather, Badsha Gazi, is also listed in the 1952 electoral roll for Swarupnagar assembly. See below:
On January 29 this year, the Bithari-Hakimpur Gram Panchayat issued a family genealogy stating that Badsha Gazi’s son, Aminuddin Gazi, had 14 children, including Sahida. Sahida’s name also appears in land records accessed by Alt News. Although Jumman’s name appeared in the final SIR list, Sahida was placed in the “under adjudication” category. However, she had appealed against her exclusion.
Following her ‘unofficial deportation’ to Bangladesh in July, Sahida’s family was able to obtain a certificate from Swarupdaha Free Primary School on August 9, which states that she studied there from 1994 to 1998. Her transfer certificate, issued by Jamia Islamia Girls’ High Madrasa located in Swarupnagar block for Class 8 in 2008, is also available.
Sahida’s Account
Speaking to Alt News, Sahida said, “I was kept at the Chembur detention camp for four days. My phone, the money that I was carrying to buy chapatis for my family and my Aadhaar card — everything was snatched away. I begged the police, fell at their feet to let me contact my family, only then did they allow me to make a call for a few seconds. After I informed my husband, he came to the Chembur crime branch office to furnish all the documents to prove my Indian citizenship, but the police didn’t even bother to see or check them,” she alleged.
“After spending four days at the detention centre, they stacked several others and me onto a bus with dark curtains, so we couldn’t see where we were going. If anybody even tried to pull the curtains slightly, the Border Security Force men would beat and abuse them. We later realised that it was the airport. From there we were boarded onto an aircraft, and they took us somewhere on the Assam or Northeast border. I don’t know any of these places, but heard it from other people in our group,” she further alleged.
According to Sahida, she was placed in a group of around 200 people who were also pushed into Bangladesh.
“After we landed, we were taken to a detention centre. From there, we were packed into buses in batches. The bus took us to several other camps. They kept us waiting in some camps for 10 hours, and in some for about 3-4 hours before moving us out. Finally around 1 am, the BSF pushed all of us back into no man’s land,” she claimed.
“We were in a marsh with the muck reaching my neck in some places. I had to wade through the mud on no man’s land to finally reach the Bangladesh side of the border by daybreak,” she added.
The others told Sahida that they could be at the Feni border, near Chattogram of Bangladesh.
Following this, according to the petition submitted in the Supreme Court by her son, Sahin, Sahida somehow managed to reach the Petrapole-Benapole border area after a few days. There, the Border Guard Bangladesh (BGB) apprehended her, but due to humanitarian reasons, she was provided shelter and was finally able to contact her family on July 31, the petition said.
“A farming family from Bhadiyali village has sheltered me, and despite their financial constraints, they are doing their best to feed me. But do I deserve this hopeless situation? Why do I have to survive on other people’s grace? I have diabetes and thyroid issues. Since July 19, I haven’t had my medicine. My family’s life has been turned upside down. My husband had to flee Mumbai, leaving his meagre employment and my younger son had to leave his studies,” she lamented.
Alt News contacted an officer from Chembur crime branch, who refused to comment on the matter, stating that they are “officially required not to speak on such matters.”
We also reached out to the officer-in-charge of Kolaroa police station in Bangladesh. He refused to comment.
Legal Tangle: Contentious SOP, Loopholes in Govt Order
On August 17, Sahin moved the apex court with a petition challenging his mother’s apprehension, detention and forcible expulsion to Bangladesh, demanding that she be brought back to India. The petition argued that the Mumbai police’s actions directly contradicted the provisions of Article 21 of the Constitution.
The petition also challenged the legality of the Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) dated May 2, 2025, titled ‘Procedure for deportation of illegal Bangladeshi nationals/Rohingyas’, and the ‘Immigration and Foreigners Order, 2025’, insofar as it permits or facilitates removal of persons apprehended within India without the safeguards prescribed by law and the Constitution.
The SOP from May 2025, published by the Union ministry of home affairs (MHA), establishes guidelines for ‘deportation/removal/expulsion’ of Bangladeshi nationals and Rohingyas. According to the SOP: “All State Governments/UT Administrations shall set up a Special Task Force in each District under the police of the State/UT to detect, identify and deport/send-back illegal immigrants from Bangladesh/Myanmar settled in the State/UT concerned.”
“If the suspected Bangladesh/Myanmar national claims Indian citizenship and residence of a place in any other Indian State/UT, the concerned State Government/UT would send to the Home Secretary of the State/UT and District Collector/District Magistrate of the District from where the suspected person claims to hail, the details including name, parentage, residential address, details of near relatives etc. The State Government/ UT/Collector/District Magistrate concerned in turn will ensure that an appropriate report is sent to the deporting State Government/UT after proper verification within a period of 30 days,” the SOP reads.
It is important to note here that the SOP doesn’t mandate an FIR under the Immigration and Foreigners Act, 2025, if a suspected Bangladeshi or a Rohingya is apprehended and due investigation, enabling anybody under suspicion of being an illegal immigrant to be simply expelled from India.
A Supreme Court advocate, requesting anonymity, told Alt News that the SOP is inhumane as it empowers the State and the border guarding forces such as the BSF to push back suspected ‘Bangladeshi and Rohingya’ infiltrators into ‘no man’s land’ without any judicial process. The SOP also mandates the handover of suspects to the relevant border guarding forces of Bangladesh and Myanmar, thus enabling the Indian border guarding forces to exercise their powers arbitrarily.
As contention around this SOP rose, the Indian government initiated ‘The Immigration and Foreigners Order, 2025’ — published in the Gazette of India on September 1, 2025, effectively overriding the provisions of the earlier SOP. According to this order, if a suspected foreign national is apprehended without his/her travel document, such as a passport, then that person’s nationality has to be first ascertained by that person’s Nation. After it has been proved beyond doubt that the person is an illegal immigrant, the deportation process will take place.
As per Chapter 3, Article 12(4)(c) of the said Order, it is clearly mentioned: “In the absence of a valid passport or other travel document, the authorities referred to in sub-paragraph (3) may immediately take appropriate steps for getting the nationality verified and for issuance of travel document in favour of the illegal migrant from the Embassy or High Commission of the country concerned in India through the Ministry of External Affairs and necessary steps shall be taken by such authorities to deport the illegal migrant from the country as soon as the travel document is received.”
Based on Sahida’s account of her ‘deportation’, however, it becomes clear that provisions of the Order were not followed. Further, even though certain provisions of the previous SOP were applied, the process, or rather the lack of it, in which she was pushed into Bangladesh, contradicts the rest of it.
In a similar case reported by Scroll.in, 66-year-old Dablu Sheikh and his three sons were picked up from their home in Suti, Murshidabad, under suspicion of being Bangladeshis. They have been missing for over 40 days. Sheikh’s father, Sk Samjani, was also a voter in the Suti Assembly constituency in 1966 and 1995, the report stated, adding that the inspector-in-charge of Suti police station said the four persons were illegal Bangladeshi infiltrators, and thus had been deported to Bangladesh. The officer further said that no FIR was registered against the four men under the Foreigners Act, as they were detained following the Union government circular from May 2025, and directly sent to the Jangipur holding centre. The report suggests that they were deported to Bangladesh from the holding centre.

A court in Japan has ruled that the human voice has legal protection after a landmark case involving a well-known actor and a TikTok account that he claimed had cloned his “lustrous” baritone voice in its AI-generated videos.
Tokyo district court said on Wednesday that voices should enjoy the same protection as publicity rights, at the end of a closely watched legal action brought against TikTok by Kenjiro Tsuda – best known for voicing the character Kento Nanami in the anime Jujutsu Kaisen.
But the court dismissed Tsuda’s request that the operator of TikTok remove the videos, noting that the user had deleted them soon after the suit was filed last November. “The unauthorised use of a performer’s voice … can be considered an infringement on publicity rights,” said the presiding judge, Aya Takahashi.
The lawsuit is believed to be the first in Japan seeking to defend an individual’s vocal identity against AI-generated copies. Japan’s voice actors, many of whom achieve star status through their “appearances” in anime, are increasingly worried that AI mimicry is threatening their livelihoods and the industry as a whole.
An actor’s voice “is the result of years of rigorous training and apprenticeship”, Yuko Sasaki, executive director of the Japan Actors Union said ahead of the ruling.
Tsuda, 55, claimed that the 188 TikTok videos uploaded on an anonymous account between July 2024 and September last year had been narrated by a “deep” and “lustrous” voice that could only be his. In response, the platform argued that the videos contained a “generic male voice” and that any perceived similarities to Tsuda’s voice were highly subjective.
The verdict is the first in which a Japanese court has declared that the human voice is protected under publicity rights, a reference to the ability to control and profit from aspects of an individual’s identity, in Tsuda’s case his distinctive voice.
The protection applies “if the purpose of using the voice is exclusively to take advantage of its commercial appeal”, Takahashi said, describing a voice to be “as symbolic of one’s personality as portraits are”.
The TikTok account, whose picture resembled Tsuda’s Jujutsu Kaisen character, combined images and AI-generated speech about urban legends, the occult and conspiracy theories.
At one point, the account had more than 200,000 subscribers and, according to the legal complaint, the clips would have earned its owner between ¥500,000 (£2,395) and ¥75,000 in monthly revenue, the Kyodo news agency said.
Describing the content as “sordid”, Tsuda’s legal team claimed the account had only attracted attention because it had cloned the “attractive voice of a popular actor”.
TikTok said in a statement it would “respect the court’s judgment while considering what steps to take after scrutinising [the ruling’s] details”. It added: “We will continue to sincerely work on the balance between technology development and rights protection.”
In 2024, actors in Japan launched a campaign called “No More” to oppose the unauthorised use of their faces and voices in AI-generated content.

Donna Langley, chairman of NBCUniversal Entertainment & Studios, is not a fan of Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery combining. “I think it is bad. I think it’s bad for everything,” she said bluntly, addressing the feature film market in particular.
“What this year has proven is, if you build it, they will come. Right? If you have the right mix of films in a steady diet for the audience, they’re going to show up. And we’re also cultivating this great habit with young people, who are coming to the cinema and we need to keep them there. So volume matters, and if we if we essentially lose a studio — which is I know not the stated plan and goal — but if we lose a studio, it’s bad … Look back at Fox-Disney. It wasn’t great, she said during a Q&A at the Bloomberg Screentime conference.
Paramount has committed to a legal settlement calling for the combined studios to release 30 theatrical films a year for the first two years post-merger, and 32 films for the following three years. The deal is expected to close next Tuesday.
Watch on Deadline
Last fall, Universal detached the prolific Tyler Sheridan from his longtime studio home at Par for a new five-year film and television deal starting in early 2029. Asked how, Langley said, “Look, I think I saw an opportunity, with disruption and instability at moments where companies are going through something. And you know they are just moments to kind of look around the marketplace and see if there’s a competitive advantage. But really, where I started talking to Taylor was about film, because I knew that he had a film deal at Paramount but it was a first look deal, didn’t have as many teeth to it as his television deal. That’s how it started, and then we just got to talking, and one thing led to another.”
Split Looming
NBCU itself is in the midst of big corporate wrangling as parent Comcast plans to spin it off with Sky into a standalone, publicly traded company. “I’m mostly excited and optimistic about it. I’m not fearful of it at all, actually. I think it’s going to be good … Not to be tethered to a legacy business, Comcast, where the stock has struggled for a while, is a good thing.
“Now we are going to be the masters of our own destiny. It is more pressure. But in our neck of the woods, when you have to open movies, you know, however many times a year, there’s no more pressure than that.” She acknowledged “the scale question, of course,” but said it will be interesting for the slimmed down company to explore “at a moment of this real historical transformational change, what else can we be doing, and where else should we be playing in terms of growth.”
The split should be completed by mid-2027.
Box Office Run
The head of the number one movie studio in the world this year in the best overall box office since the pandemic, is more cautions about next year. “I think 2027 has a different complexion to it. I don’t think it has as much potential for the kind of big billion-dollar hits like this year, if you think about the breakouts, the ones that were surprises … But I think ‘28 will be kind of back again.”
“But you know, you really never know. I mean, I think if this year taught us anything, it was so exciting because it sort of reminds you that one of the fun things about this business is that surprises can always happen, good or bad. Luckily, it was good.”
Universal’s Christopher Nolan’s epicThe Odyssey is a juggernaut led and Obsession from Focus Features one of the year’s unexpected hits.
“They were both surprises for different reasons. I felt very confident that The Odyssey was going to cross a billion and then some. But the play-out pattern was so extraordinary. I mean, the fact that in week three we actually outgrossed the second week. It was just filled with surprises all the way along.”
Obsession “was just a good old-fashioned over-performing surprise. We knew we had something that could hit the cultural zeitgeist when we apparently, according to reports, overpaid for it in Toronto … We caught lightning in a bottle.”
The studio acquired the film for $15 million and it went on to gross over $500 million worldwide.

Will 2026 finally be Warrington Wolves' year?
- Published
Britain did not have a single motorway in 1955.
We were still five years out from the MOT being introduced and cars did not require a seatbelt.
There was one television channel, provided by the BBC.
Capital punishment was still in place.
The humble postcode had not yet been rolled out across the land.
And rationing was still very much in the national memory, having only been phased out a year beforehand.
All of this paints a picture as to what life was like when Warrington last won a league championship.
On Saturday they stand 80 minutes away from ending a 71-year wait for another title and their boss Sam Burgess has the chance to lay down a marker as a coach just as he did during an illustrious playing career.
But can Super League's perennial nearly side finally get over the line and finally earn a league triumph in the modern era?
- Quiz: Name every Super League Grand Finalist 
  - Published8 hours ago
Two Wembley defeats - now Old Trafford awaits
Former England captain Burgess began his career as Warrington head coach in earnest ahead of the 2024 season - off the back of Daryl Powell's uncompetitive stint in charge of the Wire.
A legend of the game as a player, it was his first top job as a coach, five years after he retired following his enviable stint both on the pitch and as assistant coach down under with South Sydney Rabbitohs.
A first Wembley appearance came shortly after, as Wolves reached that season's Challenge Cup final, when they were undone by a Wigan Warriors side on the way to a quadruple.
Twelve months later, treble-winners-in-waiting Hull KR beat them again in the final.
Burgess' side eventually missed out on a play-off spot altogether in 2025, finishing eighth, but, in contrast, they have put together a consistent campaign in 2026 to finish third in the table, behind second-placed Leeds on points difference.
So you might expect Burgess to be feeling rather pleased with himself, and his side, as they prepare for the first Grand Final of his tenure and a meeting with Powell, who has inspired Wakefield's ascent from the Championship to the top of the sport after leaving the Wire.
Well, not quite.
"Not really," Burgess replied when asked in his pre-match media commitments whether it gave him extra satisfaction that his side had proved him right by emerging as challengers after their disappointing 2025.
"I'm pretty satisfied to be here. I guess I'll find out how satisfied I am on Saturday at about eight o'clock."
Super League Grand Final
Warrington Wolves v Wakefield Trinity
Saturday, 3 October, kick-off 18:00 BST
Old Trafford, Manchester
Listen to commentary on BBC Radio 5 Sports Extra, BBC Radio Merseyside, BBC Radio Leeds and BBC Sounds; watch highlights Saturday, 3 October from 23:00 BST on iPlayer and BBC Two on Sunday at 13:45 BST
Fifth time lucky for Warrington?
It took 14 years into the Super League era before Warrington reached their first Grand Final and this year is the fifth time they have reached Old Trafford, following previous finals in 2012, 2013, 2016 and 2018.
Tony Smith's impressive Wire side came undone against Leeds first and then again at the hands of Wigan in 2013 and 2016 - with Steve Price last leading the club to a Grand Final in 2018 when they were defeated by the Warriors for a third time in a row.
Since that point, the Primrose and Blue have failed to trouble the upper echelons of the sport, with St Helens' dominant spell starting the following year while Wigan and Hull KR have both taken turns at having a commanding stint of their own.
So far this year, they have narrowly missed out on second place in the regular season and dispatched reigning champions Hull KR and Leeds in the play-offs.
Yet when times were tough in 2025, Burgess never gave up and said that it was a belief in his side and the knowledge that Warrington had a long-term plan that kept his camp motivated.
"I could see a lot of green shoots last year where we're going," he added.
"You've got to be able to believe it to do it, and I believed in the club, I believed in the players we had, and I believed in the philosophy that we've got, so I guess we've been very consistent all year without jumping out at anyone, which is a good sign.
"We've had a lot of challenges throughout the year, we've managed them well as a club, which has been important."
Will McNamara's experience aid Wire?
Ask those in the know at the beginning of the 2026 season which two teams would contest the Grand Final and not many would have picked out Warrington or Wakefield.
"It's Warrington's year" has become something of a meme in the northern hemisphere's rugby league fandom in the past few years - describing how one of the league's best-funded and well-supported teams always looks the part, but falls at the final hurdle.
Former England coach Steve McNamara arrived at the club as an assistant coach last October following his departure from a spell at Catalans, who he guided to the Challenge Cup and two Super League Grand Finals.
He is set to join Hull FC for next season but Burgess believes their previous failures have not happened in a vacuum - but have shaped the team they have become this season.
"We've played a couple of big games over the last three years, so we've got a bit of experience," said Burgess.
"We have matured as a group and as a club. The club has matured with us, which is important. Whether it counts as much, on Saturday, we'll see."
Of course, Burgess' time as a player can be summed up by a stunning 2014 season which culminated in a victorious NRL Grand Final with the Rabbitohs, when he played on with a broken cheekbone and also won the Clive Churchill Medal as man of the match.
Asked about how he reflected on that moment ahead of his first Grand Final as a coach, Burgess said: "It's much easier as a player.
"Any experience is experience whether it's as a player, coach, staff member, assistant, whatever. We've got a bit of experience in the room.
"Steve McNamara brought a lot of experience to us this year as well, which is going to help for something.
"We've got a lot of things in our corner. Again, when the whistle blows at six o'clock, you've got to do the right jobs and get the performance on the field."

Pandora claims 'we haven't made this decision lightly' after raising prices
The SiriusXM service joins a long list of streamers that have increased rates this year.
Following the lead of streamers everywhere, Pandora is instituting a price hike. In a September 2026 email, the music streamer announced that their subscriptions would increase by at least a dollar per month beginning in October. The announcement prompted a mix of surprise and outrage from many of Pandora's millions of paid subscribers.
The change comes just months after Spotify, one of Pandora's fiercest competitors, instituted a similar price hike. Up until now, Pandora listeners have enjoyed relatively cheap subscription costs. And while many customers are sure to remain loyal to its "Music Genome Project," some are just as likely to judge Pandora's music-curation-juice as no longer worth the squeeze.
The logic behind the SiriusXM company's latest billing structure is somewhat unclear. On its support page, Pandora stated, "We're making this update so we can continue investing in the personalized listening experience Pandora is known for, including better recommendations, improved reliability, and access to the music and podcasts you love." Whether this ad-speech can be translated into a suite of AI features, an expanded software development team, or that Pandora simply needed to keep the lights on, is unclear. And while the company assures its subscribes that "we haven't made this decision lightly," some will inevitably be skeptical that increased prices will translate into a better product.
Pandora's new prices
As it stands, Pandora offers two paid subscription tiers. The first, Pandora Plus, now costs $5.99 per month, or $65.89 per year. Complete with ad-free personalized music, unlimited skips, offline listening, and ad-supported search features, the music genome project subscription is the same price as Spotify's and Apple's discounted student options.
The streamer's music-on-demand tier, Pandora Premium, is more expensive. Now costing $11.99 per month or $131.89 per year, Pandora Premium is more in line with its competitors' prices. The Ad-free service, with unlimited skips, offline listening, shared playlists, and search and play features, is much closer to the service offered by top on-demand music streamers like Apple, YouTube, Spotify, and Qoboz. And while access to the company's famous curation algorithm helps differentiate Pandora Premium from the competition, Engadget found that the service offered fewer premium features and more compressed streaming quality than its competitors. Meanwhile, Premium Family subscribers, who can grant access to Pandora Premium to six family members, will now fork up $19.99/month or $219.89/annually.
Those who subscribe to Pandora Free will continue to have access to personalized music stations, podcasts, and ad-supported unlimited skips. If you decide to cancel your paid subscription, you will return to the free curation station service.
If you subscribe to Pandora through third-party vendors, like the Apple or Google Play store, you may pay a different price. Pandora Plus and Premium users who subscribe via Apple, for instance, will see their monthly music streaming bill rise to $6.99 and $14.99, respectively. Google Play store listeners, meanwhile, will pay $6.99 and $12.99 per month for Pandora Plus and Pandora Premium. Amazon Appstore subscribers will find that their Pandora Plus subscription remains at $4.99 per month, while Roku customers can subscribe to the service's paid tiers for $4.99 and $10.99 per month. For the latter two, select annual, Premium, and Premium Family subscriptions remain unavailable.
Managing your Pandora account
New subscribers began paying the higher prices as of September 22, 2026 . Current subscribers, on the other hand, will be charged the newest rates on their next bill, starting October 22, 2026. On its announcement page, the company stated that subscribers can switch to any its three subscription tiers before the start of their next billing cycle.
If you'd like to learn more about your subscription rate, Pandora suggests referring to the notification in your email's mailbox. Alternatively, you can sign in to your Pandora account, tap the profile icon in the upper right corner > Settings > Subscription.
If you would like to change your subscription, you can do so through Pandora's website or app. If visiting Pandora's site via a computer, sign into your account, go to Subscriptions > Switch Plans. To cancel your subscription, follow the same procedure and click Cancel Subscription in the bottom corner. If visiting Pandora's website on your phone, select the three lined menu icon at the top left, tap Subscription, log into your account, and select Switch Plans. From there you can choose to Cancel Subscription. After confirming your choice, you will be returned to Pandora Free.
Critically, if you are signed up via a third party application, you will have to adjust your subscription through your billing provider. As it stands, Pandora Support is unable to help manage these subscriptions. To find billing partner-specific subscription management instructions, visit Pandora's support page.
Notably, any changes must be made at least 24 hours before the end of the billing cycle. If you decide to cancel or change your subscription, you will still have access to your most premium Pandora subscription tier's features through the end of your current billing cycle.

Britain is in talks with European allies over releasing emergency diesel stockpiles after Donald Trump threatened to cut off US supplies of the fuel.
Ministers held calls with counterparts from the European Commission (EC), Germany, France, Italy and Ireland on Thursday to discuss whether to draw down reserves after the Trump administration told Germany and France to release their stockpiles to help ease soaring global energy prices or face a US export ban.
The warning marks an escalation of pressure on Europe as Trump considers a potential wider ban to help lower domestic fuel prices before the US midterm elections in November.
Trump said Washington could ask its European allies to release strategic diesel reserves. “We may do that. They have some diesel,” Trump told reporters on a midterm elections campaign trip to Texas, shortly after the Treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, urged Europe to “immediately” release its reserves.
Bessent flagged the potential diesel cuts in a social media post, writing: “Our European partners should accelerate delivery on their existing commitments and make additional supplies immediately available to address ongoing disruptions.”
Martin McCluskey, the UK minister for local energy, was reportedly on the call with EU countries on Thursday.
The Trump administration has been frustrated with France and Germany for what it considers their not following through on commitments to release oil and petrol stocks.
Fuel stations across Europe are unlikely to run dry, because Europe produces about 70% of the diesel it consumes from domestic refineries. It also stores fuels in reserve. But experts fear that competing for cargoes on the global market would lead to higher market prices.
It was unclear whether the UK would be included in such a ban, but the loss of US supply would drive prices up sharply at the pumps because the UK does not refine enough diesel to meet domestic demand. About a third of UK diesel imports last year came from the US.
The average price of a litre of diesel in the UK hit a new all-time high on Wednesday of 199.72p, according to the motoring body the RAC.
John Healey, the chancellor, admitted earlier this week that UK diesel prices were “extreme” and said the government was in discussion with the US over trying to stop a ban.
EC commission spokesperson Anna Kaisa Itkonen confirmed that EU member states will hold urgent talks with the commission on Friday to discuss a coordinated response.
“The commission … is closely coordinating with EU member states to take stock of the situation and examine appropriate measures to tackle these high prices,” Itkonen added. Discussions will also involve the International Energy Agency.
The US energy secretary Chris Wright said he was “highly confident” Europe could help ease soaring global fuel prices by drawing down its emergency diesel inventories.
“This is a time for a coordinated release of diesel stores as we go into to harvest season and we go into winter heating oil season,” he told Fox News. “Now’s the time to bring more diesel to the market, and that diesel is available.”
Miatta Fahnbulleh, the UK energy secretary, has been in contact with Wright to raise concerns.
Earlier, a US official told reporters it was “in Europe’s best interest” to work with the US as it pursues options to boost the supply of refined products and lower costs for consumers.
The US war in Iran has disrupted energy supplies via the strait of Hormuz and sent the price of oil soaring. Before the war, in February, Brent crude – the international benchmark for oil prices – traded at about $72 a barrel. It was above $101 on Thursday.
Releasing more stocks would represent a problem for European countries, which need to balance the need to bring down domestic fuel prices with keeping high stocks for a potential worsening energy crisis over the winter if the Iran war continues.
“The UK continues to need fuels – from transport to chemicals, agriculture and defence,” said Elizabeth de Jong, the chief executive of the trade group Fuels Industry UK. The latest US threat showed the UK “cannot solely rely on overseas production for domestic energy security”, she added.
Trump has said he was “very seriously” considering a US diesel export ban to try to curb soaring prices, and has urged Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, to pause strikes on Russian oil refineries over concerns that they could further push up prices. Russia had already extended its ban on diesel exports until the end of October after Ukrainian attacks on refining companies.
A government spokesperson said: “We have a diverse and resilient supply. We continue to engage with our international partners and the UK fuel industry.”

Thirteen-year-old S. Ishaan completed a double crossing of the Palk Strait on Wednesday, setting a record as the youngest S14 para swimmer to achieve the feat.
The Chennai swimmer covered approximately 64km in 18 hours and 50 minutes, starting at 5 p.m. on September 29 and finishing at 11.50 a.m. on September 30. He swam from Dhanushkodi in Tamil Nadu to Talaimannar in Sri Lanka and back to Dhanushkodi.
The crossing followed a 5km sea swim in Goa and a 10km swim in Kochi. In preparation, he trained in different sea conditions, gradually progressing from swimming near the shore to sessions farther out at sea.
Ishaan has also built a competitive record in the pool. At the Junior and Sub-Junior National Para Swimming Championship in Bengaluru in June, he won gold in the sub-junior boys’ 100m backstroke, 100m butterfly and 200m individual medley events.
In 2025, he won gold in the 100m butterfly and silver in the 200m individual medley at the National Championships.
Across National and Tamil Nadu State competitions over the past two years, he has collected eight gold and two silver medals.
Ishaan was diagnosed with autism, intellectual disability and attention deficit hyperactivity disorder at two, according to his mother, Sharmila. He competes in S14, the category for swimmers with an intellectual impairment.
Sport initially became part of his routine to develop coordination and help him follow instructions. His mother noticed that he was more attentive in the water.
“He is very happy when he is swimming, as compared to when not in the pool,” Sharmila told Sportstar before the sea swimming attempt.
She introduced him to skating, running, badminton and table tennis as well, without initially aiming for medals. His swimming coaches subsequently identified his potential for competition and began preparing him for races.
Sharmila, an IT engineer, said she had left her job to support his development, adapting activities at home to his interests and working towards small achievements.
The sea crossing was also intended to give Ishaan a sense of joy after he encountered rejection and difficulties interacting with other children.
Sharmila said she wanted him to develop the skills and mental strength to manage daily life independently. Taking on new challenges through sport was part of preparing him for life beyond the pool.
“He needs a tough mindset to accept everything,” she added.

It was raining intermittently on a cloudy evening when a private bus on the Attingal–Venjaramoodu route entered the crowded Attingal private bus stand in Thiruvananthapuram in Keralam.
Even before the engine fell silent, the bus crew spotted another bus at the stand—a service that, according to the route schedule, should have left the stand around 30 seconds ago. Within moments, a heated argument began between the crew of the two buses. The crew of the former bus alleged that the latter bus was eating into their business by deliberately delaying its departure and poaching passengers. After several minutes of heated exchanges, the latter bus finally left the stand, with only a handful of passengers.
Though that confrontation ended there, another, milder altercation erupted inside the former bus. The owner-turned-conductor directed his frustration towards the driver. Throughout the journey, the conductor had repeatedly urged the driver to speed through the heavy evening traffic, skip some stops and ensure that the bus reached the stand on schedule.
K.N. Rajesh (name changed), a middle-aged driver with around 22 years of experience at the wheel, said no amount of skill acquired over the years could have helped him beat the heavy evening traffic in the town and the delay was unavoidable. Yet, the bus had lost a handful of passengers as it arrived about 30 seconds late. The delay will cause a cascading effect on passenger numbers at nearly half the stops along the route, he says.
“As bus workers, we try to avoid such situations. In our bid to maintain time and minimise losses, we may inadvertently commit minor traffic violations such as jumping a red signal at the last moment or skipping certain stops or services,” says Rajesh.
The episode offers a glimpse into the daily dramas unfolding across Keralam’s public transport network, where intense competition, fuelled by dwindling revenues of private bus operators, has become commonplace. The situation has worsened since the State government introduced the Priyadarshini free travel scheme on Ordinary buses of the Kerala State Road Transport Corporation (KSRTC) for women and transgender persons on June 15, 2026.
Janatha Sabu, a private bus owner and member of the Kerala Motor Transport Workers’ Welfare Fund Board, notes that the industry has been in the doldrums since the COVID-19 outbreak, with nearly a third of its passenger base switching to alternative modes of transport. The Priyadarshini scheme has now dealt another severe blow to the already struggling private bus industry, eroding more than 50% of its existing passenger base, observes Sabu.
The resulting scramble for getting passengers has intensified competition and turned bus stands across the State into venues of frequent confrontations. The scheme, a poll promise of the United Democratic Front, has now emerged as a major success, with women passengers embracing the scheme. Transport Minister C.P. John says the scheme had facilitated an average 12.93 lakh free journeys a day in 100 days, entailing a financial liability of around ₹267 crore for the KSRTC.
While acknowledging the scheme’s popularity, the private bus operators say they are not entirely opposed to it, even though it had severely affected their livelihood.
700 private buses stop operations
T. Gopinathan, general secretary of the All Kerala Bus Operators Organisation, says that around 700 private buses had ceased operations during the first 100 days of the scheme. More than half of the buses still in operation are reportedly running reduced services and earning low daily revenues.
“The State government should hike the minimum fare to ₹15 for all categories of passengers, along with an increase in student fares, to offset the losses suffered by private buses. Otherwise, the private bus sector will face a slow death,” says Gopinathan.
Daily revenue has fallen by around ₹2,000 to ₹3,000 for private buses operating in southern Keralam, where KSRTC services are more extensive than in the central and northern parts of the State.
Many operators are left with barely ₹500 to ₹1,000 in daily profit after meeting fuel expenses, employees’ wages and maintenance costs. Fuel prices alone have risen by around ₹9 a litre following the West Asia crisis, observes Sabu, who operates three buses.
An interesting anecdote about Kerala’s private bus industry is closely intertwined with the State’s enduring tea culture. Sunil Kumar, owner of Saroma Travels, which once operated a fleet of 10 buses but now runs only four services in Thiruvananthapuram city, recalls the long-standing relationship between the price of a cup of tea and the minimum bus fare. “When I entered the industry in 1994, the minimum bus fare was ₹1, and a cup of tea too cost ₹1. By 1996, both had risen to ₹2, and they continued to rise together at regular intervals,” he recalls.
Just before the introduction of the Priyadarshini scheme, the minimum private bus fare in Keralam was ₹10, so was the price of a cup of tea. But things changed after the West Asia war. While the tea prices rose to ₹15 across the State, the minimum bus fare remained unchanged despite a sharp increase in fuel prices and other operational costs, including price of spare parts and accessories.
“Besides these increases, the State government’s free-travel scheme came as a body blow to the industry that has already been struggling to survive,” Kumar says.
Private bus revenues have also failed to keep pace with the rise in the consumer price index over the years. The disparity is evident from the experience of Shaji, a bus owner and office-bearer of the Kerala Private Bus Federation. “Fifteen years ago, the minimum bus fare was ₹5, and a single bus generated ₹7,000-₹8,000 in revenue a day. Even today, buses on the most profitable routes earn only around ₹9,000 to ₹10,000 a day. The interesting part is that diesel that cost ₹35 a litre 15 years ago costs ₹104 today. The daily wage of bus crew has risen from ₹300 to around ₹1,100 during the same period,” explains Shaji.
Long day, low wages
The plight of bus crew members is even more distressing. An average crew member begins the day around 5 a.m., with most private buses starting services between 5.30 a.m. and 6.30 a.m. The workday often stretches until 9 p.m. or 10 p.m., making for 12-15-hour shifts.
Crew members who once earned around ₹1,100 to ₹1,200 a day often receive only ₹700 to ₹800 on less profitable routes because of falling revenues.
Rajesh G., who has worked as a private bus conductor on the Irinjalakuda-Triprayar route for the past 24 years, says the demanding work schedule bears little relation to the remuneration. “The only reason many of us continue in this profession is that we do not possess any other skills or means to support our families. During the COVID-19 pandemic, I tried selling lottery tickets on the streets to make a living, but the income was not enough to support my family. That eventually forced me back into the only profession I know,” Rajesh sighs.
Happy women
On the other hand, the latest turn of events has brought cheer to women across Keralam, although the major beneficiaries of the free-ride scheme are those in southern Keralam and parts of central Keralam. According to Deepa M., a native of Kallambalam and a private-sector employee, the scheme has been a boon, particularly for women working in low-paying jobs in textile shops, sales and other unorganised sectors. “Saving an average of ₹1,000 to ₹1,800 a month means a lot to an ordinary homemaker,” she feels.
However, she points out that the scheme has its drawbacks too. “My son studies in a school in Sreekaryam, Thiruvananthapuram. He travels from Kallambalam to Sreekaryam, a route where KSRTC enjoys a virtual monopoly. Student concession is available only on KSRTC Ordinary buses, which are now overcrowded with women passengers, forcing him to travel on KSRTC Fast Passenger buses, which do not offer student concession. Whatever I save through the free-ride scheme is lost on my son’s daily commute,” Deepa says.
The major grievance of private bus operators is the manner in which the State government implemented the scheme without introducing measures to shield the private bus sector from its adverse impact. The government could have extended the scheme to private buses as well. An income-based scheme applicable to both the KSRTC and private buses would ensure that economically weaker sections continue to receive the benefits while also supporting the student community, feel bus operators.
“Such a model would reduce pressure on routes inadequately served by the KSRTC and enable the State to extend the benefit to people across Keralam by making optimum use of the existing public transport network,” feels Gopinathan.
An expert committee headed by former Transport Commissioner K. Padmakumar has submitted a report to Chief Minister V.D. Satheesan recommending several measures to address the concerns of private buses numbering around 11,000, including according the sector industry status. However, private bus operators have rejected most of the recommendations, saying they do little to address their immediate concerns.
The road ahead remains uncertain for the private bus operators.

At Madison Square Garden in New York City on November 9, 2017, at the G-Shock 35th Anniversary Celebration, G-Shock creator Kikuo Ibe showed off three sapphire-crystal prototype watches: one clear, one ruby, and one sapphire blue. Because machining sapphire was so difficult at the time, each watch took over a month to produce.
These were built with, for the time, high-end Casio features such as Tough Solar power and Multiband 6 radio-controlled timekeeping—but as they didn’t meet the G-Shock shock-resistance standards, the trio was never intended for sale. They were primarily a symbol of innovation for the Japanese brand, which started in 1983 specializing in super-tough performance timepieces.
Now, nine years later, in what Casio is calling the culmination of an “eight-year project” (so presumably the ball started rolling soon after the excited reception Ibe’s crystal concepts got on stage at MSG), G-Shock is launching a three-watch collection using blue sapphire as an expression of what happens when G-Shock toughness meets Japanese engineering. The flagship model, and by far the most expensive, is the $80,000 MRG-D5000, the first-ever retail G-Shock with an outer case and bezel hewn entirely from blue sapphire crystal.
The collection is called the “Blue Rose Project” because the blue rose is viewed as a symbol of making the impossible possible since it doesn’t exist in nature. It sees the super-expensive MRG-D5000 released alongside the $9,500 MRG-B5000SA-2, and the GMW-B5000SB-1A for $850.
Only 20 of the $80,000 MRG-D5000 full-sapphire G-Shocks will be made, putting these rugged “luxury” timepieces somewhat implausibly in the same price bracket as a Patek Philippe or Porsche Macan. This is quite the flex from a company that also sells its watches for less than $90.
The 2017 concept watches required metal bracing to hold the crystal sections together, which is partly why they couldn’t pass G-Shock’s rigorous toughness tests. The new MRG-D5000, however, is a fully functional G-Shock, taking construction lessons from the MR-G engineering team who found that dividing the outer case into multiple interacting components could disperse impact more effectively than a conventional single-piece construction.
G-Shock fans will have already seen this technique employed in the titanium MRG-B5000 from 2022, but this “Multi-Guard Structure” has now been reengineered specifically for sapphire crystal, with Casio claiming the construction takes inspiration from traditional Japanese timber-frame techniques, using interlocking pieces rather than placing stress around screw holes or other details that could result in cracking.
While the MRG-D5000’s bezel and outer case are entirely machined from blue sapphire crystal ingots grown over several months, sadly—unlike the 2017 concepts—the strap isn’t matching sapphire but instead a rubber strap that repeats the brick pattern seen on the watch face in raised detail. To round off the luxe makeover, the MRG-D5000’s MR-G mark, “Shock Resist,” and other lettering on the face are in 24-carat gold.
The G-Shock development team responsible for the new collection tells WIRED the fundamental challenge was building a “near-unbreakable” watch using an inherently brittle material. Making watch cases from sapphire is not new in the high-end watch world, and many distinguished makers, including Richard Mille and Hublot, have released pieces made of the crystal.
To make the sapphire case work for a G-Shock, however, Casio had to develop a brand-new, dedicated shock-resistant structure, with the Multi-Guard construction using virtually invisible seams, alongside a completely screwless assembly method to hit the required shock performance. To do this, the outer case assembly required the development of completely new, dedicated jigs and fixtures, a process apparently so demanding that only one person at Yamagata Casio (the primary “mother factory” for Casio) can currently perform it.
All three new watches, along with the proper G-Shock resistance to knocks and drops, are water-resistant to 200 meters, solar-powered, and feature radio-controlled timekeeping, world time, stopwatch, countdown timer, five daily alarms, and a full-auto LED backlight.
If the $80K G-Shock is too steep an investment, the MRG-B5000SA-2 with two two-carat facet-cut blue sapphires and a grade-5 titanium exterior is limited to 500 pieces. The cheapest GMW-B5000SB-1A2 marries a full-metal black exterior with four round brilliant-cut blue sapphires.

Google promised Gemini 3.5 Pro in June, but it spent the summer trotting out smaller Flash models. Now, Google is ready to take on the frontier again with Gemini 4 Argon. The company claims this new AI offers industry-leading performance in coding, knowledge work, and cybersecurity, but you aren’t allowed to use it yet.
