Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee has paused executions in the state after death row inmate Christa Pike survived two lethal injection attempts on Wednesday night in what has been dubbed an unprecedented failure.
Pike, 50, was alive and loudly snoring after being given two doses of pentobarbital. She was taken by ambulance from the prison and was being treated at a hospital, but her attorneys said they hadn’t been told about her condition.
She had been scheduled for execution at 10 a.m. Wednesday for a murder she committed at age 18 and would have been the first woman executed in Tennessee in more than 200 years. An appeals court stopped the lethal injection just an hour before it was to start and hours later the U.S. Supreme Court overturned that stay.
“There are very few answers this morning. It’s very early," Lee told reporters Thursday at an unrelated event, noting he had received no updates on Pike's condition. "The people of our state deserve to have those questions answered."
He called what happened “deeply disturbing” and said it appeared prison staff followed procedure.
Lee has ordered “a comprehensive, third-party review to determine exactly what occurred” and said that the one remaining scheduled execution will not take place this year.
“Carrying out a lawfully imposed sentence is among the State’s most serious responsibilities, and the people of Tennessee expect it to be done in a manner that is not only legal and constitutional, but is effective,” he said.
The Tennessee Department of Correction said in a statement that it “followed every step of the State’s lawful, established execution protocol approved by the Attorney General’s Office.”
The state's execution protocol calls for a secondary set of drug syringes to be administered “if the inmate is not deceased” after the first set. It does not spell out what happens if the subject is alive after the second set.
Robin M. Maher, executive director of the Death Penalty Information Center, said what Pike experienced is “singular and unparalleled.”
Media witnesses detail the botched execution
Seven other people have survived medical problems due to an execution team's failure to access a vein to administer lethal injection drugs, but no one has stayed alive after receiving the drugs used in such executions, she said.
Media witnesses observing from a separate room said officials raised curtains to the execution chamber at 7:27 p.m., showing Pike strapped to a gurney.
“I’m going to leave this world the way I spent most of my life and that is in love,” she said in her “last” words. She described herself as at peace.
But Pike remained awake and at one point raised her head and asked prison officials if her arm was supposed to feel that way. It was not clear what she was referencing.
By 8:26 p.m., execution witnesses reported that the second dose of pentobarbital had been administered.
Pike continued to be heard snoring behind the closed curtain until the microphone was cut off at 8:53 p.m. At that time there was an announcement to escort media witnesses out of the area.
Lawyers for Pike filed an emergency motion late Wednesday to the Tennessee Supreme Court seeking to immediately halt and stay the execution, saying she was in “unnecessary agony” and it was violating her right to be executed free of cruel and unusual punishment. They also filed motions in the Sixth Circuit court and a district court.
It was the second time this year that Tennessee has been unable to carry out an execution. In May, state officials called off the lethal injection of Tony Carruthers, who was convicted of kidnapping and killing three people in 1994, after executioners tried and failed for over an hour to place an IV to administer pentobarbital.
Pike and her boyfriend were convicted of the fatal stabbing and beating in 1995 of 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer, their classmate at a job training facility in Knoxville. The case garnered widespread attention in part because of a pentagram that was carved on Slemmer’s body, and other elements of the crime stoked fears of Satan worship during the “satanic panic” of the 1980s and 1990s.
Stay of execution was swiftly appealed
Pike was initially scheduled to be put to death in the morning, and witnesses had gathered at the Riverbend Maximum Security Institution in Nashville when the 6th Circuit U.S. Court of Appeals voted 2-1 to issue a stay. That court said a delay was needed to consider whether Pike’s allegations of childhood sexual abuse were fully considered at her sentencing.
The attorney general’s office appealed to the Supreme Court, saying that halting the execution at the last moment traumatized Slemmer’s family and rewarded “abusive delay tactics” by Pike’s attorneys.
Later in the day, the high court cleared the way for the execution to proceed. The conservative majority did not explain their order, while the three liberal members signed a dissent that said Pike’s claims deserved a closer look.
Pike did not deny committing the killing, but her supporters argued that the state should consider her age at the time, her mental illness and her allegations of severe sexual abuse.
As the execution date drew near, debate renewed over the death penalty for young offenders.
Assistant Federal Defender Stephen Ferrell said Pike’s death sentence is an outlier because other 18-year-olds in Tennessee have had such sentences vacated.
After the killing, Pike was diagnosed with bipolar disorder and post-traumatic stress disorder. In her clemency petition, she said she only wanted to fight Slemmer but killed her in a frenzied attack when she couldn’t “put the brakes on.”
“I was a mentally ill 18-year-old kid. It took me numerous years to even realize the gravity of what I’d done,” Pike said in a statement.
Victim's mother says she is waiting for death sentence
Slemmer’s mother had traveled to Nashville in the hopes of witnessing the execution of her daughter’s killer. She told The Associated Press on Saturday that she had waited decades to see Pike’s sentence carried out.
“Every time I think about it, I think about Colleen feeling that pain and trying to get up and run,” May Martinez said.
The killing rocked the city of Knoxville. Prosecutors said Pike, fearing Slemmer was trying to steal her boyfriend, lured her to a wooded area on Jan. 12, 1995. Pike cut Slemmer with a box cutter and beat her with a large chunk of asphalt. Shipp, Pike’s boyfriend, has admitted that he was the one who carved a pentagram, a star-shaped symbol associated with Satan, into her body.
Shipp was 17 when the crime happened and received a sentence of life in prison with the possibility of parole. Pike was the only one sentenced to death.
Since the Supreme Court reinstated the death penalty in 1976, 18 women have been put to death, representing about 1% of all executions, according to the Death Penalty Information Center.
Pike would have been the 30th person executed in the U.S. this year after Florida carried out an execution on Tuesday.
Tennessee announced in 2024 that it was switching from a three-drug series for lethal injections to the single drug pentobarbital. That came more than two years after the state abruptly halted the execution of Oscar Smith and acknowledged that it had failed to ensure its lethal injection drugs were tested properly.

Conrad “Cronos” Lant, the frontman for the legendary Northern British heavy metal band Venom, has died, according to a post on the band’s social media sites and the Guardian. No cause of death was cited; he was 63.
“For more than four decades, Conrad’s voice, bass and vision were at the heart of Venom,” reads a statement from the band. “He created something that changed heavy music for ever. Venom never followed the rules. They forged their own path. And Conrad was there at the centre of it all — uncompromising, fearless and unmistakable.”
At the time Venom released its first album in 1981, the group’s imagery — including skulls, bondage gear, swords and all manner of pseudo-witchcraft and Satanism — and flamboyant stage antics were so over the top that many did not take them seriously. But their influence on heavy metal, particularly thrash, was vast and far-reaching, on bands such as Metallica, Slayer, Anthrax and even Nirvana drummer/Foo Fighters frontman Dave Grohl, who collaborated with Lant on the Probot project in 2004. Venom’s album “Black Metal” even spawned the name of a subgenre that has been taken to even greatest extremes by many Scandinavian bands.
Popular on Variety
Lant was born in London to a musical family but moved with his family to Newcastle when he was a child. At the age of 16, he joined a band called Guillotine that eventually morphed into Venom; he started as a guitarist, then moved over to bass (which he played for the rest of his career) and finally lead singer as various members left. With their name and image in place, the trio — guitarist Jeff Dunn (who went by Mantas) and drummer Tony Bray (Abaddon) released “Welcome to Hell” in 1981, which featured the single “In League With Satan,” which even included a speech about the devil (recorded backward).
The group continued on that track across five albums during the 1980s, but the one that truly brought them mainstream attention was “Possessed.” Released in April of 1985, the album’s timing coincided perfectly with the rise of the controversial Parents Music Resource Center, led by “Washington wives” Tipper Gore, Susan Baker and others, which testified before Congress about overtly sexual, violent and Satanic lyrics and imagery in popular music. “Possessed” was No. 14 on the organization’s “Filthy 15” songs chart — along with songs by Prince, Madonna, Sheena Easton, Judas Priest and even Cyndi Lauper — and brought Venom’s music to the attention of countless thousands of people who had never heard of them. (The PMRC hearings succeeded in having warning stickers attached to certain CDs and vinyl, but little else except publicity.)
Venom went on hiatus in 1988 and Lant embarked on a solo career as Cronos throughout the 1990s. But Venom reformed for another seven LPs, the most recent being 2018’s “Storm the Gates.” The band continued to tour right up until this past summer.

Decade after exit, Shankersinh Vaghela in talks to return to Congress ahead of 2027 polls
Gujarat Congress president Amit Chavda said discussions are underway with Shankersinh Vaghela and that the party would take next steps after talks with its leadership.
The Congress has opened channels with former Gujarat chief minister Shankersinh Vaghela, 86, for his possible return to the party, nearly a decade after his exit triggered a series of defections from the Gujarat Congress ahead of the 2017 Assembly election.
Gujarat Congress president Amit Chavda said discussions are underway with Vaghela and that the party would take next steps after talks with its leadership. A meeting between Vaghela and Congress leaders, including Rahul Gandhi, is also expected before a decision is taken.
Vaghela’s dramatic departure from the Congress in July 2017 following differences with the party leadership came right ahead of the high-stakes Rajya Sabha poll in August, in which late Congress veteran Ahmed Patel was seeking re-election.
Fourteen Congress MLAs, including Vaghela, left the party around the time. Three of them, including Balvantsinh Rajput, crossed over to the Bharatiya Janata Party before the Rajya Sabha elections. Rajput was subsequently fielded in the Rajya Sabha against Ahmed Patel.
The high-voltage contest ended with Patel scraping through by a single vote, saved by Bharatiya Tribal Party leader Chhotubhai Vasava. The Congress expelled eight MLAs, including Vaghela, for cross-voting.
By the time the Congress headed into the December 2017 assembly elections, the Congress had lost 17 leaders. The BJP fielded many of them. Nonetheless, the Congress delivered its best performance in over two decades, securing 77 seats against the BJP’s 99. However, continuous defections in subsequent years eroded the party’s numbers, reducing its strength significantly.
After a series of defections and by-elections, the BJP went into the 2022 Assembly election with 111 MLAs, while the Congress was reduced to 59. In 2022, the BJP fielded 37 leaders who had switched from the Congress since 2017; 34 of them won. The 37 include the 17 leaders who joined the BJP in 2017 and 20 who had joined after the 2017 assembly election.
But nothing turned out right for Vaghela.
After leaving the Congress, Vaghela launched the Jan Vikalp Morcha in 2017, then joined the Nationalist Congress Party (NCP) and later formed the Praja Shakti Democratic Party. But he couldn’t win a single seat.
His son, Mahendrasinh, also left the Congress with him in 2017 and joined the BJP in 2018. But he couldn’t stay long and exited the BJP within three months. In October 2022, Mahendrasinh Vaghela, who last won the state election from Bayad assembly seat in 2012, rejoined the Congress. The Congress fielded him from Bayad in 2022 but he lost to the BJP.
The BJP won 156 of Gujarat’s 182 assembly seats in the 2022 election, its highest-ever tally. Its strength has since risen to 162 through defections and by-election victories. The Congress, which won only 17 seats in 2022, now only has 12 MLAs.
To be sure, Vaghela had been with the BJP till 1995 when he formed the Rashtriya Janata Party and became Gujarat chief minister with Congress’s support in 1996. The RJP later merged with the Congress.
Amit Dholakia, head of the department of political science at MS University in Vadodara, said Vaghela’s political experience could help the Congress rebuild in parts of central and eastern Gujarat, including the tribal belt, but his return would also bring organisational challenges.
His return, for one, could add another layer to the Congress’s internal factionalism, particularly when it is time to distribute tickets during the elections likely to be held by the end of 2027. “His entry could add one more faction to the existing groups. It might be difficult to manage the internal factions over tickets,” he said.
Dholakia also wondered whether Vaghela could translate his political profile into votes, saying his 2022 political venture had not made a significant electoral impact. Instead, his political style could create difficulties within the party. “Existing functionaries might find it difficult to adjust to his style of functioning,” Dholakia said.
For Vaghela, Dholakia said, a return to the Congress would provide a platform to remain politically relevant, but he did not expect it to have a major electoral impact in the 2027 assembly election.
Ghanshyam Shah, a political scientist and retired professor of Jawaharlal Nehru University, doubts if Vaghela’s return to the Congress would make a difference.
“I don’t think he has a large following. Whatever he had is already lost. He may not help the Congress much. My fear is that Vaghela, knowing what he has been, might end up creating problems for the Congress in Gujarat,” Shah said.
Shah said Vaghela’s reputation as a strategist should also be viewed against his record during his earlier association with the Congress when the party could not expand its support base despite having him as head of the state party unit. “He is a good strategist, but his previous strategies did not work for the Congress,” he said.

Private equity (PE) giant TPG has now offloaded more shares of listed logistics giant Shadowfax via an open-market transaction for ₹113.6 Cr. According to BSE data, the PE major, via its entity NewQuest Asia Fund IV (Singapore), sold 40 Lakh shares of the logistics giant at ₹284.03 apiece to rake in the amount. There was no clarity on who lapped up the shares that flooded the market. The block deal was undertaken at a premium of 1.3% to the stock’s last closing price on Wednesday. This is not the first time that TPG has sold its stake in the company in the past two months. In September, the PE firm offloaded Shadowfax shares worth ₹200 Cr. It currently operates across more than 16,372 pincodes and plans to increase its network of dark stores from 47 to 100 by March 2027 as it looks to strengthen its quick commerce business. Shares of Shadowfax closed Wednesday’s trading session 0.09% lower at ₹280.5 on the BSE.

United Nations, Sep 23: In his inaugural speech at the UN General Assembly, British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said world leaders must set up global standards to oversee artificial intelligence because “fundamental decisions on this technology are too important to be left to chance”.
Burnham said the UK will try to persuade other countries to adopt rules on transparency and access to AI models - and, even tougher, to get tech companies to sign on, too.
He said AI has immense potential but will also be “a source of disruption to the way we live and work - and a multiplier of risk”.
Burnham also said Russia and other states are using AI-augmented misinformation and disinformation to corrode democracy, something he said Britain has faced in the decade since it voted to leave the European Union.
He said he has asked British security chiefs to set up a National Centre for Information Defence to counter the threat.
Burnham also chaired a meeting at the UN General Assembly on Tuesday on the Israel-Palestine issue, alongside French President Emmanuel Macron, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney and Saudi Foreign Minister Faisal bin Farhan.
He said the two-state solution to Israel-Palestinian conflict must be kept alive.
Burnham said failure to deliver a two-state solution will “corrode trust” in politicians who have talked about the issue but not taken action.
He told delegates from dozens of countries that the UK has banned trade with Israeli settlements in the West Bank because the “E1” settlement expansion plan is “a deliberate attempt to block a two-state solution.”
“We all live in an era of low trust in politics. Many people in this room, many politicians around the world, have spoken for decades about a two-state solution. But if we fail to back those words with deeds, we will further corrode trust in the political, diplomatic and international process,” the UK prime minister said. (AP)

The Embassy of the State of Palestine to India has questioned the description of the 1918 Battle of Haifa as the “liberation of Haifa”, saying that Indian soldiers who participated in the battle were serving under British command as part of an imperial military campaign that resulted in the occupation of Palestine.
In a five-page position paper titled “Rewriting of India–Palestine history: The battle of Haifa: liberation or occupation?”, the Palestinian Embassy said the terminology surrounding the battle required “careful and scholarly reflection” and argued that the event should be understood within the historical context of British military occupation of Palestine.
The Embassy said Palestine, including Haifa, was under Ottoman rule before 1918 and that British forces defeated the Ottoman Empire during the First World War, bringing Palestine under British occupation. Indian soldiers participated in the campaign as part of the British Indian Army, under British command.
It argued that describing them retrospectively as having “liberated Haifa” risked attributing to India a sovereign military decision that the country did not possess in 1918, when it was still under British rule.
The paper pointed to contemporary British terminology, saying military and parliamentary records referred to the operations in Palestine using terms such as “capture”, “take”, “fall” and “conquer”. It also noted that following the British military campaign, Palestine was administered under the Occupied Enemy Territory Administration (OETA) until its replacement by a civil administration in July 1920.
The Embassy also cited India’s own historical records, including the 2014 publication Indian War Memorials Around the World, saying it does not describe the event as the “liberation of Haifa”.
According to the paper, the publication records that the “fortified town of Haifa fell to a cavalry charge by the Jodhpur Lancers” and that the 15th Imperial Service Cavalry Brigade “broke through and took the town”.
It also referred to the Teen Murti Memorial in New Delhi, stating that the memorial was established during British colonial rule to commemorate Indian soldiers who served and died during the First World War, and was not originally intended to commemorate relations between India and Israel.
The Embassy said the memorial refers to “Palestine and some of its cities” among the places associated with the military campaigns in which Indian soldiers served.
The paper further cited official Indian records to state that 491 Indian soldiers are recorded at Ramleh War Cemetery, 109 at the Gaza and Deir el Balah War Cemeteries and 47 at the Haifa Indian Cemetery, besides soldiers commemorated at other cemeteries and memorials across historical Palestine.
The Embassy questioned why Haifa had become the centre of a commemorative narrative when Indian soldiers had fought across a much wider region, including the Suez Canal, Gaza, Jerusalem, the Jordan Valley, Damascus and Aleppo.
It also said the first formal Israeli public ceremony commemorating the Indian soldiers was held in 2010, nearly a century after the battle.
The paper argued that Britain, rather than India, was the principal military power behind the campaign, as it financed, armed and commanded the operation. It questioned why the “liberation of Haifa” narrative centred on Indian soldiers while Britain’s role was not similarly emphasised.
The Embassy also stressed that the soldiers described as “Indian soldiers” served in the British Indian Army and came from different regions, communities and religions across British India, whose geographical and political boundaries differed from those of the present-day Republic of India.
The position paper placed the soldiers’ participation within the wider history of British colonial rule, noting that Indian troops were deployed in military campaigns far from their homeland.
It also referred to the Rowlatt Act and the Jallianwala Bagh massacre, arguing that the broader record of British rule should be considered when interpreting the role of Indian soldiers in the First World War.
The Embassy cited Mahatma Gandhi’s opposition to the establishment of a Jewish state in Palestine at the expense of its indigenous population, including his statement that “Palestine belongs to the Arabs in the same sense that England belongs to the English.”
It further pointed out that India voted against UN Resolution 181 in 1947, which proposed partition and allocated Haifa to the proposed Jewish state, and questioned how the 1918 battle could subsequently be presented as a foundation for India-Israel historical ties.
The Embassy said describing the 1918 occupation of Haifa as a liberation “raises serious questions and concerns in Palestine”. It maintained that Haifa should be recognised as a Palestinian city at the time and that the battle took place in the context of the British military occupation of Palestine.
At the same time, the Embassy said its position was expressed with “full respect” for the sacrifice and memory of Indian soldiers and for India’s sovereign right to commemorate its history and fallen soldiers.
It called for historical remembrance of the Battle of Haifa to remain grounded in accuracy, balance and respect for the historical experiences of all concerned, while emphasising that the document represented the Palestinian Embassy’s perspective and was intended to contribute to discussion on the historical and legal questions surrounding the battle.

When Away launched the Carry On suitcase in 2016, it created the must-have travel accessory. It went viral for its sleek, simple polycarbonate design (plus a dash of smart social marketing). Its pioneering ejectable portable battery earned it the “smart luggage” moniker, and other bag makers quickly copied the concept.
A decade later, Away is launching the Series 3—its third generation. The battery is gone, but the features that attracted and retained a loyal following remain, with a heavy focus on invisible tech.
“We didn’t like to be called ‘smart luggage’,” Sarah Amidi, Away’s senior vice president of Brand, tells WIRED at the company’s design studio in New York City’s SoHo district. When the first Carry On was conceived, charging solutions weren’t as ubiquitous as they are today, Amidi says, which created a unique travel pain point for Away to tackle. It may have seemed gimmicky, but a quickly accessible USB port to charge a phone made sense. The ejectable design was forward-thinking, given evolving regulations around traveling with batteries.
While the battery hasn’t been available in Away luggage since 2023, Amidi says tech isn’t entirely gone; the company is looking at how technology can play the right role in luggage design. Instead, with the Series 3, Away has become more of a traditional luggage maker than a disruptor. “We design it to last the next 10 years,” Amidi says.
On the surface, every piece from the Series 3 Classic and Flex (expandable) series will look familiar to Away fans, and that’s intentional. Instead of a new design, Amidi says the company strengthened its carry-on by putting it through rigorous testing. In fact, the Series 3 launch was delayed because it didn’t fully meet expectations.
“We asked, what features solve friction and earn their place,” Amidi says. “We didn’t want to add things just to add things that take away from capacity or add weight, and we couldn’t make polycarbonate any better.”
Reinventing the Wheel, Sort Of
Amidi says the shell design still works today (with the battery option gone, it also shaved off weight and added more room), so Away looked at two areas that could use some work: the wheels and telescoping trolley handle—what travelers often complain about in luggage.
For the WhisperGlide 360 spinning wheel design, Away added an extra ball bearing and improved the threading to make them glide smoothly and quietly. Away also brought its StopLock Brakes system, first introduced in its top-opening TopSide luggage, to the Series 3. As the name suggests, flipping a switch quickly locks the wheels, effective even on slight inclines.
When I asked why quiet wheels would even matter in, say, a busy airport, Amidi refers to a time when she needed to quietly sneak out of the house for a trip without waking her family. She says these are the kinds of new travel pain points Away is looking to solve with tech.
Then there's the Infinite Height Trolley handle, which offers five times more stopping points than before—a more personalized experience for travelers of varying heights. Hooks in the trolley handle might seem like a simple design touch, but they’re handy for holding a jacket, purse, or bag of airport fast food (each hook can hold up to 11 pounds, but Away has stress-tested it up to 40 pounds).
Other improvements include redesigned interior covers that open outward to give better access, more pockets for small items, a pouch for a Bluetooth tracker, and accessories to help keep the luggage looking clean. The compression system, a signature Away feature, remains the same.
Personalization is a key selling feature. In addition to the standard colors, the Series 3 comes in purple (Electric Iris), chocolate, and chartreuse. The handles and wheels are removable and can be customized in different styles (also handy for repairs). There's also a D-ring to attach accessories like luggage tags and charms, if that’s your thing. For many people, it will be.
The Series 3 Classic style is available in carry-on, bigger carry-on, medium, large, and trunk sizes. The expandable Flex style is available in the same sizes except trunk.
Away also unveiled the Signature Bags collection, which includes a tote, weekender, commuter backpack, duffle, and underseat bags. An evolution of Away’s Everywhere series, the durable nylon is now lighter and softer, Amidi says, with updated hardware like zippers—including a reverse coil zipper in the laptop compartment for better protection—hidden pockets for easy access to often-used items, and a water bottle pocket. The laptop compartment has moved to the outside of the bag, allowing quick access during airport security checks, for example.
Overall, Away's new luggage doesn't offer anything groundbreaking. Many of these features are available in bags from other companies, and in some ways, it feels like Away is playing catch-up. But Away is leveraging its strength with a well-regarded product that already works, with a few tweaks to make it better. It’s this, not batteries, that has made it a cult favorite among travelers.

Concerns over the safety of drinking water have resurfaced in parts of Uri area of north Kashmir’s Baramulla district after residents of Gawalta village found a dead snake inside a pipeline supplying water to the locality, raising questions over the maintenance and monitoring of the public water supply network.
The incident comes weeks after a similar complaint from Karkroo Mohalla in Nambla, where residents had reported finding dead rats inside a water storage tank and supply pipelines.
Both incidents have generated severe resentment among the local population, who accused the Jal Shakti Department of not taking care of the water tanks, pipelines and other components of the supply network.
In the fresh incident, the residents said the Sokad-Gowlta Water Supply Scheme had remained non-functional for several days, leaving the village without regular drinking water.
They said that despite repeated requests to employees of the Jal Shakti Department, the problem was not addressed promptly.
“With the supply remaining disrupted, the local residents inspected the pipeline themselves on Monday and found a dead snake lodged inside it,” said Arif Hussain, a local resident.
The presence of the snake triggered concern among residents over the possibility of contamination and the overall hygiene of the water distribution system.
The residents of Gowlta have now urged the department to conduct an immediate inspection of the entire supply network, clean and disinfect the pipeline and ensure that only safe water is supplied to households.
They have also sought an inquiry into how the reptile entered the pipeline and demanded preventive measures, including regular inspection and sanitation of water infrastructure.
Residents said repeated complaints involving contamination or poor maintenance were a major issue in the area and the concerned authority should ensure monitoring of drinking-water schemes in the Uri area.

Billie Jean King has often said that she was moved to form the women’s pro tennis circuit after earning USD 600 for her 1970 Italian Open title while Ilie Nastase took home USD 3,500 for winning the men’s tournament the same year.
In 2027, nearly six decades after King’s title at the Foro Italico, the Rome clay-court event will finally award women the same amount of total prize money as men, as part a “major milestone” initiative that the WTA Tour announced Thursday.
The initiative means that all combined WTA 1000 events will award equal prize money for the first time. Besides the Italian Open, the holdouts had been the Canadian Open and the Cincinnati Open.
ALSO READ: Zverev vouches for best-of-five-sets format, says no one wants reduction
The other combined 1000 events in Indian Wells, California; Miami; Madrid and Beijing; as well as all four Grand Slams, already offer equal prize money.
“Achieving equal prize money across all combined WTA 1000 tournaments is a major milestone for tennis,” WTA chair Valerie Camillo said. “It demonstrates the WTA’s continued commitment to leading the sports industry in delivering our athletes competitive and financial equality and is a testament to the enduring nature of the founding vision of the WTA.”
In 2023, Italian Open organizers pledged to have equal prize money starting in 2025 but didn’t carry through on the promise.
The total men’s prize money this year in Rome was USD 9.6 million while the women got USD 8.3 million.
Also announced for next year was an expanded WTA 250-level tournament in Manila, Philippines, amid massive interest surrounding home player Alex Eala, who is ranked 18th.
In January of this year, the Philippines hosted a WTA 125-level tournament.
Also, the number of annual WTA 500 level tournaments required for players ranked in the top 50 was reduced from six to four, resulting in a total base playing commitment of 14 WTA tournaments plus the four Grand Slams in 2027.
The announcements come after the WTA recently selected Charlotte, North Carolina, to host its flagship event, the WTA Finals, for the next three years in an NBA arena.
“The WTA is stepping up to deliver more for players and tournaments in 2027,” Camillo said. “We have listened to player feedback on the demands of the calendar and responded with a meaningful reduction in commitments.”
ALSO READ: WTA 250 to be relocated from Chennai to Manila next year
The WTA relied heavily on its tour architecture council, a working group chaired by third-ranked Jessica Pegula.
“As players, we’re on the road most of the year, so having more flexibility in our schedules and commitments makes a real difference,” Pegula said. “The 2027 changes give us more ability to build our seasons around our own goals — competitively and personally. That’s an impactful step forward for players.”
The WTA said the updates “will be implemented as a one-year pilot” for 2027, allowing it to “evaluate the impact of the changes across the tour to inform decisions for 2028 and beyond.”

Burundi has agreed to join a clutch of other African nations in receiving migrants from other countries deported from the US under Donald Trump’s hardline immigration policy.
However, the authorities in Bujumbura, the country’s economic capital, said Burundi will only accept those not accused of crime or terrorism links, said Nancy Ninette Mutoni, a spokesperson for the country’s president, Évariste Ndayishimiye. Tuesday’s announcement gave no details of numbers, timing or financial details.
Washington has sent so-called “third-country deportees” to some half a dozen African nations as well as many other countries, often where they have no ties, have never been and find themselves detained indefinitely, under opaque deals that Senate Democrats say have cost tens of millions of dollars.
In many cases, deportees had secured legal protections from immigration courts in the US against repatriation. But rights groups say the third-country deals allow the US to circumvent those protections.
Mutoni said preparations were underway to arrange accommodation, living conditions and integration into local communities in Burundi. “Receiving them requires serious planning – where they will stay, what they will eat and how they will live alongside the local population,” she said.
“If they choose to join Burundian citizens and make a valuable contribution to national development, the law will be respected,” she said, regarding potential citizenship.
Burundi aimed to both strengthen diplomatic relations and provide hospitality to people in need, the spokesperson added.
The US state department did not immediately respond to requests for comment while a spokesperson for the Burundi foreign ministry said details of the agreement were not yet available.

Does Horner have a chance of Ferrari job? F1 Q&A
- Published
Mercedes' George Russell took his first victory since June by holding off Max Verstappen to win the Azerbaijan Grand Prix.
Verstappen's Red Bull team-mate Isack Hadjar completed the podium on his return after missing three races with a broken wrist.
Championship leader Kimi Antonelli finished fifth in Baku, meaning his advantage over team-mate Russell has narrowed to 66 points.
This weekend, Formula 1 heads to Malaysia, the host of the Bahrain Grand Prix - an event originally due to take place in April but which was postponed because of the war in the Middle East.
Before the race in Sepang, BBC F1 correspondent Andrew Benson answers your latest questions.
Does Christian Horner really want the team principal job at Ferrari, or even have a shot at it? - Ben
This topic has become a subject for conversation in recent days following an interview Horner did with the Times, external as he promotes his new book.
Horner said: "At this stage in my life, there's only one team for which I would accept non-participation in ownership."
Asked whether he would take a job there, he replied: "Would I consider Ferrari? I mean, Ferrari is the biggest brand in Formula 1. It's the dream. And arguably it's the sleeping giant of Formula 1."
Ferrari team principal Frederic Vasseur made his views about Horner's intervention pretty plain after the Azerbaijan Grand Prix when he said: "Mr Horner is looking for a job - that, everybody knows - everywhere."
Vasseur said the speculation surrounding the team meant Ferrari were "not working in the perfect serenity".
Horner's comments seem to make it clear that he would consider a job offer from Ferrari. But the key questions are under what conditions he might accept it, and whether he would be offered it in the first place.
Horner has made it very clear over the years that he believes an F1 team needs one person in charge and in overall control.
It's highly unlikely he would get that at Ferrari, where chairman John Elkann and chief executive officer Benedetto Vigna will always have more authority than any team principal.
Even at Red Bull, where Horner had theoretical leadership at the F1 team, he was ultimately answerable to headquarters in Austria and that is what led to his removal in the end.
It's hard to imagine how Elkann and Vigna could or would countenance any situation where they were removed from any input into the F1 team.
And it's even harder to imagine a situation where that was not the de facto position even if a team boss had been given assurances they would be left alone.
Then there is the question of whether Ferrari would want Horner.
Horner comes with baggage. All of the above for a start, and on top of that there is the cloud under which he left Red Bull.
There is no doubt that he was a remarkably successful team principal there, the team winning eight drivers' titles, six constructors' championships and 124 grands prix in his two-decade tenure.
However, the team unravelled in his final 18 months in charge, in the wake of the accusations of sexual harassment and coercive, controlling behaviour that were made against him by a female employee.
Red Bull dismissed those allegations after two internal investigations led by external lawyers.
But they were a key factor in Adrian Newey leaving his position as chief technical officer - along with internal politics in which Newey felt his role had been diminished by Horner.
Newey was followed out of the door by long-time sporting director Jonathan Wheatley and head of strategy Will Courtenay.
Horner was finally dismissed following a slump in form which Red Bull bosses concluded the team did not appear to be capable of arresting under his leadership.
In the Times interview, Horner says that the only justification he was given by Red Bull for his sacking was "it was more Christian Horner Racing than Red Bull Racing".
He adds at other points in the interview: "I am a bit of a Marmite character. I know I'm not everybody's cup of tea. It's impossible to be." And: "I'm the cure and the problem."
Clearly, any decision as to whether Horner is the person you want to lead your F1 team would need careful consideration.
It's also worth mentioning that Ferrari driver Lewis Hamilton has made it pretty clear over the past few years that he has little time for Horner.
Why hasn't the FIA made a decision on the final two races of the season? They've cancelled the final rounds of the World Rally Championship and World Endurance Championship because of the Middle East conflict. Surely they should be confirming the changes in the calendar now? - Nigel
To start with a point of order, it is Formula 1 that decides the calendar - as in, the commercial rights holder - not the FIA, the governing body. The FIA's role is effectively only to rubber-stamp F1's decision.
As things stand, F1 is planning to end the season as the calendar was originally scheduled - with Las Vegas followed by Qatar and then Abu Dhabi, external over the last two weekends in November and the first in December.
Although the war continues between the US/Israel and Iran, the advice F1 has been getting is that the situation in those two countries is stable, and there is not a high risk of attacks on civilian infrastructure.
The UK Foreign Office, for example, does not advise against travel to Qatar and Abu Dhabi., external It simply says the situation there "remains unpredictable" and that "there is a risk of more attacks and unforeseen escalation in the region".
And the two countries consider themselves open for business.
However, F1 has a contingency plan.
Imola in Italy is preparing to host a race on the weekend of Abu Dhabi.
If the two Middle Eastern races cannot happen as a result of an escalation of the situation in the Gulf, Imola would step in and hold the season finale on 4-6 December.
But unless and until that happens, there is no confirmation of changes to make, as there are currently no changes.
Why wasn't a virtual safety car called when Valtteri Bottas crashed right at the end in Azerbaijan? This was obviously a dangerous situation as the car was buried in the barrier. And it almost cost George Russell a well-deserved victory - Steve
Valtteri Bottas crashed at Turn 15 on the penultimate lap of the race, meaning his Cadillac was in the barriers there when leaders George Russell and Max Verstappen came around their last lap less than a second apart.
Normally, a car in the barriers on a street circuit means at least a virtual safety car.
However, in this instance a spokesperson for governing body the FIA says that race control "determined that it was safe to let the leaders race to the line - they were able to cut the apex at T15, as it's a relatively slow corner".
In the event, the Bottas incident, the FIA says, was "successfully managed by localised double yellows".
Whether this was the correct course of action, and whether the decision was influenced by wanting to prevent the grand prix finishing under caution, will remain a subject for debate.
On the one hand, it allowed the race to continue and be exciting to the end.
On the other, slowing for the incident caused a technical issue for Russell's Mercedes.
"I lifted off the power and when I went back, I had no turbo, so then I had no power," Russell said. "Max almost got me at the line."
Russell was able to mitigate this loss of power from the internal combustion engine because, it being the final lap, he could use up all his battery on the run to the flag, rather than have to keep it balanced for the following lap.
So he managed to hang on - but by less than 0.2 seconds.
Had he not, the decision by race control would have come under a great deal more scrutiny than it did.
I love your explainers. Please can you analyse the data explaining the jump Williams have made with their upgrades. It seems more significant than Aston Martin's much written-about 'leap'? What are the percentages, averages etc. - John
First of all, thanks very much for the compliment.
This is a complex topic. There is no doubt that the lighter chassis and aerodynamic upgrades introduced by Williams in Baku marked a step forward.
It was their best qualifying performance of the year in terms of positions, even if in percentage terms they were actually slightly closer to the front in Miami back in May.
But it's too early to judge the Williams upgrades - and Aston Martin provides a clue as to why.
This year, there is quite a swing in competitiveness for certain teams depending on circuit type.
Regardless of the upgrades, Williams always expected Baku to be one of their stronger circuits - short-duration corners and long straights suit their car.
But they struggle in long-duration corners, so it will be interesting to see how they go this weekend in Malaysia, because Sepang is full of them.
Likewise, Aston Martin have specific weaknesses.
Their aerodynamic upgrade in Hungary improved their chassis performance by in the region of two seconds a lap.
Hence their significant improvement there and in Zandvoort, where Fernando Alonso drove superbly to take two points for ninth place.
But, despite its upgrade for Zandvoort, the Honda engine remains the worst on the grid, in terms of overall power, driveability and energy management.
So, it's no surprise that on two hugely engine-dependent circuits such as Monza and Baku, they would struggle.
On that basis, Aston Martin can be expected to be relatively more competitive again in Singapore, with its low power-sensitivity, and where Alonso is usually outstanding.

Algeria introduces death penalty for arsonists after deadly wildfires
- Published
Algeria has adopted a law imposing the death penalty on people convicted of arson of forests or fields after a series of deadly wildfires swept parts of the country.
Members of the national assembly voted through the bill, which also made child abduction a capital offence, on Thursday.
Capital punishment has been in the country's penal code for some offences, but no execution has been carried out since 1993.
The official death toll from the blazes stands at 12, but independent news outlets believe the figure to be much higher.
Algerian President Abdelmadjid Tebboune ordered the justice ministry to introduce the changes to the criminal law after more than 100 fires in the north-east of the country during an intense heatwave in northern Africa.
Under the law, anyone convicted of deliberately setting fire to forests, woods or fields could face execution.
The death penalty has also been extended to child kidnappings that involve torture, sexual assault or mutilation.
According to news agency AFP, Justice Minister Lotfi Boudjemaa told parliament: "The adoption of the death penalty for these acts is the appropriate legal response to curb these crimes."
The tougher penalties were justified because arson had reached "the level of organised crime", with investigations suggesting links to "foreign parties", Boudjemaa said.
The upper house, the Council of the Nation, will review the law before it is officially ratified by the president.
Investigative journalist Nozha Khelalef has been gathering the names of those believed to have died in the fires from death notices posted by families and information shared by some local authorities.
Her tally, listed on the independent news website Twala, external, puts the death toll at 200.
While Algeria regularly experiences forest fires in the summer, climate change has exacerbated the intensity and severity of recent wildfires in the country.

SBI Mutual Fund, under its various schemes, acquired an additional 1.18 Cr equity shares of Swiggy via open market transactions on Tuesday, the foodtech major informed the bourses earlier today. Following the purchase, its total shareholding in Swiggy rose to 14.16 Cr equity shares or around 5.1% of Swiggy’s total equity. Assuming the trades were executed at that day’s closing price of ₹253.90, the mutual fund giant would have spent over ₹300.6 Cr to pick up the additional stake. The transaction raised SBI Mutual Fund’s aggregate holding across its various schemes past the mandatory 5% disclosure threshold under SEBI rules. It previously held a 4.7% stake, with 7.11 Cr shares or 2.58% held by its holding entity SBI Equity Hybrid Fund. Overall, domestic mutual funds held a cumulative 22.8% stake in Swiggy as of June 30, 2026. For comparison, their holding in rival Eternal stood at 31.7% on the same date. SBI Mutual Fund holds around 4% stake in Eternal as well. The stake purchase comes about a month after the company secured shareholder approval to cap its foreign ownership at 49.5%, gaining the tag of an Indian-owned and controlled company (IOCC). The move allows Swiggy to pivot the business model of its quick commerce arm Instamart to an inventory-led model. While it currently serves as a marketplace that hosts seller entities, the new model will allow it to sell products after directly procuring them from brands. This is expected to help lift up Instamart's revenues and margins. The move followed Eternal doing the same last year as the two sought to restructure their quick-commerce businesses. “The move supports management’s plan for a 1P (inventory-led) model at Instamart, which could drive a 80 bps margin upside,” brokerage Jefferies had said at the time. On the financial front, Swiggy’s net loss in Q1 FY27 narrowed by nearly 34% YoY to ₹791 Cr while operating revenue rose 36.8% YoY to ₹6,812 Cr. It also managed to achieve a milestone towards profitability with Instamart achieving contribution margin breakeven in the quarter. Shares of Swiggy ended 4.88% lower at ₹238 on the BSE.

Last week, after a Mississippi grand jury declined to bring criminal charges in the death of Nolan Wells, the 18-year-old Black college student who disappeared on Horn Island while traveling with a group of white friends and was later found dead, Black users on Threads demanded justice.
“Just so it’s abundantly clear: The state of Mississippi is covering up the murder of Nolan Wells,” user @_taexoxo posted two days after the September 21 decision. The case has incited racial tensions nationwide.
“This year a grand jury handed down an indictment for a pool of water turning green, but didn’t indict when a black kid was found floating face down in water!” commented comedian D.L. Hughley.
Black Americans have never shied away from calling out America’s racial hypocrisies—Twitter served as an indispensable tool as the Black Lives Matter movement swelled in the 2020s—but the chatter on Threads was uniquely charged for Wells. It was the latest bit of evidence showing that the platform has emerged as a vital artery of the Black social media ecosystem, at times even rivaling the influence Black Twitter once embodied.
In 2021, when I first explored the cultural expansiveness of Black Twitter, I wrote that it was “all the things: news and analysis, call and response, judge and jury—a comedy showcase, therapy session, and family cookout all in one.” Five years later, Threads is proving to be its spiritual successor, a robust digital universe where no conversation, no matter how ugly or awkward, is off limits.
As with Black Twitter, on Threads you are just as likely to come across conversations around the ageism double standard that Black women face as you are off-the-cuff TV commentary. Speaking of HBO Max’s new superhero thriller, Lanterns, one user recently commented that it’s the first sci-fi show “with a black Chosen One and a white Magical Negro.”
“The heyday of Twitter was during the Obama era. Now we’re living through the second Trump administration. Having a place to laugh to keep from crying is just as important as it ever was,” Jamilah Lemieux, a cultural critic and author who has 208,000 followers on the Meta-run platform, tells WIRED.
Lemieux was active on Twitter for over a decade, where she discussed motherhood and women’s rights, but started to pull back because the level of harassment and vitriol she was getting started to outweigh her positive interactions.
Twitter underwent a noticeable vibe shift in 2022 after Elon Musk bought the platform and renamed it X. For day-one users, the app was less functional: It was harder to see the content you wanted, hate speech and propaganda accounts surged, and moderation seemed to disappear overnight. “I’m not surprised that that happened. It was a very deliberate shift away from the progressive Black voices that had defined the platform for its earlier history,” says Lemieux, who describes the current experience of posting on X as “screaming into the void.”
Lemieux has since decamped to Threads, where she has become a power user of sorts, riffing on everything from singer Chris Brown to public versus private education. “I wanted a social media home again, but I just wasn't really sure where I fit. I have always preferred text to video in terms of the creation. And Threads offered what I loved about Twitter, which is that I could reach people with my words without having to curate visuals.”
Today, some of the biggest cultural voices on X have migrated to Threads—including author Roxane Gay, activist Brittany Packnett Cunningham, and journalist Nikole Hannah-Jones, whose recent New York Times Magazine essay about her decision to enroll her daughter in low-performing, predominantly Black public schools sparked an intense debate online around using your child to fight systemic failures.
“omg the threads convo about that article is better because NHJ is on there replying to ppl, god all the employed ppl really did go to threads,” TV writer @theashleyray posted on X, telling another user, “black twitter is there.”
Bluesky, which launched as invite-only in 2023 before opening up to the wider public a year later, initially announced itself as one of the first serious alternatives to X. But it wasn’t until Donald Trump’s 2024 presidential win that millions of users, seemingly in need of a public sphere free of the MAGA-fueled rhetoric that had overtaken X, flocked to Bluesky. They were eager to recapture the spirit of social media’s earliest days.
Emboldened by its decentralized format and the promise of improved user safety mechanisms, Rudy Fraser, a developer with a background in community organizing, created Blacksky, a custom feed and moderation service that quickly became a central meeting ground for many Black users on the platform. It has proven to be a more secure social ecosystem for Black users, but it hasn’t exactly swayed public discourse in the way Black Twitter did with #OscarsSoWhite or #IfTheyGunnedMeDown.
Part of that is a numbers game, says Rianna Walcott, an assistant professor of communication at the University of Maryland who founded the Black Digital Migration Project, a research initiative examining how Black social media users respond to changing platform conditions.
“The problems of platform fatigue and reaching a globally Black audience are probably limiting Blacksky’s visibility, as it lacks the initial buy-in that comes from an already connected platform ecosystem like Meta’s,” Walcott says. In the beginning, Bluesky’s biggest user base was concentrated among progressives, particularly journalists, academics, activists, and writers. A 2025 Pew Research Center survey found that 69 percent of respondents who were left-leaning news influencers joined the platform during its first year. And while Blacksky was fundamental to the platform’s nascent growth, Black engagement has stalled for a number of reasons; several colleagues and friends of mine stopped using it after the first few months, seemingly disheartened by its low-key atmosphere, on top of having to rebuild their social media presence in a new corner of the internet.
Threads, meanwhile, prioritizes engagement and allows users to easily join communities like Black Threads, Black British Threads, or Black LGBTQ Threads that are tailor-fit to their interests. According to a Meta blog post from December, there are over 200 groups, which include everything from TV and fitness to the NBA.
“I think it matters more to Black users where they can find each other at volume rather than the overall politics of the platform,” says Walcott.
While Spill, the image-forward social media network launched by Alphonzo Terrell, a former Twitter employee, has been successful in directly appealing to Black people, Threads has a unique advantage when it comes to onboarding new members because of its tight integration with Facebook and Instagram, platforms that have over 6 billion users combined. Threads has more than 500 million monthly active users and, in terms of sheer capacity, is on track to surpass X’s 557 million monthly active users, according to a Statista report from March.
Lemieux appreciates how seamless the platform is compared to X. “We often joke that Threads will drop you off anywhere,” she says. “A lot of the laughter and humor, it’s not just Black people coming up with hashtags like it was before, sometimes it’s just a middle-aged white woman’s Facebook post, who has cross-posted to Threads without realizing it.”
Though many of the same people and conversations that defined Black Twitter have moved to Threads, “Black Threads doesn’t feel like an exact replica of Black Twitter to me,” says Phil Lewis, an editor at HuffPost and news aggregator. He says that Black Twitter especially “shined” when users live-tweeted events, like award shows and sports events. “I haven’t seen that yet. But you can feel when a cultural moment is happening on Threads in the same way.”
Even so, the platform has been able to move the needle in surprising ways. In August, when the majority-Black city of Gary, Indiana, lost power for two weeks, causing a food shortage, among a long list of other safety concerns, Lewis says it was users on TikTok and Threads who first raised awareness about the historic blackout, which had received very little national media coverage until that point. “Then news outlets started paying attention.”
One of the most striking things Walcott has noticed about Threads as the spiritual successor to Black Twitter is how users are deliberately building and maintaining a narrative of its history. “People talk about events in Threads history like they did and do with Black Twitter,” she says. “When something happens that calls for comment, people turn to Threads for that discourse, just as they once turned to Twitter as the center of a hypernarrative web.”
User @missglowdigger certainly agrees. “Threads is single handedly thee best thing to happen to black social media,” she posted in September.
To which she was swiftly reminded: “Yes it is and I love the community BUT let us not get too comfortable … this is still a White Mans app.”

South Africa’s president has called on men to take more responsibility for violence against women as he announced measures to tackle the problem, amid anger at authorities over a recent wave of murders.
Cyril Ramaphosa acknowledged that not enough had been done to protect women. He said police would be reviewing unsolved murders, attempted murders and serious sexual offences against women and children, as well as producing a funded plan to reduce the forensic backlog for such cases, both within 60 days.
In a televised speech on Tuesday night, the president said local governments would have five months to address issues that compromised women’s safety, from broken streetlights to overgrown public spaces and abandoned buildings. He added that he had tasked five ministers to come up with a plan within 60 days to reduce alcohol-fuelled violence.
“Alcohol does not cause gender-based violence and it can never excuse it. Responsibility always lies with the perpetrator,” Ramaphosa said. “But harmful alcohol use is a significant aggravating factor in interpersonal violence and it must be addressed as part of our wider prevention effort.
“Women should not have to live in fear because government has failed to repair a light, clear a public space, process evidence or enforce a law.”
South Africa has been gripped by grief and fury after the discovery of 11 women’s bodies dumped across Ekurhuleni, the municipality adjoining Johannesburg to the east, since 15 July. Eight of the women were found in the last three weeks, including Elizabeth “Tsontso” Moselakgomo, who was discovered on 12 September after she went missing when she went for a run after work.
Ramaphosa said suspects had been arrested in connection with three of the killings and that the other cases would not be left to go cold. He added that police had not found evidence that a serial killer was responsible for all 11 killings, but that all possibilities were still being investigated.
He directly addressed South African men, urging them to challenge relatives, friends and colleagues who harassed, humiliated or abused women. “It is time for good men to stop being silent men,” he said.
“For too long, gender-based violence has been treated as a woman’s problem to solve. Women march, the women of our country organise, they speak out, they protest, they confront and they comfort survivors,” Ramaphosa said.
“Women change their routes home. Avoid going out at night and warn one another about dangerous places and dangerous men. We have placed the burden of male violence on women. That must change.”
Activists expressed their frustration that solid policy actions had not been taken years ago and scepticism that the measures Ramaphosa had announced would work.
Shenilla Mohamed, the executive director of Amnesty International South Africa, said: “These are not new issues and as a country we have been talking about ways to tackle the high numbers of [gender-based violence and femicide], especially since 2019 when women took to the streets to protest, and yet here we are again in the face of continued attacks against women.
“Amnesty International South Africa also notes the timelines put in place by the president, but this will only mean something if it results in action, and if there are consequences for inaction.”
Mpiwa Mangwiro-Tsanga and Bafana Khumalo, of Sonke Gender Justice, an NGO, said: “Our concern … is that the response remains heavily weighted towards what happens after violence has already occurred.”
They added: “Investigating unresolved cases, processing forensic evidence and repairing unsafe public spaces are necessary, but they do not constitute a comprehensive prevention strategy. It is concerning that the president is asking municipalities to do what is actually their mandate and yet they do not deliver on these.”

On Thursday, nearly one million Americans will start receiving $500 checks from the Trump administration under its new Affordable Care Act refund program.
The payments are meant for a narrow group of people who bought their own health insurance through HealthCare.gov, the federally run ACA marketplace.
To be eligible, consumers must have enrolled in a HealthCare.gov plan and paid the full cost of their premiums without receiving federal premium tax credits or other financial assistance.
In a letter accompanying the checks, Trump said the refunds are for people who use HealthCare.gov, "but who do not receive Taxpayer Subsidies to help pay for their Coverage."
The program is also limited by geography. The payments are going to eligible consumers in the 30 states that use HealthCare.gov, rather than to those in state-run ACA marketplaces.
That means people who bought coverage through state-run exchanges are not eligible for the refund program.
States highlighted in blue below are eligible for the refunds:
Trump has framed the payments as refunds for what he says were excessive charges linked to the federal marketplace's operating costs.
Eligible people do not need to apply, submit a claim, or sign up for the program. Administration officials say they have already identified recipients and will mail the $500 checks automatically to their home addresses.
Each eligible enrollee will receive a separate payment. As a result, a household with multiple people who individually meet the requirements could receive more than one check.

Trump's trade rep sounds pessimistic about deal with Canada, saying issues are 'quite difficult to resolve'
Jamieson Greer says while 'technical talks' are ongoing, there are 'a handful of outstanding issues'
U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer says he regularly speaks with his Canadian counterpart, but the two sides have reached an impasse on some trade irritants and there's no sign of a resolution any time soon.
Speaking to reporters at the G20 meeting of trade ministers in Milwaukee, Greer sounded pessimistic about the prospect of a deal with the Canadians saying while "technical talks" are ongoing between trade experts from both countries there are some fundamental disagreements.
"The reality is there are a handful of outstanding issues that are quite difficult to resolve," Greer said.
Greer said the Trump administration's policy of imposing tariffs on foreign manufactured goods to try to "reindustrialize" America is a universal one and not "focused on one country."
Canada, meanwhile, maintains that punishing tariffs on industrial products like steel, aluminum and autos make no sense given just how integrated the two economies are after decades of free trade.
The federal government has strenuously opposed U.S. tariffs designed to decimate those key Canadian sectors, saying it's no way to treat a supposed ally. Plus, Canada is America's biggest customer, purchasing more American-exported goods than any other country.
U.S. losing manufacturing jobs
Still, Greer said Canada and other countries treat the United States as "a dumping ground" for their products and the U.S. just wants to produce more of what it consumes domestically. He added that these policies shouldn't be read as "threats against Canada" alone.
Despite Greer's claims that these tariff policies are boosting industrial employment, data from the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics compiled by the Economic Policy Institute shows that some, 62,000 manufacturing jobs have been lost since Trump took office for his second term in January 2025.
International Trade Minister Maninder Sidhu, who is responsible for non-U.S. trade, met with Greer while in Wisconsin.
The conversation was focused primarily on wider world trade issues like ending forced labour and the phenomenon of some countries like China dumping heavily state-subsidized products into market economies.
But the Canada-U.S. dispute did come up, Sidhu said in an interview with CBC News.
He said he stressed to Greer that the two countries need to "find a way to work together, especially for our auto supply workers."
"I think there is energy from both sides," Sidhu said, calling it a "very cordial conversation."
"But we want a good deal," he said. "We won't accept anything less."
Greer downplays Trump's deal comments
Speaking earlier Thursday to Bloomberg News from the summit, Greer seemed to downplay President Donald Trump's assertion this week that the Canadians would come calling for a deal and that something could come together within a month.
"You've heard the president talk about this. Most recently he said, 'Well, we may have a deal with Canada in a few weeks.' I'd emphasize the 'may' in that part of the situation," Greer said.
Greer reiterated that the U.S. is open to a deal with Canada, but he suggested Prime Minister Mark Carney and his negotiators can't accept what the Americans are offering.
"The question is does Canada want to get to 'yes' on some of these things. We have a trade policy where we're not inclined to go to zero tariffs because we're trying to reshore," he said. "Gaps remain between Canada and the United States."
Those "gaps" became apparent when Canada-U.S. trade talks collapsed in August, with Carney pulling his negotiators back from Washington after what he described as a series of last-minute American changes that weren't workable for Canada.
Canada was concerned about U.S. tariffs on medium- and heavy-duty trucks, which could have made a GM plant in Oshawa, Ont., that produces Chevrolet Silverados uncompetitive and imperiled the planned production of Ford F-250s in Oakville, Ont.

Carney also said he couldn't accept language in the proposed deal that could have compromised Canada's sovereignty, namely provisions he described as limiting the government's ability to make trade deals with other countries.
U.S. opposition to Canadian policies designed to promote the "discoverability" of French-language programming on streaming services was also an issue, Carney has said.
While Greer seemingly backed down from U.S. demands on French-language content in an interview with CBC News, no apparent progress has been made on those other issues in the weeks since the bilateral talks imploded.
Carney said this week he thinks it's possible to negotiate a "mutually advantageous trade arrangement" with the U.S. at some point in the future.
"Canada stands ready to negotiate in good faith," he said.

On Sept. 28, 2026, U.S. President Donald Trump held an event at the White House to announce the planning of a new steel plant in Iowa. Joining him in the Oval Office for the event were several Iowa state leaders and officials.
Afterward, some social media users claimed Trump insulted Iowans during the event. For example, an X post (archived) displayed a video clip apparently recorded at the event and asserted, "Trump claims the federal government can 'supersede' Iowa and calls Iowans 'troubled people.'"
In the clip, Trump can be heard saying this: "And we can supersede the state, right? If we can supersede the state, it's good. Otherwise, it will never be good. They're very — they're really troubled people."
Users shared other posts claiming Trump called Iowans troubled people on Instagram (archived) and Threads (archived). Snopes readers searched the site and emailed us asking whether the claim was true.
It was not true. While the video clip is real and unedited, it omits important context that proves Trump didn't call Iowans "really troubled people." Trump was actually referring to Minnesota Gov. Tim Walz and other Democratic leaders in that state.
The remark came immediately after an exchange in which Trump asked how Walz was treating the opening of a new iron mine in Minnesota. Given that this context was omitted, we have rated the clip miscaptioned.
Videos and transcripts of Trump's remarks at the event were uploaded online by C-SPAN and Roll Call. The conversation that led to Trump making the "troubled people" comment begin at about the 6:20 mark in the C-SPAN video and 6:07 in Roll Call's Vimeo video.
At that time, John Jovanovic, the Trump-nominated chairman and president of the Export-Import Bank of the United States, begins describing the opening of an iron mine in Minnesota that is meant to supply the Iowa steel plant (emphasis ours):
JOVANOVIC: Thank you, Mr. President. So, what we're really talking about today is America's economic security. And Mr. President, it's your plan in action, but it all starts mining more in America. The mine you mentioned is the first mine opened in America in 50-plus years focused on iron ore. EXIM financed it, but most importantly, it's found on the Iron Range in America, which for 145 years has been the most prolific iron ore deposit in the world. It helped build America. It helped win two world wars. You're helping resurrect it, Mr. President, with this first iron ore mine. That is why this plant is possible, because we are creating one American supply chain. And what you see again here today, Mr. President, is private capital flowing in to rebuild America and to build America's future, so we can assure that the warfighter of tomorrow in America is always well-equipped and that everyday Americans have what they need when they need it most. And this is what it's going to take to continue to deliver the American dream, Mr. President, for another 250 years.
TRUMP: And how is the governor treating you? Because I freed up the iron ore in that place, and I absolutely won the election, but they wouldn't — they cheat like hell. But how is the governor treating you? Because I freed it up and then they closed it, and the people were devastated because it is the finest iron ore in the world, they say. So how is the governor and these other people that don't — I mean, it's one of the worst-run places I've ever seen. How are they doing?
JOVANOVIC: You know, Mr. President, we were there only 10 days ago, actually, to initiate the mine. We set off 1.3 million pounds of explosives that put it into operation and that will be the iron ore that feeds this plant and to make steel in America the —
TRUMP: And we can supersede the state, right?
COMMERCE SECRETARY HOWARD LUTNICK: Yes.
JOVANOVIC: [unintelligible, cut off by Trump]
TRUMP: If we can supersede the state, it's good. Otherwise, the state will never be good. They're very — they're really troubled people. Thank you very much; great job you're doing, too, by the way. Secretary Lutnick, please.
The mine Jovanovic referred to is owned by Mesabi Metallics in northern Minnesota, where part of the American Iron Range is located. Mesabi Metallics is the same company investing in the steel plant in Iowa.
Local news reports on the fraught history of the mine suggest its struggles have largely been tied to the parent company of Mesabi Metallics, Essar. The India-based company first started work on the mine and an accompanying steel mill in 2007 before shuttering its plans for the mine in 2015 and filing for bankruptcy in 2016. Essar still owes Minnesota more than $22 million in infrastructure debt, according to Iowa news channel KWQC.
As Jovanovic said, Trump administration officials were at the opening of the iron mine in Minnesota about 10 days earlier. If Trump's concern was about opening the mine, he'd have no reason to call for the federal government to "supersede" Minnesota. According to Essar itself, Minnesota State Auditor Julie Blaha said in 2024, "After years of uncertainty, it's encouraging to see Mesabi Metallics breathing new life into this major mining operation."
While the context makes it clear that Trump was referencing Walz and his administration in Minnesota, not Iowans, Snopes reached out to the White House to seek confirmation on whom exactly Trump believed to be "really troubled people." We'll update this story if and when we receive a response to our question.

Another wave of landslides and heavy rain has killed about 30 people in Nepal, as the Himalayan nation reels from August's catastrophic flooding that left 1,400 dead and thousands more missing.
The national disaster management authority says more than 1,900 families have been affected since late last week with more than 240 homes damaged. Roads, buildings and bridges have been swept away.
Hundreds of trekkers on the Annapurna Circuit - crucial to Nepal's economy - have had to cut short their hikes to get to safety.
Many have been helicoptered out of the districts of Manang and Mustang, from a hiking circuit that usually takes up to three weeks to complete.
Communities in several parts of Nepal are mourning loved ones.
Speaking from a damp, blue tent in Battar, a town north-west of Kathmandu, Buti Tamang told BBC Nepali: "We used to live in a hut, but now there is nothing. We have lost so many of our relatives."
"Now it is raining and the tent leaks, so we've been facing a difficult situation. We have nowhere to go," said Ramesh Ghale, who also had to flee his home.
Several trekkers and their guides say their journeys back down the mountains have been treacherous, taking up to three or four days and requiring them to pass collapsed roads and swept-away bridges.
Jake Stacy, a 21-year-old from Suffolk, found himself stranded with his guide in Yak Kharka, upper Manang, due to heavy snowfall last week and decided not to continue to the Thorang La pass, the highest point of the circuit.
"We made our own paths on mountain slopes," he said, after returning to base camp in Pokhara on Tuesday night. "It was quite steep and we were clambering because there was river below… It was very muddy and very wet.
"Many trekkers were helicoptered out," he added.
Australian Andrew Graham and his guide Prem KC said they had to cross more than 15 landslides after they decided to return from Manang village. "A few of them were quite dangerous, the residual risks have grown now."
The two got stuck when they reached the village of Chame, which had been evacuated due to the risk of landslides, and had to spend a night in the jungle, Graham said.
A massive landslide has partially blocked a river which passes through Chame, causing a temporary lake that has inundated houses and a key bridge. Authorities have been trying to release the water for the past three days using excavators but have not been very successful, locals told the BBC.
Meanwhile, trekking guide Tse Ring Doma said she and her group had to cross 28 landslides. The mental stress was more difficult than the physical challenge, she said, given the fresh memory of last month's enormous disaster: "Even thunder would make us run and come out to see if anything was coming our way."
Her client, Norwegian Ellen Wahlström, said visitors were fortunate - they would only have to leave some of their items behind, while locals risked losing their houses and land. She added that authorities had been clearing many of the landslides "surprisingly fast".
While road damage in Manang has been serious, with several bridges swept away and communications down in some areas, no one had been killed in the trekking region, chief district officer Mukti Prasad Khanal said.
But four bodies have been recovered and 12 people remain missing after an avalanche near the base of Himlung Peak, close to the border with Tibet.
A representative of the local trekking authority, the Annapurna Conservation Area Project, said some 700 trekkers were still waiting in Pokhara to embark on the Annapurna Circuit.
"We have been holding back all these people who want to go to the Annapurna Circuit trek, although we are under pressure from the trekking industry to announce the route open," he said.
Indian visitors who often visit the ancient temple Muktinath on a Hindu pilgrimage had been asked to fly from Jomson to Pokhara instead of drive down, due to a cut-off road, he added.
Most of the old trekking trails on the Annapurna Circuit have been unused in recent years after the introduction of roads, except for small pockets of Manang and Mustang districts.
But now operators say many trekkers have been using these abandoned paths to return, as the main roads have been washed away in some sections of the circuit.
