A court in Shopian on Tuesday sentenced a man to life imprisonment for the murder of a person in 2019, observing that the case did not fall within the “rarest of rare” category warranting the death penalty.
Principal Sessions Judge Shopian Mehmood Ahmed Chowdhary awarded life imprisonment and a fine of Rs 1 lakh to Bilal Ahmad Seh, who was convicted under Section 302 of the Ranbir Penal Code (RPC).
The court said the convict had been in custody since his arrest on April 21, 2019, and had spent nearly seven years in custody during the trial.
The case, registered as FIR No. 19/2019 at Police Station Zainapora, initially involved charges under Sections 302, 307, 147, 148, 506, 109, 341 and 34 of the RPC.
While deciding the quantum of sentence, the court considered the mitigating and aggravating circumstances and referred to the Supreme Court’s guidelines on awarding the death penalty.
The court noted that the case was based on four eyewitnesses as well as circumstantial evidence. It also took into account that the convict was a first-time offender, was a farmer by profession and had been supporting his family.
The court observed that there were no aggravating circumstances of such an exceptional nature as to warrant capital punishment.
“Life imprisonment is the appropriate punishment to be awarded to the convict for commission of murder of the deceased,” the court said.
The court also noted that other accused named in the case, including the convict’s brother and two sisters, had been acquitted, while proceedings against another accused had abated following his death. A juvenile accused in the case is facing separate proceedings before the Juvenile Justice Board, according to the case record.
Since the sentence is one of life imprisonment, the court directed that the case file and judgment be submitted to the High Court of Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh for confirmation of the sentence as required under law.
The convict was directed to be sent to Special Jail Pulwama to undergo the sentence. The court also informed him of his right to appeal against the judgment and sentence before the High Court within 15 days.

Elon Musk returns to US government for Pentagon war study
He will co-lead Project Meridian with Palmer Luckey, the co-founder of defence tech firm Anduril Industries, and former House speaker Newt Gingrich
Tech billionaire Elon Musk will make a return to officially advising US President Donald Trump’s government by co-leading what the Pentagon called a study on the future of war.
Musk served as the head of the Department of Government Efficiency before departing in May last year, having publicly fallen out with Trump.
In a speech at the Quantico military base, Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth said “Project Meridian” will be “an effort led by America’s best minds to study the future of warfare”.
“We are leveraging a unique source of American advantage, one our adversaries do not have: our innovators, our senior leaders and our technologists,” Hegseth said.

Hurricane Polo is barreling towards the Baja California region of Mexico, the latest system in a Pacific hurricane season that has been notably active in recent months. On 22 September, a measurement of 892 millibars was registered for Hurricane Polo, making it the second-most intense hurricane on record in the east Pacific. It is fuelled by exceptionally warm waters across the Pacific Ocean, providing favourable conditions for the system to maintain its considerable strength.
Polo is expected to turn towards the west-north-west, before taking a more north-westerly trajectory on Saturday. It has maximum sustained winds of around 150mph, with even stronger gusts occurring within the most intense parts of the hurricane. Hurricane-force winds extend outward for approximately 40 miles from the centre, while tropical storm-force winds reach as far as 125 miles. These powerful winds, combined with torrential rainfall and dangerous seas, could have significant impacts. Although some fluctuations in intensity are possible over the coming days, Polo is expected to remain powerful as it tracks north-westwards.
In India, a deep 988-millibar low-pressure system – a tropical storm in this case – is centred along the east coast, bringing widespread and potentially disruptive weather conditions to Odisha and surrounding areas. The system is producing heavy rainfall across the region, with the latest forecast models suggesting totals could exceed 200mm in some locations over a 24-hour period. Rainfall rates are expected to be particularly intense at times, with hourly totals potentially exceeding 30mm in the heaviest downpours. Such intense rainfall could cause significant surface water and localised flooding, particularly in low-lying areas and places with poor drainage. Strong and gusty winds are also affecting coastal parts of Odisha. Winds are forecast to reach around 50-60mph, creating hazardous conditions in exposed areas and potentially causing disruption to travel, infrastructure and power supplies. Authorities have closed numerous schools across the affected districts for safety reasons.
Meanwhile, in Iberia, the relentless heat of summer is extending into meteorological autumn, with temperatures rising into the high 30s celsius on 23 September. Alvega, in Portugal, recorded a maximum temperature of 41.7C, smashing many July records from previous decades.

Poor diet, sedentary habits, and prolonged screen use are contributing to metabolic disorders among young people at increasingly younger ages, said Challa Suresh, Scientist ‘G’ and Director Grade, Head of the Cell Biology Division, AcSIR Coordinator at the ICMR-National Institute of Nutrition, at an oration organised by Sri Ramachandra Institute of Higher Education and Research recently.
Delivering the Prof. S.P. Thyagarajan Endowment Oration on ‘The Modern Lifestyle Paradox: Why are Young People Developing Metabolic Disorder Earlier?’, Prof. Suresh stressed the importance of nutritious food and healthier lifestyle habits in preventing lifestyle-related illnesses.
He advised young people to choose wholesome, nutrient-rich foods, and limit processed and packaged foods, which he linked to rising obesity. He also called for reducing screen time, noting that prolonged use of digital devices encourage sedentary behaviour and affect memory and overall well-being.
The event was attended by university officials, academicians, clinicians, researchers, and students.

New Delhi, Sep 23: The Congress on Wednesday alleged that for the Modi government, the UCC is not an instrument of considered legal reform but an instrument of division, disruption and diversion, as well as a tool for stoking prejudices and keeping society in a state of permanent polarisation.
The opposition party's assertion comes after former Bombay High Court judge Justice R C Chavan resigned from the Maharashtra government's panel to prepare a draft for implementing the Uniform Civil Code (UCC), citing serious reservations over its decision to restrict public feedback on crucial social issues to a "Yes/No" format.
Congress general secretary in-charge communications Jairam Ramesh said the resignation of a former high court judge from the Maharashtra government's committee to draft a UCC for the state raises larger questions, apart from his several concerns on the functioning of this committee.
Posting his statement on X, Ramesh said, "A retired High Court judge has shown courage to resign from a committee set up by the Maharashtra government to prepare a uniform civil code for the state. Here is our statement on the non-uniform 'Uniform' Civil Codes (UCC) the HM is trying to bulldoze through in every state."
"Did the Constituent Assembly ever imagine a situation in which every state would enact its own separate version of a UCC? The answer is a resounding no," Ramesh said.
Did the architects of our Constitution led by Dr B.R. Ambedkar ever conceive states competing with one another to have different UCCs according to the political machinations and calculations of one political party, he asked.
"Again, the answer is a resounding no," Ramesh added.
He pointed out that on June 17, 2016, the Modi government referred the question of the UCC to the 21st Law Commission of India for detailed examination.
"After extensive research, the Commission published its Consultation Paper on Reform of Family Law on August 31, 2018. Its conclusion appearing in paragraph 1.15 on page 7 of the Consultation Paper was clear: 'The formulation of a Uniform Civil Code is neither necessary nor desirable at this stage'. Instead it recommended addressing nor discrimination within individual family laws while preserving India's legal and cultural diversity," Ramesh said.
The Modi government has chosen to disregard the findings of the very Commission it tasked with examining the issue because the facts, as usual, did not align with its political agenda, the Congress leader said.
Over the last three years, one BJP-ruled State after another bulldozed through its own version of a UCC, Ramesh said.
The UCC came into effect in Uttarakhand from January 27, 2025. Subsequently the Gujarat Assembly passed the UCC Bill on March 24, 2026, the Assam Assembly on May 27, 2026 and the Madhya Pradesh Assembly on July 21, 2026," he pointed out.
Ramesh said these State-level UCCs, never envisaged in the Constitution, are not uniform.
"They contain different provisions, different penalties, different procedures and significant exemptions. Contrary to claims, the Uttarakhand UCC, the only one in force, continues with a number of patriarchal traditions and is creating many problems for perfectly law-abiding residents of the state," Ramesh argued.
Union Home Minister Amit Shah has made a typically bombastic announcement that a UCC will be implemented in all NDA-ruled States before the 2029 Lok Sabha election, he said.
Evidently other NDA parties have lost their voices and are being silenced by the BJP, the Congress general secretary said.
"For the Modi Government, the UCC is not an instrument of considered legal reform to be implemented after the widest possible consultations and public debate and with the broadest possible consensus. It is, in reality, an instrument of division, disruption and diversion, a tool for harassment and intimidation, stoking prejudices and keeping society in a state of permanent polarisation," Ramesh said.
Later, asked about the statement, he said, "The UCC bulldozer is to permanently polarise society."
In a letter to the panel chairperson Justice Ranjana Desai (retd), former Bombay High Court judge Chavan criticised the committee's approach, stating that reducing complex societal questions, such as delayed marriages, perversions, infertility, and rising matrimonial disputes, to binary options undermined the primary purpose of consensus-building.
The former judge said he had misunderstood that the committee aimed to gather views of the people of Maharashtra and to generate a consensus to remedy the issues of late marriages, infertility, unstable marriages, time-consuming dispute resolution mechanism and so on.
"Now that the misunderstanding is removed, I realise that the aim is to just provide an opportunity to people who may care, to share their responses, in a 'yes or no' format to the questions posed so that analysis of data becomes easy," the letter said.
In July, the state government set up a seven-member committee headed by retired Supreme Court Justice Ranjana Desai to draft a framework for implementing the UCC, which seeks to establish equal laws across religions on issues about marriage, divorce, and property.
Justice Chavan, a former high court judge, resigned from the panel on September 19.
The Congress' statement also comes days after Shah said the BJP-led NDA governments in 21 states will introduce UCC before 2029. The next Lok Sabha polls are scheduled for 2029.

Union Petroleum Minister Hardeep Singh Puri, along with the Petroleum and Natural Gas Regulatory Board (PNGRB) and city-gas distributors, on Thursday launched National PNG Drive 3.0, stepping up efforts to accelerate the shift towards piped natural gas (PNG) for households.
The latest phase, which will run until the end of FY27, targets 50 lakh new domestic PNG connections, conversion of 40 lakh existing connections into active consumers and onboarding another 50 lakh domestic PNG registrations.
The initiative builds on the second phase, which ran from January 1 to June 30, 2026, and added around 13.4 lakh billed connections, while generating more than 15.3 lakh domestic PNG registrations.
PNGRB data showed a sharp acceleration in adoption during the second phase. Average daily additions of domestic PNG connections rose 43% to 6,690 from 4,702, while daily additions of billed consumers increased more than two-and-a-half times to 7,392 from 2,781.
The third phase would focus on improving utilisation of existing city-gas infrastructure. The government also plans to accelerate PNG adoption in newly connected areas, particularly semi-urban and rural markets.
According to PNGRB, around 6.9 lakh inch-km of pipeline infrastructure has been laid across the country, including approximately 2.5 lakh inch-km of steel pipelines and 4.42 lakh inch-km of MDPE pipelines. This network has the potential to support around 1.3 crore domestic PNG connections.
In a social media post, Mr. Puri said “this will strengthen India’s vision of increasing the share of natural gas in the primary energy mix from around 6% currently, while providing a cleaner, reliable and affordable energy source.”

There’s a common assumption that anxiety about artificial intelligence is universal — that everyone, everywhere, is bracing for the same disruption. But, a new Pew Research Centre Survey of over 42,000 adults across 37 countries, suggests otherwise.
The survey’s data points out that worry about AI tracks closely with wealth. The richer the country, the more its people fear AI will take their jobs, widen inequality, and disrupt daily life. The poorer the country, the less its citizens fear AI as they simply haven’t formed an opinion on it yet.
The researchers split 36 core countries into 18 “high-income” and 18 “middle-income” nations, using World Bank’s classifications built on gross national income per capita. The gap between the two groups shows up in nearly every question that was part of the survey.
A median of 55% of adults in high-income countries said AI will lead to fewer jobs in their country over the next decades. In middle-income countries, that figure drops nearly 20 points lower to 36%. People in poorer countries aren’t necessarily more hopeful; they’re more uncertain.
Roughly a third of the adults in middle-income nations said they simply don’t know how AI will affect jobs, compared with about a fifth in wealthy ones.
The same pattern holds for inequality. A median of 35% of adults in high-income countries believe AI will widen the gap between rich and poor, versus 22% in middle-income countries.
In general, 40% of the respondents in the wealthy nations said they were more concerned than excited about AI’s growing presence in their daily lives, compared with 31% in middle-income nations.
A clear divide
When the researchers plotted individual countries against their GDP per capita, the correlation between GDP per capita and the belief that AI cost jobs was strong. On AI awareness — the share of people who said they’ve heard or read ‘a lot’ about AI — the connection was even stronger.
Respondents in two Asian nations capture this divide. In Singapore, for instance, where GDP per capita is close to $100,000, 53% of its adults said they’ve heard or read ‘a lot’ about AI. In Bangladesh, where GDP per capita is about $2,600, just 4% of its adults reported the same level of awareness.
Loss of jobs fear follows the same pattern as roughly seven in ten or more adults in Australia, South Korea and the US expect AI to shrink the job market over the next two decades. But in Kenya, Nigeria and the Philippines, that expectation is far less common as they are yet to form a strong view on the technology.
Nearly half of Americans said the technology will widen the gap between rich and poor. In India, however, which is classified as a middle-income country, only 13% said the same.
This divergence in attitudes of people in high-income and middle-income economies seems to be a function of the level of awareness of new technologies.
People in advanced economies are far more likely to have encountered AI tools directly that have visibly threatened their job prospects.
In middle-income nations, however, where informal labour and manual work still make up a large share of employment, AI’s impact can feel more abstract.
Pew Research Centre found that in many middle-income countries, it’s the wealthier and more educated people within that country who are most likely to say AI will cost jobs or deepen inequality.
Much of the gap traces back to the same driver: people with less income and less formal education are simply more likely to say they’re unsure of this technology. Uncertainty fills the space where worry would otherwise occupy.
The bottomline is that familiarity with AI predicts concerns about AI, and that is a function of income.
Beyond income
Apart from income, age plays a major role in how respondents perceive AI. Younger adults are dramatically more aware of AI than their elders. In Spain and Greece, the awareness gap between 18-to-34-year-olds and those 50 and older exceeds 50 percentage points.
And in several wealthy nations, that awareness is translating into a distinctive kind of unease with a mix of concern, excitement and a rising tide of job-related anxiety among the young.
In the US, share of adults under 35 who say they’re concerned about AI has jumped from 40% to 55% in the last 18-24 months. In Sweden, there is a starker shift as a year ago older Swedes are more worried about AI than younger ones. But now the two groups have converged with younger adults’ concern rising.
This shows that young people in wealthy countries are the most digitally immersed, AI-literate, and most anxious lot — a combination that upends the idea that youth are optimistic about new technology.
In India, just 13% of adults surveyed said they’ve heard or read ‘a lot’ about AI. This is one of the lowest figures in this survey, trailing far behind high-income countries.
And the belief that AI will cost jobs is comparatively muted too. Among Indians 50 and older, just 20% expect fewer jobs over the next two decades, rising to 30% among those 35 to 49 and 33% among adults under 35 — a meaningful generational gap.
That youngest-oldest pattern on jobs fits the broader global trend of younger adults being warier of AI’s economic disruption.
But India breaks from the pack on general sentiment as it is one of the few countries in the survey where older adults (24%) are more likely than the youngest adults (15%) to say they’re primarily concerned rather than excited about AI in daily life — the opposite of what shows up almost everywhere else.
The implication of this survey is double-edged for citizens and governments. Concern is often what drives demand for regulation and worker protections. That means the countries best positioned to frame laws around AI’s disruptions may be exactly the ones already feeling the most anxious about it.
Meanwhile, in the middle-income economies, the absence of alarm may reflect not resilience, but simply not having been asked the question loudly enough yet.

- The Skeleton Key can be found in a buried chest within the Nightmare Neighborhood POI in Fortnite.
- The Secret Room that can be opened using the Skeleton Key is found in the basement of the house located in Nightmare Neighborhood.
- The quality of loot you find solely depends on which Secret Room you open in Fortnite.
The Skeleton Key was added with the Fortnite update 42.30 on October 1 for Fortnitemares 2026. It is a master key of sorts, able to open different types of locks, especially those that lead to Secret Rooms in Fortnite. If we’ve piqued your interest, here’s everything you need to know about the Skeleton Key in Fortnite, how to get it, and how to use it to open Secret Rooms.
Where to Find the Skeleton Key in Fortnite: Map Location
To find the Skeleton Key in Fortnite, you need to dig up a buried chest found within a random mausoleum that’s located in the graveyard. It is adjacent to the newly added Nightmare Neighborhood POI on the Fortnite Chapter 7 Season 4 map.
There are a total of three mausoleums that you can find inside the graveyard, but only two of them have buried chests within. We’ve attached some images to help you see exactly where you need to go to dig up the chest and open it to get the Skeleton Key in Fortnite.
That said, the Skeleton Key is a unique item that’s limited to the Nightmare Neighborhood POI (it spawns nowhere else on the island) and will be vaulted when Fortnitemares 2026 ends. You can find two Skeleton Keys in every Fortnite Zero Build or Battle Royale match.
How to Find the Secret Room in Fortnite
Once you have the Skeleton Key in Fortnite, equip it and head inside the main building that’s located next to the graveyard. After entering, take the first left, open the door, and go down two flights of stairs. We recommend that you equip the Skeleton Key, as it points the way, making it easier for you to reach your destination.
At the bottom of the staircase, three doors appear in front of you. Using your Skeleton Key, you can open any one of these doors in Fortnite. The choice is completely yours, and there are no wrong answers. However, we strongly suggest you only open the door that the Skeleton Key has marked.
Don’t worry about jump scares, as Epic Games hasn’t introduced any in this location with the Fortnite update 42.30.
Which Secret Room to Open Using the Skeleton Key in Fortnite?
So, you don’t want to risk opening the ‘wrong’ secret door in Fortnite using the Skeleton Key, do you? Well, unfortunately, as we mentioned, there are no wrong answers. The prize or loot behind each door is randomized in every match. Which means there’s no guarantee of what you find. To that end, here’s what we found behind each door:
- Door 1: Common weapon and ammo.
- Door 2: Rare Chests (x2).
- Door 3: Regular Chests (x2).
To maximize your odds of opening the door that leads to the room filled with rare chests, we suggest listening carefully for audio cues. Turn on the “Visualized Sound” option from the menu to improve your odds of opening the ‘right’ room every time. If you’re lucky, you can get one of the many Exotic weapons in Fortnite by opening the rare chests.
That’s all you need to know about the Skeleton Key in Fortnite and how to use it to get high-tier loot. Remember to make use of audio cues to open the door that has the most loot behind it. If all else fails, you can always go and open a Vault in Fortnite to get powerful items/weapons.
Let us know in the comments below which Secret Room’s door you opened first using the Skeleton Key in Fortnite and what you found behind it.
How to get the Skeleton Key in Fortnite?
You can get a Skeleton Key in Fortnite by digging up and searching buried chests located inside mausoleums with the premise of the Nightmare Neighborhood POI.
What do Skeleton Keys do in Fortnite?
Skeleton Keys can be used to open a ‘ Secret Room’ that grants you loot.
What sort of loot is found behind the Secret Room in Fortnite?
Depending on which ‘Secret Room’ you open, you can either get basic loot or rare chests.

A decade ago, actor Deepika Padukone said in an ad campaign: ‘My body, My choice.’ But, in reality, when it comes to older people, society often wrests that agency from them. Last week, as the world observed both International Day of Older Persons (October 1) and Gandhi Jayanti (October 2), Mumbai-based Sumira Roy’s documentary film Bhangaar (Obsolete), raised the question of dignity in death and the right to die for the elderly.
The yet-to-release Marathi film, which won the National Film Award for Best Non-Feature Film last month, was screened by the Kriti Film Club in Delhi NCR.
Bhangaar trains the lens on Narayan and Iravati Lavate, an octogenarian Maharashtrian childless couple, who petitioned for active euthanasia in 2018. Iravati succumbed to cancer in 2023, Narayan lives in an old-age home. His eyesight and memory, too, have deserted him. After the news of the National Award came in, Roy wanted to share the moment with Narayan. She rang up Prakash Joshi, the brother of Iravati, who also appears in the film. Joshi told her that due to Narayan’s present old-age health and impediments there of, nothing would register with man.
While Nilesh Maniyar and Shonali Bose’s documentary A Fly on the Wall (2024) is also on the same subject and travels with Chika Kapadia to Switzerland for his last days, Roy’s documentary shows how only privilege can afford that right.
Monisha Advani, Bhangaar’s producer and partner, Emmay Entertainment, calls the film personal, “My late mother was a Maharashtrian and while growing up, the frugality of my maternal grandparents’ lives somewhere was mirrored in the Lavates. Sumira has given me the opportunity, in a private way, to pay tribute to my familial pedagogy."
Excerpts from an interview with director Roy:
You are from an advertising background; how, when and why did you transition into filmmaking and documentary films at that?
Since I’ve been a student, I’ve been passionate about films and documentary films and had even sat for the FTII entrance examination. But the women in my family were against me going to Pune and feared the casting couch in the film industry. Years later, when I went to Japan for work, I did a postgraduate course in Japanese cinema, theatre and painting. I was just hooked on when I saw [films by Yasujirō] Ozu and all the greats there. So, I thought, there’s a roundabout way to do films through advertising films. There’s a great amount of discipline in ad films; you shoot minimally and you have only 30-40 seconds to tell your story. Ad films [at Ogilvy and JWT] also gave me a lot of exposure to a lot of things that you need in documentaries. For instance, understanding human behaviour. And then, in documentaries, I learnt how to listen… to people’s stories. I went on foreign location shoots and for post-production. All that’s helped me now. In 2011, I left advertising and started two agencies, mainly for production. I was a little bit jaded and cynical, trying to do these falsehoods to make people buy things they didn’t need.
Did the Central Board of Film Certification raise any objections in Bhangaar?
Only to the title. The censor board didn’t like the word bhangaar [obsolete] and called it insulting. I had to keep going back to explain to them that the word is what Narayan uses [in life and in the film]. It’s his, not mine. After some time, they agreed but asked me to carry a disclaimer in Marathi at the start of the film that this is the character’s interpretation of the title. That was fine by me.
There seems to be a thematic continuity between your documentaries Last DaysLast Shot (2017) and Bhangaar. Tell us about the earlier film.
I have an idea, and then I make a film. I don’t just go and make documentaries, because I’m not an activist or an investigative filmmaker. As Narayan says in the film [Bhangaar], the day you’re born is the beginning of death. He echoes the Myth of Sisyphus when he says there’s no purpose to life; it’s absurd. I am drawn to existentialism, and like diving into the interior of minds.
For my earlier film, I was interested in exploring the philosophy of moksha and nirvana. I went to Banaras [Hindu] University, and walked around in the gullies and ghats. People would pop out from the woods to say, ‘Come listen to my poem.’ There, I found a Bengali poet-artist who had gone to Japan and become famous. He returned to Varanasi with his Japanese wife [they ran the Kumiko Guest House]. By the time I shot him, he looked like Rabindranath Tagore. He was about 80 or 81. He told me his idea of moksha: to dissolve the ego. Then I met a 26-year-old Dom in Harishchandra Ghat cremation ground, who [told me he] hardly got a chance to light the fire, and couldn’t make money with it. So, he bought a camera and started shooting the relatives of the dead. He said from his experience that a good person’s corpse burns faster than a sinner’s.
What drew you to Iravati and Narayan Lavate’s story?
It’s a personal reason. My long-widowed mother was quite active in life. She’d drive, have a social life, her body and mind intact. A year before she passed away, she started saying, ‘I want to die with dignity.’ I was a documentary filmmaker, but I never listened to her nor asked her what she meant. I was petrified of her dying. [After] she passed away, I was stricken with grief and regret. I came across the Lavates’ story in Mid-Day; they asked for the right to die together with dignity. That struck me, and I went to meet them in their 12x12 room in a Mumbai chawl, to get closure for what I hadn’t done with my mother. They taught me so much about Marathi literature and theatre. Narayan looked like Picasso to me. He knew the Constitution by heart. I asked, how could they want to die. He said, ‘It’s time to go.’
They had this fixed spiel they would rattle to the media/news channels. They would do the same during our initial days of shoot. I just told them not to look at the camera and go about their days. I had to be a fly on the wall and filmed them over four years. Afterwards, they forgot there’s a camera. My DOP is brilliant because it was a boot camp for her, with no lights, no space to set up the camera. The aerial shot of them playing cards was shot from atop a washing machine.
In India, the elderly population is growing rapidly even as the birth rate declines. What did your research throw up about ageing and caregiving?
The elderly are growing three times faster than the population of the youth. Palliative care exists only for the rich. There’s no geriatric care and no focus on what is going to happen to the elderly population. All of us are in some stage of caregiving. We are either watching our parents or grandparents.
Gandhi spoke of self-rule. Swaraj is not just political self-rule but also the rule/autonomy over oneself. Does that idea of self-determination versus duty get complicated when it comes to an older person’s choice to die?
Loss of personhood and loss of autonomy, which older people fear, is exactly why they [Irawati and Narayan] asked for it [active euthanasia]. We do not connect with our families. Our conversations revolve around whether they have taken their medicines, if the oxygen tank is running low, if the nurse administered the injection. That’s our only conversation with them. The elderly feel like they are [outdated] machines. We have moved away from joint families to nuclear families. As a society, we have forgotten how to respect someone who has lived longer than expected. We keep talking about Gen Z and loneliness, but loneliness is far worse among the older generations. We hardly talk about it. Even our films don’t.
We’ve read about the Aruna Shanbaug case. This year, the Supreme Court gave its landmark judgment permitting passive euthanasia for Harish Rana who was in a vegetative state for over 13 years. What has been the impact of the Lavates’ petition?
Narayan and Iravati are the pioneers of this, at least in our country, or in South Asia. The courts are getting more and more petitions since. The press doesn’t cover many of these.
Bhangaar (Obsolete) screens on October 1 at the India Habitat Centre, Delhi, and on October 4 at Museo Camera, Gurugram at 4.30 pm.

Each rare disease affects very few people. However, there are around 8,000 rare diseases, and they cumulatively affect hundreds of millions of people. In India, 1,004 rare genetic disorders have been reported so far.
It used to be that because the number of patients for a rare-disease drug was very small, so the pharmaceutical industry’s interest in developing such drugs was limited. Therefore they were called orphan drugs.
In order to overcome this hesitancy, many governments have incentivised companies to develop orphan drugs. Examples include the Orphan Drug Act, which the U.S. passed in 1983 to provide tax incentives, seven years of market exclusivity for the first approved product for a given condition, grants, regulatory fee waivers, etc.That is, it reduced the costs of developing the drugs and enabled companies to make a good profit.
This allowed companies to diversify into rare-disease drugs. Before the passage of the Orphan Drug Act, only 38 relevant drugs had been approved in the U.S. But after that, by 2022, there had been 1,122 approvals. Subsequently, several countries and regions, including Japan, Australia, and the European Union had approved similar legislation encouraging pharmaceutical companies to develop and manufacture orphan drugs.
Because of the small market, companies tend to set very high prices for these medications, and it is not unusual for a rare disease patient to find that a year’s worth of the drug costs around $100,000 (Rs 1 crore) or more. This puts the medication out of reach for virtually all patients around the world unless a health insurance scheme or government health service covers it. Samples of such high-priced pharmaceuticals are described in the table.
Two challenges
Although the Government of India supports rare disease patients with up to a total of Rs 50 lakh for their treatment, this is often insufficient to cover the necessary costs even for a year, and patients may have to resort to crowdfunding to raise the required capital.
For example, in mid-2025, Rs 9 crore was raised through crowdfunding to pay for gene therapy for a 16-month-old child in Kolkata. In fact, almost 4,000 children are listed on a Government of India crowdfunding platform, with the cumulative annual cost of treatment for these patients amounting to over Rs 9,000 crore.
Many drugs for rare diseases have been developed, but they cater to only about 5% of rare diseases and associated conditions. Therefore, most patients lack suitable drugs, even those available at high cost.
Two key challenges in developing new orphan drugs are identifying a patient cohort for conducting clinical trials and determining endpoints in these trials. Once a drug is approved, undertaking small-scale manufacturing and distribution that is affordable and of high-quality are other major challenges.
In this article, the authors present here a possible solution to these issues. These solutions touch on how foreign companies that tend to develop novel drugs can work with India both for clinical trials and manufacturing.
Trials for new drugs
With an overall population exceeding 1.4 billion, India has a large number of patients with any given condition. And due to high rates of endogamy in certain social groups, the prevalence of a particular rare disease is even higher than might be expected based on its prevalence elsewhere.
For example, research has shown that in particular ethnic groups, the prevalence of beta-thalassemia in India can be 10.5% whereas, per a 2023 review, the prevalence in India’s general population is 3.7%. Indian patients have also become increasingly organised in recent years, with a proliferation of patient advocacy groups focusing on specific diseases.
On the research front, for example, one longitudinal study has been tracking a group of 70 people with a rare condition called GNE myopathy. Patient groups pertaining to Rett syndrome have a registry of more than 400 patients. The gene pool of the Indian diaspora also has unique mutations, often across different ethnicities.
In all, there is a large number of rare disease patients, which should help in finding a suitable patient cohort for trials. However, patients from India are not usually participants in international trials for orphan drugs.Therefore, there is considerable scope to increase their involvement in such trials. The government could foster the collaboration of foreign companies and local organisations, as it does in the area of chip manufacturing. It also could invite multinational drug companies to set up drug-development centres vis-à-vis rare diseases in India, in collaboration with patient groups.
If Indian patients are important participants in developing such drugs, they are also likely to be more interested in accessing the resulting drugs than in any monetary compensation. Put another way, Indian patients may be willing to help drug development but only if they see themselves as beneficiaries of the approved drugs.
Overpriced drugs that they cannot access serve no local purpose. To this end, the authors propose that India decide on the price of drugs sold within the country or in the Global South. The company developing the drug can be free to set prices in the rest of the world.
The authors say this with reference to the concept of benefit-sharing. Recently, country representatives and medical experts discussed this concept in the context of the Pandemic Agreement of the World Health Organization (WHO). The idea is that in the event of a pandemic, countries will rapidly share information about pathogens, including their genetic information, with the rest of the world. That way, pharmaceutical and biotechnology companies can develop diagnostics, drugs, and vaccines as early as possible. The catch is such products must be shared across countries, fairly and equitably.
Notably, U.S. and Chinese companies are locked in a charged race to develop drugs for rare diseases. Chinese companies will usually have access to enough patients, and also to low-cost manufacturing. Likewise, companies from the Western nations may find it worthwhile to explore opportunities of collaboration in India.
Manufacturing in India
India has been called the “pharmacy of the world” due to its production of small molecule generics, which fill 47% of the prescriptions for generics in the U.S. India also has the largest number of manufacturing sites approved by U.S. regulators outside the U.S.
Indian firms also manufacture and export biosimilars to the U.S. and the European Union and supply 15% of all biosimilars sold in the U.S. Of late, facilities in the country have been producing a relatively novel therapy personalised to each patient for particular cancers, called CAR-T, to international standards.
In effect, India can manufacture various categories of high-quality drugs at low cost. Local manufacturers are also ready to do this for small volumes, whereas manufacturers in Western nations are often unwilling to do so.
After understanding how foreign companies could develop and manufacture orphan drugs in India, we can consider how existing orphan drugs that have been approved abroad can be produced in India.
Under Rule 101 of the New Drugs and Clinical Trials Rules 2019, the Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation (CDSCO) has specified six countries — including the U.S. and the U.K.; if one of these countries approves a drug, the drug need not have a new clinical trial conducted in India before its maker seeking the Indian regulator’s approval.
This provision can be a major incentive to manufacture and market certain generic drugs in India. However, this policy can benefit from greater transparency, including guidance documents to help drug developers and sponsors file applications to the regulator. Regulatory agencies abroad routinely develop such documents to ease the applications process.
As a rule, the approval of such drugs should be based on bioequivalence, i.e. their behaviour in the body should be the same as that of the original drug; safety and toxicity studies; and the drug’s effectiveness once it is on the market.
Such a pathway will require appropriate safeguards for quality, safety, a system that looks out for adverse events after the drug is on the market (i.e. pharmacovigilance), and manufacturing standards — but it will also considerably reduce the need for duplicate paperwork.
What the state can do
We also have an opportunity to take advantage of India’s expertise in generic drugs to create a global orphan drug manufacturing industry. The government should draft policy that reduces the financial barriers to producing such drugs locally. A useful model could be developed along the lines of the production-linked incentive schemes for manufacturing. That is, companies investing in the manufacture of selected orphan drugs could receive incentives linked to production, investment, exports, and patient access.
The financial incentives could include tax incentives for investing in orphan drug manufacturing and production-linked incentives for approved orphan drugs. Other kinds of support could include support for technology transfer and process development in collaboration with a national laboratory, advanced market commitments (AMCs) by the government, committing to buy a certain output at a certain price point, and distributing it through the Centres of Excellence on Rare Diseases, the Central Government Health Scheme, and the Pradhan Mantri Bhartiya Jan Aushadhi Kendras. Manufacturers could also benefit from predictable demand during the early stages of production, and incentives for exporting to low- and middle-income countries.
The overall objective should not simply be to subsidise companies. Instead, the government should de-risk the initial investment enough to make orphan drug manufacturing commercially viable.
With a streamlined regulatory pathway, appropriate financial incentives, and government procurement, India could build a globally competitive rare-disease pharmaceutical sector.
Taken together, India has already shown the world how to make drugs affordable. The next challenge is to show the world how to make rare-disease drugs accessible.
Gayatri Saberwal, Rakesh Mishra, and Alok Bhattacharya are with the Tata Institute for Genetics and Society. Bhattacharya is also with ‘World Without GNE Myopathy’.

Hundreds Detained in France as Some Student Protests Turn Violent
French high schoolers are protesting teacher shortages and overcrowded classrooms, in France’s latest flare-up over education and public services.
French authorities have detained at least 440 people during protests this week led by high school students who are angry about the state of the country’s education system.
Students have held demonstrations in hundreds of schools across the country, in some cases barricading the entrances with obstacles like e-bikes, throwing projectiles and setting fire to trash cans. On Tuesday night, Laurent Nuñez, the interior minister, said in a television interview that police had detained 440 people on Monday and Tuesday, many of whom were minors.
By Wednesday morning, nearly 80 people had been injured in the unrest, including students and staff members, according to France’s education minister, Édouard Geffray.
A union of high school students said they were protesting a “lack of teachers and staff, dilapidated schools, overcrowded schedules and classrooms.” It also highlighted the stress caused by a state-run website that students must use to apply for admission to higher education programs, including undergraduate university places, and which is perceived as opaque and impersonal.
Mr. Geffray called their demands “legitimate” and worthy of debate, but said the violence had gone too far. One young person, who was using a firework launcher, lost use of part of a hand, he said. Teachers had been chased and principals had been targeted with such launching tubes, he added.
“No demand can justify such acts,” Mr. Geffray said.

With the 2026 midterm elections fast approaching, polling increasingly suggests that the GOP is in for a bad time. As the Iran war drives up inflation and fuel prices, Republicans are on the back foot not just in swing states like Michigan, but in redder parts of the map: Iowa, Texas, and maybe even Kansas, among others. (Not to mention Georgia and North Carolina.)
What Democrats are still getting wrong about voters
Sarah Longwell explains how Democrats could win 2026 — and still lose the bigger fight.
It’s shaping up to be a Democratic wave, in other words, and a major repudiation of President Donald Trump. According to Sarah Longwell, the publisher of political news site the Bulwark, there’s a clear reason why this is the cycle that things seem to be falling apart for Trump, who has dodged scandals and bad poll numbers before. “The average person is often voting on instinctual things,” she explains, “and those instincts are a lot of your animalistic desires for things to be okay materially.” And for many voters right now, things are not okay materially.
Longwell would know: She regularly speaks with voters for her podcast, The Focus Group, and she’s the author of the new book How to Eat an Elephant: One Voter at a Time.
Longwell talked with Vox’s Astead Herndon for a special live recording of the America, Actually podcast at the Texas Tribune Festival earlier this month about why voters are both more and less complicated than punditry sometimes suggests, what the future holds for the Republican Party post-Trump, and the lesson Democrats need to learn to capitalize on their wins.
Below is an excerpt of Astead’s conversation with Longwell, edited for length and clarity. There’s much more in the full show, so listen to America, Actually wherever you get your podcasts or watch it on Vox’s YouTube channel.
One of the themes in the book is to talk to voters like real adults. What does that mean?
There was a long period of time in our history where the artifice of politics was part of the performance of politics.
You could give a good speech. You’d do a debate. Those are not the rules of politics in this communications environment anymore. Every single one of you, if you’re a Bulwark person, you interact with me. I am in your ear, and we’re having a conversation.
We have a parasocial relationship. I walked in here and met a bunch of people, and they were like, “I feel like I know you.” And people want to feel like that about their political leaders now. And so they want to know what makes you tick. Are you a real person? And so the artifice of a debate on CNN is starting to feel really stupid, no offense to CNN.
People demand more now. And a lot of it is just that artifice is falling away for voters. Donald Trump understood that as a person who had been in people’s living rooms as a performer. Democratic politicians still have not figured it out.
One of the things that comes through in both the book and I think the work that we both do is how voters don’t always fit into those neat ideological boxes.
I always tell the story about when I was at the Iowa caucuses, and I remember in 2019 in the Democratic primary, someone telling me they were stuck between Bernie [Sanders] and [former New York City Mayor Michael] Bloomberg, and asking, “How did you get there?”
And what was the answer?
I think the short answer was they liked a strong guy where they knew what he believed in. And they did not care which side of that coin that was, as long as it felt consistent and something they could put their hands around.
If ideology is not the controlling paradigm for voters, how should we think about the different ways people are sorting themselves right now?
My answer is genuinely not to sort them as much. This is the reason people say things like, “It’s the economy, stupid,” and then everybody gets bored with that answer, and they want to talk about 10 other things because they’re like, “Well, that’s so straightforward.”
But I try in the book to say it really is about improving people’s material well-being and ensuring their safety. So you go back to: What are the most human things that people want? They want to be able to afford gas. They want a job. They want a job [where] they think that they can go up the ladder.
They want their kids to get a good education. Then they want to be safe. They want to know that they’re safe in their community. They want to know they’re safe in the places that they go. And Donald Trump and Republicans really do understand: People vote with weird animal instincts.
Now, I bet a lot of the people in this room are college-educated suburban voters, but the average voter in a general election is a 55-year-old white guy without a college degree.
The average person is often voting on instinctual things, and those instincts are a lot of your animalistic desires for things to be okay materially — your cost of health care, and then for you to be safe. And so if you think about those base-level desires and then think about what Democrats spend most of their time talking about, you’re like, “Is that the thing that captures all these people?”
When I watch Democrats as somebody who’s an immigrant into the Democratic ecosystem, there’s a lot of, like, “And you get a policy, and you get a policy, and you get a policy.” And I don’t really understand that because everybody needs cheaper gas.
Everybody needs groceries that they can afford. And so talking about the things that unite us or that everybody needs, to me, is the secret sauce for how Democrats should think about policy.
Three years ago, Democrats thought that being against January 6th was a thing that united everybody. There was a belief that pro-democracy arguments were going to unite people across ideology. Why did that fail in 2024?
I’ve been thinking about this a lot as Trump gets terrible poll after terrible poll, and this is my point.
The coup, all of the horrible things he said about women, all of the lawsuits — I mean, he told everybody an election was stolen. Why is he underwater right now? Because of gas prices, because of a war in Iran, because the negative personal consequences of his policies are hitting people.
I know that it frustrates people. I’m so aware of the frustration where people are like, “Why are people so selfish? Why don’t they think about the bigger picture of democracy?” And one of the things I try not to do is magic words — consultant stuff, because a lot of consultants do that. They’re like, “Say freedom,” and “Say affordability.”
There’s nothing to back it up. But the one magic word I do think that Democrats should start using is “America,” and swap it in for “democracy.” And the reason is, voters practice democracy in America by its individual things.
They practice free speech. They like rule of law. They like checks and balances. So they like the elements of democracy, but they don’t think about them up here as democracy. And also the word democracy now is very polarized, right? Republicans think that Democrats are a threat to democracy because they stole the 2020 election. And Democrats think Republicans are a threat to democracy because they lied about the election being stolen and then tried to overturn the entire government.
I think one side of that equation is more right than the other. But I think that’s why it didn’t work.
I want to look ahead. Our show focuses on building a roadmap for American politics without Trump, and part of that question has been about Republicans.
They have made themselves into a new kind of America First-esque party. But what does that mean without Trump at the center of it? When you’re in your focus groups, is it clear what values or principles Republicans believe in besides what Donald Trump says to them?
Absolutely not. They don’t have anything. This is why I wrote the book. I wrote the book because we have 2026, we have 2028, and we have 2032.
By 2032, there’s going to be a new census, and things are going to get worse for Democrats. Hear me on this. People are not grokking this yet. The map — people are leaving California for Texas, people are leaving New York for Florida, and it’s just going to get harder for Democrats to win if this same trajectory that we’re currently on holds.
But there is a generational opportunity right now, and it’s why I desperately wanted to bring this book and get it out there. The Republican Party at this moment is as hollowed out as ... Donald Trump is going to leave it in shambles. There is no Trump heir who can do what Trump does, who has the longstanding parasocial relationship with voters where they give him this blank check that other people don’t get.
But my concern is that 2026 will go really well and that Democrats will say, “See? It’s fine. Everybody likes us.” They don’t.
This was the big mistake in 2022. The midterms were extrapolated [to signal] Biden’s re-election, and those were not the same thing.
They are not the same thing. And again, the average voter is a 55-year-old white man without a college degree. And you can just hold that in your head and picture that guy and say, “Do we have candidates who can appeal to that guy?”
I was being annoying when I was flying here, tweeting things, and there’s a new poll out for [Pennsylvania Gov.] Josh Shapiro. He is beating his Republican opponent by 21 points in the poll right now. This is the largest swing state in the country, and Democrats hate Josh Shapiro.
Hate feels a little strong. I think the left doesn’t like Josh Shapiro. I don’t think that’s the whole party.
That’s a good point.
I’ll just say, as a slight Josh Shapiro stan, perhaps I feel more than most people’s antipathy to the idea of Josh Shapiro running. I get a lot of people just being like, “Absolutely not. He’s a corporate centrist. We would never consider him. And also he’s Jewish slash Zionist.”
And a lot of this is Twitter discourse, but it feels like he doesn’t get the same buzz or interest, which seems insane to me when you’ve got somebody that popular in such a big, important state that Trump was able to win twice.
The electoral argument for the Josh Shapiros of the world is clear.
Twenty-one points in Pennsylvania at any rate is impressive, but let’s use him as an example, because I do think it speaks to where some Democrats have gone in the last couple years. The polling will tell you that the majority of Democrats want to see their party reshift its relationship with Israel and want to see things like an arms embargo.
Polling would tell you that the majority of Democrats believe that they shouldn’t be taking corporate money, or that things like AIPAC money are bad. How does a Josh Shapiro — let’s use him as an avatar. … Is that compatible with where the Democratic base is right now, even if it’s clearly compatible with Pennsylvania?
The way that you just said it doesn’t sound compatible. But I don’t think that it’s incompatible.
This is a book about what the voters think, and the voters want a new relationship with Israel, hands down. Without question. They want America to reevaluate our relationship with Israel. And the next Democratic presidential candidate is going to have to do that.
And I have a theory about this. I do think that the 2028 nominee is very likely to be a Jewish person who is highly critical of Israel, because I think that it helps to heal the deep divide right now on this issue within the Democratic Party.
Now, do I think it’s more likely that that is the very handsome Jon Ossoff? I kind of do. But I just ... a big part of this book is, “Don’t you want to win? Don’t you guys want to win?” Like, do you want to win more than you want to be right about everything?

The story so far: On September 17, 2026, the Union government agreed to the Supreme Court’s suggestion of reducing the qualifying percentile for the 2025 National Eligibility-cum-Entrance Test-Super Speciality (NEET-SS) from 50% to 30%. Following this, the Medical Counselling Committee (MCC) has commenced a stray round from September 25 to fill the remaining 1,857 vacant seats. The Centre also agreed to give the 40 vacant in-service seats in Tamil Nadu back to the State.
What is the NEET-SS examination?
The NEET-SS is the only entrance examination for admission to DM (Doctorate of Medicine), MCh (Master of Chirurgiae), and DrNB (Doctorate of National Board) super-speciality courses in India. It is conducted by the National Board of Examinations in Medical Sciences (NBEMS), an autonomous body under the Union Health Ministry. There are over 7,000 seats in the country, with around 15,000 applicants every year.
NEET-SS is not a single unified examination. The courses offered under it are divided into 15 groups: general medicine, general surgery, orthopaedics, paediatrics, obstetrics and gynaecology, anesthesiology, radiology, respiratory medicine, microbiology, pathology, psychiatry, pharmacology, ENT, critical care, and medical oncology. Each group covers multiple specialty subjects. For example, general medicine covers cardiology, nephrology, neurology, and seven other subjects. Each group has a different question paper; that is, there are 15 question papers in total, and the cut-off for each paper varies.
Why were seats going vacant?
Super-specialisation provides advanced clinical training and teaching for doctors. In India, it is in high demand in private corporate hospitals. “The market factor plays a big role. Doctors are taking super-speciality seats which give more chances for better practice and more money. If the seats they prefer are not available for their ranks this year, they will try the next time. This is a major reason why seats are going unfilled,” Dr. Ravindranath, general secretary of Doctors’ Association for Social Equality, said.
Cardiology, neurosurgery, medical oncology, and gastroenterology are among those subjects which are highly competitive with lower vacancies. Seats mostly go vacant in those courses which do not have as much demand. For example, cardiovascular and thoracic surgery has witnessed a drop in demand as medical treatment now relies on drugs and radioactive interventions over surgery. Super-specialisation in paediatric surgery has a lower demand due to competition from doctors in other specialisations.
Candidates prefer top-ranking institutes for pursuing their super-specialisation, and hefty fees in private colleges lead to vacancies.
A long-pending problem in courts
In 2023, after 1,003 seats remained vacant, a Supreme Court Bench led by Justices B.R. Gavai and Vikram Nath asked the Centre to find a solution. The Bench called these vacant seats a “wastage of resources”. Following this, the Medical Counselling Committee (MCC) announced that the 2023 candidates with zero percentile were also eligible to secure a seat if they opt for it; however, many seats still remained vacant. In 2024, around 600 NEET-SS seats were vacant after two rounds of counselling, which led to mop-up rounds following court intervention.
In 2026, while hearing the case filed by Tamil Nadu Medical Officers Association, the court said the large number of vacancies in the 2025 NEET-SS admissions presented the case for reduction of the qualifying percentile “compelling.” The Bench of Justices B.V. Nagarathna and Joymalya Bagchi said access to super-speciality for in-service government doctors must become easier as they are appearing for the exam while providing service to the public at the same time.
What was the demand of doctors from Tamil Nadu?
Under G.O. Ms. No. 462, Tamil Nadu has reserved 50% of NEET-SS seats for in-service doctors in State medical colleges. This quota was upheld by the Supreme Court in 2022.
In the 2025 cycle, the State had reserved 219 seats for in-service doctors, of which only 68 were filled. Over 111 candidates remained on the waiting list. In the petition, the Tamil Nadu Medical Officers Association challenged the “premature diversion” of 152 seats reserved for in-service doctors working in State hospitals into the All India Quota. Senior advocate P. Wilson, for the petitioner, said that many candidates, particularly from rural parts of the State, were awaiting a reduction in the qualifying percentile. This is relevant as there is no caste- or religion-based reservation in this exam. He also sought protection of the in-service quota. This led to the Centre giving 40 vacant seats back to the State.
Is this adequate to address the problem?
“Reducing the cut-off might address this problem to an extent, but it cannot prevent seats from going vacant,” Dr. Ravindranath said. He added that the low number of government seats in States like U.P., Bihar, and the Northeast is worsening the issue. Along with this, employment and promotion opportunities have not increased for super-specialists. This is because in government hospitals, new departments for such specialisations have not been established. The low stipends and heavy workload in the course are also factors that discourage candidates from pursuing super-specialisation.

Bigg Boss 20 Week 4 has had its share of fights, nominations, task drama and shifting equations, but the overall energy inside the house has remained relatively subdued. With Friday set for the Weekend Ka Vaar shoot, there are several issues from the week that deserve to be put under the spotlight. From Love Gill’s increasingly complicated group dynamics to Gullu’s captaincy and Qazi Touqeer’s growing disconnect with his own allies, here are four things Salman Khan should address.
Bigg Boss 20 Weekend Ka Vaar: Love Gill’s group dynamics, Gullu’s captaincy and Qazi Touqeer’s blind spot, 4 things Salman Khan needs to discuss
1. Love Gill needs to STOP playing peacemaker at her own expense
Love Gill’s biggest problem right now may not be her game, but her tendency to constantly keep the peace within her group.
Across the past few weeks, Love has repeatedly found herself apologising to her friends and group members after confrontations. One of the earliest examples came after Yung DSA lost his life, with the group suspecting that Gullu had played a role in the decision. At the same time, Gullu’s equation with Love, including their flirting, appeared to create discomfort among some members of the group.
Aamrapali Dubey subsequently confronted Love over the situation. While Love initially stood her ground, she eventually apologised to Aamrapali.
View this post on Instagram
A similar pattern emerged when Aasif Khan expressed his frustration over Love seemingly prioritising Scout OP and Yung DSA and relying more heavily on their opinions.
The latest incident involving Yung was even more telling. After Love danced on Gullu’s bed, Yung made a comment that she found inappropriate. Love confronted him, but the situation escalated, with Aamrapali also getting involved. Love eventually apologised to Yung.
The most interesting part is that Love herself has admitted to Aasif that she does not feel she can completely be herself within the group.
That is precisely where Salman could ask her to take a step back and assess her game. Being diplomatic is one thing, but constantly trying to keep everyone happy can prevent a contestant from establishing an individual identity. Love has shown that she can stand her ground. The question is whether she will continue doing so when it comes at the cost of keeping her group happy.
2. Gullu needs to move beyond the safety net of captaincy
Kushal Tanwar, aka Gullu, entered the Bigg Boss house with expectations attached to him. As a winner of MTV Roadies XX: Double Cross, he already had a reality-show history built around tasks, strategy and confrontations.
Yet, three weeks into Bigg Boss 20, his contribution to the central drama has often felt quieter than expected.
His biggest advantage has been his position as captain. Gullu has managed to keep himself safe for two consecutive weeks, but that also means his game has not been tested in the same way as several other contestants.
Salman had already questioned Gullu during the previous Weekend Ka Vaar after he failed to take a strong stand while serving as sanchalak during the diss battle. Bigg Boss also took a dig at him over his relatively passive approach.
This week, Gullu became captaincy contender again, but even his leadership came under scrutiny. During the housemates' rose-based assessment of his captaincy, several contestants criticised him for being careless, people-pleasing and insufficiently strict. The messy-house footage shown by Bigg Boss further added to the criticism.
View this post on Instagram
Salman does not necessarily need to question Gullu simply because he has not been involved in every fight. Instead, the bigger question is whether he is using his position to actively shape the game.
If Gullu wants to establish himself beyond the captain's badge, this could be the week to ask him to take more decisions, drive tasks and take clear positions instead of relying on safety.
3. The entire house needs a wake-up call
If there is one larger issue Salman should address, it is the overall energy of the house.
Week 4 has had individual incidents, but very few moments have managed to sustain momentum. The ration and captaincy task created some conflict, the Love-Yung argument added another layer to the group dynamics and Qazi's remarks sparked a confrontation with Kanika. Beyond these moments, however, the house has often felt quieter than it should at this stage of the season.
That is where a larger Weekend Ka Vaar intervention could help.
Kanika Mann, in particular, is an interesting case. She has had strong opinions on several issues and has not shied away from calling out behaviour she disagrees with. Her objection to Qazi's use of the word “lollipop” during their interaction was one example. However, she has also frequently chosen to discuss her frustrations with the cameras rather than directly with the person involved.
View this post on Instagram
The latest confrontation with Qazi showed that Kanika is capable of taking the issue directly to the person concerned. That side of her game could potentially be more impactful than repeatedly discussing the same concerns privately.
The same applies to the rest of the house. At this point, the contestants need to realise that simply reacting to one another is not enough. They need to actively play the game.
4. Qazi Touqeer needs to realise what is happening within his own group
Qazi Touqeer has been involved in several conversations and confrontations this week, but there is another aspect of his game that could make for an interesting Weekend Ka Vaar discussion.
While Qazi appears to be comfortable with his group, some of the people around him have also been critical of him behind his back.
His recent clash with Kanika over the “lollipop” remark is already one issue Salman could revisit. Kanika had objected to the word earlier, and the matter eventually became a direct confrontation. But beyond that incident, Qazi could benefit from being made aware of how some of his own group members perceive him when he is not around.
The purpose would not simply be to create another fight. Instead, it could force Qazi to reassess his equations and understand whether the people he considers allies view the relationship in the same way.
That could also test how Qazi handles uncomfortable information when it comes directly from Salman rather than through another contestant.
This Weekend Ka Vaar needs to shake things up
Week 4 has not been completely devoid of drama. There have been nominations, ration cuts, captaincy politics, personal clashes and questions around individual gameplay. However, the bigger issue is that very few contestants have managed to consistently drive the narrative.
That makes this Weekend Ka Vaar particularly important. Love needs to examine whether keeping her group happy is coming at the cost of her individual game. Gullu needs to prove that his captaincy is more than a route to safety. Kanika needs to take her opinions directly to the people involved, while Qazi may need to look more closely at the equations within his own group.
If Salman addresses these issues, the focus can move beyond simply revisiting isolated fights and towards the larger question of how each contestant intends to play Bigg Boss 20 from here.

Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Tuesday lauded the rhino conservation efforts in the country and said the Project Rhino has been initiated for financial and technical support to the range states for protection, habitat management, and understanding population dynamics of the endangered species.
On the occasion of World Rhino Day, Modi said the country celebrates the magnificent greater one-horned rhinoceros and lauds all those at the forefront of its protection.
“Assam now holds nearly 80 per cent of the world’s rhino population and Kaziranga’s efforts to end rhino poaching have been extensively appreciated,” he said in a post on ‘X’.
The prime minister said on one hand, rhinos have either returned or are well protected in parts of Bihar and West Bengal, on the other hand, success of reintroduction of rhinos in Dudhwa (Uttar Pradesh) is creating history.
“This shows the sustained commitment of our people towards animal protection and active wildlife management in the range states,” he said.
Taking species conservation in the country forward, Modi said he was happy to share that Project Rhino has been initiated for financial and technical support to the range states for protection, habitat management, genetic improvement and understanding population dynamics.
World Rhino Day is a day of awareness for all five rhino species and the work being done to save them. Since 2011, World Rhino Day has been celebrated internationally on September 22 by rhino experts and advocates around the world.
The day is especially important to raise awareness of the plight of rhinos because they are regularly poached for their horns which are sold illegally and used in traditional medicine — despite no scientific proof that these remedies work.

Trump touts having the best numbers of any president, despite his dismal approval rating
Facing electoral humiliation in Texas, Trump claims press isn’t doing enough to sell his successes

Donald Trump claimed once again that he had the “best numbers” of any president, even as his approval poll ratings continue to slide and Americans are feeling serious economic pains stemming from the war in Iran.
The president was in Denton, Texas, on Thursday at a manufacturing plant on Thursday as part of a two-state swing that will also include a visit to Choctaw tribal lands in Oklahoma. He spoke to a crowd of a few hundred people as he tried — not for the first time this week — to convince voters that it was merely an image problem from which the GOP and his presidency are suffering.
"We have the greatest numbers of any president in the history of our country, and I can't get the word out,” the president complained. “The only thing we’re doing bad at is public relations.”
It’s far from the first time he has said this. Going back months, Trump has insisted that the country’s economic numbers are better than at any point in history, even as interest rates remain high and wages remain just barely ahead of inflation, and not enough for many Americans to deal with surging prices in several key areas, including food prices and gasoline.
The president said at his event on Thursday that Americans worried about affording those commodities were wrong.
“They say, ‘yes, but affordability?’ And everyone thinks that the prices are high because of me, but they're not. We're the ones bringing down the prices. I just hope you can know. The one good thing about [the president’s critics] is, they have a great line of bull***t.”
“You know, they came up with the word affordability. So from day one, they said, ‘what about your prices?!’ And then they came up-- you know, they always come up with these words.”
Though the crowd was cheering for his early remarks, it had largely grown silent by the time Trump made his remarks about affordability, in part due to the length of the president’s speech, which began 40 minutes late and lasted a full hour. His remarks were punctuated with calls for voters in the state to support Ken Paxton, a sign that the president sees a real possibility that Paxton will lose his upcoming Senate election against James Talarico, his Democratic opponent. Talarico led Paxton by 51 percentage points to 49 in a Fox News poll released this week, a devastating sign for the Republican candidate in Texas and a worrying sign for the GOP in other areas as well.
Trump faces a 41 percent approval rating in the state of Texas, where Paxton is running to preserve a Senate seat for the GOP that has now cost the party more than $100m in total in advertising and other expenses, thanks in part to the bloody primary fight between Paxton and the Republican incumbent, John Cornyn. The senator has not endorsed his would-be replacement and has already said he won’t campaign or fundraise for him.
Paxton’s own spotty record also makes the race harder to win for Republicans, and those Republicans aligned with Cornyn spent the duration of the primary highlighting those issues for voters. The attorney general of Texas, Paxton, was nearly impeached by the state legislature for abusing his office amid reports of affairs and a messy divorce battle with his wife, Angela Paxton, who is a Republican state senator.
His controversies aren’t the only problem weighing down his candidacy, though, as Trump’s war with Iran has become staggeringly unpopular and by far the least popular of Trump’s stances among his own voters. Three in four Americans disapprove of Trump’s handling of relations with Iran in a recent CNN/SRSS poll, and other surveys have shown that Americans broadly doubt that the president has a solid strategy for extracting the U.S. from the conflict.
Trump has pledged to spend much of October on the road campaigning for Republican candidates. Democrats are hoping to win Cornyn’s seat as well as three others to obtain a Senate majority, and polling suggests that the party is competitive in as many as a half dozen or more seats currently held by Republicans.

New Mexico wants Meta to pay up to $40 billion in penalties after data privacy trial
Oct 1 : The state of New Mexico asked a judge on Thursday to order Meta Platforms to pay between $35 billion and $40 billion in penalties after a jury found the company had misled consumers about the privacy of their data on Facebook in a case that came out of the Cambridge Analytica scandal.
Attorneys for New Mexico made the request at a hearing in a lawsuit brought following revelations that the British political consulting firm, which worked on Donald Trump's 2016 presidential campaign, harvested personal data from as many as 87 million Facebook users through a third-party app without their consent.
The jury returned its verdict on September 25. Judge Francis Mathew, who oversaw the trial in Santa Fe, will decide how much Meta must pay in financial penalties.
Attorneys for Meta and New Mexico clashed at the hearing over how much was appropriate to order, with Meta arguing that the penalties the state was seeking don't match the conduct the state focused its case on at trial.
"Well, when the parties go to trial, they roll the dice," said Mathew. "They have to accept the consequences of their decision to go to trial, do they not?"
TRIAL FOCUSED ON MISSTATEMENTS
The lawsuit, filed in 2021, accused Meta of lying to Facebook users in the state about who had access to their data, how the company handles hate speech and misinformation posted on the platform and other internal policies. The company knew that third parties had broad access to users' personal data, and it tolerated hate speech or other harmful content when it benefited the company's bottom line, the state said.
Jurors examined 29 statements made by the company and its leadership on those issues and found 26 of them misleading. They said the company had committed more than 43 million violations of New Mexico’s consumer protection laws, based on the number of Facebook users or New Mexico residents who were the audience for each misleading statement.
Attorneys for Meta had argued at trial that the statements were cherry-picked snippets, and the company had repeatedly acknowledged its handling of misinformation or privacy issues was not perfect.
State law allows the judge to decide how much to fine Meta per violation, up to $5,000.
At the hearing on Thursday, Randi McGinn, a lawyer for New Mexico, said applying the full $5,000 penalty to the number of violations would create too large of a penalty under the US Constitution’s protections on due process.
But the judge should order a significant payment that will impact the company, McGinn said.
"This court should speak to Meta in the only language it understands, which is money, and the value of its stock price," McGinn said. She said $35 billion to $40 billion, which represents about 20 per cent of the possible penalties that could be awarded under state law from the verdict, would impact the stock price while complying with Meta's right to due process under the Constitution.
At the hearing on Thursday, Matt Nicholson, a lawyer for Meta, called the state's request an "astronomical penalty that would obviously violate a host of constitutional provisions."
In court filings, Meta urged Mathew to cap the penalties at $3.45 billion. The jury may have said it found Meta’s statements misleading, but the evidence shows that Meta does not sell user data and New Mexico did not prove that any consumer had actually been misled, the company said in court filings.
The judge said he expected to issue a ruling later this month.
The case is State of New Mexico, et. al., v. Meta Platforms, Inc., case number D-101-CV-2021-00132 in the First Judicial District Court of New Mexico.
