In September, a rumor spread online about an Australian man riding high after entering a cannabis plant in the tomato category of a local garden competition — and winning the first place prize.
For example, a Facebook page called The Local Situation posted the claim alongside an image purportedly showing the 83-year-old budding "tomato" gardener with his alleged gold medal cannabis plant (screenshotted). The caption says the man is from Ulladulla, a coastal town in southeast New South Wales.
"Panellist Marjorie Budd said the panel was so taken by its lush foliage and rich aroma that nobody asked where the tomatoes were," the post adds.
The rumor spread elsewhere on Facebook (screenshotted).
Snopes readers searched our website to determine whether the story was rooted in truth or just blowing smoke.
In short, the claim is labeled as satire. The Local Situation Facebook page was the first to post the rumor. The account's content is dedicated to fake stories based in Australia.
"Real local issues with a satirical edge," the page's account description reads (archived).
The person behind The Local Situation said in an email to Snopes that the story was satire and had no connection to any real stories.
"I regularly do Cannabis related satirical posts to raise awareness for medical cannabis driving rights and cannabis legalisation in Australia," said the account owner.
Growing and consuming cannabis for recreational purposes is illegal in New South Wales and in most of Australia.
The image in The Local Situation's post was also generated using artificial intelligence, according to OpenAI's detector tool, which checks for an invisible AI watermark known as SynthID. (OpenAI is the company behind ChatGPT; its detection tool can only tell if the image was created using the company's own AI software.) The Local Situation also confirmed that the image was created using AI.
(OpenAI)
Other indicators the image is AI-generated include distorted faces in the background and unreadable text on name tags and labels.
Pangram, which is considered a leading AI text detection tool, determined that 100% of the text in the original post was also AI-generated. (Despite Pangram's comparative reliability, it is worth noting these tools are still fallible.)
If this story were true, reputable local news media outlets would likely have reported on it. Searches using Google, DuckDuckGo and 
These searches did, however, find several Australian news stories about men who were busted or arrested on charges of growing cannabis, who either claimed they were growing tomatoes or were actually reportedly growing tomatoes near the cannabis plants.
Snopes has debunked similar fictional rumors, such as a claim that Canada faced a major donut shortage shortly after the country legalized recreational marijuana use.
Since the effectiveness of satire is subjective, we use "originated as satire" or "labeled satire" ratings based on creators' description of their work. It's your call on whether you agree.

In the 80th minute of India’s international friendly against Panama last week, Ashique Kuruniyan played a bouncing cross into the far post from the left side of Panama’s box. It evaded Panama’s backline and came to Edmund Lalrindika, who missed the entire goal, which was at his mercy.
“You cannot score every goal. Sometimes you score, sometimes you miss. When you score, you feel like you are the best. But once you miss, everyone blames you. It’s really hard,” Edmund had told Sportstar in an interview ahead of the game.
“(But) I like challenges,” he followed up immediately.
For Edmund, the miss will feel like a tiny hiccup compared to the adversities he has overcome. Years before he was East Bengal’s target man, Edmund suffered a spine injury that kept him off the field for a year and a half and even threatened to end his career.
“That (injury) was one of my biggest challenges,” Edmund recalled. “It was during my time with Bengaluru FC, and after that I didn’t have any club; I didn’t have any offer. So it was really a tough time for me.”
However, his grit to get back on the pitch impressed newly formed Inter Kashi, which took a gamble on him in 2023. Two years down the line, he bagged four goals and five assists in 19 appearances as the club became champion of the Indian Football League (formerly I-League).
The title meant promotion into the Indian Super League, which he then won with East Bengal, whilst being the joint-highest Indian scorer (4).
But perhaps the 27-year-old’s crowning moment came during the Durand Cup 2026 final against archrival Mohun Bagan SG in August, when he bagged a scintillating first-half hat-trick as the Red and Gold Brigade went on to lift the trophy at the Salt Lake Stadium in Kolkata.
ALSO READ | One of the best results of my tenure with India: Khalid Jamil after Panama draw
And now, as record World Champion Brazil awaits at the same venue on Saturday, Edmund will be looking to pick up right where he left off. “It’s a dream, you know, playing against a top country. I will be very happy if I get to play, if the coach gives me a chance,” he said.
Edmund, however, will be slightly sad to not be playing against his idol Neymar Jr., who retired from international football earlier this year. The admiration may stem from the fact that Edmund himself started as a winger in professional football, despite playing as a striker in his younger days.
“I played my whole youth career as a striker. But in the ISL, every coach (usually) prefers foreigners in that role. So when I signed a professional contract, I decided to start playing more as a winger,” he noted.
He credits his Inter Kashi and current East Bengal head coach Antonio Habas for returning him to the striker role. “He always wanted me to play as number nine, and I refused initially. But after I scored a hat-trick in the Durand Cup final, he told me that he always wants me to play as number nine,” Edmund said with a slight chuckle.
However, in the national team, being the centre forward comes with a lot of added pressure, especially as the search for a true successor to Sunil Chhetri continues. But Edmund was quick to ward off any comparisons, saying that “no one can replace” the former India captain.
“I have my own path, and I still have a long way to go. I am just trying to improve every day,” he asserted.
And what better stage to announce himself to the world than against giants of the sport like Brazil and Uruguay, especially in front of the Kolkata support.
Edmund pointed out how he is eager to see a stadium usually filled with fans divided by club rivalries cheer together for a change.
“I think it will be really special because it will be in Kolkata. I know the atmosphere of a Kolkata derby. I think it is far the best atmosphere in India,” he said, adding, “And now East Bengal and Mohun Bagan fans will be together. I know the atmosphere will be on a different level. So I’m really excited, and I hope we can give some joy to our fans.”

Jammu, Sep 23: The Special Operations Group (SOG) Jammu has arrested three alleged members of the Khauf gang from Delhi, including its key member wanted in 13 FIRs.
Officials said that Karanjit Singh alias “Gugga,” son of Arjun Singh, resident of Dablehar, Tehsil R.S. Pura, was apprehended from Delhi. He had 13 FIRs pending against him and is an accused in the Gataroo murder case and several other cases involving attempt to murder, assault, rioting, criminal intimidation and possession of illegal weapons.
Police said Karanjit Singh had earlier escaped from the R.S. Pura Observation Home along with two Pakistani inmates. During the escape, police personnel on duty were allegedly assaulted and injured in firing inside Observation Home. Accordingly, FIR No. 39/2026 was registered at R.S. Pura.
During the same operation, two other alleged associates of the gang were also arrested from Delhi. They have been identified as Naresh Kumar alias “Major,” son of Kamal Kumar, resident of Arnia, who is stated to be a close associate of absconder Sunil Kumar alias “Gokul” and is involved in cases relating to violent assault, rioting and illegal possession of weapons; and Rahul Kumar alias “Sundi,” son of Bishan Dass, resident of Makhanpur, Bishnah, involved in a case relating to alleged smuggling of narcotics into jail premises and booked under NDPS Act and Prisons Act.
Police said arrests are part of ongoing efforts of Jammu Police and SOG to trace absconders and investigate activities of organised criminal networks. Further investigation is underway and additional arrests may follow.(GNS)

Tonight’s episode of Asit Kumarr Modi’s Taarak Mehta Ka Ooltah Chashmah will see Taarak Mehta, Jethalal and Ratan together in the Gokuldham compound. During their conversation, Taarak introduces Ratan to a popular food shop located near Jethalal’s Gada Electronics. He describes the shop’s samosas, kachoris and bhel, which leaves Ratan keen to try the food.
Taarak Mehta Ka Ooltah Chashmah: Taarak’s food plan takes an unexpected turn as Anjali bhabhi appears
As the conversation continues, Jethalal suddenly screams, “Anjali Bhabhi!” Taarak and Ratan are taken by surprise, only to discover that Jethalal was joking. Taarak then announces that they will visit the food shop the following day and enjoy the snacks together.

Amid increasing competition in AI, Google has now unveiled its new, most powerful model Gemini 4 Argon. The model is targeting long-running workloads across software engineering, enterprise knowledge work and cybersecurity. Argon is initially being rolled out to a select group of “trusted cyber defenders” through Google's Fairwind programme, with wider access planned for developers, enterprises and consumers. Google said paid API customers and Google AI Ultra subscribers will get access to Gemini 4 Argon first, although it is yet to announce a broader public release date. “It shows frontier performance in complex workflows, cyber defense and software engineering. Teams are using it extensively at Google, from coding to quantum computing, great feedback,” Google CEO Sundar Pichai said. Google said Gemini 4 Argon will launch at an introductory price of $2 per a million input tokens and $10 per a million output tokens. Cached input tokens will be priced at a 95% discount to the standard input-token rate. One of the biggest changes with Gemini 4 Argon is its 1 Mn-token output limit, up from the previous 64K-token limit. Google said the expanded capacity allows the model to sustain longer reasoning trajectories and work through complex, multi-step tasks in a single run. “Google engineers have been using Argon for their daily tasks, from everyday debugging to large-scale codebase migrations and algorithm designs. It sets a new state of the art on DeepSWE v1.1 (77.9%), which measures a model’s performance in real-world long-horizon software engineering tasks,” the tech giant said. Beyond coding, Google said Argon is designed for knowledge-intensive work across areas such as finance, legal research and drafting. As per Google Deepmind's tests, Argon performs strongly across a wide range of real-world tasks. In its testing, Argon scored highly in areas such as professional knowledge work, coding, scientific problem-solving and handling very large amounts of information. Its particularly strong long-context results suggest it can work with large volumes of information while still finding and using relevant details. The model also has multimodal capabilities for professional use cases. Google said Argon can analyse charts, understand long videos and work across multiple documents to support tasks that require visual and contextual understanding. Google Puts Cybersecurity At The Centre Of Argon Cybersecurity is a major focus of Gemini 4 Argon. The model is said to autonomously identify, validate and patch software vulnerabilities. The model is available without its usual cyber guardrails to the initial users and Google's internal teams. Cybersecurity company Wiz is already using Argon through its “Scan for Good” initiative, as per Google. In an early demonstration, Google said Argon identified a critical vulnerability exposing sensitive personal information in healthcare software used by hospitals globally. Google is taking a phased approach to the rollout because of the model's cybersecurity capabilities. The company said it is strengthening safeguards against misuse, including cyberattacks and CBRN-related threats, while also working on protections against indirect prompt injection attacks. The AI Race The developments come as Google, Anthropic and OpenAI are engaged in an intense competition to build and deploy models that offer superior performance while are more cost effective. Earlier in September, OpenAI launched its "most capable model yet", GPT-6 Astra, a more autonomous AI model. The model supports reasoning efforts ranging from low to maximum and comes with a 1.05 Mn-token context window and a maximum output of 1.28 Lakh tokens. Anthropic also recently launched Claude Opus 5.5, claiming that the model delivers performance comparable to its more powerful Claude Fable 5.1 on most tasks while costing 40% less to run than Claude Opus 5 on typical workloads. Claude Opus 5.5 is priced at $4 per Mn input tokens and $20 per Mn output tokens, with Anthropic also cutting cache-read costs by 60%. The company is positioning the model for agentic coding, computer use and knowledge work. On a different note, Google has also been expanding its AI push in India beyond model development. Earlier in September, the company selected four Indian startups (Terrastack, Varaha Climate, Farmers for Forests and Climitra Carbon) for the inaugural Google DeepMind Accelerator: AI for the Planet (APAC). The startups are part of a 16-member APAC cohort and will receive access to Google's AI stack, technical support and mentorship to develop AI-led solutions for environmental challenges.

K-pop star convicted of violating military service law
- Published
A South Korean court has handed a suspended one-year prison sentence to K-pop singer Song Min-ho after he was convicted of violating the country's military service law.
The 33-year-old member of the boy band Winner was found to have been absent multiple times at a community centre in Seoul, where he had worked as a social worker from 2023 to 2024.
All able-bodied men in South Korea have to serve at least 18 months in the military. But some are alternatively assigned as social service personnel for health reasons.
The prison sentence handed on Thursday is suspended for two years. That means he can avoid incarceration if he does not commit any crime during that two-year probationary period.
The court heard that Song, who is also known by his stage name Mino, had recorded 102 unauthorised absences during his 21-month stint as a social service agent.
Military service is a duty to be performed "faithfully", and social service agents are "no exception", the court said.
But the court also noted that Song had admitted to the charges and shown remorse.
Authorities launched an investigation into Song shortly after he was discharged in 2024, when local media reported that he was frequently absent from his social service duties and took excessive sick leave.
Song's supervisor at the social service centre was also given a suspended jail sentence for helping him dodge his duties, including falsifying records to make it look like Song had reported to work.
The conscription of South Korea's entertainers has long been a topic of national public debate.
Gangnam Style singer Psy famously had to enlist twice, once in 2003 and another time in 2007, after a Seoul court ruled that he had neglected his duties by continuing his showbiz activities during his first national service stint.
Steve Yoo, one of the country's biggest pop stars in the 1990s and early 2000s, was embroiled in a national scandal after he was found to have evaded military service in 2002. South Korean authorities banned him from the country after he renounced his citizenship and became a US national shortly before he was due to serve in the military.
Going on hiatus to serve in the military is often a threat for budding careers in South Korea's fast-moving entertainment industry. But the evasion of military service also comes with intense public scrutiny and legal repercussions.
Ahead of the ruling on Thursday, Song told reporters that he regretted his actions and was "sorry toward the people who gave me so much love", Seoul Economic Daily reported.
But he did not answer a question about whether he would re-enlist to serve the mandatory duty.

International Oscar Submissions: Cuba, Denmark, Vietnam, Italy, France and More Join the List
The campaigns for the Oscar for international feature film are gaining momentum, with final submissions due by Oct. 1. The Oscars shortlists will be revealed on Dec. 15, with 15 international films selected to be voted on by Academy members in all branches who commit to watch all 15 films. Oscar nominations will be revealed on Jan. 21.
This year’s entries include titles like Romania’s “Fjord,” which won the Palme d’Or at Cannes; Germany’s “Everytime,” which won Cannes’ Un Certain Regard prize; France’s “Minotaur,” which won the Cannes Grand Prix; Spain’s “La Bola Negra,” Poland’s “Fatherland,” which won the best director award at Cannes, and Denmark’s “Woman Unknown,” which won the Golden Lion at Venice, and also earned its star Mathilde Arcel the Coppa Volpi for best actress.
Meanwhile, a new Academy rule allows any film that wins the top prize at one of the six biggest festivals — Cannes, Berlin, Venice, Sundance, Busan and Toronto — to be entered in the international feature race even without a national committee’s backing.
	
- 
			Hanging by a Wire (Pakistan)Mohammed Ali Naqvi’s documentary thriller “Hanging by a Wire” has been selected as Pakistan‘s submission for the International feature film Oscar at the 99th Academy Awards, marking the first time a documentary has represented the country in the category. “Hanging by a Wire” is directed by Naqvi and written and produced by Naqvi and Bilal Sami. The film revisits the August 2023 cable car emergency in Battagram, in northern Pakistan, in which eight passengers, including six schoolboys on their way to school, were left suspended roughly 900 feet above a ravine after a cable snapped. The resulting rescue effort was followed live across Pakistan and internationally. 
 The film draws on footage from witnesses, testimony from survivors and staged reenactments involving people who took part in the rescue to build its account.“Hanging by a Wire” debuted at the 2026 Sundance Film Festival, in the World Cinema Documentary Competition lineup, before going on to play the Tribeca Festival. The film is produced by EverWonder Studio, Universal Pictures Content Group, Mindhouse Productions and 64th Street Media. Dogwoof holds theatrical distribution rights in the U.K., with Abramorama handling U.S. theatrical release. The film is set for a streaming release on Paramount+.
- 
			One Woman, One Bra (Kenya)Kenya is submitting Vincho Nchogu’s “One Woman, One Bra” as its entry to the Oscars international feature race. The film follows Star, a Sayit villager at risk of losing her home. While her fellow villagers are about to receive title deeds — marking the first time in centuries they will claim legal ownership of their land — she does not know her parentage and is unmarried. A photograph of her younger self then sparks a journey to find her estranged mother as she considers several options to claim her land. “’One Woman, One Bra’ is a film rooted in an authentic Kenyan story and cultural experience,” said Eddah Kiruhi, chairperson of the Kenya Oscars Selection Committee. “Its originality, performances, visual and sonic treatment, and purposeful storytelling were among the elements that distinguished it during the selection process.”
- 
			Variations on a Theme (South Africa)South Africa has selected “Variations on a Theme,” an Afrikaans-language drama written and directed by Jason Jacobs and Devon Delmar, as its entry to the Oscars international feature race. Starring Hettie Farmer, the film follows an “elderly goat herder in the mountains of Namaqualand, South Africa, who falls victim to a scam promising long-overdue reparations for her father’s service during the Second World War,” according to its synopsis. “Waiting for money that will never come, she faces her family’s decision to move her to the city and strip away the last of her independence.” “Variations on a Theme” world premiered at the International Film Festival Rotterdam, where it won the Tiger Award. It went on to be awarded best African film at the Joburg Film Festival and best film at Zagreb Subversive. It was produced by the filmmakers in association with Kraal Stories, Meria Productions and Interakt (Netherlands). “Being selected to represent South Africa as the country’s Oscar submission is an incredible honor,” producer Annemarie du Plessis said. “The fact that we get to share the beautiful community of Kharkams, who are truly the heartbeat of this film, with the world makes it even more special. We are so grateful to everyone who believed in this film and helped us get here. We hope that this moment can serve as an inspiration to other filmmakers and storytellers to keep going, to be bold and to trust in the stories they want to tell.”

Aref Jaber is on a neighbor's roof, trying to get home.
At 51, he is clambering over a wall into the next backyard, up onto the next roof, along the line of stone houses that stand between him and his own front door. He has no choice. Alleys and side streets in his neighborhood have been sealed with cement blocks and barbed wire, and a single point of access, called Checkpoint 160, is the only way in or out for the 140 families who live there.
But Checkpoint 160 is closed again; Jaber is not sure why. The whim of a soldier, a crash in the scanning system, breaking news in the region—it could be anything.
For the last three years, he says, this has happened at least two days a week. So the community has devised a system of alternative routes. Jaber calls his neighbors to ask if he can come through. They check their windows for soldiers, and then Jaber scales ladders and traverses roofs. “When I finally get home,” he says, “it feels like I’ve achieved something monumental.”
The enclosure of Jaber’s neighborhood is a dense microcosm of what life is becoming across the occupied West Bank—for Palestinians, that is. At the same time that deadly Israeli settler violence robs communities in the West Bank of their land, and amid the genocide in Gaza, Israel has expanded its infrastructures of military control and domination.
Since 2023, Israel’s fragmentation of Palestine, underway for generations, has accelerated. The West Bank has, for the nearly 3.5 million Palestinians who live there, ceased to exist as a contiguous territory. According to the most recent UN data from December 2025, at least 925 fixed and temporary checkpoints, metal gates, roadblocks, and earth mounds divide the West Bank. (A Palestinian governmental commission reported this month that the number is now 942.) This fracturing has torn families apart, stifled the economy, and obstructed access to essential services such as hospitals and schools.
Aref Jaber climbs onto the roof of a neighbor's home to get to the street in the Jaber neighborhood in Hebron.PHOTOGRAPH: SAMAR HAZBOUN
Israel has never publicly listed the checkpoints it operates, their staffing hours, or their closure times. On the ground, Google Maps is practically useless for Palestinians; it is blind to the checkpoints and tries to route drivers onto roads reserved for Israeli-plated cars. Instead, citizens have developed their own ad hoc networks to inform each other of closures.
As far as we know, no organization has used that network—combined with new datasets and on-the-ground reporting—to measure what this does to daily life.
Over 18 months, WIRED, Lighthouse Reports, Arab Reporters for Investigative Journalism (ARIJ) and the Palestine Reporting Lab investigated the system that has carved the West Bank into cantons and measured what it cost people to move through it.
We analyzed tens of thousands of Telegram messages Palestinians sent to navigate daily checkpoint delays and closures
Working with the Institute for Social and Economic Progress (ISEP), a Palestinian research organization, we polled hundreds of people across the West Bank to find out how checkpoints shape their lives.

The average West Bank commuter—someone who drives several times a week—loses about an hour and a half each week to additional travel time in an effort to avoid checkpoints. Over the course of a year, that amounts to 77 hours lost.
For some, the delays are far longer. People going from Ramallah to Al-Eizariya, on the edges of Jerusalem, could do so in 27 kilometers/48 minutes. Instead, it's 45 kilometers/100 minutes.
Our data shows that people have to take all sorts of complex routes to avoid checkpoints.
Using the median route taken in our dataset, someone who commutes back and forth four days a week would lose nearly seven hours in additional travel time every week.
Anyone who commutes four days a week from Ramallah to Hebron is robbed of over 12 extra hours of travel time.
One pair of towns, Anabta and Beit Lid, are 8 kilometers apart.
It used to be a 10 minute drive. It now routinely takes 50 minutes each way.
Our data analysis found that checkpoint delays have increased by more than 50 percent in the aftermath of October 2023, frequently exceeding hours at a time.
Together, Palestinians in the West Bank lose about 30 years every day.
Data can count the checkpoints, clock the closures, and tally the hours lost at the gates. But how does the system upend the life of a single family?
Losing Access to an Education
More than a decade ago, Amal and her family left the US. They moved back to a home in Al-Janiya, where they built a house with a garden, and a mountain view. “Mashallah,” she says of it still. (The names have been changed due to safety concerns.)
By the time the family arrived, Al-Janiya's main entrance had already been closed for over a decade. Israel sealed the eastern road in 2003; it now serves as an entrance to Talmon, an Israeli settlement built on the village's land.
The only way in or out of Al-Janiya that Amal's family has ever used runs west, through the neighboring village of Ras Karkar. Fifteen minutes down that road is her husband's shop in Ramallah.
A little further on, a local university, where her daughter Lina studies software engineering.
With open roads, Lina's commute could be around 12 kilometers/20 minutes.
With the detour because of a checkpoint, it became 32 kilometers/47 minutes.
Amal’s eldest, Dana, went farthest, to another university to study dentistry. She is set to be the first doctor in the family.
Dana's commute should be around 35.5 kilometers/47 minutes. It is now often a 90-minute drive.

Every day that Dana and Lina drive to their universities, they each lose about an hour on the circuitous route and at checkpoints. Over the course of an academic year, they have lost about three days each due to the detours.
“You loop and loop and end up at the same point… I swear, I get dizzy… By the time you arrive, you're just sad. You sit there asking yourself: what is this life?” Amal said. "You can take it once. Twice. For a year. Then it crosses some limit and you can’t.”
Thirty percent of people in the West Bank said that checkpoints have prevented them from starting or completing a university education. Most students living outside major cities cross at least one checkpoint on the shortest route to their nearest university.
Last summer, Amal's family decided they couldn’t spend another academic year in Al-Janiya, and they moved near Ramallah. “We grieve leaving our village,” Amal said, “but it’s not really a choice.”
They join more than one in ten people in the West Bank who say they’ve moved to other cities or regions because of checkpoints, along with 31 percent who say they’re considering moving for the same reason.
An Inheritance of Loss
Roads that once tied Palestine together have been closed off again and again, first by militarized borders and barriers, then by permits, and finally by hundreds of checkpoints.
Khalil Tufakji, a Palestinian cartographer and expert on Israeli settlements, has watched Israel assemble this system for decades. The purpose of checkpoints is the fragmentation of space, he said—“every city closes in on itself”—and in this way, the homeland shrinks to a city.
The system that confines Palestinians was built in layers. Under British colonial rule, Palestinian communities were at times subjected to roadblocks, systemic and capricious searches, border barriers, and a system of permits that restricted who could move by vehicle across the territory.
In 1948, in what is known as the “Nakba” or “catastrophe,” Zionist forces expelled more than 750,000 Palestinians from their homes. Hundreds of villages were depopulated or destroyed, and people were driven into exile.
Those who remained were placed under Israeli military rule for the next 18 years, forbidden to work, trade, study, or seek medical care beyond their towns without an Israeli permit.
In 1967, when Israel seized the remaining Palestinian territories, it reconstructed the same permit system there. Palestinians were sorted into categories, the color of an ID card determining who may go where.
In 1988, UN Special Committee reports classified the closing of areas in the occupied territories as collective punishment.
In 1995, the Oslo Process resumed. It was meant to lead to the establishment of a sovereign Palestinian state. Instead, it further fragmented Palestinians by dividing the West Bank into administrative islands.
By the early 2000s, this system of closures and permits had become the status quo. In 2002, Israel started building the 713-kilometers-long separation wall, 85 percent of which runs through the West Bank.
And since 2007, Israel has imposed a blockade on Gaza, isolating it from the rest of Palestine.
In the years that followed, the restrictions intensified.

This has meant that every generation of Palestinians since 1948 has inherited a smaller world than the one before it. Grandparents in Jenin, a city in the northern West Bank, tell stories about driving to have lunch in Jerusalem or a weekend in Beirut.
Parents from West Bank towns mention visiting Gaza. Their children remember school trips to Jericho's ancient sites, to an amusement park in Tulkarm and to the zoo in Qalqilya. Most people in the West Bank today have never been to Gaza, according to the ISEP poll. Over 40 percent of respondents said they had never seen the sea, though from high points, in places like Ramallah, you can see it in the distance.
A Palestinian family on the beach of Gaza on August 25, 1997.PHOTOGRAPH: ANTOINE GYORI/GETTY IMAGES
Today, people in the West Bank are living through another period of fragmentation. Three-quarters of those living in the West Bank have close relatives in other governorates. A quarter of parents said their children have never met close relatives who live in other parts of the West Bank. A generation is being locked in: Nearly a third of people under the age of 25 say they’ve never even left their own governorate.
In response to WIRED’s questions, the Israeli Military said, “Decisions regarding the placement of roadblocks, their opening or closing, are made in accordance with operational situation assessments and security considerations alone.” It is a policy that is “continuously adjusted according to the situational assessment on the ground, while balancing the residents’ ability to move freely throughout the area and security needs.”
In a letter addressed to Israel’s Central Command and top military officials, as reported by the newspaper Haaretz in June, the legal adviser to the Israeli military, Colonel Cobi Marcus, advised that the current system of checkpoints and movement obstacles has intensified beyond any legal justification. Haaretz reported he “warned” that since October 2023, the proliferation of movement restrictions, imposed on residents without authorization, may violate basic rights and the principles of international law.
Rema Hammami, an anthropologist at Birzeit University who has researched checkpoints, calls the current situation unprecedented. “Every single community, village, every single Palestinian city is going to be a separate prison. And if there's no pushback on it, they’re just going to keep going forward with it.”
There have been military checkpoints in other parts of the world, like Sri Lanka and Iraq. But Hammami says nowhere compares to the "density, scope, and comprehensiveness” of the system in the West Bank.
A Family Split
Route 60 was part of Reem Yassin’s life for six years. It’s the West Bank's central highway and the main road connecting Ramallah, the West Bank’s political hub, with Nablus, the commercial center of the north.
Yassin was the senior resident anesthesiologist at An-Najah National University Hospital, a leading medical facility in Nablus, which is 45 kilometers away from her home in Ramallah, in the central West Bank.
Yassin says the drive took her around 40 minutes in 2020, when she began her residency—an annoying but manageable commute. After October 2023, the Israeli military erected an additional three checkpoints on the most direct route between Ramallah and Nablus, and she says existing checkpoints began to close far more frequently.
When she gave birth to her first daughter, Yara, she would drop the baby off at her parents house in ’Asirah al-Qibliyah, a village south of Nablus, which meant she had to pass through a different checkpoint, Al-Muraba’ah, off Route 60.
Data analysis shows that since October 2023, Al-Muraba’ah has been one of the most congested checkpoints in the West Bank, often becoming a chokepoint as other routes into Nablus were closed. It would routinely take drivers 20 to 30 minutes to cross, but delays of several hours weren’t uncommon.
To make it work, Yassin would pack the night before, like she was catching a long flight: snacks, a breast pump, clothes for herself and for Yara. She would leave the Ramallah apartment in the dark, before 6 am, to drop Yara in 'Asirah before crossing Al-Muraba’ah.
"I didn't have a life anymore," she says. "I’d go to work and see my daughter for an hour at night. The rest of the time was at the checkpoint." She is one of a third of West Bank parents who say that checkpoints regularly prevent them from seeing their children during their waking hours.
The patterns are unpredictable. One moment, cars pass the checkpoint without much delay; at another, it can take hours. Events that should have little bearing on West Bank mobility can suddenly trigger a lockdown. On June 13 and 14, 2025, when Israel began bombing Iran, about 70 percent of checkpoints were suddenly closed, according to our analysis of Telegram data, an almost 350 percent increase from the week before.
Alexandra Rijke, a cultural geographer who spent years researching checkpoints in the West Bank, calls unpredictability one of the occupation's core mechanisms. Not knowing whether you can go to work or school, or what will get you punished, has a huge impact on people's lives. "Arbitrariness is incredibly violent," she said.
Across the West Bank, the roads between whole regions converge at a handful of checkpoints.
Their closure can divide north from south, force drivers away from their destination before they can turn back toward it, and leave an entire city dependent on a few guarded exits.
The Divide
Every journey we mapped from the southern West Bank toward the center and north narrowed to Wadi an-Nar.
The Divide
When its gates close, it cuts the West Bank in two.
The Detour
The fastest road from Ramallah toward East Jerusalem and the southern West Bank passes through Jaba checkpoint.
The Detour
When it closes, often to give settlers an open road on the other side, drivers must head north before they can turn east and south again.
The Enclosure
Qalqilya city reaches the rest of the West Bank through only a few roads.
The Enclosure
When the main entrance closes, drivers are forced south before they can turn back east.
The Enclosure

Yassin follows a protocol for crossing. Windows down before the soldiers ask. Then the script, which she can recite: "Hand over your ID. Where are you going, where are you coming from, what do you do?" Sometimes the soldier holds his phone up close and takes photos of her face with her ID and license plate. One time, she said, a soldier leaned in through the window: "You're beautiful," he said.
She often saw men pressed face-down against the hoods of their cars, hands behind their backs, the soldiers shouting. Sometimes, on her way back, the same men are still detained.
When asked, nearly two-thirds of people say humiliation or fear most characterize their feeling about checkpoints. Of people stopped at a checkpoint in the last six months, nearly 40 percent said their vehicle was searched by a soldier, and more than 20 percent said they were physically searched. About one in seven said a soldier had pointed a gun toward them.
Eventually, even dropping her daughter off in the morning stopped making sense. Yassin began staying at her parents' house near Nablus most nights. Her husband Montasir stayed in Ramallah and visited on some weekends. He usually left them Saturday morning, before the settler traffic on Route 60 picked up and checkpoints got worse.
As Yara grew older, she began to ask questions. When she opened her eyes in the morning, she’d ask: "Mama, why didn't you take us to Baba?" Then, because she already knew the answer, she’d say, "Is the road closed?"
In the end, the checkpoints proved too great a barrier for Yassin too. The move to her parents’ wasn’t enough. She was still losing hours at the checkpoint. After her second child was born earlier this year, Yassin decided not to go back to work. She extended her maternity leave and was weighing what comes next: a pause, a position closer to home if she can find one, perhaps something abroad. "I can't do it again," she said. Since then, Yassin has left her job at the hospital.
Deadly Delays
In the summer of July 2024, a young man from Reem Yassin’s village was shot by Israeli forces in the leg. The injury itself was not life threatening. But after soldiers held his ambulance at a checkpoint for almost an hour, he entered severe hemorrhagic shock, Yassin recalled.
Yassin, who was completing part of her medical residency at Rafidia Surgical Hospital in Nablus, was the doctor who received him. Recognized immediately by his family, she worked to stabilize him as his blood pressure plunged.
"We almost lost him," Yassin recalls. "We had to keep pumping blood into him." He survived, luckily, but his situation is far from unique: Nearly two-thirds of people in the West Bank say checkpoints have been a barrier to their access to medical care.
Between October 2023 and August 2026, the Palestine Red Crescent Society (PRCS) documented 237 access denials and 240 mission delays by Israeli forces. In early 2026, incidents included soldiers detaining a medical crew at the Sarra checkpoint, soldiers throwing an ambulance crew’s keys down a mountainside at Huwwara, and a Palestinian woman in labor being transferred between vehicles across locked gates. (In response to questions on medical delays, the Israeli Military said, “In accordance with international law, the IDF allows freedom of movement for medical vehicles, including ambulances, for the purpose of providing medical treatment and evacuating the wounded.”)
These delays carry fatal consequences. The Red Crescent attributes 25 deaths since 2023 to the obstruction of its medical teams. In July 2026, a Palestinian infant, Ahmad Zaid, died after Israeli soldiers at a checkpoint blocked the vehicle transporting him for more than an hour.
In response, the Red Crescent has begun bringing facilities to the people, building makeshift medical points inside villages since ambulances are now so often delayed and cannot reliably access hospitals. Doctors Without Borders (MSF) also started providing first aid training to medical and nonmedical volunteers so they can respond to urgent medical needs in cases when an ambulance is delayed or stopped at a checkpoint.
Sleeping at the Factory
After October 2023, delay times at checkpoints across Nablus spiked to levels beyond anywhere else in the West Bank. Commuters in Nablus spent an average of nearly an hour and 50 minutes avoiding checkpoints. Ali Haj Ali has worked at Sama Pharmaceuticals, a medicine factory east of Nablus city, for over a decade; now, at 37, he supervises the maintenance of the company’s production lines. When he leaves at the end of his shift at 4:30 pm, he has stopped expecting to reach his home before 8:00 pm, even though it’s only 16 kilometers away.
Some nights, he doesn't get home at all. He sleeps at the factory, in an arrangement Sama built during Covid-19: Two offices hold a bed and a dozen mattresses for whoever can’t make the trip home.
When checkpoints close, Sama’s employees sometimes have to sleep on site.PHOTOGRAPH: Lama Rabah
“My three kids, my wife, my mother, my father, I’d barely see them,” he said. “And forget about seeing friends.” But this is the best job he thinks he can find, so he keeps going.
On a recent afternoon, Ali sat in a room at Sama Pharmaceuticals, along with his colleague, Ohood Khatatbeh. In minutes, they were filling in the details for one another, recounting what they call “Nablus’ checkpoint crisis” in 2024 and 2025. Ali would sometimes reach the checkpoint, sit there for hours, then just turn around and go home.
"Nothing is guaranteed, that's just how it is here. It's like a lottery," Ali said.
Ohood, the factory’s quality assurance manager, is 38 years old, and the mother of three sons. Her town, Beit Furik, is southeast of Nablus. It has a single gate, in or out. Her whole day is dictated by that gate.
The town has had to come up with its own protocol, as Ohood calls it: For every three private cars, one shared taxi gets through. What they cannot control is the pace, interrupted by the soldiers’ change of shifts.
Best case, if the Beit Furik gate is open and traffic is moving freely, the drive home can take 15 minutes. But for a year and a half, it routinely took her more than 5 hours daily. On the worst day, it took 10 hours. In 2024, Ohood's teenage son had finished a final exam in biology at his school in Nablus just before she was finishing her shift. They found each other at the Beit Furik gate at 4:30 pm, in a line that packed the road several cars wide, all heading for the single entrance to a town of almost 16,000.
Ohood and her son waited in line together until 3 am the following morning.
"The regular employee, the one not separated from work by a checkpoint," she said, "would be home, eaten, showered, asleep, and already dreaming, while I'm still at the checkpoint."
Across the West Bank, checkpoints have begun to reshape how businesses like Sama operate. The company has started rejecting highly qualified candidates after assessing the checkpoints they would have to cross to get to work, Ohood said. It’s even started writing it into the job postings, as a requirement: Candidates must live in Nablus. About half of people polled said checkpoints have impacted their or their spouse’s ability to get a job.
In late 2025, Ohood’s one-week-old baby, Aws, came down with jaundice. She and her husband drove him out of town to the hospital. But on the way back, as she remembers it, they they found the soldier already closing the gate.
"Go back," the soldier yelled in Arabic from the other side of the gate in Beit Furik.
"Go back where?" her husband asked. "We have a sick child with us."
The soldier raised his rifle and pointed it toward them. "For God's sake," Ohood told her husband, "let's just go back." He tried once more anyway, offering to turn around himself if the soldier would just let Ohood and the baby cross the gate on foot. The soldier lost his temper. "I'll shoot you," he said.
They turned around, the baby crying in their arms, and waited in line for an hour and a half until the soldier opened the gate again.
A Different World
By 2000, Aref Jaber says every road in and out of the Jaber neighborhood in Hebron, named after his family, was sealed with earth mounds and concrete slabs. By 2010, he says, iron gates were installed and checkpoints were manned by soldiers. Three years ago, new closures were installed on the very entrances to people's homes, and iron fencing was wrapped around the gates so no one could squeeze through.
The neighborhood sits between the Ibrahimi Mosque, the settlement outposts in the old city in Hebron, and the Kiryat Arba settlement, and has only one way in or out: a turnstile, an inspection room with digital scanning, a metal gate, and a military watchtower, called Checkpoint 160. It’s “as if we’re entering another country,” Jaber says of crossing it. Except the country on the other side is his own house.
For months after October 2023, Israeli forces imposed a curfew on the neighborhood every night, from 10 to 7 in the morning. Now it's every weekend, Aref said. From Friday afternoon until Sunday morning, the checkpoint is closed. No one in, no one out. Jaber says the people who die on Sundays are lucky, because you can bury them the same day. Die on a Saturday, and there is nothing to be done until the checkpoint opens again.
The Palestinians in the neighborhood need to wait for Israeli approval for things big and small: whether they want to evacuate a patient, hold a funeral, or bring in a canister of cooking gas. Locals cross the checkpoint on foot and climb the hill, carrying the sick, carrying groceries up to the neighborhood, dragging suitcases down toward the checkpoint. Jaber’s 6-year-old grandson should be able to go to the school 50 meters away. But it now sits behind an earth mound wrapped in barbed wire, and reaching it would mean a three-kilometer detour on foot, along settler-dominated roads. Jaber waves at his cousins, who live behind the same earth mound. "They have a whole different life there," he says. "We're in the closed zone."
Houses belonging to Palestinians who have been forced to leave them or use a different entrance by the Israeli Military and Israeli settlers are seen in the Jaber neighborhood of Hebron.PHOTOGRAPH: SAMAR HAZBOUN
Even amid the unrelenting pressure of apartheid, people can still imagine a different life. On January 6, 2026, at around 3:00 pm, a Palestinian driver approached Wadi an-Nar, the checkpoint controlling the only road linking the north of the occupied West Bank to the south since 2000. He noticed something strange. No soldiers stood in the way. The checkpoint was open. He took out his phone, recorded a twenty-second video, and posted it in a local Telegram channel.
Within the hour, the clip spread through the West Bank. Everyone was confused. Did Israel remove its checkpoints? Was this really happening?
At 5:57, admins of the “Road Conditions” Telegram group were joking about crossing checkpoints off their lists.
At 6:10, the admins posted that the soldiers had returned. At 6:12, they said the gates were shut.
There was never an explanation. Some assumed it was a drill for Israeli forces. Others, simply a change of shifts. But for three hours, people allowed themselves to imagine a West Bank without checkpoints. A West Bank you can drive the full length of, 130 kilometers from north to south, in less than two hours.
And for a moment, they inhabited a world where they could plan the next day, the next hour. Where Amal’s daughters would reach their lecture halls in minutes. Where Reem wouldn't have to give up a job to keep her family together. Where Ali would walk through his front door before his son fell asleep. Where Ohood would take her baby to the hospital without a rifle raised at her. Where, perhaps, you just keep driving: to Haifa, to Gaza, anywhere you want.
And Aref Jaber would walk down his own street, past the ladders he no longer needs. He would open his front door, and be home.

Buried beneath every American city is a mysterious jumble of cables, pipes, and gas lines, entangled like a pair of wired headphones the moment you pull them out of your pocket. Every time a contractor sticks a shovel in the asphalt, they embark on a high-risk excavate-by-dots obstacle course, dodging color-coded clusters of spaghetti-like power lines, gas mains, sewers, and fiber-optic cables. A line of blue spray paint means water. Red means power. Yellow is gas. Orange is telecom.
Disney World solved a problem that could save America billions every year
Our cities are built atop a dangerous obstacle course of cables. The Magic Kingdom found a better way.
About 700,000 times a year — that’s once every 47 seconds — something goes wrong.
A backhoe slices into a cable and cuts off a 911 call center, or a woman comes home to find her dryer and hot water heater on fire after a contractor pierced her electrical line. Just last week, a contractor accidentally severed a single telecommunication cable that proved critical enough to ground flights at some of the nation’s largest airports on the eve of the UN General Assembly, ensnaring even world leaders like Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney in delays.
The ground beneath our city streets has never been so crowded, driven by a furious race to lay fiber optic cables carrying the data that fills your social media feeds and transmits your ChatGPT queries. Nor have the systems we use to find out where it’s safe to dig — namely, a hotline and all that colorful spray paint — ever felt so catastrophically insufficient.
“If the locator mismarked the line, if the line wasn’t marked, if there was no map that even said the line was there,” said Sarah Magruder Lyle, president of the Common Ground Alliance, a trade association focused on underground damage prevention, “there are a variety of issues that could happen before the excavator even puts a shovel or a backhoe in the ground.”
According to Common Ground, such incidents cost the US about $83.2 billion per year, roughly as much as we invest in public transit annually nationwide. But the actual financial toll may be even higher, because every time a crew stumbles across a mislabeled power line or a gas pipe everyone else forgot about, it can delay construction for months on end. As Magruder Lyle put it, “if they get out there and they find something that they’re not supposed to, you have to go back and reengineer the whole project.”
Such surprises can also lead to tragedy. A 5-year-old named Alistair Lamb was killed in Missouri last spring after a contractor drilled into a gas line near his home, spewing fumes that leveled his house when his unsuspecting father flipped a light switch. And just this May, another unmarked gas line killed three people when contractors struck it, leading an apartment complex in Dallas to explode.
Yet the messy underbelly of our cities remains largely invisible, with accountability for issues foisted upon and at times evaded by a hodgepodge of finger-pointing private utility companies, agencies, and contractors. And that’s a shame because there is, in fact, a better way to bury the cables and pipelines that our modern lives depend on, and a multitude of better ways that we can find the ones we’ve already buried.
What Disney World gets right about the stuff we bury
To understand one utopian vision for how all this could work, look no further than the happiest place on Earth. That’s a moniker Disney World has earned, in my mind, not for its Mickey Mouse waffles (though my niece may disagree), but for its world-class utility corridors, also known as utilidors.
Directly beneath the Magic Kingdom is a sprawling network of tunnels. Initially designed to shepherd around Mickey and his friends, the system now also serves as one of the largest utility corridors ever created. Unlike the rest of America, where cables are typically dumped in ditches before being covered with dirt, the electrical lines that power Cinderella’s castle quite literally get the princess treatment.
Alongside water pipes, sewers, and animatronic control systems, these power lines lace the walls and ceilings of the utilidors, meaning they’re protected from weather and changes in the soil. They are also easy to monitor, catalog, and access if something needs fixing. While the cost of building a controlled system like this is much higher upfront than burying directly in the ground, the practice virtually eliminates the risk of accidentally rupturing a gas main or slicing a fiber optic cable during routine maintenance. Once they’re built, they can also drastically reduce costs in the long run because you no longer need to tear up a street every time a utility needs fixing.
“Obviously, it’s expensive,” said Debra Laefer, a professor of civil and urban engineering at New York University, “but in the long term, it would be hugely cheaper,” especially “in areas where we are digging all the time, there’s a direct business case for moving towards these utilidors.”
As fantastical as Disney World’s imagineered system may seem — and it was, to be clear, predicated on a not-easily-reproducible master plan — the idea of storing utility lines in easy-to-access tunnels is not just for amusement parks. It is possible even in places where most of those lines are currently lying in the dirt, as Prague proved back in the 1970s, when the city decided it was fed up with destroying its precious cobblestone streets every time a buried pipe or cable needed fixing. The city now boasts a sprawling utility tunnel network, occasionally patrolled, evidently, by a couple of robot dogs tasked with mapping out every cable.
Singapore has also spent years building out walkable utility corridors that operate much like the Magic Kingdom’s, transmitting water, data, and energy from the safety of well-organized underground tunnels. Some of Tokyo’s largest districts store their cables and gas lines in huge concrete utility ducts, and many Parisian water lines and fiber optics are kept across the city’s centuries-old sewer system, a catacombs of waste made easily navigable by blue-and-white street signs that correspond to the avenues above. Many university campuses across the US also boast their own sprawling utilidors.
In most cases, cities chose not to relocate utilities all at once, a feat that would probably be financially prohibitive and deeply disruptive. Rather, they took advantage of all the times they’ve needed to relocate utility lines anyway, a standard (and expensive) practice for big building projects like the Wallis Annenberg Wildlife Crossing or the Second Avenue Subway, a major transportation project in New York City that’s been consistently delayed by unmapped utility lines. A group of graduate students found that building such a tunnel in parts of NYC would likely cost at least twice as much as dropping a utility line in the ground, but could recoup the costs within 47 years.
“There are streets in New York City that have been excavated at least once a year, every year for the past 30 years,” Laefer said. If you just prioritize those streets, gathering the piping in a “big concrete box” underground, you could allow workers to complete most repairs without needing to disturb the streets or sidewalks above at all.
But building new utility tunnels would require that we first come to better understand the wires and piping already entangled under our cities, which if you recall, we have only a surprisingly flimsy picture of in most cities today. But if every surprise utility line is an opportunity to move it somewhere better, it is also an opportunity, at the very least, to map out where it is.
To that end, a few years ago, Laefer led a $1.2 million pilot funded by the National Science Foundation to create a test case for 3D-mapping New York City’s underground utilities, a project that’s since been adopted into a citywide initiative. The city says it plans to roll out the spruced up utilities locating system in 2028. The UK debuted a similar digital map of over 3 million kilometers of underground pipes and power, owned by hundreds of utilities and agencies a few years ago. The nation projects that it could help save over $500 million per year by minimizing delays and accidental damage. In places where Singapore has not yet stuffed its utilities into walkable tunnels, the city’s own mapping and utilities coordination has already saved it an estimated $230 million in avoided clashes since 2024. Not bad for an intervention that doesn’t even require any physical rebuilding.
So why hasn’t every American city copied London or Singapore?
Well, US cities tend to be plagued by even more private utilities and patchwork local and state norms and regulations than a nation like the United Kingdom. Getting them to pool together what they often consider proprietary underground data is challenging, and few local officials have opted to prioritize such efforts. But this may well change as more and more fiber optics go into the ground, more flights get canceled, more apartment complexes explode, more power lines flicker off, more sinkholes form, and more Americans come to be all too acquainted with the perils lurking just beneath our feet.
“I think at this point, it’s more about political will and money than any technical obstacle,” Laefer said. “Technically, we’re there. It’s just a matter of doing it.”

When the Chinese scientist He Jiankui announced in 2018 that he had created the first gene-edited babies, the experiment was widely condemned as reckless and premature. It ended with He in prison.
But that hasn’t stopped the push for gene-edited human embryos, with biotech entrepreneur Cathy Tie arguing that doing so isn’t just urgent—it’s a “moral imperative.”
Tie is the 30-year-old founder of Origin Genomics, a company that launched in March with plans to bring gene-edited embryos to IVF clinics. In a new commentary published in the journal Trends in Genetics, she argues for public funding and new regulatory pathways to advance gene-edited babies and eventually move into clinical use.
But questions remain about what evidence researchers will need to determine whether gene-edited embryos are safe enough to attempt a human pregnancy—and what risks might remain for the resulting children.
“There are cautionary tales of first human trials where there was really no flashing red light, and people died,” says Hank Greely, a law professor and director of the Center for Law and the Biosciences at Stanford University.
So-called germ-line gene editing involves modifying cells involved in human reproduction, like embryos. Any changes made could be passed on to future generations. That could mean, for example, correcting a devastating genetic mutation for good. But accidental DNA edits elsewhere, known as “off-target effects,” could introduce new health risks that could also be passed down. Those high stakes are part of why dozens of countries have banned gene-editing of human embryos intended for pregnancy.
People at risk of passing a genetic disease on to their children can use IVF combined with genetic screening to identify disease-free embryos before transfer to the womb. Critics of embryo editing argue that screening tools make the need for it very small. Gene-editing embryos, Greely says, would be helping “a fraction of a fraction of a fraction.”
The drawback of the current approach is that IVF is inefficient; viable embryos can be hard to come by, even for people without an inherited disease risk. Ian Watts and Cheyenne Ziegler, for example, underwent three rounds of IVF in their attempt to have children that do not carry the genetic variant responsible for Watts’ Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease, a degenerative neurological disorder that impacts fine motor skills and mobility. With any IVF cycle, eggs regularly don’t fertilize, and those that do often stall in development or have chromosomal abnormalities. Adding additional screening for disease means that some viable embryos also don’t make the cut.
In Watts and Ziegler’s case, three rounds of IVF have produced eight chromosomally normal embryos, but only three without Watts’ variant. Those three embryos are likely not enough to give the couple the three or four children they hope to have one day.
“The choices currently available are either not having children or doing lots of IVF,” says Watts, a 36-year-old engineer in Long Beach, California. Gene editing could give people like him more chances at a future family. It could also help couples in the extremely rare situation where every embryo would inherit a disease-causing mutation, such as partners who each have two copies of a harmful variant.
“We’re here to treat these diseases, not just exclude embryos and call it a day,” says Tie, a former Thiel fellow who’s alluded to herself as “biotech Barbie.”
The invention of CRISPR raised the possibility of gene-edited babies more than a decade ago, and newer forms of gene editing offer increasing precision. In June, researchers at Columbia University revealed that they had edited early-stage human embryos using a technique called base editing with incredible accuracy. Tie cites this work in her commentary, arguing that precision editing is now well within reach.
If medicine can safely and effectively prevent a disease, she writes, deciding whether to use that treatment should be part of a patient’s reproductive choice. “The obligation of medicine is not only to avoid causing harm but also to prevent avoidable suffering when effective interventions exist,” she writes. Tie says, though, the technology shouldn’t to enhance traits such as intelligence.
And people seem to want the choice: A European survey released in July found that more people supported than opposed human embryo editing.
Tie says that New York City–based Origin is currently working on “optimizing” base- and prime-editing tools on human embryos that IVF patients have donated for research. (The company is currently only testing it in human embryonic stem cell lines.) She expects the company to have significant data in the coming months showing that its embryo-editing tools are safe and efficient. Tie’s first human embryo-editing company, Manhattan Genomics, abruptly shuttered this year after operating for only a few months.
But while the Columbia work demonstrated that precise genetic changes to human embryos are possible, the researchers didn’t correct disease-causing mutations. Some of the editing tools they developed also resulted in unwanted and inconsistent genomic changes, leading them to conclude in a paper published this month that “undesirable consequences” meant the technology was not ready for clinical use.
Variability also means that one editor working doesn’t establish that another will be safe.
“Each and every mutation will therefore be a new medicine,” says Dieter Egli, who led the Columbia work. On top of the added technical challenges, that could make embryo-editing especially time-consuming and expensive to develop.
Tie is clear that she does not think embryo editing is ready for human patients, but she argues it’s close enough that it’s time to address the legal and funding barriers that stand in the way of developing it for use in US clinics. Federal funding for human embryo research is currently legally restricted, and the Food and Drug Administration is barred from considering clinical trials involving embryos with heritable genetic modifications.
Many scientists working on embryo editing believe it will one day come to clinics. Where they differ is when and what it will take to establish it as safe enough.
Doing so, says Paula Amato, a professor of ob-gyn at Oregon Health & Science University who also advises gene-editing company Preventive, will require rigorous assessment of embryos in the lab before moving to trials in nonhuman primates. Those studies should also follow several generations to make sure there are no unexpected changes. Origin, though, is not currently working with animal models, nor does it have immediate plans to do so.
But even with an editing tool that appears to perform perfectly in studies, it will be impossible to ensure that any embryo implanted in a human is free of unintended genetic changes. Before transfer, edited embryos would likely undergo genetic testing. Embryo biopsies sample only a few cells, though, which may not reflect whether different cells carry different genetic changes.
Undetected off-target effects could manifest years later, after a gene-edited baby has grown up and had children of their own.
“You can never be sure that you did your homework,” says Shoukhrat Mitalipov, director of the Center for Embryonic Cell and Gene Therapy at OHSU. “You think that it's safe, but you’re transferring a kind of black box.” (Mitalipov advised Manhattan Genomics.)
Patients, Amato says, will have to be counseled on these risks.
Watts and Ziegler say that the risks of a novel technology would be worth it for the chance of giving one of their affected embryos a disease-free life. Ziegler is currently 20 weeks pregnant with one of their unaffected embryos, but they have continued to hold on to the ones with Watts’ variant in hopes that correcting them will be an option one day.
“If the choices are to discard or to give a new technology a chance, I would lean toward giving new technology a chance,” Ziegler says.

Additionally, 4A Games is also implementing community-led bug fixes and quality-of-life features in the updates.
The developers have also confirmed that Metro Redux’s next-gen update will run at native 4K 60 fps and upscaled 4K at 120 fps on applicable monitors and TVs on consoles. On Xbox, players will get TSR upscaling and anti-aliasing support on Xbox Series X, and Spatial Audio support on eligible Xbox platforms. 4A Games clarifies that this isn’t a remake or a remaster, but rather the perfect way to play through the original Metro experience before Metro 2039 launches in 2027.
The last glimpse of Metro 2039 came at Gamescom 2026, leaving fans with little to look forward to since then. Thankfully, the Metro Redux next-gen updates should keep players busy until the next entry arrives on February 4, 2027.

The government on Thursday revised guidelines for vehicles registered under the Divyangjan category. The beneficiaries will receive an exempted FASTag based on the disability percentage shown on their disability certificate, Unique Disability ID (UDID) card or other applicable records.
The Ministry of Road Transport and Highways revised the guidelines for issuing and renewing exempted FASTags for eligible beneficiaries to promote ease of living for citizens and further simplify toll-related procedures for Divyangjan and persons with disabilities (PwD).
Earlier, guidelines mandated renewal of exempted FASTags for Divyangjan on an annual basis.
However, under the new guidelines, the exempted FASTag’s validity will be determined by the percentage of disability.
FASTags issued to persons with 70% to 100% disability will be valid for five years, while those issued to persons with 40% to less than 70% disability will be valid for three years, the Ministry said.
According to the Ministry, the exempted FASTag may be renewed thereafter, subject to continued eligibility and compliance with the provisions of the National Highways Fee Rules, 2008.
The revised provisions are aimed at making the National Highway tolling ecosystem more accessible, transparent and user-friendly for eligible beneficiaries, while ensuring that toll exemptions continue to be administered in accordance with the prescribed rules and eligibility requirements.

Salah out of Egypt game because of artificial turf
- Published
Egypt have left Mohamed Salah out of their Africa Cup of Nations qualifier against South Sudan because the match will be played on artificial turf.
The former Liverpool forward, now with Turkish club Trabzonspor, has not travelled with the squad to the capital Juba for Tuesday's game.
The 34-year-old started Friday's goalless draw with Angola in Cairo but was substituted by coach Hossam Hassan after an hour.
"The Egypt national team's technical staff, led by Hossam Hassan, has decided to rest Mohamed Salah for the match against South Sudan scheduled for 29 September because of the playing surface," the Egyptian Football Association (EFA) said.
"It was agreed between the national team's technical staff and Mohamed Salah before the Angola match that he would not play against South Sudan, and the technical staff preferred this approach in order to protect the player," it added.
There is a perception of increased risk of injury on artificial surfaces despite technological improvements, though studies have shown, external there is no evidence of a greater risk of injury.
Salah left Liverpool at the end of last season after nine years during which he made 442 appearances and scored 257 goals, winning nine major trophies.
In six Turkish Super Lig games for Trabzonspor this season he has seven goals and two assists.
