How both parties have changed since 2024
The 2026 midterms will test Republican disillusionment with Trump — and Democrats’ new appetite for a fight.
Depending on your political appetite and your geographic location, you absolutely do not need me to remind you of the upcoming midterm elections. But for those of you unencumbered by an unhealthy attachment to political news, and unassaulted by the onslaught of ever-more-brazen political ads, consider this your official notice that the midterms are approaching. Fast.
In less than six weeks, Americans will head to the polls to decide which party controls Congress, along with a slew of state and local offices. The stakes are arguably unusually high: Voters will choose whether to check the power of a president who has bulldozed over historical norms and limits.
So starting this evening, I’m partnering with my colleague Astead Herndon and Vox’s Midterms, Actually team for five weekly editions on the biggest issues shaping the 2026 midterms. Together with outside experts, we’ll break down one issue each week and suggest further reading and races to watch in November.
Up first, and without further ado: the profound shift that both parties have experienced since the 2024 election. These are not your mother’s Democrats. Or Republicans.
Go a little deeper
To kick this series off, I asked Astead to imagine a hypothetical world in which he hadn’t followed politics since 2024. (An outlandish counterfactual: Astead is acutely plugged into politics.) But in this alternate universe, I asked, what would surprise him most about 2026?
Easy, he said. The GOP’s disillusionment with President Donald Trump, who remade the party in his image.
Let’s put some numbers on that phenomenon, to start. Trump’s approval rating has dipped to record lows, even among Republicans. According to an NBC poll conducted in mid-September, just four in 10 Republicans strongly approve of Trump’s performance, down 11 percentage points from the spring.
Republicans have soured on Trump over his handling of the economy and attacks on Iran, which violated his promise to keep America out of foreign wars. Trump’s delayed release of the Epstein files also fueled distrust in his base by exposing his own ties to the dreaded “elite insiders.”
In response, some Republican candidates have worked to distance themselves from Trump, even defying him in campaign ads. But it’s unclear whether that tactic will win over disillusioned or disengaged Republicans. If enough stay home, Astead said — especially with Democrats eager to vote — Democrats could flip the House and/or Senate and make Trump’s last years in office far more difficult.
And speaking of Democrats…they’re also undergoing a major transformation after their 2024 presidential defeat. That loss disproved their previous theory of Trump-era politics: namely, that Trump’s rise was an aberration that competence, decency, and normalcy would eventually overcome.
By contrast, today’s Democrats want a party that “fights,” Astead told me. “The open question is who they’re fighting: The oligarchy? Big Tech? The Billionaire/Epstein class? Trump’s Republican Party?”
Democrats face ideological questions, too. Since 2024, voters have lost trust in the establishment and in party leaders’ ability to pick the best candidates; left-wing candidates have thrived in that vacuum. It’s pretty wild, when you think about it, that a Muslim democratic socialist in New York ranks among America’s most popular Democrats.
For both parties, then, November 3 is a test of their respective visions for America. Not just between the parties — as in, Republicans vs. Democrats — but within them, as well. That, in turn, will help determine the rest of Trump’s presidency…and the 2028 presidential election.
But it’s only October 1. Let’s not get ahead of ourselves.
➨ Races to watch: Michigan’s Senate race, where progressive Democrat Abdul El-Sayed faces Republican Mike Rogers; Florida’s 27th District, where Republican María Elvira Salazar publicly broke with Trump; and the Nebraska, Idaho, and South Dakota’s Senate races, where independent candidates will test both sides’ exhaustion with the two-party system.

New space station crew launches from Florida on SpaceX's Crew Dragon capsule
KENNEDY SPACE CENTER, Fla. — Despite concerns about thunderstorms and gusty winds, SpaceX launched four people on NASA's Crew-13 mission to the International Space Station.
The Falcon 9 rocket leaped off the launch pad at the Cape Canaveral Space Force Station and soared northeast, over the Atlantic Ocean. It will take the capsule about eight hours to catch up with and dock to the space station. The four crew members will spend up to six months living and working aboard the outpost before returning home.
The crew includes two NASA astronauts. Commander Jessica Watkins, a geologist, is making her second trip to space, previously launching to the space station on the Crew-4 mission in 2022, and totaling 170 days in space (She was the first Black woman to serve on the space station, and has the most time in space of any Black woman). Pilot Luke Delaney, a naval aviator, is making his first trip to space. He's from DeBary, Fla., around 50 miles from the Space Coast.
"I did grow up pretty close to here," he said ahead of his flight. "I got to watch Space Shuttle launches, and now I'm going to get to see it from a little bit different perspective."
Deltona High School — where Delaney attended — declared Thursday "Luke Delaney Day" as students gathered outside to watch him take flight.
Mission specialists from Canada and Russia are joining the crew. Canadian Space Agency's Joshua Kutryk and Roscosmos' Sergey Teteryatnikov are both making their first trip to space.
Their capsule is named Grace and is the fifth and final Dragon spacecraft built by SpaceX. It's only made one trip to the space station, ferrying four private astronauts on the Axiom Ax-4 mission.
The mission name is similar to a well-known NASA mission in history: Apollo 13. An explosion just 55 hours into that mission in 1970 crippled the Apollo 13 crew's spacecraft, and NASA raced to find a solution to bring the crew home safely.
While not superstitious themselves, the members of Crew-13 incorporated elements of the Apollo 13 mission into their mission patch, remembering the ingenuity and bravery that saved that crew.
"I think it really represents what we can do when we're faced with extremely challenging and dire circumstances," said NASA's Dana Weigel. "I give the crew a lot of credit for giving the nod to Apollo 13 and kind of giving credit to that and representing that in the mission patch that they chose."
The Crew-13 members will spend their time on the space station performing maintenance on the orbiting lab and conducting science experiments – some even on the crew themselves. They'll work on a stem cell investigation that will help researchers better understand the treatment of Parkinson's disease, investigate crop production in space to prepare for long-duration missions, and test new medical equipment for monitoring crew health.
The mission was delayed in August after a leak of oxidizer was detected on the Dragon capsule during processing. NASA and SpaceX pushed the mission from a mid-September launch to find and fix the issue.
"It took a lot of effort, time, [and] many, many hours in determined troubleshooting to put us on the right path for launch," said Lori Glaze, NASA's head of human spaceflight.
Crew-13 will relieve members of the Crew-12 mission, which launched to the station in February. They'll make the trip back to Earth next week, splashing down off the coast of Southern California.
This mission is SpaceX's 13th operational mission for NASA, and 14th total for the agency. (SpaceX launched a test flight carrying two astronauts to the station in 2020.) The company has flown additional private missions to space as well, both to the space station and orbital missions. NASA's current administrator, Jared Isaacman, funded and flew two of those missions before taking the agency's top job.

In Summary
- Xiaomi released a number of power banks in the Indian market recently.
- The most eye-catching of the new power banks is the Xiaomi UltraThin Magnetic Power Bank, which is the successor to the Ultra Slim power bank launched last year.
- The UltraThin Magnetic Power Bank is the slimmest power bank in its class – it is a mere 6 mm thin, and less than 100 grams in weight. It also comes with a super premium design, with a metal build and a fiberglass wireless charging area.
- It has a premium design and feel, but the Xiaomi UltraThin Magnetic Power Bank comes with a stiff price tag of Rs 5,999, which many might find outrageous for a 5000 mAh power bank. But it could be perfect for many others!
Power banks and “beauty” are seldom used in the same sentence. They are notorious for being bulky, heavy, and brick-like. Even the ones that can be slapped on the back of your phone and attached magnetically often feel uncomfortable to use along with a smartphone. Unless one is using the Xiaomi UltraThin Magnetic Power Bank.
Xiaomi pleasantly surprised us all with a super thin power bank last year, the Xiaomi Ultra Slim power bank, which was so slim and compact that many of us had mistaken it for a card holder. It, however, lacked wireless charging, so it could not be stuck onto the back of a phone. The UltraThin power bank fixes this shortcoming. It comes with a 5,000 mAh battery with up to 15W wireless charging support, and 22.5W charging support (up from 20W on the Ultra Slim). While these numbers are nothing to rave about, it is the design and build of the power bank that are showstoppers. But can its lightweight make up for its rather heavy price tag of Rs. 5,999? Let’s find out:
Xiaomi UltraThin Magnetic Power Bank Design and Appearance: A treat to hold and carry!
It is difficult to think that anything out of the ordinary can be done with the design of power banks, given just how simple and functional the devices are, but Xiaomi has managed to make the design of the UltraThin power bank its biggest USP. As the name suggests, the power bank is truly “ultra thin.” In fact, at 6mm, it is almost half as thin as the Ultra Slim power bank that impressed us last year, and is the thinnest power bank we have used to date.
The power bank is quite compact as well. It is 98.5 mm tall, 71.5 mm wide, and weighs just 98 grams, which means that it will not only easily fit on the back of any phone out there, but will add only about as much weight as a routine phone case. Even though the Xiaomi UltraThin powerbank is quite sleek, it still feels very sturdy. The body is made of an aluminum alloy shell, giving it that reassuring solid feel, and the wireless charging side comes with fiberglass.
The power bank is available in three different colors – Graphite black, Glacier Silver, and Radiant Orange. While we received the black color option, we think all three colors look very good – the bright orange is the exact shade of the iPhone 17 Pro series’ orange and will basically blend with your iPhone 17 Pro or Pro Max (Apple seems to have stepped away from the shade in its latest iPhones, though).
Our unit came with a matte finish, and the back has a small “Mi” logo in a glossy contrast. The thin sides curve softly around the edges, while the front (which is the part that connects wirelessly to your phone) has a huge circular mark to highlight wireless charging connectivity, along with some information. All the sides are bare except the base, which has a small power button, a USB Type-C port for charging, and four tiny LED lights highlighting the amount of charge in the power bank.
The Xiaomi UltraThin Magnetic power bank is a treat to both hold and carry. It exudes premiumness, and its thin form factor makes it easy to carry around, regardless of whether you hold it in your hand, carry it in your trouser pocket, or in your bag. Or even on your phone. It was so thin and light that we actually used it as a bookmark from time to time.
Xiaomi UltraThin Magnetic Power Bank Specs and Hardware: Decent, rather than exceptional
The Xiaomi UltraThin Magnetic Power Bank is more about style and convenience than specs. It comes with decent enough specs, but nothing that will make people sit up in surprise. The power bank comes with a 5,000 mAh battery, which is a touch more than the UltraSlim, which had a 4900 mAh battery. Xiaomi has used an advanced silicon carbon battery instead of the usual lithium-ion one, which allows more mAhs to be packed in a much smaller form factor.
In terms of charging speed, the Xiaomi UltraThin Magnetic Power Bank offers up to 15W wireless charging support and 22.5W wired charging support (up from 20W on the UltraSlim). That sounds brisk enough, but this 15W wireless charging speed is only delivered with the Xiaomi 17 series. For other smartphones that come with wireless charging support, you will get 7.5W charging speed, including the iPhones (MagSafe is supported, but the charging speed remains slow).
Xiaomi has added a number of safety features in the power bank as well. The brand says there are ten layers of safety protection on the device, including foreign object detection, overcurrent, short circuits, overvoltage, overcharging, overdischarging, and over-discharging, amongst other safety features.
Xiaomi UltraThin Magnetic Power Bank Performance: Super convenient, but not super fast
The Xiaomi UltraThin Magnetic Power Bank’s spec sheet means that it cannot fully charge most modern smartphones from 0-100 percent – while it has a capacity of 5000 mAh, its rated capacity is lower (3000 mAh), as in most power banks. As a result, it was able to take our iPhone 17 (which comes with a 3692 mAh battery) from 20 percent to nearly full only once. And as its wireless charging speed for iPhones is fairly sluggish, it took comfortably over an hour. And it took even longer to charge our Pixel 10 Pro XL. That said, thanks to its slim size and light weight, you can just stick it to the back of your phone and forget it.
If you need relatively faster charging, you can connect your phone to the power bank with a Type-C cable and enjoy 22.5W wired charging speed, which is pretty much three times the 7.5W wireless charging speed with non-Xiaomi 17 series phones, and does get the phone charged much faster in comparison. However, if your phone comes with a relatively big battery (and many phones these days are comfortably above 5000 mAh), the power bank might only be able to get them up to 40 or 50 percent charged before needing charging assistance itself.
While you can use the power bank to charge two devices at once – wired and wirelessly – that compromises speed and its charging capacity a fair bit, as both get divided. The power bank also gets fairly warm while charging a phone wirelessly, which can make the temperature of the phone attached rise too. Our iPhone 17 often got very warm while charging.
The magnetic hold of the power bank is very strong. It latched on very easily to our iPhone and did not budge when we kept the pair of them in our pocket or bags, or even while using the phone. This is by far the most comfortable and convenient power bank to use with a phone – you hardly feel its weight.
Xiaomi UltraThin Magnetic Power Bank Review Verdict: Pricey, premium and a convenience contender
The Xiaomi UltraThin Magnetic Power Bank comes with a very steep price tag of Rs 5999. You can get power banks with way more mAh, more ports, and much faster charging speeds at a lower price from Xiaomi itself. Other brands also have their version of slim power banks at far lower prices – Boat has the Magnacharge at Rs 1,599 and URBN the One Premium MagSafe at Rs 1,999. However, none of them brings the sleek form factor and the premium build that the Xiaomi UltraThin Magnetic Power Bank offers, nor the long-term assurance that the brand offers. In fact, its only real competitor would perhaps be Samsung’s Galaxy Magnetic Wireless battery pack, which comes with a similar capacity and 15W wireless charging, but is bulkier and not exactly super affordable at about Rs 4,900.
If you are in the market for a power bank with more mAh in capacity and more Ws in charging speed, and what’s more, want both for a small price tag, the Xiaomi UltraThin Magnetic Power Bank is not for you. However, if you are someone who wants to invest in an ultra-portable, very premium power bank which can simply give your smartphone a power-packed nudge without adding too much bulk to your gadget life, or even to your device itself, the Xiaomi UltraThin Powerbank might be perfect for you. Yes, it is expensive, but it brings with it terrific design, ease of use, and convenience, which is likely to be coveted by many premium phone users, especially those who use iPhones and Pixels!
The Xiaomi UltraThin Magnetic Power Bank’s style is its substance. And it is substantially stylish. Yes, it does have a big price tag, but then, convenience can also be a powerful feature of a power bank.

- Good magnetic connectivity

Australia are due to play their first Test in South Africa since the sandpapergate scandal rocked the cricketing world eight years ago.
To mark one of the biggest controversies the game has ever seen, Test Match Special is asking which is Test cricket's biggest scandal.

Bodyline
On the 1932-33 tour of Australia, England needed a plan to stop the great Donald Bradman. Douglas Jardine, England's charismatic captain, came up with a tactic that would change the game forever: Bodyline.
Jardine instructed his fast bowlers, Harold Larwood and Bill Voce, to bowl hostile, short-pitched deliveries at the Australians. In an era when batters wore no upper-body protection, England's method was criticised as unsporting and against the spirit of cricket.
The bad blood between the two teams escalated to the administrators of the game in each country and even turned into a diplomatic incident, threatening to strain relationships between governments.
England won the series 4-1, a result almost lost in the infamy of the entire episode.
The D'Oliveira Affair
In 1968, England were due to tour South Africa, a country then operating under a system of racial segregation known as apartheid.
In line for selection was Basil D'Oliveira, a mixed-race all-rounder born in South Africa, who had emigrated to and qualified to play for England.
Despite scoring 158 in the final Test of the summer against Australia, D'Oliveira was initially left out of the England squad, only to then be called in as a replacement for the injured Tom Cartwright. His inclusion was criticised in South Africa and the tour was called off little more than a week later.
South Africa played one more Test series – at home to Australia the following year – then spent two decades out of international cricket. In the intervening time, a number of rebel tours to South Africa took place, with huge consequences for the players involved.
'George Davis is innocent'
Australia were defending the Ashes in England in 1975. The series was shortened to four Tests because of the inaugural men's World Cup earlier in the summer.
At 1-0 down, England had a huge chance to level the series in the third Test at Headingley. At the close of the fourth day, Australia had reached 220-3 in pursuit of 445. A thrilling finish was in prospect.
Overnight, the pitch was vandalised. Holes were dug and oil was poured on the surface. The damage was caused by supporters of George Davis, who had been jailed for armed robbery the previous year. "George Davis is innocent" was written on the wall around the ground.
The Test was abandoned as a draw, meaning Australia retained the urn and ruining the prospect of a decider at The Oval.
Davis was released in 1976 when his conviction was adjudged to be unsafe, and it was overturned entirely on appeal in 2011.
- George Davis appeal win sparks Headingley Ashes memories 
  - Published24 May 2011
World Series Cricket
In the mid-1970s, Kerry Packer, one of the richest men in Australia, wanted to boost the ratings of his Channel Nine TV network with live sport. He approached the Australian Cricket Board with a lucrative offer, one that was rejected in favour of keeping live cricket on the Australian Broadcasting Corporation.
So, Packer created his own product: World Series Cricket. The plan was simple – Packer recruited the best players in the world to stage his own matches.
Most significant was the signing of England captain Tony Greig, who effectively acted as an agent. Greig was stripped of the captaincy and Australia's 1977 Ashes tour of England was overshadowed by the emergence of Packer's outfit.
World Series Cricket lasted for two seasons – 1977-78 and 1978-79 – comprising one-day matches and 'SuperTests' between teams representing Australia, West Indies and a World XI. Meanwhile, traditional cricket rolled on. In 1978-79, England embarked on Ashes tour they won 5-1, beating an Australia side decimated by Packer defections.
Later in 1979, a truce between Packer and the board was brokered, and Nine earned TV rights to the game in Australia. Many of the innovations of WSC – coloured clothing and day-night cricket among them – shaped the game as we know it today.
Mike Gatting and Shakoor Rana
England had already been frustrated by the decisions of a home umpire in losing the first Test on their tour of Pakistan in late 1987.
Shakoor Rana was appointed to stand in the second Test, much to England's displeasure. Rana had previously clashed with New Zealand skipper Jeremy Coney.
On the second day in Faisalabad, Rana was at square leg when he appeared to halt the game to object to one of England captain Mike Gatting's field placements.
Gatting was furious, confronting the official in footage that has been replayed over and over. The following day, Rana refused to take the field, leaving England waiting in the middle for play that did not get under way.
The match eventually resumed on the fourth day and the cancellation of the tour was narrowly avoided, but mistrust and ill-feeling between England and Pakistan lingered for years later.
Dirt in the pocket
In the mid-1990s, ball-tampering was the most emotive topic in Test cricket. In 1992, Pakistan's tour of England was overshadowed by allegations and innuendo. Two years later, the England captain found himself at the centre of a similar row.
In the Lord's Test against South Africa, Michael Atherton was caught by TV cameras rubbing dirt on the ball. Atherton's explanation was that he was trying to maintain the condition of the ball, rather than alter it. Trouble was, he told the match referee he was using the dirt to keep his hands dry.
The story was headline news, topped off by a chaotic news conference when Atherton was, in his own words, "fed to the lions". Atherton considered resigning, but escaped with a fine and remained captain for another four years.
Hansie Cronje
Former South Africa captain Hansie Cronje was one of the most revered figures in his country. He was even close to Nelson Mandela.
Yet he became involved with Indian bookmakers and gradually made suggestions to fix matches, or parts of them. Cronje targeted impressionable team-mates to become part of his scheme.
Cronje's most infamous plot came in a dead-rubber fifth Test against England at Centurion Park in 2000. The match had been badly affected by rain, but Cronje was adamant the teams should do all they could to ensure it did not end in a draw.
He negotiated with England skipper Nasser Hussain for both teams to forfeit an innings, leaving the tourists with a final-day run-chase, which they completed. England were unaware, but Cronje had engineered a result.
Cronje confessed months later and would eventually give public testimony at the King Commission. He was banned from cricket for life and was killed in a plane crash in 2002.
- Hansie Cronje, match-fixing and plane crash that left a complex legacy 
  - Published30 July 2025
The forfeited Test
This scandal had roots in past attitudes towards Pakistan cricket and ball-tampering.
Pakistan had already lost the series in England in 2006, yet were cruising to victory in the final Test at The Oval.
However, Australian umpire Darrel Hair, himself no stranger to controversy, asked for the ball to be changed midway through the afternoon session on the fourth day. Ball-tampering was suggested and Pakistan refused to play after tea.
Confusion reigned. Pakistan captain Inzamam-ul-Haq relented and tried to resume the Test, but by then umpire Hair and partner Billy Doctrove had awarded the match to England.
Years of back-and-forth followed, with the result first changed to a draw, then reverted back to an England win. Inzamam was cleared of ball-tampering, while Hair served a ban from officiating. The match remains the only Test in history to have been forfeited.
Pakistan spot-fixing
No-balls deliberately bowled in the 2010 Lord's Test between England and Pakistan ultimately resulted in three of the tourists' players spending time in jail.
A sting by the News of the World newspaper paid a middleman - cricket agent Mazhar Majeed - for details of three no-balls.
Majeed arranged for Pakistan captain Salman Butt and pace bowlers Mohammad Asif and Mohammad Amir to execute the no-balls, then the News of the World broke the story while the Test was still ongoing.
All three players received bans from the International Cricket Council, then were found guilty of conspiracy to cheat at gambling and conspiracy to accept corrupt payments.
Butt was sentenced to two and a half years in prison, Asif a year and Amir, who was aged only 17 at the time of the no-ball plot, six months.
- How Pakistan cricket betting scam unfolded 
  - Published1 November 2011
Sandpapergate
In the third Test of Australia's bad-tempered tour of South Africa in 2018, TV cameras picked up touring fielder Cameron Bancroft appearing to rub the ball with a small, yellow object.
Bancroft, along with captain Steve Smith, admitted to attempting to alter the condition of the ball. Days later, it was revealed Bancroft was using sandpaper.
The outcry engulfed the Australian team and the entire nation. Prime minister Malcolm Turnbull said he was "bitterly disappointed".
Smith was sacked, along with his vice-captain David Warner, the architect of the plot. All of Smith, Warner and Bancroft served lengthy bans from playing for Australia.
Coach Darren Lehmann was cleared of having knowledge of the ball-tampering, but he too resigned.

Rows of hardware and car-part shops line Garstin Bastion Road, with faded signs crammed together above their shutters. By day, the street is one of Old Delhi’s busiest commercial thoroughfares. But as dusk falls, GB Road, as it is known locally, transforms into one of the city’s most notorious red-light districts.
An estimated 2,800 sex workers live and work in brothels that occupy the upper floors of the dilapidated buildings, their entrances tucked behind narrow stairways and unmarked doors. Women sit on plastic stools beneath the stairways, calling out to men passing on the street, while others watch from windows above, their eyes following the movement below before customers are directed upstairs.
The challenges the women of GB Road face are numerous and well documented – from health risks to abuse, debt to poor sanitation. Now they face a new struggle: India’s controversial electoral reform process. The Election Commission’s special intensive revision, or SIR, is a nationwide exercise in which electoral rolls have shrunk by more than 58 million voters across the 13 states covered in the first two of three main phases. In Delhi, covered in the third phase, the scale of exclusion is the highest recorded as a percentage: 4.76 million names – 33% of the city’s previous electorate – do not appear on the city’s draft roll published on 31 August.
The government says SIR is meant to “purify” the electoral rolls by removing ineligible voters, including alleged undocumented migrants, but critics have accused Narendra Modi’s government of using it to target minority voters and reshape electoral rolls in ways that could benefit his Bharatiya Janata party (BJP).
On GB Road, the proportion of those excluded is even higher. Data shared by officials overseeing about 1,300 voters in the area show that about 650 were sex workers on the previous electoral roll. Of these, at least 500 have either been marked as “shifted”, meaning they have moved home or location, or have been unable to establish their eligibility because of missing documentation – more than three-quarters of the sex workers on the local roll.
One of them is 36-year-old Beauty*, who has lived on GB Road for more than two decades. She got her first voter ID in 2008. At the time, the address where she lived and worked as a sex worker and verification by a government official called a booth-level officer (BLO) were enough to put her on the electoral roll. She voted in previous elections.
But under the new rules, voters had to establish eligibility by proving their link to the relevant previous electoral roll or by producing prescribed documents such as a passport, birth or education certificate – a paper trail Beauty struggled to reconstruct. Trafficked at 16 and brought to the brothels of GB Road, she has no contact with her family. She does have an Aadhaar card, India’s biometric identity document used widely to establish identity and access government services, with her GB Road address. But Aadhaar is not proof of citizenship and does not, by itself, establish eligibility to vote under the SIR process.
She tried to get a copy of her matriculation certificate, which is evidence of schooling, from the village in Rajasthan where she grew up. One of her regular customers of the past 10 years – a man she refers to as her husband, agreed to help track down the old record but failed.
“If I had the papers to show my father’s birth certificate, or even my own matriculation certificate, then I could prove who I am,” she says. “But how can I go back to my village to ask for these things when my trafficking has brought so much shame to my family that they no longer accept me?”
Now Beauty has lost hope – and, for now, her vote. Her name was left out of Delhi’s recent draft electoral roll. For her, the voter ID had meant more than a piece of identification. Sex workers, she says, are accustomed to being treated as immoral, degraded and less worthy than others.
“We all shit. That is what makes us equal as human beings. Voting is the same in the realm of rights. When I stand in that queue, nobody is more or less than me. It reminds me that whatever people think about my work, I am still equal to everyone else.”
Beauty is not alone in struggling to prove her eligibility. The SIR requirements have exposed the precarious paper trails of women across GB Road, a roughly 1.5km stretch running between two of Delhi’s historic landmarks, Ajmeri Gate and Lahori Gate.
Of the nine sex workers interviewed for this story, none had successfully completed the SIR process: six said they had never received the enumeration form distributed by BLOs to verify voters’ details and collect information for the electoral-roll revision, while the remaining three were unable to meet the documentation requirements.
According to Kiran Deshmukh, a sex worker and coordinator at the National Network of Sex Workers (NNSW), many have spent years, even decades, in Delhi but possess few documents establishing their family histories or links to earlier electoral rolls. “Some were trafficked as children and lost contact with their families; others never attended school or have moved between rooms and brothels without leaving a stable documentary trail,” says Deshmukh. “It is impossible in such circumstances to prove such rigid eligibility requirements under SIR.”
The process is so cumbersome that even people who are literate and have institutional and organisational support can struggle to establish their eligibility. “The process of receiving the enumeration form, knowing when you have not received it, reaching out, then trying to create a paper trail is so daunting that the entire burden of proving your eligibility is placed on the citizen to protect their own constitutional right,” says Deshmukh.
Sagrika Rajora, a researcher and member of Voter Adhikar Manch, a citizens’ collective, argues that the burden falls particularly heavily on people whose lives do not fit neatly into the categories used by the verification process. “To identify people of such marginality is a tedious task. These categories of ‘shifted’ become an easy way forward for booth-level officers, when finding people on the ground is already time-consuming.”
BLOs are often drawn from occupations such as auxiliary nurses or health workers, adding electoral duties to already demanding jobs. Some have raised concerns about the workload and unrealistic timelines of the exercise. Yet, Rajora says, there has been little effort to streamline the process to ensure that “no eligible citizen is left out”, the aim outlined by the Delhi chief electoral officer, Ashok Kumar.
“There is so much discretion vested in one BLO. Even if you leave citizenship aside and talk only about voter rights, the entire process of delivering and collecting these forms depends on that one person. There are no grounds for entrusting one person with such a huge responsibility without any accountability at all,” Rajora says.
“It is not surprising that sex workers are among those being excluded. When people have lives that are so complex and mobile, you are going to be untraceable, absent from the system. These are the people for whom such a verification system is simply not designed to work.”
The gaps also cause problems for workers’ children when they reach adulthood. “Children may not possess documents establishing parentage in the manner expected for verification. Some are raised by relatives, guardians or members of the community, while others grow up in institutional care, making conventional family records difficult to establish,” says Deshmukh.
For 23-year-old Dinesh*, whose mother was a sex worker, the problem is not abstract. His mother died three years ago, but she never had a birth certificate. Without one, obtaining her death certificate became nearly impossible, leaving Dinesh with little documentation through which to establish his maternal lineage.
When Dinesh submitted his enumeration form, he relied on his matriculation certificate as proof of his identity. But the booth-level officer pointed out that it did not have his father’s name. “If my mother gave birth to me, why do I need a man’s name on any official certificate?” he asks.
Dinesh says his name is missing from the draft electoral roll. He is still unsure why, but suspects the absence of his father’s name may have been a factor.
The NNSW has written to the chief electoral officer seeking special measures to ensure that sex workers and their children are not excluded from the SIR. But the joint chief electoral officer, Balram Meena, told The Hindu there was no separate process for sex workers. “If their mapping can’t be done and there are no documents either, their names will be removed as per the process.”
The fear of losing the vote is not only about voting rights. In West Bengal, where the SIR has already been completed, the BJP government has used lists of voters deleted during the exercise to scrutinise eligibility for welfare schemes. The BJP chief minister, Suvendu Adhikari, says welfare programmes will continue under a “transparent process”, but adds: “No deceased person, illegal infiltrator, or non-Indian individual will be allowed to avail benefits meant for citizens of the state.” The government has excluded about 3 million beneficiaries from its new Annapurna Bhandar welfare for women scheme, using SIR deletion data in its verification process.
In Delhi, the next stage of the SIR process – issuing notices to those whose eligibility or previous electoral-roll details could not be established or matched, and dealing with claims and objections – has now begun and will continue until 29 October. Those excluded from the draft roll can challenge their omission. But Dinesh says he does not intend to.
After years of being asked to produce documents that his family never had, he is unsure what more he can submit to prove that he exists.
“Even if my mother were alive today, I don’t think that would be enough to prove anything. She never had the documents they are asking for. So how am I supposed to get those documents now, especially after her death?”
* Names have been changed. Workers and residents did not permit any photography during the Guardian’s visit

The “Fast & Furious” TV series, first revealed to be in development earlier this year at the NBCUniversal upfronts, is closer to reality. Peacock announced Thursday that it has greenlit a new scripted television series based on the franchise.
Vin Diesel, who revealed that a “Fast & Furious” scripted series was in development during the upfront presentation in May, is an executive producer along with One Race’s Sam Vincent (One Race), Original Film’s Neal H. Moritz and Pavun Shetty, and Jeff Kirschenbaum and Chris Morgan Productions’ Chris Morgan.
Mike Daniels (“Sons of Anarchy,” “Shades of Blue,” “The Rockford Files”) and Wolfe Coleman (“Shades of Blue,” “911: Lone Star”) will serve as co-showrunners, pilot writers and executive producers.
Popular on Variety
According to Peacock, the streamer is looking to premiere the “Fast & Furious” series by 2028.
Premiere would coincide with the next film installment, “Fast Forever,” which has been slated to hit theaters on March 17, 2028.
Universal Television, a division of Universal Studio Group, is the studio.
“For the last decade, we have realized that the fans have wanted more,” Diesel said at the upfront in May. “They wanted us to expand the legacy characters, their stories. And for the last decade, the desire has been for us to enter the TV space that Fallon has mastered. And I had to wait till it was right… It became right when Donna Langley started to oversee it all, because that’s when I knew that the integrity of the characters, the international appeal, what makes us all feel like family would be protected in the TV space… The news that I have here today is that Peacock is launching four shows from the ‘Fast and Furious’ universe.”
Previously in TV, Netflix aired the animated series “Fast & Furious Spy Racers” for six seasons between 2019 and 2021.
In case you’re one of the few out there who doesn’t know what the “Fast & Furious” franchise is about, here’s NBCU’s explainer: “This year marks the 25th anniversary of the launch of one of the most iconic film franchises in cinema history. On June 22, 2001, Universal Pictures released “The Fast and the Furious,” a high-octane thriller set amid the street-racing culture of Los Angeles. The film — starring Vin Diesel as Dominic Toretto, Paul Walker as Brian O’Conner, Jordana Brewster as Mia and Michelle Rodriguez as Letty — would ignite a cultural phenomenon.”

The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) has proposed a draft amendment to the Food Safety and Standards (Prohibition and Restrictions on Sales) Regulations, 2011, to restrict the manufacture and sale of analogue products as “Paneer” and prevent consumers from being misled about the nature and composition of such products, noted a release issued by the Union Health Ministry on Thursday.
The proposed Food Safety and Standards (Prohibition and Restrictions on Sales) Amendment Regulations, 2026 seek to insert a new clause under Regulation 2.1.1 of the existing regulations, specifically covering “paneer made of constituents not derived from milk”.
Under the proposed amendment, products already licensed or registered under the ‘Analogue in Dairy Context’ category would be required to discontinue the use of the term “Paneer” in their nomenclature, labelling or marketing.
The proposed amendment is aimed at ensuring that the nomenclature and presentation of food products accurately reflect their nature and composition, thereby enabling consumers to make informed choices.
As the notification is a draft regulation, FSSAI has invited objections and suggestions from stakeholders and members of the public. The draft regulations will be taken into consideration after the expiry of 60 days from the date on which copies of the Official Gazette containing the notification are made available to the public.

‘Brain fog’ is used to describe a feeling of mental slowness, difficulty concentrating, finding words, remembering information or processing things as quickly as before. But it is not a medical diagnosis, and persistent cognitive difficulties should not automatically be attributed to brain fog.
What brain fog feels like
Brain fog is a subjective description of changes in cognitive functioning. People may feel that their thinking has become slower or more effortful, that they cannot concentrate on a task, lose their train of thought, struggle to find words or read something without absorbing the information.
“Brain fog is basically a subjective feeling that you are cognitively slow, that you are mentally slow, that you are not able to do your daily activities as quickly or as deftly as before,” says Srividhya S., associate consultant, department of neurology, Rela Hospital, Chennai.
It is different from the occasional forgetfulness that occurs when a person is tired, distracted or stressed. Forgetting where the keys were kept or briefly forgetting a name, for instance, does not by itself indicate a cognitive disorder. Tiredness is also not the same as brain fog. Fatigue is primarily a feeling of reduced physical or mental energy, while brain fog refers more specifically to difficulties with attention, memory, processing or mental clarity.
T. Swathi, consultant, neurology, SRM Prime Hospital, Chennai, says people with brain fog are often aware that they are not functioning as efficiently as before. This also distinguishes it from some memory disorders, where relatives may be the first to notice changes such as repeated questions, difficulty managing regular tasks or getting lost in familiar places.
Health factors
The causes of brain fog can be varied, and more than one factor may be involved. Poor or inadequate sleep is a common contributor. Sleep apnoea can also disrupt sleep repeatedly without the person being aware of it.
Stress, anxiety and depression can affect attention and processing speed. Other possible contributors include thyroid disorders, diabetes, anaemia and nutritional deficiencies such as vitamin B12 and folate. Migraine and hormonal changes, including those during pregnancy, the postpartum period and menopause, can also be associated with cognitive symptoms.
Medicines should also be considered. Sedatives, some sleeping medicines, antihistamines, anticholinergic medicines and some anti-seizure drugs can affect alertness or cognitive function. Alcohol and dehydration may add to the symptoms.
“Brain fog has several possible causes and can be due to more than one,” says Arulselvan V.L., senior consultant in neurology, Apollo Hospitals, Greams Road, Chennai. “It is crucial to not think that all brain fog is neurological.”
Cognitive difficulties can also occur during or after infections. A recent systematic review of 47 studies involving more than 25,000 people with long COVID estimated the pooled prevalence of brain fog at 30%. However, various studies use different definitions and assessment methods. There is so far no comparable prevalence estimate because brain fog is a symptom description and not a defined medical diagnosis.
When tests are needed
There is no fixed duration after which every case of brain fog requires investigation. Persistence, progression and its effect on daily functioning are important.
Doctors advise evaluation when symptoms continue despite adequate sleep and lifestyle measures, recur frequently or gradually worsen. Repeatedly forgetting important information, struggling with previously familiar tasks, difficulty following conversations or unusual changes in work performance are also reasons to consult a doctor.
Symptoms lasting for several weeks without an obvious explanation, particularly when they affect work, studies or relationships, should be assessed. New symptoms such as persistent fatigue, weight changes, breathlessness, tingling, low mood or excessive daytime sleepiness can provide additional clues.
Evaluation usually begins with a detailed history. . A neurological examination may then be performed.
Depending on the history and examination, doctors may check blood counts, blood sugar, electrolytes, thyroid function, kidney and liver function and nutritional markers such as vitamin B12.
A brief cognitive assessment may be useful when there are concerns about memory, attention or language. Brain imaging such as an MRI is also not routinely required for uncomplicated brain fog. It may be considered when symptoms are progressive, the neurological examination is abnormal or there are other features suggesting a structural or neurological cause. A sleep study or EEG may be considered in selected cases.
Certain symptoms, however, require prompt attention rather than being attributed to brain fog. Sudden difficulty speaking, facial drooping, weakness or numbness on one side, sudden problems with vision or balance, seizures, fainting or severe confusion can indicate an acute neurological problem such as stroke. A sudden, severe or unusual headache also requires urgent assessment.

India’s Nitesh Siwach entered the final in the Men’s Greco-Roman 97kg event at the Asian Games 2026 on Thursday.
In the semifinal, Nitesh outclassed Mongolia’s Gankhuyag Ganbaatar 9-0 to earn a victory by technical superiority.
In the final, the 23-year-old Indian will take on Japan’s Yuri Nakazato, with the bout scheduled to happen at 3:35 p.m IST on Thursday.
If Nitesh beats Nakazato, he will become the first Indian to win an Asiad gold in the Greco-Roman wrestling in 64 years.
Who is the last Indian to win a Greco-Roman wrestling gold medal in Asian Games?
Ganpat Andalkar and Malwa Singh won gold medals for India in Greco-Roman wrestling at the 1962 Asian Games.
Andalkar won the Men’s Greco-Roman +97 kg title, in addition to the silver medal in freestyle wrestling in the same weight category. Singh won gold in 52kg category and added a bronze in the freestyle discipline.
India has already won a Greco-Roman wrestling medal in Aich-Nagoya through Sunil Kumar, who bagged bronze in the men’s 87kg event.

1962, Jakarta
1974, Tehran
2010, Guangzhou
2023, Hangzhou

Canada fast-tracking oil pipeline designed to diversify economy away from US
The new pipeline could make Canada a major global energy supplier, as Asia looks outside the Middle East in the wake of the Iran conflict
Canada will fast track the approval process for a new proposed crude oil export pipeline to its west coast that could generate over C$20 billion (US$14 billion) a year in GDP, Prime Minister Mark Carney said on Thursday.
The pipeline, which was announced in July, is a crucial part of Carney’s bid to diversify the economy away from the United States and help lessen the effect of US President Donald Trump’s tariffs.
Carney said Ottawa would officially list the Pacific Link pipeline as a project of national interest, which enables it to proceed through a single federal regulatory review process. He said Ottawa aimed to complete the process by September 1, 2027.
“A pipeline to the west coast is part of our mission to transform our economy, to double our non-US exports over the next decade … [and] to unlock our full potential as a global energy superpower,” he told reporters in Fort McMurray, hub of Alberta’s oil sands industry.

'It's a nightmare.' Former refugee, professor on Trump's new Medicaid policy
For stories on the science of healthy living, subscribe to NPR's Health newsletter.
Mustafa Rfat has been getting frantic phone calls recently from refugees with disabilities. As of Oct. 1, refugees are losing access to Medicaid across the country because of H.R. 1, the Trump administration's major budget bill Republicans passed last summer.
"I spent these past two weeks just talking with so many of them, literally just terrorized by the reality that their children with disabilities are losing coverage," he says. "For example, a father is a refugee with disabilities, with two kids with disabilities, and he's just confused how he's going to get the medication."
Rfat is a professor of social work at the University of Nebraska at Omaha, and his research focuses on refugees with disabilities, an experience he knows firsthand.
When he arrived in the U.S. as a refugee from Iraq in 2011, the chronic condition that affects his spine was severe. "I was in a very bad situation," he says. "I couldn't walk. I was in so much pain. I missed my medications for a long time. I didn't see a doctor. So it was a very, very difficult and vulnerable situation."
As he moved from Alabama to Illinois to West Virginia trying to find housing and continue his education, Medicaid was a lifeline, Rfat says. "I had to climb this big mountain of acclimating into the culture here, learning English, dealing with the traumas of the war, the loss of family members, the challenges that I faced, being alone with a disability," he says.
"I was determined and in this determination, Medicaid was the big factor that made my dreams come true." In fact, he says one of the specialists who treated him wrote his first reference to apply for college. He has since become a U.S. citizen with a family, a doctorate, and a job as a professor.
Now, he's trying to help refugees with disabilities facing the challenges of navigating life in the U.S. without that lifeline. As of Oct. 1, refugees are among the groups that will lose Medicaid coverage.
Hundreds of thousands will lose coverage
Only a small portion of legal immigrants have been eligible to enroll in Medicaid, including refugees and asylum seekers. Because of the changes to "Alien Medicaid Eligibility" in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act that Republicans passed last summer, an even smaller subset now have access. An estimated 280,000 people will lose Medicaid in October, according to an analysis by KFF Health News.
That includes immigrants admitted to the U.S. on humanitarian grounds who are waiting to be approved for a green card, explains Ben D'Avanzo, senior strategist at the National Immigration Law Center.
"The people who are losing Medicaid and CHIP [the Children's Health Insurance Program] are among some of the most vulnerable immigrants — people who have experienced violence in their own homes or on their journey, who may have physical and mental conditions, who are fleeing persecution and war," he says. "These are people who we have long, in the United States, welcomed, and populations who have had very strong, historic bipartisan support."
Rfat points out that refugees are more likely to have serious health conditions than other groups. "More than one third of them have at least one type of disability — this is what the research tells us," he explains. In refugee camps and during war access to doctors and medication is difficult, and simple conditions can become serious and complex.
That was his own experience with an inflammatory condition called ankylosing spondylitis. "By the time I arrived in the U.S., a lot of doctors told me, 'You are one of the worst cases that we are seeing,'" he says. "And that is the case for a lot of refugees that come here."
In a statement to NPR, the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services wrote that they are enacting the law passed by Congress working with states to accurately implement the policy. They did not respond to a follow up question about the effect of the policy on refugees with disabilities.
"Once these changes take place, these groups of immigrants will be left with very few options for affordable, comprehensive coverage," says Drishti Pillai, director of immigrant health policy at the nonpartisan health research organization KFF.
"They could still buy full price coverage from ACA marketplaces, but that is often unaffordable," Pillai says. "Employer-sponsored coverage is also an option, but many immigrants, especially those who are on Medicaid, don't work in jobs that don't offer employer-sponsored coverage, such as jobs in construction, agriculture, food service."
She says a few states are creating their own coverage options for these groups, but many have tight budgets and are facing even bigger Medicaid cuts in January. Most states have also opted in to allow Medicaid to continue to cover pregnant women and children who would otherwise be losing coverage.
D'Avanzo points out that the categories of people losing coverage now will eventually become green card holders who are eligible for Medicaid.
"So these are people who are going to put off preventative care, who are not going to treat their chronic conditions, who are going to forgo important medication," he says. "And then when they are Medicaid eligible again in the future, once they've received their green card, they're going to be needing much more specialized care and much more costly care."
Hope for change
Mustafa Rfat is headed to his alma mater Washington University in St. Louis, Missouri this weekend to meet with a few dozen refugees with disabilities and share some of his recent research. He says the loss of Medicaid and food benefits will hang over the event.
"It's a nightmare for the community," he says. He hopes Congress will reverse course.
He's decided to devote part of the event to teaching about civic engagement. "To understand the importance of voting when they become citizens, to understand the importance of being aware of the policies, being aware of who their representatives are, how to communicate with their representatives," he says.
"These are new Americans," he adds. "These people are going nowhere. By making their health and well-being worse, it's not going to benefit anyone."

To say Italy is my happy place would not be an exaggeration.
I've visited all 20 regions, most at least twice, and spend about five months a year there. As such a frequent visitor to the country, I am often asked, "What's really worth seeing in Italy?"
It's a valid question: There are some tourist attractions that never get old, even for people like me who have seen them dozens of times. Others, I'm not particularly rushing back to.
If you're headed to la dolce vita and are seeking some guidance on which sights are worth it, here are three to include in your itinerary, and two to skip.
The Colosseum is a world wonder, and it's an absolute must-see.
If you only have time for one attraction in Italy, make it the Colosseum. Just plan strategically to optimize your experience: Visiting in the early morning can help you beat the heat and avoid the crowds, especially in the summer.
I'd also recommend scheduling a tour ahead of time. If you aren't interested in history, though, you might find the interior boring — in that case, you should still visit, but head there at night to catch a glimpse of the massive monument from the outside.
One of my favorite late-night strolls in Rome involves grabbing a gelato from Gelateria Dell'Angeletto while staring at the Colosseum's arches.
Napoli Sotterranea is an underground history lesson.
Many tourists just get a glimpse of Naples while on their way to the Amalfi Coast. Don't be that person, and get to know this beautifully misunderstood city by taking a tour of Napoli Sotterranea.
While about 130 feet below ground, you'll find narrow historical caves dating back over 2,400 years. A tour — which is the best way to see the city underground — covers the city's history through World War II.
You'll even learn a myth or two about the corniciello, the "Italian horn" that is often worn as a necklace, and how some use it to ward off bad luck.
Visiting the Trulli of Alberobello is like wandering through a fairytale village.
Puglia has seen an influx of tourism in recent years.
Activities like boating through Polignano a Mare's caves and marveling at Lecce's Baroque architecture have made Puglia a hot spot for good reason. The trulli of Alberobello are one of the most popular things to see in the region — and still, very much worth it.
A UNESCO World Heritage Site, Alberobello's trulli are cone-shaped houses made of limestone and provide a unique look into southern Italy's history.
It's believed that, centuries ago, the people of Alberobello built these houses because they were easy to dismantle — and, therefore, they were able to avoid paying property taxes.
Today, many trulli have been turned into bed and breakfasts, and visitors can sleep in one. Alberobello is a popular day trip from Bari, and although you can easily see the town in just a few hours, sleeping in a trullo is an experience well worth it if you have a night to spare.
On the other hand, the Trevi Fountain used to be one of my favorite sights in Rome … but it's lost some charm.
As much as I understand the desire to recreate the iconic "Lizzie McGuire" shot — something I've personally done myself — the Trevi Fountain no longer feels like a must-visit spot in Italy to me.
The fountain is now enclosed by metal gates and regularly monitored by employees. If you want to get closer to the fountain during peak hours, you have to pay a 2-euro admission fee.
This admission fee was implemented in 2026 to help address overcrowding and better protect the historic structure. However, up to 400 people are still allowed within the small confines of the Trevi Fountain — meaning that, despite these regulations, it often still feels crowded.
If you do want to get close to the Trevi Fountain without the crowds and admission fee, I recommend stopping by during off-peak hours, such as 5 a.m. or 2 a.m. Or, you can view it from the street for free.
Cinque Terre can be enjoyable, but not on a day trip.
Many visitors to Florence take a day trip to Cinque Terre, a string of five villages in Italy's Liguria region.
Although Cinque Terre — and Liguria itself, for that matter — are worthy of a visit, I believe that trying to tackle this as a day trip from Florence is pure foolishness. I've found that even the fastest journeys from Florence take about two hours by train or car.
Then, you're trying to rush through five villages, each full of beaches, hikes, cliffs, and great restaurants.
It's simply too much for a day, so if you want to visit Cinque Terre, choose one or two villages and spend some proper time there, instead.

Reversing a downward trend over the past two months, monthly electric two-wheeler (E2W) registrations bounced back in September. As per Vahan data, total E2W sales for the month of September stood at 2.07 Lakh units, up 12.2% month-on-month increase from 1.84 Lakh units registered in August. Important to note that Inc42 had reported 1.72 lakh E2W registrations for August based on the data available on August 31, while the latest Vahan data puts the month at 1.84 lakh units, a 7% upward revision. From a year-on-year (YoY) lens, September’s total registration almost doubled 1.05 Lakh units registered in September 2025. The top three traditional OEMs — TVS Motor, Bajaj and Hero MotoCorp — together accounted for around 61% of September registrations, with all three recording month-on-month growth. In contrast, new-age players such as Ola Electric, Ather and BGauss saw more mixed performance. While Ather’s registrations rose 4.9%, Ola declined 3.5% and BGauss was broadly flat. The September rebound also comes against a broader strengthening of India’s electric mobility market. As per reports, total EV registrations rose 64.6% YoY to 3.15 Lakh units in the month. In this, E2Ws accounted for the bulk of this growth. The growth could partly reflect the build-up to the festive season, when automakers and dealers typically step up inventory and promotional activity. Established two-wheeler manufacturers are also expanding their EV portfolios and distribution reach, making electric scooters more accessible to mainstream buyers. This shift towards mass-market products could further support volumes as manufacturers target buyers beyond the early-adopter segment with more affordable models and wider retail networks. While Ather launched its ₹99,999 scooter, Konarc, in late August, Ola Electric launched the S1Z scooter, priced at ₹79,999, around the same time. Incumbents Maintain Lead E2W market leader TVS Motor led the charge in September as well, with its market share now at 26%. The original equipment manufacturer (OEM) recorded 53,989 E2W registrations in September, an almost 10% MoM increase from 49,284 units recorded in the month prior. After capturing over a quarter of the Indian E2W market, TVS Motors has now embarked on an international expansion effort which includes establishing and expanding presence in countries like Nepal, Kenya, Sri Lanka and now, Indonesia, where it is planning to set up a manufacturing facility. With its current monthly manufacturing capacity at 40,000-45,000 units currently, it plans to raise that to 50,000-plus units in three to four months. Meanwhile, Bajaj Auto is hot on the trail, strengthening its position further in September with 48,383 registrations recorded in September, a 17% jump from 41,341 units recorded in August. Its total market share now stands at 23.4%. The OEM is on track to launch an electric motorbike in the coming months, and is meanwhile expanding its market position through its portfolio spanning premium to mass-market offerings. HeroMotocorp, while failing to re-enter the top three ranking, saw registrations soar 27% in September to 24,306 units. The OEM is nevertheless planning to launch its own electric motorcycle in 2027 alongside new e-scooter variants, while doubling down on manufacturing. Ather, Ola Lose Market Share In comparison to larger OEMs, Ather Energy saw tepid growth in September, with registrations inching up 5% MoM to 30,479 units from 29,068 in August. Its market share, meanwhile, fell 110 basis points to 14.7% during the month. Important to highlight that Ather’s overall sales have now crossed the 8 Lakh mark, making it the fourth OEM in the country to achieve the milestone. It expects sales momentum to accelerate as its newly launched affordable scooter Konarc picks up, and could make up for half of its sales within two years. Meanwhile, Ola Electric continued its downward trajectory in terms of registrations, which dipped 3.5% MoM to 13,449 units in September. The September decline comes as Ola attempts to rebuild its distribution network through dealer-led stores, targeting a network of more than 500 outlets, while also pushing cheaper products and its in-house Bharat Cells. E-scooter maker E-Sprinto recorded a blockbuster 16X MoM increase in registrations during the month to 1,997 units.The OEM is planning to substantially increase its presence on Indian roads in coming months, buoyed by plans to launch an affordable family scooter with a claimed range of 130 km on a single charge. Meanwhile, electric motorbike maker Oben also recovered substantially in September, registering 1,417 units in September, a 120% MoM surge from 642 units in August. On the other hand, its rival electric bike maker Ultraviolette saw registrations dip over 12% MoM to 536 units. The startup raised $85 Mn in equity funding during the month as it plans to shore up manufacturing and enter new markets in US, Latin America, and Southeast Asia. Besides Ultraviolette, River raised $120 Mn in August to expand its manufacturing as well. The e-scooter maker saw its registrations increase 6.4% to 5,549 units. Simple, which raised $180 Mn earlier this week, saw its registrations dip 19% MoM to 1,351 units in September. It plans to focus on a new manufacturing facility, higher production, an expanded distribution and service network, and the next generation of products. The startup recently launched the Simple Wave, an affordable family scooter series starting at ₹1.10 Lakh.

South Korea has demanded an apology from North Korea over a landmine blast that injured three soldiers, saying they were hurt by North Korean mines on the southern side of the border.
Kang Hyun-woo, the director of operations at South Korea’s joint chiefs of staff, demanded an apology and “responsible measures” from Pyongyang over the blast, which occurred on 21 September during a search operation south of the border.
He also called for an immediate halt to North Korea’s mine-laying and border fortification, which he said violated the armistice and the spirit of inter-Korean agreements. North Korea would bear “all responsibility” for any future developments, he said.
The incident echoes a 2015 mine blast in the demilitarised zone between the countries that seriously injured two South Korean soldiers and prompted Seoul to resume propaganda broadcasts over loudspeakers. North Korea responded to the move with artillery fire across the border before expressing regret during high-level talks.
The US-led UN command (UNC), which oversees the 1953 armistice that halted but did not end the Korean war, said on Wednesday that a joint investigation with South Korea’s military had identified a live North Korean anti-personnel mine on the southern side of the military demarcation line (MDL), the de facto border.
The UNC said an armistice violation had occurred and that it was addressing the issue through “established armistice mechanisms”.
The explosions occurred about 10 metres south of the MDL on the western front, as troops searched an area where North Korea was suspected of laying mines.
Two blasts went off about a minute apart, seriously injuring a battalion commander, whose foot was reportedly severed at the ankle, and an engineer. A third officer was present and has minor injuries from the explosion.
On Monday, South Korea’s military said interim findings showed the blasts were “highly likely” to have been caused by North Korean mines
North Korea has denied involvement. In a statement carried by state media on Wednesday, Kim Yo-jong, the sister of leader Kim Jong-un, called the incident “an obvious self-staged farce”.
“Our soldiers have never once crossed the border,” she said, warning that if South Korean troops fired directly at North Korean soldiers, border units would carry out “immediate and merciless retaliation”.
Chris Green, a senior consultant at the International Crisis Group, said the investigation findings would not settle the matter politically because the North would always have “guaranteed plausible deniability”.
There are no working communication channels between the two Koreas. Pyongyang severed ties in 2024, declared South Korea a hostile state and has since laid mines and built fortifications along the border. “Accidental escalation on the Korean peninsula is always just a few steps away and it’s fewer steps now than it was in 2015,” Green said.
The blast presents a challenge for South Korea’s president, Lee Jae Myung, who has sought to revive diplomacy with Pyongyang. Last week, he told the UN general assembly that Seoul would be a “pacemaker” for peace, and urged Washington to ease sanctions in exchange for a freeze on North Korea’s weapons programmes.
The incident has also fuelled political tensions at home. Opposition politicians questioned whether the investigation had been delayed to avoid overshadowing Lee’s UN speech, a suggestion the presidential office denied.
The conservative People Power party has also called for the return of the propaganda loudspeakers, which were switched off and dismantled under Lee last year.
The mine blast adds to other diplomatic difficulties facing Lee. On Monday, Seoul demanded an apology from Ukraine after its president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, disclosed the transfer of two North Korean prisoners of war to South Korea.
Seoul said the two sides had agreed to keep the transfer secret, citing the men’s safety and diplomatic and security considerations. Some critics said the secrecy was about not upsetting Pyongyang.

An investor lawsuit against UnitedHealth Group will move forward after a federal judge on Wednesday declined the company’s motion to dismiss allegations that it juiced its earnings to the tune of $3.3 billion in 2024 to conceal weakness in its Medicare Advantage business.
It wasn’t all good news for the California Public Employees’ Retirement System, or CalPERS, though. U.S. District Judge Jeffrey Bryan dismissed most of the pension fund’s allegations that UnitedHealth’s leaders deceived investors about multiple aspects of their business in order to artificially inflate the company’s stock. Bryan agreed with UnitedHealth that most of the company statements CalPERS cited weren’t specific enough or represented typical promotional “puffery” that investors wouldn’t act on.
One of the lawsuit’s central allegations was that the Minnesota-based conglomerate concealed an illegal practice of making its Medicare Advantage patients appear sicker on paper to siphon more money from the government. On that front, CalPERS cited the company’s statements that home visits kept its members healthy and that its clinicians made independent clinical decisions. In fact, reporting has since shown that UnitedHealth used those visits to add diagnoses to patients’ records for which they received no follow-up care and pressured its doctors to do the same using bonuses. .

Flydubai passenger describes hugging his children as plane nosedived during attack
- Published
A man has described how he hugged and reassured his two young children as their plane suddenly descended after one pilot stabbed the other in an attempt to seize control of the flight.
A Flydubai plane plunged more than 17,000ft (5,200m) in less than two minutes around two hours into its journey from Dubai to Tel Aviv on Wednesday, before passengers and crew overpowered him and retook control to land safely.
Adam Polovincik told BBC Newshour that he hugged his six-year-old son and three-year-old daughter "really hard" and tried to stay calm for them as the attack unfolded.
He praised the pilot who was stabbed and passengers who fought off and subdued the attacker, saying they were "true heroes".
The stabbed pilot is in a stable condition in hospital, while the alleged attacker has been arrested.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has said it was too early to say whether Iran was involved in the attack, but that the alleged attacker had undergone "Islamist radical indoctrination".
Polovincik, who was sitting in aisle 13, was flying home with his wife and children after an "amazing" holiday in Singapore and Thailand.
He said there had been a "huge degree of panic" on the plane as there was a "very, very, very sharp decrease in height".
- What we know about stabbing on Flydubai flight to Israel 
  - Published12 hours ago
He thought at first that this was simply because of an air pocket, but "it took a lot of time, almost a minute".
Everyone who had not been seated fell to the floor, the 40-year-old said.
"After a couple of seconds, we started to hear screams. 'There is blood, there is stabbing, we need help'," Polovincik said.
"At the end of the day, you understand very, very quickly that literally there is nothing that you can do at this point in time," he said.
Polovincik, a performance marketing analyst, said he tried to "be cool" for his children.
"You just tell them, yeah, everything's going to be all right. It's just a malfunction in the aeroplane, there is a crew under control, the passengers are helping them, [you] hug them really hard and try to keep your face so it doesn't look very panicked, try to keep your tone of voice."
But he said there was naturally a "high degree of panic" on the flight.
There were lots of families with children on the plane because the flight took place towards the end of a Jewish holiday period.
After about 10 to 15 minutes, he said a passenger in the cockpit told them the incident was "under control" and other staff were flying the plane.
In a video released by Netanyahu's office, passenger Yaniv Hayun described putting the attacker in a chokehold and pulling him out of the cockpit before other passengers helped pin him down.
Two other pilots who were onboard the flight then took over the controls and safely landed the plane, which had been carrying more than 150 passengers.
Polovincik said: "After they told us that the situation is, again, 'under control', then it was a bit harder to tell the kids that it's malfunctioned because people start to walk around the aeroplane covered with blood."
Polovincik was praised Indian pilot, Capt Smit Machchhar, who fought off his attacker and opened the door to the cockpit, allowing passengers to step in.
"Without him opening the door, we're probably not speaking here right now," he said, adding that he "can't even start saying our gratitude for this human being".
Polovincik said that, although he was not religious, he could not escape "the feeling that it was the hand of God yesterday" that had put "the pieces on the board in the way that they did".
"It's remarkable."
After the situation onboard was brought under control, the flight was diverted to Saudi Arabia, where Polovincik stressed the passengers, who were almost all Israeli, were treated well.
"They brought us water and food and coffee and even sweets for the kids - even though we don't have any diplomatic relationship between Israel and Saudi Arabia," he said.
The alleged attacker, who was arrested in Saudi Arabia, is expected to be transferred to the United Arab Emirates, from where the plane departed, Netanyahu told Fox News.
The passengers were taken to Tel Aviv on another flight later on Wednesday and were greeted at the airport by crowds of onlookers playing music, singing, dancing and waving Israeli flags.
Polovincik said it had been "such a terrible ending" to an amazing family trip and that it would take some time for his family to come to terms with what had occurred.
