Bhopal (Madhya Pradesh): Directorate of Enforcement (ED), Indore, has filed a prosecution complaint before the Special Court, Indore, against 21 accused persons and entities in the bank fraud case involving M/s Ruchi Global Limited, now known as M/s Agrotrade Enterprises Limited, on Thursday, said officials.
The court has issued notices to the accused for a pre-cognizance hearing.
ED initiated an investigation on the basis of an FIR registered by the CBI, Bhopal, against M/s Ruchi Global Limited (RGL) and its directors, alleging wrongful loss to the consortium banks.
Investigation has revealed that the company fraudulently availed non-fund-based credit facilities, such as Letters of Credit (LCs), aggregating Rs 66 crore, from the consortium banks in favour of related associate concerns.
These LCs were opened under the guise of purchasing agro-commodities against fabricated documents, including forged bills of exchange and fake lorry receipts. Upon discounting of these bills through negotiating banks, the proceeds of crime were rapidly layered through a network of shell, layering entities and integrated back into the bank accounts of the company within one to three days.
Due to non-payment by RGL on the due dates, all LCs devolved upon the issuing banks, resulting in a wrongful loss to the consortium banks. Earlier, during the investigation, ED conducted search operations on Dec 23, 2025, leading to the seizure of unaccounted cash amounting to Rs 23.50 lakh and the freezing of bank accounts.
Furthermore, a provisional attachment order was issued on Feb 18, 2026, attaching immovable property valued at Rs 5.13 crore.

Subhash Chandra Bose took Sanskrit as optional paper in civil services exam back in 1920: PM
Prime Minister Narendra Modi, at the UPSC's centenary celebrations, recalled that Subhas Chandra Bose took Sanskrit as an optional paper in the civil services exam in 1920 despite British rule. Modi also praised Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel for building India's "steel frame" and urged the UPSC to focus on the next 25 years.
Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Thursday hailed freedom fighter Subhas Chandra Bose for writing his civil services exam in Sanskrit in 1920, when the British were in power.
Modi was attending the centenary celebrations of the Union Public Service Commission (UPSC) here at Bharat Mandapam.
In his address, the prime minister called the event a celebration of aspirations of millions of young people.
"It is a celebration of the trust that every Indian places in this institution. During this century-long journey, generations changed, governments changed, technology changed, and syllabi changed, yet the trust in the UPSC remains just as unwavering today, and that is one of your greatest assets," Modi said.
He also asked everyone to go through the gallery set up at the venue.
"While viewing the gallery, I saw the details regarding the time - back in 1920 - when Subhas Chandra Bose also went through this very process. It struck me that although the British were in power at the time, there used to be a Sanskrit paper, and Subhas Babu wrote his exam in Sanskrit," the prime minister said.
Contrasting the institution's British Raj origins with its post-Independence evolution, he said that the system successfully shifted its focus to fulfil the dreams of a free nation.
Modi said that while the UPSC discharged its historical duties, the focus must now pivot toward the next 25 years.
The prime minister paid his homage to Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel (the first home minister of Independent India) for giving the newly formed nation a solid structure for governance.
He praised Sardar Patel for transforming and empowering the institution into a premier pillar of Independent India.
"The steel frame that was needed for the reconstruction of the nation was provided by Sardar Patel," Modi said.
April 21 is celebrated as Civil Services Day every year.
The day commemorates Patel's 1947 address at Metcalf House, Delhi, to civil services officers on probation, whom he called the "steel frame of India."
Civil Servants for the East India Company used to be nominated by company directors and trained at Haileybury College in London before they would be sent to India, according to the UPSC documents.
Following Lord Macaulay's report of the Select Committee of the British Parliament, the concept of a merit-based modern civil service in India was introduced in 1854. For this purpose, a Civil Service Commission was set up in 1854 in London, and competitive examinations were started in 1855.
UPSC's institutional journey began with the formation of India's first Public Service Commission on October 1, 1926. It became the Federal Public Service Commission on April 1, 1937.
After the Constitution of India came into effect on January 26, 1950, the Federal Public Service Commission became the Union Public Service Commission.

The cost of borrowing money is moving unrelentingly higher, with profound implications for savers, borrowers and the U.S. government's fiscal outlook.
The big picture: The bond market moves over the last few weeks have pushed most risk-free interest rates north of 5%.
Barring a rapid reversal, expect pain to come in interest-sensitive sectors like housing, new stress on federal government finances and greater risks of financial disruption.
It is better news for savers, who have taken paper losses on existing bonds in recent weeks but can now deploy cash safely with the best prospective returns seen in decades.
Zoom out: It is clearer than ever that the era of cheap borrowing and abundant capital that lasted from 2008 to 2021 is well and truly over.
Every individual looking to take a home mortgage or car loan is in competition with the voracious capital needs of the AI giants and the U.S. government.
While the Federal Reserve has gotten out of the business of forecasting its next moves, it is now looking out of position. Its leaders increasingly believe that it has set its policy rates too low to control inflation amid a growth boom, and are now looking to adjust course, which means last week's rate hike won't be the last.
Rate hikes may not deter much AI investment or government borrowing, which leaves all other interest-sensitive sectors to bear the brunt of bringing the economy into better balance.
Zoom in: The surge in rates has been driven for the most part by a rise in real yields — implying a stronger growth outlook, not an outburst in expected inflation.
Investors can now buy a 30-year inflation-protected Treasury security that pays 3.26%, the highest since 2002. This time five years ago, that number was negative.
The forward earnings yield of the S&P 500 is about 5%. With the 30-year nominal Treasury bond yielding around 5.5%, bonds look more attractive relative to stocks than they have in ages.
State of play: The recent surge in longer-term rates is poised to push 30-year fixed-rate mortgages to near 8%. Mortgage News Daily on Thursday clocked the 30-year rate at 7.45%, or 7.55% for jumbo loans.
Mortgage rates got that high briefly in the fall of 2023, but the last time they were above that level on a sustained basis was in 2000.
Over time, the housing market can find a balance. But in the near term, surges in rates just mean pain as the market freezes up.
People can't afford to buy houses with 7.5%+ rates, and sellers don't want to cut their prices, so there is a standstill, as witnessed in the fall of 2023, until either rates fall or prices adjust.
The intrigue: Higher rates, if sustained, will make America's fiscal situation considerably thornier.
The U.S. government's debt service costs were already projected to reach new highs in the coming years — but that burden will be much worse if the rate surge of the last few weeks is sustained.
By the numbers: In projections that the Congressional Budget Office produced last February, net interest costs are already at $1 trillion this year and on track to reach $2 trillion by 2035, meaning that much of federal spending is needed just to service old bills.
But those projections assumed 10-year Treasury yields were in the ballpark of 4.3%. They're now nearly a full percentage point higher than that.
In startling numbers that CBO released this week, in a scenario in which interest rates were 1 percentage point higher than its baseline, debt held by the public would grow to 222% of GDP in 2056, 47 percentage points higher than the baseline.
Reality check: Higher interest rates don't flow through to government debt service costs immediately. Longer-term bonds gradually mature over time.
So a reversal in rates would help the fiscal arithmetic (at least so long as it wasn't caused by a recession or productivity slump).
The bottom line: If the 5% world is here to stay, it commands a rethinking of the U.S. government's tax and spending policies, the price of assets, and more generally what we consider normal in an era of steep global demand for capital.

India’s food market, estimated at $550–$600 billion is growing at 6–7% CAGR, supported by economic growth and urbanisation, Devesh Deval, Joint Secretary, Ministry of Food Processing Industries said.
He said food processing, accounting for nearly 8% of gross value added in manufacturing, is strategically important as it creates greater value for farmers, attracts investment and is the second-highest employment creator in manufacturing.
“The government’s focus is to increase the level of processing across all 16 broad sub-sectors and ensure greater value reaches farmers,” Mr. Deval said on the on the sidelines of Anuga Select India and Anuga FoodTec India 2026 global food & beverages show organised by Koelnmesse in Mumbai.
“Cereals, meat, fruits and vegetables and dairy remain key segments, with India being the world’s second-largest producer of fruits and vegetables and the largest producer of milk. Fisheries, marine products and animal husbandry also receive dedicated policy attention, while healthier and plant-based foods are emerging areas of innovation,” he emphasised.
Stating that protein was particularly relevant given India’s large vegetarian population, he said there was a need to meet growing protein requirements.
Tarun Bajaj, senior consultant, Agricultural and Processed Food Products Export Development Authority (APEDA), speaking on the occasion, said India exported $53 billion worth of agricultural and processed food products in 2025–26, placing the country among the top 10 exporters globally.
“Despite geopolitical challenges, exports continue to grow, with rice, meat, marine products, coffee and tea among the leading products, while processed food exports are steadily increasing,” he said.
“This growth reflects the development of infrastructure at both the macro and micro levels, supported by conducive government policies and strong performance by farmers,” he said.
Speaking at the show Martina Englhardt-Kopf, Vice Minister, Ministry of Food and Agriculture, Federal Republic of Germany, said “At a time when geopolitical tensions, the pandemic and disruptions to global supply chains have highlighted the importance of resilience and food security, strong regional value chains must go hand in hand with stable, transparent and rules-based international trade.”
She said the conclusion of the India–EU Free Trade Agreement was therefore “an economically significant milestone, creating a market of around two billion people and liberalising trade covering 99.3% of EU and 96.6% of India’s trade value.”
Addressing delegates Silvio Erkens, Minister of Food Safety, Fisheries & Horticulture, Kingdom of the Netherlands, said “The food sector stands at the crossroads of opportunity and responsibility, with climate change, geopolitical instability and energy shortages creating new challenges for food production, trade and processing.”
“This makes international partnerships, innovation and business collaboration essential,” he said.
According to Milind Dixit, managing director, India & SAARC Region, Koelnmesse Pvt. Ltd. India’s food processing industry is entering an important phase of expansion, driven by rising domestic consumption, greater value addition, technology adoption and stronger integration with global markets.
“The sector has already reached around $382 billion in FY25 and is projected to approach $689 billion by FY34, while processed food now accounts for more than 20% of India’s agricultural exports,” he added.

The Treasury Committee has written to the chief executive of HM Revenue and Customs (HMRC) to ask about the tax implications of the Premier League's investigation into Manchester City.

The overhead conditions in Srinagar on Thursday were pristine. It meant that the Sher-i-Kashmir Stadium was bathed in sunshine for most of the opening day of the Irani Cup fixture between Jammu & Kashmir and Rest of India. But the surface beneath, imperative as it is to how the action unfolds, had a healthy covering of grass.
It put the onus on the pace bowlers to seize the day. J&K’s attack, despite the absence of Auqib Nabi due to his involvement in India’s ODI series against the West Indies, didn’t disappoint.
With Sunil Kumar and Lone Nasir making three inroads each, the host bowled out the Rishabh Pant-led outfit for 237. It could have been a day of utter dominance for Paras Dogra & Co., but RoI’s pacers, namely Mukesh Choudhary and Akash Deep, nabbed a wicket apiece as the shadows lengthened in the final hour. J&K was 21 for two at stumps.

To establish a comprehensive framework for registration of allied and healthcare professionals (AHP) in both the State Registers and the Central Register, the National Commission for Allied and Healthcare Professions (NCAHP) under the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare notified the Registration of Allied and Healthcare Professionals Regulations, 2026 on August 31, 2026, and published it in the Gazette of India on September 15, 2026.
(Sign up for THEdge, The Hindu’s weekly education newsletter.)
Under the new regulations, all allied and healthcare professionals spanning 57 vocations across 10 broad disciplines, including physiotherapists, dietitians, lab technologists, forensic psychologists, among others, will soon have to register in the State and Central registers to practise in their chosen fields.
Registration certificates, including digital certificates featuring the Unique Identification (UID) number and a secure QR code, will be issued to the professionals by the Commission or the respective State Council. This will facilitate identification and verification of registered professionals and support greater transparency in the delivery of allied and healthcare services. The registration and payment of the fee will be processed on a dedicated online portal developed by the Commission.
“These regulations mark a leap towards streamlining the allied and healthcare workforce. Unless and until the professional gets the UID, he/she will not be able to practise/work. There is a penalty of up to 6 months to two years’ jail term under the NCAHP Act-21 if the professional practices without registration,” Dr. Yagna Unmesh Shukla, chairperson of NCAHP said.
“The regulations also aim to bring uniformity in the registration of allied and healthcare professionals and ensure renewal. With this registration, the actual number of qualified professionals will be available, as well as the difference between qualified and non-qualified professionals, which is also one of the key objectives of the NCAHP Act-21,” she added.
Public access
Highlighting that the registration process is the first of its kind in the history of allied and healthcare professions, Dr. Shukla says that the regulations provide a real-time synchronisation between the State Registers and the Central Register through an integrated online system.
Further, the Central and State Registers will be accessible to the public through the websites of the Commission and the respective State Councils, which will display the prescribed particulars of registered professionals.
Since only persons meeting the prescribed eligibility requirements, including recognised qualifications and the applicable exit examination requirements, will be eligible for regular registration, this will provide an important safeguard for patients and service users by promoting the practice of appropriately qualified professionals.
The public will be able to verify the registration status and relevant details of allied and healthcare professionals through the websites of the Commission and the respective State Councils. Professionals residing in a State or Union Territory where a functional State Council has not yet been established may register directly with the Central Register.
A key feature of the Regulations is the flexibility they give to allied and healthcare professionals to register in one State and practise in another State. “This will mitigate the hassles professionals face when applying for registration in another state. All they now need to do is fill out the form and inform the state in which they reside of the state where they intend to practise, so that this information remains on record. Since each registered professional is provided with a UID number, all their records are documented, facilitating the smooth transfer of registration details from one state to another,” Dr. Shukla said.
Apart from registration certificates, including digital certificates featuring the UID and a secure QR code, registered allied and healthcare professionals will also have access to a Good Standing Certificate. It will help professionals pursue any foreign education or profession or participate in student exchange programmes outside India. “There is a big difference between registration and a Good Standing Certificate. Registration is the licence to practise in India, whereas a Certificate of Good Standing is issued by the State Council when required by various countries for professionals who wish to work or study in those countries,” Dr. Shukla says.
Registration of foreign-qualified professionals
The Regulations establish a pathway for Indian citizens holding foreign qualifications in allied and healthcare. A foreign-qualified allied and healthcare professional will be considered eligible to apply for registration provided his qualification is recognised by the Commission, or he has completed the prescribed credential equivalency evaluation, and has also passed the relevant exit examination, where applicable. “It is important to have an equivalence process of foreign qualified professionals in place for the safety of the patients,” Dr. Shukla adds.
There is also provision for temporary registration for eligible foreign-qualified Indian professionals for specific, time-bound purposes, including postgraduate or specialty education, fellowships, clinical research, observerships, advanced workshops, expert visits, and voluntary community service. Such registration remains subject to the conditions laid down in the Regulations and applicable regulatory guidelines.
Validity period
Under the regulations, the registration will remain valid for five years, renewable upon the fulfilment of Continuing Professional Development (CPD) requirements through approved online and offline modes. This means that professionals must upgrade themselves professionally (15 hours per year) by attending seminars, conferences, workshops, training programmes and faculty development programmes.
“It is important for professionals to update and upgrade themselves in their respective professions. Since the regulations are being implemented for the first time, flexibility in the CPD programme is being permitted. This explains why 50% of these participations in online mode are being considered,” Dr. Shukla said.
Additionally, the Commission is making efforts to introduce provisional registration for professionals currently practising in the allied and healthcare sector who lack the prescribed primary qualifications. Such professionals will be provided with an option to undergo a bridge course to attain eligibility for regular registration. The Commission is making concerted efforts to introduce provisional registration for professionals currently practising in the allied and healthcare sector who lack the prescribed primary qualifications.
“Those who are practising for many years and are not qualified as per the provisions of the Act will be registered under the Provisional Registration Act and will have to undergo a prescribed Bridge course within the given time period to attain eligibility for regular registration,” Dr. Shukla said.
Interim registrations
The Regulations have also introduced provisions for interim registration for students enrolled in recognised institutions who are undertaking internships, clinical training, observerships, or practical coursework required to complete an allied and healthcare qualification. Interim registration must be initiated by the recognised institution and obtained from the concerned State Council. No fee will be charged for interim registration applications, the NCAHP regulations stated.
(Rajlakshmi Ghosh is a journalist with over three decades of experience in media houses and educational institutions)

Tsawwassen First Nation identifies 2 elders killed in crash outside mall
2 more people in hospital in critical condition after Wednesday crash, police say
The Tsawwassen First Nation has identified the two elders who were struck and killed outside the Tsawwassen Mills mall on Wednesday while a National Day for Truth and Reconciliation event was taking place.
In a social media post, the nation identified the victims as wilapiya (Barb Joe) and Virginia Splockton.
The nation described Joe as a "cultural pillar, knowledge keeper and matriarch" who was responsible for reviving the hən̓q̓əmin̓əm̓ language.
Splockton is being remembered as beloved family member and pillar of the community with a deep love for crafting, drumming, singing and who "was always willing to lend a helping hand to those in need."
The elders' families, in the social media posts shared by the First Nation, thanked the community for the outpouring of support they have received in the wake of the tragedy.
The deadly collision occurred around 10:25 a.m. PT on Sept. 30, when police say a vehicle struck four pedestrians outside the mall.
Two were killed, while two others were taken to hospital.
The driver of a the vehicle received medical attention following the crash and has since been released from hospital.
In an update earlier Thursday, police say the two people taken to hospital remain in critical condition, with "serious, life-altering injuries," according to Delta Police Department Staff Sgt. Mike Whiteley.
The two people who were injured are not members of the Tsawwassen First Nation, Whiteley added.
"This was a very tragic event," Whiteley told reporters at a news conference on Thursday afternoon.
"It was very difficult for our first responders, but also for our community, and especially for the Tsawwassen First Nation."
While the crash happened while a Truth and Reconciliation Day Walk was taking place elsewhere on the mall property, police say there is no evidence linking the collision to the event.
Police said Wednesday that the male driver of the vehicle may have suffered a medical emergency in the moments leading up to the crash. They did not elaborate on what that medical emergency was.
"At this time, there is no information to suggest the collision was intentional," Delta Police said in its Thursday news release.
Video from the scene of the crash on Wednesday shows a pickup truck with the logo for the company Alpine Building Maintenance printed on its side.
In a statement Thursday, the company confirmed one of its vehicles was involved in the collision.
"We are co-operating with the appropriate authorities to support their investigation. Our thoughts are with everyone affected," it said.
No charges have been sworn as of Thursday afternoon, police said.
"If the evidence warrants us forwarding charges to Crown counsel, then we'll be doing that," Whiteley said.
Prime Minister Mark Carney and leaders on the B.C. election campaign trail — David Eby, Emily Lowan and Lorne Doerkson — expressed their condolences to the families and the First Nation after the crash on Wednesday.
The Indian Residential School Survivors Society said in a post on social media that the loss of the two "beloved" elders is devastating, while the Huu-ay-aht First Nations on Vancouver Island said it feels the tragedy deeply as an elder who died was a grandparent of one of its citizens.
In a statement issued Thursday, the Tsawwassen First Nation requested privacy as it grieved the loss of the two elders, adding that its offices would be closed on Oct. 1 and 2.
"Two beloved [elders] from our community lost their lives. Our hearts are with their families, loved ones, and all those affected by this devastating loss. We are also holding close in our thoughts those who were injured and everyone who witnessed this tragedy," the statement reads.
"We recognize the profound impact this tragedy has had on our community as a whole. During this incredibly difficult time, we are grateful for the care, compassion, and support that has been extended to Tsawwassen First Nation."
With files from Michelle Gomez, Simon Little and The Canadian Press

SpaceX's Crew Dragon "Grace" spacecraft stacked atop its trunk section during preparations for the Crew-13 mission at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station, Florida.
Credit:
SpaceX
SpaceX's Crew Dragon "Grace" spacecraft stacked atop its trunk section during preparations for the Crew-13 mission at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station, Florida.
Credit:
SpaceX
A four-person crew rocketed into orbit Thursday from Cape Canaveral Space Force Station, Florida, heading for a six-month expedition on the International Space Station.
Riding a Falcon 9 rocket and Dragon spacecraft, the four crew members departed from Space Launch Complex-40 at Cape Canaveral at 11:10 am EDT (15:10 UTC) Thursday. Nine minutes later, they were in orbit to begin closing in on the space station for docking Thursday evening.
The launch was delayed from mid-September to replace a balky valve in the Dragon spacecraft’s propulsion system, a task that involved cutting into a propellant line inside the ship to swap out a faulty component.
Jessica Watkins, a 38-year-old geologist turned astronaut, leads the four-person crew sent into orbit Thursday, becoming the first Black woman to command a spacecraft. Watkins is the only veteran astronaut on the mission—designated Crew-13—after spending 170 days in orbit on a long-duration spaceflight in 2022.
Pilot Luke Delaney, a Marine Corps veteran, was seated next to Watkins for the Dragon spacecraft’s ascent into orbit. Two international crew members rounded out the Crew-13 team: Canadian astronaut Joshua Kutryk, a former pilot in the Royal Canadian Air Force, and Sergey Teteryatnikov, a Russian cosmonaut who served as a naval engineer before his selection to the Roscosmos Cosmonaut Corps in 2021.
Kutryk and his wife Heather are expecting their third child later this year. It’s rare, but astronauts have been off the planet for their child’s birth before. Most recently, NASA astronaut Randy Bresnik, set to command the Artemis III mission next year, was flying aboard the Space Shuttle Atlantis in 2009 when his wife gave birth to their daughter, Abigail Mae, in Houston.
“Leaving these three (plus one on the way) is the hardest thing I’ve ever done. But that has always been the nature of exploration,” Kutryk wrote on X.
Watkins and her crewmates were on course to reach the International Space Station (ISS) about eight hours after launch, the fastest-ever launch-to-docking transit to the ISS by a US spacecraft.
NASA astronaut Jessica Watkins, commander of the Crew-13 mission, arrives at Kennedy Space Center, Florida, ahead of launch.
Credit:
NASA/Kim Shiflett
NASA astronaut Jessica Watkins, commander of the Crew-13 mission, arrives at Kennedy Space Center, Florida, ahead of launch.
Credit:
NASA/Kim Shiflett
“What an epic ride. What an epic ride it was,” Delaney radioed mission control soon after reaching orbit. “Today, we proudly continue the streak of humans living and working in orbit, building on the legacies of yesterday to pave the way for the future of space exploration.”
The ISS has been permanently staffed since 2000, with crews flying to and from the orbiting outpost on NASA’s Space Shuttles, Russian Soyuz spacecraft, and most recently, SpaceX’s Crew Dragon. NASA and its international partners plan to keep the space station operating through at least 2030. SpaceX’s plans to retire the Crew Dragon vehicle around 2030 have prompted NASA to work more closely with Boeing to bring its troubled Starliner crew capsule into service.
Honing their craft
Thursday’s flight was the 13th crew rotation mission launched by SpaceX under a multibillion-dollar contract with NASA, and SpaceX’s 21st human spaceflight overall, including test flights and fully commercial missions.
The company’s success with the Crew Dragon spacecraft restored the country’s ability to launch astronauts into orbit after a nine-year gap following the Space Shuttle retirement in 2011, ending NASA’s sole reliance on Russia for crew transportation. NASA’s other commercial crew provider, Boeing, has repeatedly stumbled on a series of test flights with its Starliner spacecraft.
SpaceX’s plans to retire Crew Dragon and the Falcon 9 rocket mean the fleets are now well beyond halfway through their operational life. SpaceX has nine more Crew Dragon flights in its backlog, including three additional crew missions to the ISS that NASA recently secured in a $946 million contract extension, bringing NASA’s total contract for 17 SpaceX crew missions to $5.92 billion.
That figure is a drop in the bucket next to SpaceX’s projected revenues from its ever-growing Starlink broadband service, the Starship/Super Heavy rocket, and orbital data centers. SpaceX, now a publicly traded company, is prioritizing its most lucrative lines of business, and flights to the ISS aren’t among them.
Canadian Space Agency astronaut Joshua Kutryk poses for a photo with his wife, Heather, and children after walking out from the Neil Armstrong Operations and Checkout Building at Kennedy Space Center, Florida, ahead of his launch aboard a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket.
Credit:
Paul Hennesy/Anadolu via Getty Images
Canadian Space Agency astronaut Joshua Kutryk poses for a photo with his wife, Heather, and children after walking out from the Neil Armstrong Operations and Checkout Building at Kennedy Space Center, Florida, ahead of his launch aboard a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket.
Credit:
Paul Hennesy/Anadolu via Getty Images
Bill Gerstenmaier, SpaceX’s vice president of build and flight reliability, declined to say in a prelaunch press conference Wednesday if there is a “hard cutoff” for when the company will no longer offer Crew Dragon flights to NASA. The recent contract extension may be the last.
“We were just awarded Crew flights 15, 16, and 17, so I think our real focus is to make sure we get the most out of those flights,” Gerstenmaier said. “So we’re working really super hard to make sure that our vehicles are ready, things are ready to go fly, and we’ll keep moving forward.”
Notably, SpaceX is winding down Crew Dragon and Falcon 9 at the top of their game. Gerstenmaier pointed to the valve replacement inside the Crew Dragon spacecraft for the Crew-13 mission as evidence of SpaceX’s commitment to fulfilling its contract with NASA.
NASA announced a postponement for the Crew-13 launch in late August to give ground teams time to resolve an oxidizer leak inside Dragon’s propulsion system detected during launch preparations at Cape Canaveral. SpaceX traced the leak to a valve. The spacecraft was already loaded with nitrogen tetroxide, or NTO, the volatile, toxic oxidizer used by Dragon’s control thrusters in combination with hydrazine fuel.
Teams devised an unprecedented bit of spaceship surgery to replace the valve without draining the propellant and disassembling the spacecraft, steps that would have triggered a much longer delay. The fix involved cutting into the propellant line, removing and replacing the valve, then welding the line together again. It was the first time SpaceX has performed such a repair with a fully assembled Dragon spacecraft loaded with propellant.
A SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket carrying the company’s Dragon spacecraft lifts off on the Crew-13 mission to the International Space Station.
Credit:
NASA/John Kraus
A SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket carrying the company’s Dragon spacecraft lifts off on the Crew-13 mission to the International Space Station.
Credit:
NASA/John Kraus
“By cutting it out, we physically went in and actually cut the valve out of the line,” Gerstenmaier said. “It was welded in place, and then we actually re-welded a new valve in place.”
Engineers are testing the bad valve to diagnose the cause of the leak, but NASA officials were pleased with the fix. No leaks were detected during final preparations for launch Thursday, and Dragon’s propulsion system appeared to be functioning well after arriving in orbit.
“We looked at the plans, all of the data coming out of that, the welds, the leak, everything looks great,” said Dana Weigel, NASA’s program manager for the International Space Station. [We’re] really happy with how that repair was done.”
SpaceX’s preference to cut out the valve in place, rather than take a longer stand-down, kept the Crew-13 mission on track to arrive at the space station in time to replace Crew-12, which will return to Earth in mid-October after eight months in orbit.
The Crew Dragon spacecraft was inside SpaceX’s fueling and hazardous processing facility, known as Area 59, at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station, not at the company’s usual maintenance hangar a few miles away.
“I actually went down and looked at the vehicle itself, got in the clean room, and took a look to see where they actually had to cut the valve out,” Gerstenmaier said. “There was not a lot of room, but there was good access up on the platform. I think the unique aspect of this was the location where it was being done.
“We also did it with oxidizer onboard the vehicle, and the oxidizer tank was full, so we made sure that was all clear,” Gerstenmaier said. “We had to get special permission from the [Space Force’s Eastern] Range to do these activities, to do ‘hot work’ with NTO, with nitrogen tetroxide on the vehicle.”
Stephen Clark is a space reporter at Ars Technica, covering private space companies and the world’s space agencies. Stephen writes about the nexus of technology, science, policy, and business on and off the planet.

World Contraception Day on September 26 offers an opportunity to look closely at a part of family planning that receives very little attention: contraception for men. The key question here is why the range of methods available to men and women remains so different.
Women today have options including oral pills, injectables, implants, intrauterine devices and permanent sterilisation, though access and affordability to safe and reliable contraception in our country continues to remain a major challenge. For men, the practical choices are still largely limited to condoms for reversible contraception and vasectomy for permanent contraception. Male and female reproduction are governed by the same broad hormonal axis, yet the biology, anatomy and mechanics of preventing conception create very different problems. Understanding those differences helps explain why a male equivalent of the pill has remained elusive.

Police may have new ways to access data on locked iPhones
A training video reportedly demonstrates how police can evade an Apple security feature.
Privacy is one of Apple's core tenets, and in 2024, the company began equipping many iPhones with an inactivity reboot feature. This automatically restarts the device if it has not been unlocked for more than 72 hours. In practice, this has meant that law enforcement officials have been unable to access information on a smartphone. However, 404 Media reported that it has seen a training video made for law enforcement that allegedly demonstrates how tools made by Magnet Forensics can access data usually made unavailable by iPhones' inactivity reboot.
"This is an absolute game changer for iOS forensics and a function that I wish we had years ago," a Magnet employee reportedly says in the video. Magnet Forensics makes GrayKey, which it primarily sells to police as a means of unlocking smartphones. According to the new video, the company has developed a workaround for iPhones' inactivity reboot both in a new GrayKey Preserve tool and in a new Evidence Preservation Mode for GrayKey.
Although the video does not explicitly state how these resources work, 404 Media suggested that Magnet was able to put the phone in a state referred to as After First Unlock. More information can be accessed than when a device is in AFU compared to Before First Unlock. In the latter state, it is more difficult for anyone other than the owner to unlock the device and more of the data it contains is in an encrypted state. A Magnet rep is quoted as saying in the video that "Even if that device does reboot for any number of reasons, memory maintenance or the power is lost or whatever, the AFU state is not lost."
Magnet workers claimed that the new products would also be able to prevent automatic iPhone features that delete some data after a certain number of days, including cached locations as well as recently deleted iMessages and photos. It's an unsettling development at a time when both local law enforcement teams and multiple federal agencies have faced accusations of skirting the lines of citizens' digital privacy.

The setting for perhaps the country’s biggest exercise in public debate was quintessential rural India: fields of green paddy, a pond, a temple. On a normal day, as dusk falls in the village of Ajgara, in Uttar Pradesh, people gather beside the pond to chat about the price of crops, the weather, or the theft of a goat.
But for more than a month, metaphysics and ethical dilemmas replaced the usual topics. Is it permissible to use deceit to defeat an evil enemy? Is a lie justified to save a life? What is the nature of reality?
The debating tournament was the brainchild of Abhishek Pandey, district magistrate of Pratapgarh district in Uttar Pradesh. When he took up the post two years ago, he knew the area was rich in archaeological treasures connected to the ancient Indian epic, the Mahabharata.
Throughout the text, Yudhishthira, one of the central characters, debates the nature of human existence. In Ajgara he answers a string of philosophical questions to save the lives of his four brothers.
Pandey, 35, like most Indians, grew up on this story and was proud of the intellectual depth of the dialogues. When he attended Oxford University on a fellowship, he admired the debating society, which has a 200-year-long history. But India’s tradition of sophisticated public debate is much older, going back more than 3,000 years.
Pandey started to question why the tradition had not survived. “Indians have celebrated certain traditions for centuries,” Pandey says. “Why have we ceased to celebrate the legacy of debate and questioning?” Was it possible to revive this noble tradition, particularly when it was a vital component of a democracy?
He decided that the annual fair held in Ajgara in September would be a good time to stage the event. In the run-up to the fair, Pandey and his team arranged 1,500 debates across the district.
Age and education were no bar. The youngest participant was a 10-year-old schoolboy, the oldest an 80-year-old farmer. In debating for and against a motion, participants were judged on reasoning and moral clarity.
The overwhelming public response dumbfounded Pandey. Thousands of people participated in multiple rounds, and were whittled down to eight finalists – two women and six men.
While villagers milled around, enjoying the food, watching folk theatre, buying local crafts and taking a ride on a ferris wheel, a silence descended inside the debating tent.
The finale of the Great Ajgara Debate 2026 on 17 September lasted about six hours.
One topic was women’s rights. A finalist, Vivek Singh, argued that women might have equality on paper but society’s expectations of them impeded the exercise of these rights.
Another, Prajjwal Shukla, 24, argued that the real question was not what role society assigned to women but who had the authority to make those choices. Whether a woman chose a career, household responsibilities, or both, should be her choice and hers alone, he said.
“What amazed me the most was not the intellectual quality of the debates (which was great), but the atmosphere. Everyone listened respectfully, patiently, without interrupting. No one got personal. People sat for hours,” says Pandey.
Marx’s adage that history repeats itself, first as tragedy and then as farce, is a perfect description of how debate in India has descended from the sublime to the farcical.
In television studio debates everyone shouts at the same time. No one can finish a point. Personal abuse and gibes fly while the anchor whips them into ever greater frenzies.
Sadhana Dwivedi, one of the two women to progress into the last round of the Great Ajgara Debate, despises this new format.
“People need to learn to listen, to understand there may be value in another person’s point of view,” she says. “In a democracy, it is crucial for all opinions to be aired so that we can get to the truth.”
The turnout was a good demonstration of the thesis posited in economist Amartya Sen’s book The Argumentative Indian that India had a rich tradition of questioning authority and entertaining heterodoxy.
It is only in recent years that dissent has been suppressed, notably by the ruling Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata party, which values conformity.
“It’s ironic, because the BJP wants to recreate a Hindu state but is not even acquainted with the traditions of ancient Hindu civilisation, such as that of debate and being open to different ideas,” says author and commentator Parsa Venkateshwar Rao Jnr.
At the end of the tournament, the eight finalists were garlanded and driven around in an open-top car to much cheering, feted as “intellectual heroes”. The winner was Shukla, who is preparing to sit exams to enter the civil service.
“I can’t believe I am the winner of a debate that took place at the exact same spot as in the Mahabharata all those centuries ago. I participated just because I wanted to hear other people’s thoughts,” he says.
Pandey is still processing the public enthusiasm. “My deputy asked me if we should get some police deployment because the turnout everywhere was so big, but I laughed and said no. That would be a sad affair.”
He hopes to spread the event across other Indian states and perhaps nationwide. “We have to inculcate a culture of debate. It’s the hallmark of a democracy.”
Meanwhile, he has planted his flag. The inscription on the stone slab he has installed at the site reads: “The Great Ajgara Debate. First Debate 3152 BC: Yudhishthira. Second Debate 2026: Prajjwal Shukla.”

Donald Trump has said he may ask European countries to release some of their diesel reserves as he mulls a ban on US exports of the fuel amid a global shortage.
The comments followed his Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent urging for Europe to immediately ready and release such supplies. "American farmers, truckers, and businesses should not be left carrying the burden" as prices soar, he argued.
The US has threatened to restrict diesel exports amid surging costs due to the war in Iran. The issue is top of mind for US voters ahead of the crucial midterm elections.
On Thursday, Britain held talks with European partners about the potential release of diesel reserves in response to any ban.
The US is a vital supplier of diesel to the world, exporting between 1.2 and 1.5 million barrels per day, with experts warning a ban on shipments abroad could put further pressure on prices in other countries.
"We're thinking about it very seriously," Trump said of an export ban at the weekend.
On Thursday Trump added that he may ask European countries to release some of their diesel reserves, while Bessent said they should do so "immediately".
"Our European partners should accelerate delivery on their existing commitments and make additional supplies immediately available to address ongoing disruptions," Bessent said in a post on social media.
The plans come weeks ahead of November elections in the US, where control of Congress will be up for grabs. The president is set to travel across the US campaigning for Republicans in hopes of keeping control of the House and Senate.
Diesel prices in the UK hit record highs this week and are hovering just under 200p per litre, according to motoring organisation the RAC.
Britain's Energy Minister Martin McCluskey was on a call with European counterparts on Thursday to discuss the potential ban.
A source familiar with the discussions told the BBC it was prudent to prepare a co-ordinated response with other countries, including those across EU, but added that there were still European reserves left from a coordinated release of strategic fuel stocks earlier in the year.
"We have a diverse and resilient supply. We continue to engage with our international partners and the UK fuel industry," a government spokesperson said. The government has stressed that there is no cause for concern about potential diesel shortages, though prices are expected to rise further.

A video is being shared on social media (here, here, and here) with claims that it allegedly shows the Chief of the Army Staff, General Dhiraj Seth, dancing with Supreet Sapra, described as the wife of an Army major. The video features a purported CNN headline stating, “Indian Army Chief Dhiraj Seth Spotted Dancing with Army Major’s wife Supreet Sapra,” giving the impression that CNN published the video. Let’s verify the truth behind the video in this article.
Claim: The video shows Chief of the Army Staff General Dhiraj Seth dancing with Supreet Sapra, the wife of an Army major.
Fact: The video has been digitally manipulated to make it appear as though Chief of the Army Staff General Dhiraj Seth is dancing with Supreet Sapra. CNN has not published any report or headline matching the one shown in the viral video. The original video, shared in March 2026, features a different man and woman dancing at a gathering. Supreet Sapra has also clarified that she is not an Army major’s wife and that the woman shown in the viral video is AI-generated. The Indian Army’s fact-check wing has also confirmed that the video is digitally manipulated. Hence, the claim made in the post is FALSE.
To verify the claim, we conducted a Google search using relevant keywords but found no credible reports carrying the viral footage on CNN’s official website or any report or headline matching the one circulating with the video.
Upon closely reviewing the viral video, we noticed several inconsistencies. Though the man and woman appear to be dancing while holding glasses, the liquid inside them does not move or splash naturally as they dance. In one frame, the man’s ear and cheek area also appear smudged, while the faces of people in the background appear heavily blurred. The man’s face remains almost completely frozen with a wide smile throughout the video, further raising signs of AI manipulation.
We then ran the video through multiple AI detection tools, including DetectVideo AI and Meta AI’s verification platform. Both assessed the clip as likely AI-generated and detected AI signatures in the video.
The viral video contains an inset photograph showing a woman with a different man wearing a defence uniform. To learn more about the photograph, we conducted a reverse image search, which led us to an Instagram post (archived) by @sufimeranaam, dated 22 February 2026, featuring the same image. Newschecker contacted the account user regarding the viral video. She identified herself as Supreet Sapra and said, “I am Supreet Sapra, but I am not a major’s wife. My husband retired four years ago. The woman in the video is AI-generated, so apart from the name, everything is misinformation.”
Further investigation led us to an Instagram post (archived) by Rhythm Gupta, shared on 11 March 2026, with the caption, “Always dancing weirdly.” The video features a man and a woman dancing at a gathering. Their dance movements, the way they hold their glasses, and the song playing in the background are the same as those in the viral video. Although the background differs in colour and certain visual details, the overall setting and arrangement of elements are similar, and the movements of people around the dancing pair also closely resemble. This indicates that the viral video was likely manipulated using the earlier footage to make it appear as though the Army Staff chief was dancing with an Army major’s wife. Comparison of screengrabs from the viral clip and the Instagram video can be seen below.
The Indian Army’s fact-checking wing also clarified in an X post (archived) on 29 September 2026 that the viral video is digitally manipulated and fake.
To sum up, this viral video of Chief of the Army Staff General Dhiraj Seth dancing with Supreet Sapra, the wife of an Army major, is AI-manipulated.

South African white genocide does not exist, new ambassador to US tells BBC
- Published
South Africa's new ambassador to Washington has a personal reason to challenge Donald Trump's assertion that there is a genocide against white Afrikaners - he is "a born Afrikaner" himself.
"Is he talking about us?", Roelf Meyer remembers thinking, when he first heard President Trump say it.
His response to the US president's claim is blunt.
The notion of a mass attack on the white Afrikaner minority in South Africa does not exist, he told the BBC, adding that his identity gave him the legitimacy to say so.
Meyer was one of the chief mediators to end white-minority rule known as apartheid in South Africa in the 1990s. He was appointed ambassador to the US in April, after diplomatic relations between the US and South Africa plummeted.
In an interview with the BBC, Meyer said the facts about violence in South Africa had been misrepresented and he never got a clear answer about where this "misdirection of information" was coming from.
Last year, Trump accused South Africa of white genocide in a meeting with President Cyril Ramaphosa at the White House and launched a US refugee pathway for Afrikaners.
Since last year, nearly 13,000 refugees were admitted to the United States and all but three were South African.
Among them was Lielie, the name she uses publicly, who moved with her family to Texas from South Africa, where they had lived on her stepfather's farm, growing macadamia nuts and bananas.
Despite walls around the house, an electric fence, and eight bull terriers, she said she felt "fear the whole time" and that on three occasions she saw people entering her property.
"Nothing was stolen, we weren't harmed, but there are friends of my husband, people that lived around us, they were brutally attacked," she said.
She said since moving to the US under the Trump administration's refugee pathway her life had changed, she felt safer walking around, and "my kids can actually play outside".
The Trump administration is planning to admit up to 17,500 additional white Afrikaners as refugees over the next 12 months, according to a notice sent to Congress on Tuesday.
In a statement to the BBC, a White House spokeswoman said: "President Trump has provided a lifeline for Afrikaners, who are being raped, maimed, killed and driven off their property across South Africa.
"While the South African government and many in the media have brushed off the horrific lived experiences of this community, the Trump administration continues to process applications for refugee status because the president has a humanitarian heart."
SJ Du Venage, who lives on South Africa's west coast, has been trying to move to the US under the new scheme.
Du Venage is a council member of the Freedom Front Plus, a right-wing Afrikaner party, and argues that there is a "political drive towards killing white people, and killing the farmers on the farms".
"There's absolutely an agenda to wipe us out here," he says.

An Afrikaner lobby group is holding a vigil on Saturday with thousands of white crosses on Washington's National Mall to commemorate what it says are victims of "farm attacks".
Claims of genocide against white South Africans have been discredited by every political party in the country, including by those representing Afrikaners.
"I'm an Afrikaner from South Africa myself," Ambassador Meyer said, "and I can say that I've never experienced something of that kind."
Meyer said he would like to have a conversation with Trump about the reality of the situation, saying that as a "born Afrikaner", he has the "legitimacy" to speak about the subject.
The ambassador helped negotiate an end to apartheid on behalf of the National Party, which was responsible for it, with now-president Cyril Ramaphosa also a key negotiator for the African National Congress party.
He said the "trust" between the two men was one reason President Ramaphosa appointed him to help mend US-South Africa relations, as well as "the fact he also saw the value of me being an Afrikaner".
"But I'm not here to represent the Afrikaner only," Meyer says.
Last week, the Trump administration announced visa restrictions for those South Africans who it said were responsible for "race-based discrimination" against white people. It also warned of further punitive actions if South African leaders did not address the issue.
Police data shows the majority of victims of crime in South Africa, including on farms, are black. Farm violence, often motivated by robberies, is an issue but represents a smaller number of homicides in the country.
While no politician disputes that crime is a problem in South Africa, many experts say this does not qualify as "persecution".
Larry Bartlett, the former director of the US Refugee Assistance Programme, said it could even be "unlawful" to appropriate a programme defined in law for people who "really have no chance to go home".
He said white people who were unlikely to qualify as refugee in law were taking scarce opportunities meant for those fleeing war or ethnic cleansing.
The programme has its critics among Afrikaners in South Africa too.
"Why single out the white Afrikaner to say this group qualifies to flee to the US? This country suffers gender-based violence. Why not single out women?" Rudi Swanepoel, a pastor from Johannesburg told the BBC.
Swanepoel thinks it is not persecution but a "loss of privilege" that is causing some Afrikaners to feel aggrieved.
"To use the metaphor of a cake, 30, 40 years ago the white people of South Africa controlled the cake," he says. "Since democracy came, the obvious reality was we had to now start sharing that cake and those privileges."
Alongside "rural safety", the Trump administration has raised other concerns about South Africa, including targets for companies to increase non-white employment and a law allowing the state, in exceptional circumstances, to expropriate land without compensation. These are aimed at redressing historic racial inequality.
Meyer wants Trump's executive order against South Africa, which underpins the refugee pathway, revoked.
He said South Africa had never prevented people from leaving and had addressed all the US concerns, stressing that the land expropriation law is awaiting a court judgement.
"South Africa has challenges with the prevention of crime and with the combatting of crime," he said.
But he added: "It's a problem all around. It's not rural. It's not farm attacks only. If you look at the total picture, the huge levels of crime in the black townships of South Africa are the biggest concern, proportionally, far more than anything else."
He said he would encourage the US to help South Africa with resources on combatting crime, including by providing equipment to speed up reaction times.
Meyer also has a message for Afrikaners protesting against "farm attacks" by laying white crosses in Washington.
"It doesn't help us to raise a voice outside, if we are not committed to doing something inside the country," he says.

Three takeaways from Trump's 'Super Intelligence' summit
- Published
US President Donald Trump hosted a meeting of top technology bosses on Tuesday for what he called "an extraordinary gathering" of the minds that are "building America's Golden Age".
The guest list included leaders from OpenAI, Anthropic, Nvidia, SpaceX, Meta and Google - all key figures in the US AI industry.
The meeting came as some tech executives and experts have called for tighter oversight of AI, citing concerns about the potential risks it poses to humanity.
Here are three key takeaways from Trump's tech summit at the White House.
1. AI 'self-regulation' pact
Trump took questions from the media for around 30 minutes alongside top tech leaders after the closed-door meeting.
The president said the executives had signed a "morally binding" document that would serve as a "form of protection" from AI's potential risks.
Under the agreement, which Trump posted online, external, the companies are responsible for ensuring the safety of their own technology.
The firms also agreed to implement safeguards to keep models operating as intended and quickly detect and fix any issues.
They will also work with "independent auditors" to assess whether their AI systems are working as intended and ensure their platforms do not "hack or access technical systems in unintended ways."
The accord was signed by Trump, Google boss Sundar Pichai, Anthropic chief Dario Amodei, Meta's Mark Zuckerberg, OpenAI President Greg Brockman, SpaceX's Elon Musk and Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang.
"It's almost like a constitution, in a way," Trump said, referring to the agreement. "And the biggest people in the world signed that, and I signed it as president."
Trump added that he will set up a board to oversee the safety of AI tools. He did not specify who would be on that board.
Zuckerberg said the accord gives the "American people and customers the confidence that the technology works" as intended, calling the meeting a "historic conversation".
Amodei called it was a way "to win safely", referring to the president's comment earlier this month that "whoever wins AI, wins".
But not all experts are impressed with the accord.
Nanyang Technological University AI governance researcher Jose Miguelito Enriquez said the pact shows "emerging consensus" but does not address whether AI developers should be held accountable for incidents.
It is "deeply unimpressive" and comes despite calls from some world leaders and industry figures for tighter regulations over the technology, said law professor Kimberlee Weatherall from the University of Sydney.
The agreement appears to allow firms to "define what counts as safety" and does not state what consequences there are to any breaches, Weatherall said.
"The accord should be ignored, for the distraction it is," she added.
- Why Trump is all-in on AI despite the warnings 
  - Published16 September
- Why are there concerns AI could threaten humanity, and how real are they? 
  - Published17 September
Trump has repeatedly downplayed concerns about AI's risks, even as major AI firms have called for tighter oversight over the technology.
On Monday, OpenAI said it had scrapped the release of its latest flagship AI model, GPT-6.1 Astra, over safety concerns.
The company's security controls have come under intense scrutiny after high-profile incidents involving its technology, including its models accessing Australian government platforms without authorisation.
Jeannie Paterson from the Centre for Artificial Intelligence and Digital Ethics at the University of Melbourne said self-regulation could mean that companies set "only minimal safeguards".
The agreement inspires "very little confidence" as recent incidents of AI going rogue suggest companies have been undisciplined in their approach, she added.
2. Doubling down on data centres
Trump also reiterated his support for the rapid expansion of data centres - the crucial computing infrastructure that powers AI.
The rollout of data centres has drawn pushback around the country over concerns about electricity usage and their potential impact on from communities.
Data centre construction has also emerged as a potential political obstacle for Trump's Republican party ahead of the US midterm elections in November.
A survey conducted by Marist Poll in partnership with NPR and PBS News, external earlier this month found that 65% of registered voters opposed data centres being built in their areas.
Responding to those concerns, Trump said tech companies would work to make people "happy" about the construction of data centres.
"These big, powerful, very rich, very smart companies are going to be making massive contributions to communities," Trump told reporters.
Trump previously said on social media that the only reason communities should oppose data centres is if they "want to end up being backwards and poor".
Huang from Nvidia, which produces computer chips essential for running AI, said after the meeting that data centres should be called "super intelligence factories".
These facilities are "reindustrialising the United States", creating jobs across the economy, he added.
3. It's now 'Super Intelligence'
Also on Tuesday, Trump signed an executive order instructing US government departments and agencies to start using the terms "SI" and "Super Intelligence" and should no longer acknowledge the use of term artificial intelligence.
SI will take the place of AI in "official correspondence", websites, reports and other forms of communication, the order said.
"As these capabilities continue to improve, they increasingly represent not merely artificial intelligence, but a new era of Super Intelligence," the order said.
During an address to the United Nations General Assembly last week, Trump said the word "artificial" made the technology "sound fake".
Some tech leaders, including Zuckerberg and Musk, and other people close to the president have already started to use the term.
With tech leaders adopting the term, the US "may well be able to set the nomenclature," Paterson said.
But some experts said after Trump's UN speech that they thought the term was unlikely to gain widespread traction because it is a name typically used to refer to more advanced systems.

South Korea September inflation eases to 2.9% y/y, matches forecast
SEOUL, Oct 2 : South Korea's annual consumer inflation slowed to the 2 per cent range in September, driven down by government price control measures and falling agricultural costs, official data showed on Friday.
The Consumer Price Index (CPI) rose 2.9 per cent in September from a year earlier, according to the Ministry of Data and Statistics.
That marked a moderation from the 3.1 per cent annual gain recorded in August and matched the 2.9 per cent median forecast in a Reuters poll of economists.
On a monthly basis, consumer prices edged up 0.3 per cent, picking up slightly after a 0.2 per cent gain in the previous month.
The finance ministry attributed the deceleration to active policy measures, noting that price caps imposed on domestic petroleum prices helped curb inflationary pressures.
"Agricultural, livestock, and fisheries prices fell year-on-year for a second consecutive month, supported by targeted government measures ahead of the Chuseok holiday," it said in a statement.
By category, prices for agricultural, livestock, and fisheries products fell 0.3 per cent from a year earlier, helping to moderate headline inflation.
Upward pressure remained across import-related costs. Industrial product prices rose 4.2 per cent from a year earlier, driven largely by petroleum products, which jumped 11.8 per cent. Diesel prices surged 20.0 per cent.
Transport costs rose 7.7 per cent, while prices at restaurants and hotels increased 2.8 per cent compared with the same period last year.

Temperamental traits and adverse experiences during childhood may together offer clues to vulnerability to major psychiatric disorders, a transdiagnostic study by researchers at NIMHANS has found.
The study, published recently in the Journal of Affective Disorders, examined 1,162 adults, including 532 people with psychiatric disorders, 457 unaffected first-degree relatives (FDRs) and 173 healthy controls. The participants were drawn from 393 multiplex families - families in which multiple members had been diagnosed with psychiatric disorders - involving schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) and alcohol use disorder (AUD).
The researchers examined four broad dimensions of adult temperament - negative affectivity, extraversion/surgency, effortful control and orienting sensitivity - along with adverse childhood experiences (ACEs).
“Our findings suggest that temperament does not map onto psychiatric disorders in a simple, one-to-one manner. Rather, different combinations of temperamental characteristics are associated with different disorders, and some of these characteristics are also seen among unaffected family members,” said Srinivas Balachander, corresponding author and one of the lead researchers of the study.
Temperament shared within families
Using data from the erstwhile Accelerator programme for Discovery in Brain disorders using Stem cells (ADBS) project, (funded by the Department of Biotechnology and Pratiksha Trust), now known as the Rohini Nilekani Centre for Brain and Mind, at NIMHANS, the researchers found evidence of familial sharing across all four temperamental domains.
This was observed despite considerable variation in the psychiatric diagnoses within the same families. The finding is of interest because temperament is known to have a substantial heritable component, although the study did not directly establish that the temperamental characteristics observed were caused by specific genetic variants.
“In our study, considering the significant within-family heterogeneity in terms of different diagnoses, there was still a significant degree of shared temperament,” Dr. Balachander said.
Among affected participants, schizophrenia and bipolar disorder were associated with lower extraversion/surgency and orienting sensitivity. OCD was associated with higher negative affectivity and orienting sensitivity, along with lower effortful control and extraversion/surgency. Participants with AUD showed higher negative affectivity and orienting sensitivity and lower effortful control.
Some of these patterns were also observed among unaffected first-degree relatives. Relatives of people with schizophrenia showed lower extraversion/surgency, while relatives of people with OCD showed higher negative affectivity and lower effortful control.
“These findings are particularly interesting because some temperamental characteristics were evident even in individuals who did not have the disorder but belonged to families carrying a higher degree of familial risk,” Dr. Balachander said.
Childhood adversity and alcohol use disorder
The researchers also examined whether adverse childhood experiences altered the relationship between temperament and psychiatric disorders.
The clearest evidence for an interaction between temperament and childhood adversity emerged in alcohol use disorder. The overall ACE score was significantly associated with AUD, and interactions between childhood adversity and two temperamental domains - extraversion/surgency and effortful control - were also observed.
“Childhood adversity appears to add another layer to the relationship between temperament and psychiatric vulnerability. In our study, the evidence for this interaction was particularly apparent in alcohol use disorder, rather than uniformly across all four disorders,” Dr. Balachander said.
The researchers, however, cautioned against interpreting the findings as evidence that a particular temperament or childhood experience causes a psychiatric disorder.
The study was cross-sectional, meaning that the assessments were made at one point in time. The adult temperament measures were self-reported and could be influenced by current illness, treatment, illness duration or an individual’s perception of their own past Reports of childhood adversity may also be affected by recall and measurement biases.
Testing the findings
To examine whether the findings extended beyond the genetically enriched family sample, the researchers tested their statistical model using an independent community-based cohort from the Consortium for Vulnerability to Externalizing Disorders and Addiction (c-VEDA).
The analysis included 2,485 adults aged 18 to 23 years for whom the relevant temperament, ACE and psychiatric assessments were available.
The model showed an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.822 for alcohol use disorder, 0.742 for bipolar disorder and 0.752 for OCD. Its performance for schizophrenia was close to chance level, with an AUC of 0.526.
“The external validation gives us some indication that the associations identified in the family-based sample may extend to community populations for some disorders. However, the findings for schizophrenia did not replicate well, which is an important limitation and needs further investigation,” Dr. Balachander said.
The researchers said the findings point to the need for prospective studies that follow unaffected family members over time. Such studies could help determine whether particular temperamental characteristics precede the onset of psychiatric illness or are partly consequences of illness and its treatment.
“Temperament and childhood adversity may eventually become useful components of broader risk assessment frameworks, but we need prospective longitudinal evidence before we can say that they have predictive or preventive value,” Dr. Balachander said.
The researchers said that studying temperament alongside childhood adversity could eventually provide a more nuanced understanding of psychiatric vulnerability than considering family history alone. However, they stressed that the present findings do not establish that these measures can predict who will develop a psychiatric disorder.
The researchers said continued longitudinal follow-up of the cohort would be important to establish whether the observed temperamental patterns have value in identifying individuals at increased risk before the emergence of clinically significant symptoms.
