TVK candidate cries, 'sweet bro' consoles: DMK accuses Vijay of staging drama
DMK accused Vijay and TVK of staging bypoll candidate Sathyabama's tears at a campaign event, drawing a sharp rebuttal from TVK minister A Rajmohan and Congress leader Manickam Tagore.
DMK leader Kanimozhi on Thursday accused Chief Minister Vijay and his party, TVK, of staging a "drama" during a campaign event in Dharapuram, where party candidate P Sathyabama broke into tears during her speech and Vijay hugged and consoled her.
Kanimozhi alleged that the emotional moment was scripted to win public sympathy ahead of the upcoming bypoll.
“Minister Rajkumar gets a phone call, picks it up and speaks. Then he says something into Sathyabama’s ear. Within seconds, Sathyabama, who was speaking well, begins to cry, saying she is under stress as a woman. Then sweet bro (CM Vijay) hugs and consoles her. Immediately, the crowd starts cheering. Be it on stage or during a political campaign, Vijay is doing drama like this,” Kanimozhi alleged.
The remarks drew a sharp response from Tamil Nadu Minister for School Education A Rajmohan, who called the charge "sheer malice" and strongly criticised Kanimozhi.
Speaking to reporters on the sidelines of an event in Chennai to mark actor Sivaji Ganesan's 99th birth anniversary, Rajmohan said he had only asked Sathyabama to finish her speech quickly.
"This is sheer malice. I am shocked by what akka (elder sister) Kanimozhi said. I register my strongest condemnation," he said.
Rajmohan said such requests were routine at public meetings, especially when schedules were tight. Recalling his earlier experience as a professional stage anchor, he said even senior figures such as Rajinikanth and Kamal Haasan had been asked to keep their speeches short during the centenary celebrations of late DMK patriarch M Karunanidhi.
"I swear on my mother, these allegations are completely baseless and wild. The organisers only said, 'Make it fast,' because the Chief Minister had been travelling for more than eight hours in the scorching heat, completely drenched in sweat, while large crowds of people had been waiting under the sun for hours. Asking a speaker to make it quick under such circumstances is routine, not a political drama," Rajmohan said.
He also said that while coordinating high-profile political events for former Chief Minister MK Stalin and former deputy CM Udhayanidhi Stalin, stage organisers regularly sent prompts to manage time.
"It is a basic reality of public events. For a senior leader to twist a woman's tears and peddle negativity for political mileage is unacceptable," he added.
At a separate tribute event for Sivaji Ganesan's 99th birth anniversary, Tamil Nadu Congress Committee president Manickam Tagore also criticised the DMK for calling others' campaigns "drama".
Rejecting the allegations as false, he said, "Let them say whatever they want. When they go to the people, it is campaigning, but when others reach out to the public, it becomes a drama? Where is the fairness in that? They are simply speaking lies, and responding seriously to such talk is just wasting your time and mine."

Explosions heard in Ethiopia's capital after drone flights banned
- Published
Explosions were heard overnight in Ethiopia's capital, some in the area of the military headquarters in the west and another in the south of the city, residents and diplomatic sources say.
The blasts came hours after drone flights were banned over Addis Ababa and a week after fighting erupted in the north between the army and a newly launched alliance of armed groups including forces from the Tigray region.
A source linked to the opposition fighters told the Reuters news agency they were behind what they said were drone strikes.
"It was very loud. It was strong enough to set off car alarms," a resident in a southern area of the city, near the base of the secret service, told BBC Amharic.
He estimated that he heard the explosion in the Gotera neighbourhood some time around 00:30 local time (21:30 GMT).
Another resident told the BBC that he and his friends were playing games when they heard an explosion.
He lives in the western suburb of Torhayloch, a neighbourhood close to the military headquarters.
There were no official reports confirming the cause of the explosions, the exact locations affected or whether there were any casualties or damage.
The office of Ethiopia's Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed, the defence ministry as well as the federal and Addis Ababa police have not responded to BBC requests for comment.
Meanwhile, Ethiopia's foreign ministry has said it is closing its embassy in neighbouring Eritrea and expelling 10 Eritrean diplomats "for involvement in activities that pose a direct threat to Ethiopia's national security".
Earlier, in a BBC interview, Eritrea's government denied that it was backing the new rebel alliance.
- Are Ethiopians marching back to war in Tigray? 
  - Published5 days ago

  - Published3 days ago
Clashes broke out last week after months of tension between the government and the party that controls Tigray, the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF).
They both accuse each other of violating a 2022 peace deal that ended a brutal two-year civil war, which according to an Africa Union mediator is estimated to have cost 600,000 lives.
Last month, seven armed movements, including the TPLF and an Amhara militia known as Fano, formed an alliance with the stated aim of removing the government in Addis Ababa.
There is disagreement over which side started the latest fighting.
The TPLF says it was responding to a federal offensive, including drone strikes, while the government says Tigrayan forces attacked first after seizing control of airports in the region.
The BBC is unable to report from Tigray and surrounding areas.
It is difficult to verify what is happening on the ground and access to the internet and the main telecoms service provider in Tigray have also been cut.
Within Tigray, the national army and a pro-government militia appear to be advancing towards the region's main city of Mekelle.
In the southern Tigrayan town of Alamata, a medic told the BBC on Wednesday that 52 civilians had died in three days of heavy fighting.
The TPLF is also reported to be fighting in neighbouring Afar region, a strategic area which connects landlocked Ethiopia to Djibouti and its ports.
A humanitarian source has estimated that tens of thousands have fled their homes in Afar, according to the AFP news agency.
Fighting around Lalibela in the Amhara region, a Unesco world heritage site where foreign tourists have been stranded for more than a week, has involved the national army and Fano fighters, now allied to the TPLF.
The government has accused neighbouring Eritrea of backing these groups.
One pro-government militia commander fighting in Tigray told the BBC that Eritrean soldiers were involved on the front lines.
But in a rare response to the BBC from Eritrea's government, Information Minister Yemane Gebremeskel dismissed the allegations.
He accused Ethiopia's ruling Prosperity Party (PP) of seeking external scapegoats for the country's mounting challenges.
"The PP regime has made it a habit to apportion blame to its neighbours in order to deflect attention from the myriad internal conflicts that it is fomenting in various parts of the country," he told BBC Tigrinya.
Eritrea was a key ally of Ethiopia during the Tigray war, fighting against the TPLF.
But relations between the two neighbours have since deteriorated largely over the Ethiopian prime minister's ambition to take ownership of one of Eritrea's Red Sea ports.
Ethiopia lost access to them when Eritrea seceded in 1993.
Abiy has even hinted at taking the port of Assab - about 60km (37 miles) from the border - by force as he sees direct access to the sea as important for Ethiopia's long-term future and economic prosperity.
As concerns over security mount in Ethiopia, the country's National Intelligence and Security Service (Niss) announced on Wednesday that it was imposing an indefinite ban on drone flights in Addis Ababa and surrounding areas.
The agency said it would not issue permits for drone operations and warned that legal action would be taken against anyone flying drones in restricted areas.
Niss said the measure was necessary to protect national leaders, critical infrastructure and major public events.

A purported Dainik Jagran newspaper clipping (here & here) claims that the Rajasthan High Court has given a judgment that provides for six months of imprisonment and a ₹50,000 fine for any candidate who fails to secure at least 100 votes in the Sarpanch elections. Let us verify the authenticity of the claim made in this post.
Claim: A Dainik Jagran newspaper clipping claims the Rajasthan High Court has ordered a six-month jail term and a ₹50,000 fine for Sarpanch candidates securing under 100 votes.
Fact: The viral newspaper clipping is an AI-generated fake image. The Rajasthan High Court has given no such judgment, Dainik Jagran published no such report, and Indian electoral laws contain no provision imposing jail time or fines for low vote counts. Hence, the claim made in the post is FALSE.
First, an initial search confirmed that the Rajasthan High Court has not issued any such judgment regarding low vote counts in Panchayat elections. Additionally, we found no news reports published by Dainik Jagran corroborating this matter. Moreover, no such law, Court order, or judicial mandate exists under the Election Commission of India or Indian electoral statutes (such as the Representation of the People Act, 1951) penalising candidates with imprisonment or fines purely for receiving a low vote count. Under current election rules, the only major consequence for a poor electoral performance is the forfeiture of the security deposit, which applies if an unelected candidate fails to secure more than one-sixth of the valid votes polled.
Further, we ran the viral newspaper clipping through the OpenAI content detection tool, which confirmed that the clipping is an AI-generated image created using OpenAI tools. Earlier, we debunked a similarly fabricated clipping that falsely claimed a woman gave birth to puppies in the United States.
To sum it up, the viral newspaper clipping is a fabricated AI-generated image, and there is no legal provision or court order mandating jail time or fines for securing low votes in a Sarpanch election.

President Donald Trump says he isn't sure he would want a data center in his backyard.
"I would like to have data centers," Trump told Time Magazine as part of a cover story interview published on Thursday. "It doesn't mean I want them right next to my house, but certainly I like them in my county."
Trump has repeatedly defended the benefits of data centers and the AI industry more broadly, as polling shows widespread public skepticism. Republican governors have also begun to rein in incentives for data centers.
Communities that don't welcome data centers, Trump said, are also passing up on potentially lucrative tax revenue. As he has before, the president portrayed communities that oppose data center development as wrong and impoverished.
"If you want to be poor, you want to have no money, if you don't want to have a job, and if you want to live in a crime-infested area, squalor, all the things that go along with it, you should not have a data center," he said.
Amid the growing backlash against data centers, some AI and tech leaders have begun considering other ways to supply the compute they need to train and then run cutting-edge AI models. SpaceX CEO Elon Musk is pursuing orbital data centers. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman has suggested data centers are better suited for deserts.
As he welcomed AI executives to the White House on Tuesday, Trump told reporters that data centers would become "very popular" as residents see what their cooperation will bring to their communities.
"They're going to make the community happy," Trump said. "That might be supplying oil and gas. It might be supplying education. It may be helping teachers along financially, helping people along financially."
Trump described how, in some cases, a data center can be "right next to a guy's house," a reality some residents in Loudoun County, Virginia, face.
Loudoun County, home to the famed "Data Center Alley," once allowed many data centers to be built by right, including some near residential neighborhoods. In 2025, county supervisors ended by-right approvals for new data centers. New proposals must now go through a review process that includes public hearings, among other steps.
Trump's hope for a data center in his county is also complicated.
Last week, the Palm Beach County Board of Supervisors unanimously approved a one-year moratorium on the construction of large-scale data centers. Before the vote, the commissioners rejected a proposed plan for a hyperscale data center, WPTV reported.
A smaller data center plan for the site, which was previously approved, is expected to proceed.

Q: I get headaches whenever I use my phone or computer for a long time. Are screens damaging my brain?
A: Screens are not known to damage the brain simply through use, but prolonged use can cause eye strain, dry eyes, blurred vision, neck and shoulder tension and headaches. Poor posture, glare and inadequate breaks can worsen symptoms. Follow the 20-20-20 rule: every 20 minutes, look about 20 feet away for 20 seconds. Adjust brightness, reduce glare and blink regularly. Frequent or severe headaches, especially without screen use, need medical evaluation.
Q: Is every headache a migraine?
A: No. Headaches can result from stress, tension, dehydration, poor sleep, eye strain, infections, sinus problems, stomach problems or migraine. Migraine may cause throbbing pain, nausea and sensitivity to light or sound, though symptoms vary. A new, unusually severe or rapidly worsening headache, especially with weakness, confusion, fainting, seizures, vision changes, fever or difficulty speaking, needs urgent medical attention.
Q: I have a headache, so I take a painkiller immediately. Is that okay?
A: Occasional appropriate use may be fine for some people, but frequent painkiller use can cause medication-overuse headaches and, depending on the medicine, stomach, kidney or liver problems. If you regularly need painkillers for headaches, find the cause rather than repeatedly treating the symptom.
Q: Do I really need a flu shot if I usually get only a mild flu?
A: Influenza can be mild but can also cause serious illness, especially in high-risk people. Flu vaccination reduces the risk of influenza and its complications, though it does not prevent every cold or respiratory virus. Because influenza viruses change, seasonal vaccination is recommended for many people according to individual risk. Ask your doctor if it is appropriate for you, particularly if you have chronic diseases, are pregnant or belong to another recommended group.
Q: Can the flu shot give me influenza?
A: No. Injectable flu vaccines do not contain live influenza virus capable of causing influenza. Soreness, tiredness or a mild fever can occur briefly after vaccination and usually reflect an immune response. You can also catch another respiratory virus around the same time. Remember that protection takes time to develop.
Q: My eyes burn after looking at my phone for hours. Do I need “screen glasses”?
A: Not necessarily. Digital eye strain can cause burning, dryness, temporary blurred vision and headaches because we blink less while concentrating. Take regular breaks, blink consciously, reduce glare and keep the screen at a comfortable distance. Prescription glasses may help if you have an underlying vision problem. Blue-light glasses are not a magic solution. Persistent pain or significant vision changes need an eye examination.
Q: Does using a phone in the dark permanently damage eyesight?
A: Ordinary phone use in a dark room has not been shown to permanently damage eyesight, although the bright screen against a dark background can cause strain, dryness or headaches. Keep some ambient light on and adjust screen brightness. Persistent blurred or double vision, eye pain or headaches should not simply be blamed on the phone.
Q: I use my phone until I fall asleep. Does it really affect sleep?
A: It does. Screen use keeps the brain engaged, while light from screens can affect the body’s sleep-wake rhythm. Messages, videos and social media can be particularly stimulating. Keep the phone away from the bed, choose quieter activities before sleep and maintain a regular bedtime. Persistent sleep problems need further evaluation.
Q: Can sitting in front of a screen all day cause neck and back pain?
A: Yes. Prolonged sitting and poor posture can cause neck, shoulder and back pain, while looking down at a phone can add neck strain. Change position regularly, keep the screen at a comfortable height, support your back and move around during the day. Exercise and strengthening can help. Persistent pain, numbness, weakness or pain spreading into an arm or leg should be assessed.
Q: I feel dizzy and get a headache after spending hours on my phone. Is it because of radiation?
A: There is no good evidence that ordinary mobile-phone use causes headaches or dizziness through the radiation emitted by phones. However, prolonged use can indirectly contribute through eye strain, poor posture, dehydration, lack of sleep and inactivity. Look at the whole pattern and take regular breaks. If headaches or dizziness keep returning, particularly without screen use, consult your doctor.
Q: Are “sugar-free” foods healthy?
A: No. “Sugar-free” does not mean nutritious. Sugar-free biscuits, chocolates and snacks may still be high in calories, refined flour, saturated fat or salt. Some contain sugar alcohols or other sweeteners that can cause gas, bloating or diarrhoea when consumed in excess. They may also keep our preference for very sweet foods alive. Sugar-free is a label, not a health certificate. Always check the complete nutrition label.
Q: Are zero-sugar drinks harmless?
A: Not necessarily. They can be a better choice than sugary drinks if you are trying to reduce sugar and calories, but they are not automatically healthy. Some sweeteners can cause gas, bloating, abdominal cramps or diarrhoea, particularly in people with sensitive digestion or IBS. If a particular drink repeatedly causes bowel discomfort, stop it and see whether symptoms improve. Zero sugar does not mean zero consequences.
Public Advisory: Not every health problem needs a tablet—and not every health myth deserves to be believed. From WhatsApp remedies and “natural” cures to advice from friends and relatives, health information can easily become distorted. Before starting, stopping or changing a treatment, ask the doctor—not the WhatsApp group.
NOTE: These responses are for general awareness and do not replace professional medical advice. Older adults often have multiple illnesses and medicines, so individual medical advice should be taken from a qualified healthcare professional.

The Soviet Union famously churned out tens of thousands of new apartment buildings in the 1960s, ’70s, and ’80s — some assembled in as little as 12 days — together comprising tens of millions of individual apartments. Such speed is not unique to communist command economies, or even to grim concrete mega-blocks. In Sweden and Japan today, modern, high-quality new homes can be factory-built and assembled in a matter of weeks using the same basic method — prefabrication — as the Soviets.
The astonishing gap between America’s fastest- and slowest-building cities
It shouldn’t take five years to build an apartment building.
The US, alas, evinces no such urgency to build housing.
In some of our highest-cost cities — San Francisco, New York, Miami — it takes, somewhat astonishingly, nearly five years to erect a modestly sized apartment building, from the time an application is first submitted to building completion. That was one of the top-line findings of a remarkable new economics working paper on housing construction timelines across 60 US cities. The gaps between the fastest and slowest cities were just as striking: In Raleigh, North Carolina, a builder can complete a 20-unit apartment building in about as much time as it takes just to approve the permit for one in San Francisco, where applications languish for more than a year. In Indianapolis, a single-family home can be built in six months from proposal to completion, less than one-eighth the time it takes in San Francisco.
Such delays have costs — in delayed housing supply at a time when America is millions of homes in the hole, in lost staff time that developers ultimately bake into the cost of the new homes, and in homes that simply never get built because the process is discouraging to anyone but the best-resourced developers. The authors, Leonardo D’Amico, Evan Soltas, and Audrey Wang, found that longer permitting lengths are correlated with higher housing prices and lower rates of housing production, though they don’t claim to have shown that these are causal relationships. The research (which has not yet been through peer review and, like any working paper, may be revised before final publication) represents the first such comprehensive dataset comparing homebuilding timelines across the US. To build it, the researchers assembled 1.1 million permits covering 2.7 million housing units between 2000 and 2025 — about one in 13 new homes permitted nationally over that period, they write.
It probably won’t come as a shock to you that housing can be built faster in Sioux Falls, South Dakota, than in Los Angeles or pretty much anywhere in California. But perhaps the most notable takeaway (to me, anyway) from the paper was how massively home permitting times have lengthened across the board over the past 25 years. Across the cities in their sample, the researchers estimate that permitting time for a standardized multifamily building rose from 0.6 years in 2000 to 1.5 years in 2023, and, for a single-family home, from 1.6 months in 2000 to 4.9 months in 2023.
Is there really any good reason why we should take nearly a year longer to approve an apartment building than, Soltas joked in a recent interview, “the barbarians of 2006”? Shouldn’t we be getting faster and more efficient at building housing over time, not slower — especially at a time of acute housing scarcity?
You would think. So what is going on here?
One building, very different wait times
Permitting refers to everything that happens after a developer submits an application to build a house or multifamily building, before they’re allowed to break ground. The proposal is then reviewed for compliance with a range of different sets of rules, from building safety and energy codes to plumbing to zoning and, in some places, aesthetic design. Initial applications will often be found noncompliant and then sent back to the builder for revisions, Soltas, an assistant professor of economics at Princeton, told me.
The gulf between housing starts in California and Texas has become something of a meme in housing abundance circles. But, for all that, we have until now lacked rigorous apples-to-apples comparisons of permitting and building times in different metro areas, Soltas said. That gap in seemingly basic knowledge, what should be “step zero” facts for the national housing reform debate, became apparent to him when he was teaching an urban economics class, which became one of the impetuses for the new paper. “I realized if I needed that information to teach my students, that it might be useful for other people,” he said.
Rather than merely pulling permits from different cities and comparing how long whatever happened to be built in each city took to approve, the researchers used the data to estimate how long an identical, standardized project would take in each place between 2015 and 2019, keeping constant its size and the density of the surrounding neighborhood. Their uniform archetypes were a 2,800-square-foot detached single-family home on a 0.15-acre lot and a 20-unit multifamily building with 1,200 square feet per apartment.
Cities with longer permitting times also tended to have longer construction periods — the longer it takes to get an application approved, the longer it then takes to do the building itself, which compounds the gap between the fastest- and slowest-building cities (it’s possible that “cities that make the permitting process difficult also put in lots of burdens that slow the construction process,” Soltas said). One advantage of the researchers’ method is that the differences across cities can’t merely be chalked up to something like the complexity of building within already-dense environments like Manhattan — the analysis already controls for that. So the enormous gaps between different places become harder to dismiss as inevitable features of development in big cities.
The study wasn’t designed to answer the “why” of it all — those will be questions for future research. “Our paper doesn’t directly identify any smoking guns,” Soltas said. Still, some of the culprits are likely obvious — California, for example, has long subjected some housing projects to extensive environmental review requirements under the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA). Apartment buildings, especially larger ones, are more likely to have to go through CEQA review, though they’re more environmentally friendly than single-family homes (recognizing this as an obstacle to housing affordability, California has been moving to exempt many housing projects from such reviews).
Why are we taking so much longer to permit housing?
But why, as the study finds, is permitting becoming slower across the country, not just in the most regulated cities? “We estimate that, in 2000, our standardized multi-family project had a 71-percent probability of approval within six months of applying for a permit,” the researchers write. “In 2025, that project had a 44-percent approval probability within six months.” Permitting times have come down a bit since 2023, but it’s unclear whether that just represents the reversal of pandemic-era highs, or if it reflects real progress from the pro-housing policies that have been passed in many cities and states in recent years.
That discovery dovetails with other economics research finding that zoning codes, which were first widely adopted in the US in the early-to-mid 20th century, have continued to become more restrictive even in recent years, making it harder to build housing.
Without knowing why exactly permitting lengths have ballooned, it’s hard to say whether those increases have occurred for good reasons. At least some of it may have to do with the aforementioned intensification of zoning and other land-use restrictions, which, I can say from having written a lot about zoning, tend to be pretty ill-conceived and hard to justify.
The slowdown may also be connected to expanding building code requirements. I’ve written at length about that issue, too; although ever-more stringent rules might seem like a great idea — who could be opposed to more safety? — they tend to be biased against multi-family housing and likely inflate the cost of building, all without having to show that the benefits are worth the costs. Particularly the cost in housing supply that never gets built, which has the effect of keeping more Americans living in older housing stock. And do we really think a home built to 2005 standards is dangerously subpar today?
We might ultimately decide that many of today’s building requirements — particularly ones like stronger energy efficiency standards — are worth it, but first we’d need to determine what their full costs are, which we remain far from doing.
At a minimum, it seems unlikely that an apartment building that’s okay to build in Grand Rapids today would be unsafe for New York. So what, exactly, is all that extra permitting time buying the city? Now, at least, Mayor Zohran Mamdani can put an exact number on the delay.

Judge dismisses lawsuits claiming Google's AI Overviews siphon web traffic
Google may have a monopoly in search, but neither lawsuit made a compelling case the company was leveraging it.
A federal judge has dismissed lawsuits from publisher Penske Media Corporation (PMC) and ed tech company Chegg that alleged Google's AI Overviews illegally pulled readers away by repackaging their online content, Reuters reports. In a memorandum opinion on both lawsuits, Judge Amit Mehta, coincidentally the same judge who ruled that Google maintained a monopoly in online search services in 2024, said the companies failed to argue the search provider violated antitrust laws.
PMC and Chegg's original lawsuits claimed that Google was using AI Overviews and its vast index of the web to siphon traffic away from their online ad businesses, hurting their revenue. Chegg additionally said that Google was effectively forcing websites to offer their content up for AI scraping or face being excluded from search results.
Judge Mehta dismissed both claims for a variety of reasons, but broadly found that neither company convincingly argued that Google was leveraging its monopoly to get them to provide free material for its AI, or that the search provider was trying to gain an unfair advantage in digital publishing. "Plaintiffs have pleaded only that they have an 'expectation' that Google will send them search traffic if they make their content available for free," Mehta wrote. "But an expectation is not an agreement. It is simply how a general search engine works."
Engadget has asked PMC and Chegg to comment on the memorandum opinion. We'll update this article if we hear back.
Other publishers have raised concerns about how their content contributes to Google's AI search features, but the situation isn't entirely clear-cut. Publishers can exclude webpages from being used for AI Overviews, but they will still be listed in traditional search results. With more and more of the search results page taken up by AI Mode and AI Overviews, though, it's easy to see why that might not be a satisfying compromise.

The story so far
The groundwater resources of Kerala have been under severe stress due to changes in rainfall pattern following climate change, high population density as well the fact that approximately 62% of the population relies on groundwater from an estimated 6.5 million open wells for their domestic needs. The State’s fragmented wastewater management system and the unscientific construction of septic tanks and pit latrines at homes close to shallow and open wells have resulted in persistent faecal contamination of ground water in the State, which has been documented by several studies.
A 2024 study in the Journal of Environmental Management reported that 7.4% of the State’s population could be making do with poor quality of groundwater and estimated that 0.59 million people in 252 local self government bodies in the State could be continuously exposing themselves to health risks from consuming ground water from wells which may not be chlorinated regularly.
And the latest report on E.coli contamination comes from Pala, where a water quality assessment conducted in flood-affected areas along the Meenachil river detected E. coli bacteria in 67% of the samples, raising concerns over the safety of drinking water sources in and around Pala.
Researchers attributed the spike in bacterial contamination to the recent floods, which may have allowed contaminated surface water to enter water sources.
How is contamination taking place?
It is a dangerous combination of high population density, unplanned urbanisation with hundreds of septic tanks and wells sitting close to each other in small plots and the State’s natural hydrogeological features that allow surface pollutants to reach the water table quickly. In recent years, unpredictable and heavy rainfall has been adding to the State’s woes, as oversaturation of the soil and the overflow of drainage systems can quickly allow pollution and microbial contamination to infiltrate ground water.
Environmental scientists explain that groundwater is drawn mostly from shallow, unconfined aquifers, which are recharged directly by rainfall and surface infiltration. In most areas the local water table might be sitting just below the level of the river bed and it naturally leaks water downwards to recharge the underlying unconfined aquifers. If rivers are polluted, then all groundwater resources in the surrounding area would also be carrying the same pollutant.
What is the extent of groundwater contamination in Keralam?
A community-level GIS study of 449 households in an urban area of Thiruvananthapuram in 2018 had reported that most of the wells were in an intermediate-high contamination risk state, with more than 77% of wells having a septic tank within 7.5 m radius. Coliform contamination was prevalent in 73% of wells, and the groundwater was predominantly acidic with a mean of 5.4, rendering it unfit for drinking.
This picture could be true for the rest of the State also. Because of the State’s unique geography and highly dispersed, continuous rural-urban settlement pattern, just about 5-6% of major urban zones are connected to a centralised pipe-based sewerage network system. The State’s sanitation strategy relies heavily on onsite sanitation systems, with individual household septic tanks and soak pits for sewage disposal.
Unscientific construction of these household sanitation systems has rendered much of the groundwater resources unsafe for human consumption, unless properly treated.
What are the health impacts?
Safe drinking water is one of the crucial social determinants of health. It is thus unfortunate that a State which has made enviable strides in developing its public health sector has paid little attention to ensuring that people have access to safe drinking water. While people in urban areas have to a large extent, access to treated water supply, in many rural areas of the State serviced by local small water supply schemes, water distribution lines often run close to sewerage lines and even small breaks in the pipelines can lead to the contamination of drinking water
Recurrent outbreaks of water-borne diseases like Hepatitis A, Shigellosis and norovirus outbreaks have been the bane of the State in recent years, especially in the northern districts of the State, indicating the scale and impact of groundwater contamination. Hepatitis A in particular has been taking a heavy toll on the State since the last three years, with significant mortality and in many instances, leaving people with severe morbidities
Epidemiological studies conducted by the ICMR and Health department into amoebic meningoencephalitis, which has emerged as a significant public health problem in Keralam in recent times, has traced the infection to the use of non-chlorinated well water which has high concentration of E.coli, in which free-living amoeba thrive
What is the sewerage infrastructure status?
To modernise sewerage infrastructure, the State is executing projects under the AMRUT 2.0 Mission, a Central initiative aimed at ensuring universal access to safe water and reliable sewerage connections across urban areas. The CAG’s 2025 report stated that at the closure of the AMRUT Mission (Atal Mission for Rejuvenation and Urban Transformation), Kerala’s overall achievement was just 11.25% and only 0.13% households got sewerage connections.
Keralam’s geography, population density, lack of vast tracts of uninhabited land means that many proposed treatment plants end up being close to residential areas, which triggered huge public protests. Such protests led to the cancellation of multiple approved septage treatment plant projects in many parts of the State. There are also reports about the State’s financial crunch affecting project payments leading to delays in implementation

World Grand Prix Darts: Luke Humphries and James Wade storm into quarter-finals as Gary Anderson eliminated
Luke Humphries goes at 74 per cent on his starting doubles and 64 per cent on his closing ones as he sweeps Jermaine Wattimena 3-0, will face Niels Zonneveld in last eight after Dutch debutant dispatches Gary Anderson; James Wade excels against Stephen Bunting
Friday 2 October 2026 00:23, UK
Luke Humphries put in a much-improved display as his doubling prowess and a 10-dart finish secured a 3-0 rout of Jermaine Wattimena and a spot in the World Grand Prix quarter-finals.
There were also 3-1 victories for James Wade and Niels Zonneveld over Stephen Bunting and Gary Anderson respectively, while Gian Van Veen came through a deciding-set cracker with Ryan Searle to triumph 3-2.
Humphries - the title favourite after defending champion Luke Littler's shock defeat to Luke Woodhouse on the opening night - had averaged only 80 and gone at 26 per cent on his closing doubles in a scruffy 2-0 win over Dave Chisnall on Tuesday evening.
Two nights later, the 2023 champion and 2024 and 2025 runner-up averaged 94.11 and secured a finishing-double percentage of 64, although his starting-double percentage of 74 was the most eye-catching stat as he peppered double 16 early in legs.
'Cool Hand' - who will face Wattimena's fellow Dutchman Zonneveld in the last eight on Friday - hit his 10-darter at the start of the third set, while Wattimena twice hit the wrong double in the opening set.
Humphries said afterwards: "I've got a good chance of winning this. At the moment I'm a bit up and down, but if I can put that right I'm going to be tough to beat.
"It wasn't the best performance, but it was a good performance. It was a lot better than it was on Tuesday.
"I think I got in every time with my first three darts. When you're doing stuff like that, it's going to take a top performance to beat you."
Wade: Double start is 'hellish'
Wade, meanwhile, delivered a starting masterclass to reach his eighth World Grand Prix quarter-final, hitting an opening shot of 160 five times during his win over Bunting.
The sixth seed dropped his standards in the third set but was electric in the other three as he set up a meeting with Van Veen.
Wade said: "I am so grateful as it is so hard to win with a double start. We can all play it cool and pretend to be relaxed but it is awful, it is hellish, really hard work.
"I don't feel anywhere near my best but I am having to play better against better players. I have loads more gears to go - but talk is cheap.
"And I am full of cheap talk!"
Van Veen wins thriller to secure Wade showdown
Elsewhere, Searle - who landed a 167 checkout, the highest of the week - threw for the match against Van Veen after breaking the Dutchman with a finish of 100 in the fourth set, only to be broken straightaway in the deciding leg.
Van Veen, who had led 2-0 in the penultimate set before being pegged back to 2-2 by Searle, then blitzed the final set 3-0.
The third seed said: "When I was 2-1 down in sets, I was like, 'oh no, this is not how I want to go out'.
"As good as double 16 went for me in the first round, it kind of bothered me today. But at the end it really came good.
"I was quite happy with my scoring, but just missed a couple of darts at a crucial time. Luckily I got the job done."
Anderson tumbles out as Zonneveld's run continues
Van Veen's compatriot Zonneveld followed his opening-round win over Josh Rock by dumping out Anderson, starting by winning a first set in which every leg went against the throw.
Anderson made a terrible start to the match, hitting single one and then suffering two bounce-outs, while he was the victim of another bounce-out in the fourth set as he aimed for a leg-winning bullseye.
Zonneveld subsequently broke before closing out victory in the next leg.
The 28-year-old said: "Especially in this tournament, it is one of the biggest things in my whole career.
"I have achieved many things Pro Tour-wise and Euro Tour-wise but not on the main stage, just once at the World Series Finals.
"I have become a dad so less sleep and all that but I feel in rhythm again."

Here’s a fun history lesson for you. Don’t worry, we’ll make it quick! In 1966, nearly 51,000 people died on US highways. The overwhelming evidence suggested that many lives could have been saved with modern seat belts, which by then had been around for several years. The automotive industry responded by rallying together, and, in a triumph of self-regulation, voluntarily put the safety feature in every new vehicle that rolled off the line.
Kidding! Of course they didn’t do that. In the fall of 1966, Congress established the Department of Transportation and then passed the National Traffic and Motor Vehicle Safety Act as well as the Highway Safety Act, giving the federal government sweeping new authority to set safety standards. By 1968, seat belts were required in every new car. Despite a massive increase in highway traffic in the last 60 years, far fewer fatalities happen on the road today.
I was thinking about this while watching various AI CEOs huddle around US president Donald Trump on Tuesday, congratulating themselves and each other on having signed an AI safety accord. My colleague Maddy Varner wrote about the specific stipulations here, but the short version is that it’s largely up to the AI labs to keep themselves in check.
Or, as Trump put it even more succinctly in the Oval Office on Wednesday: “They’re gonna police, and they’re gonna police each other, and they’re gonna self-police, they’re gonna police themselves. It’s going to work out very well.”
So this is the current state of AI safety regulation. On one side are the AI executives, employees, and tech luminaries, who are all saying that there need to be clear, thoughtful, tactical rules introduced to avoid potential disaster. (Bill Gates, for instance, has been on a media blitz playing Cassandra about an AI apocalypse.) On the other side is Trump’s magical thinking that if you say something enough times, it must be true.
That’s not to say any of this is simple or easy. The question of how to properly “pace the frontier,” as some of those same executives like to say, remains open. Even if all of the major AI labs were to agree to a slowdown, there’s no good way to keep them to their word, and China would likely continue on its own path regardless. The US economy is increasingly propped up on the AI industry, which itself has become an ouroboros of financing deals and circular investments; any meaningful crackdown risks major instability that reaches well beyond Silicon Valley.
The automotive industry is also admittedly an imperfect analogy for all kinds of reasons. There’s no seat belt equivalent for AI, no straightforward solution that can demonstrably reduce risk overnight. (It also took decades for the majority of states to pass laws mandating that people actually wear them.) The potential harms are less certain and less quantifiable. AI doomers will tell you the technology could result in human extinction in a decade; skeptics argue that’s sci-fi marketing malarkey.
We’ve talked about various AI risk scenarios before, but no one can say for certain what’s going to happen next. If you’re looking for data points to calculate your own personal p(doom), I’d point to a recent CNN report about how the US military supposedly nearly boarded a Chinese ship in part because a false AI-generated report said it was carrying nuclear materials. What, if anything, does the AI accord accomplish to prevent similar incidents from happening in the future? Unclear.
The correct answer to all this uncertainty surely isn’t “I guess we’ll find out.” But that’s exactly what self-regulation encourages. To its credit, OpenAI has delayed and even canceled the release of its most advanced models over security concerns. But not before they went on various, extensive hacking sprees, new details about which are still trickling out at a steady pace.
In an interview with TIME published on Thursday, Trump suggested that the Department of Justice and the Federal Bureau of Investigation were sufficient “guardrails” for the artificial intelligence industry. Are they? It’s far from clear if AI companies can even be held legally responsible when their models go rogue. And it’s not like AI agents themselves are being served subpoenas.
The truth is, no one knows how to solve for AI safety right now. It’s going to take massive amounts of coordination, resources, and regulatory authority to develop the right framework and enforce it, which is exactly the kind of thing governments are designed to provide. Instead of even attempting to work through any of that, the Trump administration is getting out of the way and telling everyone to step on the gas. Don’t bother buckling up.

At a Make America Healthy Again event Tuesday, anti-vaccine Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy opened a “fireside chat” with Vice President JD Vance on the topic of artificial intelligence. While MAHA generally coalesces around things like healthy lifestyles and mistrust of drugmakers, Kennedy quickly turned to extolling the potential of artificial intelligence, surprising Vance, who said he was expecting to discuss “weight loss and acid, not AI.”
Kennedy boasted that the Trump administration is “making it easy for every American to use AI,” which he claimed would free us from the “medical tyranny” of doctors and health experts. He suggested Americans should start using AI to get second opinions about medical recommendations, saying AI is “better informed than any doctor in the country.” He also suggested that the technology would confirm his misinformation about vaccines and contrarian views on public health guidance.
“We’re never, ever again going to be able to be dominated by public officials who tell us trust the experts, because every American will be able to check their own medical advice,” Kennedy said.
AI >>> Kennedy
Kennedy, who has no medical, scientific, or public health experience, then laid out specific examples in which he suggested AI would contradict health and medical experts and vindicate his own views:
“If somebody tells you masks work, trust the experts, AI may tell you otherwise. If somebody tells you social distancing works, trust the experts, AI may correct that. And if somebody tells you that a vaccine will prevent transmission and infection—oh, you need to take it to protect your grandmother—AI may say it actually doesn’t do that”
AI may contradict or “correct” experts, but does it actually? We checked—the answer was nope.
When we asked Google’s Gemini: “Do masks work to prevent spread of infectious diseases?”
The AI chatbot responded (including its emphasis): “Yes, masks work to reduce the spread of respiratory infectious diseases, operating primarily as physical barriers to outgoing and incoming infectious particles. Their real-world effectiveness depends heavily on mask quality, fit, and population-level adherence.”
ChatGPT offered a similar answer, responding: “Yes. Masks can reduce the spread of some infectious diseases, particularly respiratory infections transmitted through droplets and aerosols.”
Doctors and experts >>> AI
Chatbots provided similar affirmative answers to the question of whether social distancing works at preventing infectious diseases. “Yes, social distancing is an effective public health measure for reducing the transmission of infectious diseases, particularly respiratory pathogens,” Gemini responded.

Srinagar has an estimated 64,416 stray dogs, according to a scientific survey conducted by the Srinagar Municipal Corporation (SMC) in 2023, the Government stated today. It said nearly one-fourth of the dogs in Srinagar, that is 15,266 stray dogs, were sterilised between June 2023 and September 2025.
The figures have been provided by the Housing & Urban Development Department (H&UDD) in a written reply to a starred question raised by MLA Zadibal Tanvir Sadiq. According to the reply, the 2023 survey carried out by SMC used the Lincoln-Petersen Formula to estimate the stray dog population within SMC limits. The Animal Welfare Board of India has recognised it as a scientific survey and it found approximately 64,416 in Srinagar.
The government has stated in the reply to the question of the legislator that from June 2023 to September 2025, SMC sterilised 15,266 stray dogs and immunised 15,725 dogs. The surgeries and vaccinations were carried out at Animal Birth Control (ABC) centres at Tengpora and Shuhama.
The government also said dog-bite cases in J&K were being recorded and monitored through the State Surveillance Officer under the Integrated Disease Surveillance Programme (IDSP). The IDSP operates under the Directorate of Health Services, Kashmir.
It has also said that SMC currently has ABC centres at Tengpora Bypass and Shuhama in SKUAST. Together, these facilities have a combined kennel capacity of 121.
An additional ABC centre at Ahal Chatterhama is also coming up, with the kennel capacity of 60. The three centres will have an aggregate kennel capacity of 181, once the third one is ready, according to the government.
The department said ABC/ARV programmes are also being implemented in Jammu. The Jammu Municipal Corporation (JMC) has sterilized 50,000 dogs since 2014.
“However, keeping in view the scale and geographical spread of the stray dog population in the urban areas of the Union Territory, the existing infrastructure and operational capacity require further augmentation and strengthening to ensure wider, effective and sustained coverage,” the reply states while acknowledging gaps in efforts to control stray dog population.
It listed its strengthening efforts as: the expansion of ABC centres, strengthening veterinary manpower and dog-catching facilities, augmentation of holding/isolation and post-operative facilities, expansion of sterilisation and ARV coverage, scientific identification and record-keeping of sterilised/vaccinated dogs, regulation of designated feeding points, improved solid-waste management and intensified public awareness.
The government has said that veterinary surgeons/doctors have been deputed to municipal corporations and urban local bodies to for helping in ABC/ARV programme.

Tiny image sparks big backlash in Nikon photo contest
- Published
The winning entry of a prestigious scientific photography competition is being re-evaluated following criticism from other scientists that it was made with AI.
Nikon's annual Small World In Motion contest accepts photos and video taken using powerful microscopes, and has run annually for the last 15 years.
The winner was a short video submitted by Dr Ning Xu, a researcher at Tsinghua University in China, which claims to be footage of tiny, hair-like structures called cilia moving inside the airways of a child with a rare disease.
Xu did not respond to the BBC's request for comment, but has posted online denying he broke the competition rules.
In a response to a post by Nikon on LinkedIn, external, he did not dispute using AI within the image processing but said he remained within the rules of the contest.
"AI was not used to generate the experimental movie, the cilia, or their motion," he said.
Xu's video is artificially brightly coloured - common in microscopy and permitted in the contest - which is usually done manually using stains and dyes on the sample itself.
He accepted AI was used "to distinguish and visualize features in the reconstructed grayscale images".
But the challenges made by other scientists include claims that the video contains shapes and movements which did not fit with normal cell structures or behaviours, and that the cilia seemed to be too big.
Commenting on Nikon's social media post, Edward Phelps, associate professor at Florida University, observed some of the structures "pop in and out of existence" and the cilia "appear from nowhere".
Meanwhile PhD student Ian Donovan from UT Southwestern Medical Centre said the source image appeared to contain a distinctive watermark indicating it had been AI generated.
Additionally, two former competition judges said they also had concerns about whether the image was real.
'Respectfully complying'
Nikon said Xu was "respectfully complying" with its investigation and had provided it with additional technical documents.
Dr Patrick Hickey, who came fifth in the 2026 Small World contest, said the recognition the award represents means more than the $3,000 (£2,250) prize itself.
"If you spend a lot of your time in a dark room looking down a microscope, it's really nice to be able to show people and to show the public," he said.
"There's an interesting fusion between science and art, and a lot of the images that scientists are making have some very abstract and artistic qualities to them."
Hickey said it would be unfair on other entrants if it turned out the winning video was unfairly altered by AI.
"There's a specific set of rules in the contest, and one of them was quite clearly that you couldn't use generative AI to produce things, and the other was obviously that it has to be taken under a microscope," he said.
So far, Nikon is standing by its procedures but it said there would be an update soon.
"At this time, we don't see that any rules were violated," it said in a statement.

The World Health Organization said on Friday, September 25, 2026 that the Ebola outbreak caused by the Bundibugyo virus in the Democratic Republic of the Congo has spread to two additional health zones, bringing the total number affected to 63 across seven provinces.
The newly affected zones are Bulu in Sud Ubangi province and Dungu in Haut-Uele province, which borders South Sudan.
As of September 23, Congo had reported 7,890 confirmed cases and 3,799 deaths, according to the WHO.
WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said conflict and population displacement were making it more difficult for health workers to reach affected communities and trace people who may have been exposed to the virus.
"It's very difficult to see Ebola in isolation because even our response in Ebola is affected by the conflict because there is displacement and there is access problem to some areas," Tedros said. He said restricted access could leave contacts untraced, while displacement and crowding increased transmission risks.
Tedros said cases were declining overall and that contact tracing, safe burials and community engagement had improved, although transmission remained uneven across affected areas.
The lack of approved vaccines and treatments for the Bundibugyo strain was also complicating the response and could make people reluctant to seek care at treatment centers, Tedros said, adding the WHO was working to accelerate clinical trials of vaccines and treatments.
Turning to the risk of future global health emergencies, Tedros said countries needed to strengthen pandemic preparedness. “Ebola will not be a pandemic, but there could be a respiratory pathogen that can become a pandemic," he said. "Before that hits, we need to prepare."
The World Health Assembly adopted the Pandemic Agreement in May 2025 to strengthen global prevention, preparedness and response to future pandemics.
"We continue to see significant mis- and disinformation about the WHO Pandemic Agreement, with false claims. It's a power grab that cedes sovereignty to WHO," Tedros said. "This is completely untrue."

Venus is shrouded in a veil of mystery. The yellowish “lower haze” at the bottom of its atmosphere was discovered by the Venera and Pioneer Venus probes in the 1970s. These spacecraft were some of the first to successfully send images of the planet back to Earth, but the haze they saw went unexplained for decades. Now the mystery Venus was keeping has been unveiled.
What nobody knew then was that the haze is an accumulation of particles from meteorites. “Shooting stars” that burn up in the atmosphere leave behind cosmic dust particles, and after sulfuric acid interacts with these particles, it leaves behind a haze. Planetary scientist Hiroki Karyu and his research team at Tohoku University in Sendai City, Japan, finally figured out how the haze formed using a microphysical model. This type of model involves microphysics—the micro-scale processes that create clouds and precipitation on Earth and other bodies.
“The continuous influx of cosmic dust is sufficient to sustain this lower haze layer with the particle size distribution observed by the entry probes,” Karyu said in a study published in Nature Astronomy. “These haze particles of cosmic origin act as efficient condensation nuclei, promoting cloud formation in the main cloud deck even far from their initial source.”
Hazed and confused
Previous speculation suggested the haze formed from volcanic ash. Venus is known as the most volcanically active planet in our Solar System, with signs of volcanism first observed by the Magellan spacecraft in the early 1990s. Recent studies discovered the planet is more volcanically active than previously thought, but the researchers found that ash belched out by Venusian volcanoes is not the source of haze particles.
Surface dust was also ruled out. Karyu found that even if there were much larger influxes of volcanic or surface dust on Venus, the particles would still not be able to interact with the atmosphere’s sulfur in the right way to form the haze.

A second US federal judge has blocked President Donald Trump’s $100,000 fee on new H-1B visas, providing temporary relief to Indian technology professionals and US companies that depend heavily on the programme.
US District Judge Haywood Gilliam in Oakland, California, ruled that US Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) and the State Department had failed to follow required rule-making procedures before implementing the fee. The ruling follows a separate decision by a Boston federal judge in June that also blocked the charge. A federal appeals court subsequently declined to pause that ruling.
The latest decision does not permanently eliminate the $100,000 fee. Instead, it blocks the agencies from implementing the fee while the underlying legal challenge proceeds.
The development is particularly significant for Indians because they account for the largest share of H-1B beneficiaries.
USCIS data show that people born in India accounted for 283,755, or 71%, of all H-1B petitions approved in fiscal 2024. China was a distant second with 46,722 approvals, or 11.7%. For initial employment alone, Indian beneficiaries accounted for 80,449 approvals, or 57% of the total.
That means any major change in the cost or availability of new H-1B visas can have a disproportionate effect on Indian professionals seeking to work in the US.
The immediate significance of Wednesday's ruling is that the $100,000 charge cannot simply be treated as an uncontested new cost for employers seeking to sponsor affected workers while the litigation continues. The legal status of the fee, however, remains unresolved.
For Indian IT professionals, the ruling could ease some of the uncertainty surrounding US job opportunities that require new H-1B sponsorship.
The H-1B programme is widely used by technology companies to recruit foreign professionals in specialised occupations. The programme provides for 65,000 regular visas each fiscal year, plus 20,000 additional visas for people with qualifying advanced US degrees.
The $100,000 charge represented a dramatic increase from the typical H-1B fee burden, which Reuters reported had generally been around $2,000 to $5,000, depending on the circumstances.
Because employers generally bear the visa-related costs, the increase could affect companies' decisions about whether to sponsor workers from overseas.
The latest ruling therefore removes, at least for now, one major cost uncertainty for employers considering new H-1B hires. It does not, however, guarantee that an individual Indian applicant will receive an H-1B visa.
The ruling is important for US technology companies because the H-1B programme is a major channel through which they recruit specialised foreign talent.
A $100,000 charge could substantially alter the economics of sponsoring a new worker, particularly for employers that sponsor large numbers of employees. The court's decision means companies challenging the fee have another legal ruling supporting their argument that the administration did not follow the required rule-making process.
The US Chamber of Commerce has separately challenged the fee, while a coalition of unions, employers and nonprofits brought the case before Judge Gilliam.
For companies, however, the latest ruling should be viewed as temporary legal relief rather than a final resolution. The litigation over Trump's authority to impose the fee remains active.
Another important factor is the administration's separate effort to establish a permanent H-1B fee of about $103,000.
The Department of Homeland Security moved in August to adopt that charge. If finalised, it is expected to face another round of legal challenges. Reuters noted that those cases would involve different legal questions from the lawsuits surrounding Trump's existing $100,000 fee.
In other words, Wednesday's ruling does not necessarily settle the broader question of whether a six-figure H-1B charge could eventually become part of the US immigration system.
The latest case concerns the new H-1B fee, rather than ending the H-1B programme itself.
For Indian professionals who already hold H-1B status, the ruling therefore does not by itself change the basic validity of their existing visas. The H-1B programme continues to allow US employers to temporarily employ foreign professionals in specialised occupations.
The more immediate issue is the cost and conditions attached to new H-1B applications and sponsorship.
The administration has defended the fee as part of a broader effort to reshape the H-1B programme.
Trump has said the programme has been abused by companies that replace American workers with cheaper foreign labour. His administration has also introduced enhanced vetting of H-1B applicants and proposed a selection system that would favour higher-skilled and higher-paid workers.
Trump recently extended the $100,000 fee for another year after it had been due to expire on September 21.

Czech Prime Minister Andrej Babiš’s government survives no-confidence vote
The Czech government led by populist billionaire Andrej Babiš survives a parliamentary no-confidence vote
PRAGUE -- The Czech government survived a parliamentary no-confidence vote on Thursday after the opposition challeneged its widening budget deficit and raised conflict of interest concerns over populist billionaire Prime Minister Andrej Babiš.
Only 83 opposition lawmakers in Parliament’s 200-seat lower house voted to dismiss the three-party coalition government. At least 101 votes were needed to bring it down following a three-day debate.
The opposition parties that called the vote condemned the government's draft 2027 budget, which projects a deficit of 386 billion koruna ($18 billion), the second-largest in Czech history. This year’s deficit is expected to reach 310 billion koruna.
Many economists and opposition lawmakers have criticized the proposed deficit at a time when the Czech central bank expects the economy to grow by 2.7% next year.
The government says the spending is necessary to boost investment and fund priorities, such as health care, pensions and public-sector salaries.
Babiš, one of the country's richest people, has faced criticism that he has not done enough to resolve potential conflicts of interest between his private dealings and his political status.
After his ANO (YES) movement won last October’s election, Babiš has moved about 200 of companies under his Agrofert conglomerate to an independent trust fund to comply with conflict-of-interest legislation, without which his businesses would be ineligible for Czech and European Union subsidies.
His investment in the health care sector has not been affected by the move.
The European Commission said last month that the trust arrangement did not sufficiently resolve the problem, saying Babiš remains in a potential conflict of interest and suspended some payments to Agrofert.
The opposition has also criticized Babiš for his verbal attacks on independent courts, judges and media.
Babiš has formed a governing coalition with two small political groups whose agenda includes reducing support for Ukraine and rejecting some key EU policies.

CJP founder Dipke briefly detained after placard protest at Marine Drive
CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke was taken to Marine Drive police station after appearing with placards. The incident came before his party's October 2 protest, which police have not permitted.
Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) founder Abhijeet Dipke was briefly taken to the Marine Drive police station on Thursday after he was spotted carrying placards at the iconic Mumbai promenade, ahead of his organisation's proposed October 2 protest.
Dipke had gathered at Marine Drive with a group of supporters holding placards, according to a police official. A team including a woman inspector approached him and escorted him to the police station in a police van.
According to the official, the woman officer asked Dipke about his identity and hometown while taking him to the police station.
Mumbai Police, however, denied detaining Dipke. Officials said he was at Marine Drive around 5 pm, where he was meeting people and asking questions of police personnel deployed there.
Dipke later gave a different account of the incident. He said a woman police officer asked him to accompany her for a cup of tea, following which he was taken to the police station and later told he could leave. He claimed the officer told him, "Your chai is pending with us."
Dipke said he was not served tea at the station and alleged that the episode was aimed at wasting his time. He also suggested that the officer may have received instructions from senior officials to release him.
The incident came a day before the CJP's proposed protest on Gandhi Jayanti. Dipke has announced that his organisation would seek the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over alleged irregularities in the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls.
Mumbai Police has denied permission for the proposed protest, citing restrictions governing gatherings at Shivaji Park, the absence of required civic permission and concerns over traffic movement and the passage of emergency vehicles.

The Supreme Court on Tuesday (September 29, 2026) expressed concern over the sharp disparity between the prices charged to retailers and consumers for essential medicines, particularly cancer drugs, observing that steep mark-ups placed an enormous burden on taxpayers and amounted to “carnage”.
A Bench of Justices Vikram Nath and Sandeep Mehta questioned the Centre on why the 16% retailer margin provided for under the Drugs (Prices Control) Order (DPCO), 2013 should not be applied uniformly to essential medicines to curb steep mark-ups over the price to retailer (PTR).
“Why not keep the 16% margin on MRP, which is prescribed in the DPCO, on everything? ... Ultimately, the loser is the taxpayer. This is carnage, as simple as that,” the Bench remarked.
The observations came while the top court was hearing petitions filed by advocate Kishan Chand Jain and paediatric surgeon Sanjay Kulshrestha, seeking its intervention to regulate the prices of drugs, medical equipment, and generic medicines, and make them more affordable.
Justice Mehta pointed, in particular, to the nearly ten-fold mark-up on an essential cancer drug, which was supplied to retailers for around ₹3,000 but sold to consumers for ₹27,000. He questioned who ultimately benefited from the nearly ₹24,000 difference. “You tell us why this difference... Where does this chunk of money go? Ten times...” Justice Mehta remarked.
Solicitor General Tushar Mehta, appearing for the Centre, acknowledged the concern and said the government would have to find a way forward while “balancing equities”. He, however, said it was private hospitals, rather than pharmaceutical companies, that benefited from the steep mark-ups. “The pharma company is not the gainer. The gainer is the private hospital,” the Solicitor General submitted.
The Bench also flagged the practice of private hospitals insisting that patients purchase medicines from their in-house pharmacies, leaving them with little choice to procure the same drugs at lower prices elsewhere.
It also pointed to the impact of such inflated prices on public finances, observing that when treatment is covered under government-funded health schemes such as Ayushman Bharat, the cost is ultimately borne by taxpayers.
“Suppose the patient is taking treatment through government services... The government doesn’t pay, the taxpayer pays. This affects a larger section of society,” the Bench remarked.
Mr. Mehta sought time to place before the court details of the existing mechanisms governing drug pricing and assured the Bench that he would make his submissions on the next date of hearing. The Bench accordingly posted the matter for further hearing on October 12, 2026.
The petitions have sought directions to make drug formulations more affordable by curbing alleged overpricing of essential medicines by pharmaceutical companies and retailers. They have also sought stricter enforcement of price controls under the Drugs (Prices Control) Order, 2013 to prevent violations of the prescribed pricing mechanism and disproportionate profit margins across the drug supply chain.
Earlier, the top court had described the wide difference between the price to retailers and the MRP of medicines as “dacoity”, while drawing attention to the financial distress faced by patients struggling to meet treatment costs.
“The MRP is 10 times the rate at which it is provided to the retailers. If this is not extortion, then what is it? People sell their houses, ornaments to get treatment,” the Bench had remarked.

Cockroach Janta Party founder Abhijeet Dipke said on Thursday (October 1, 2026) that the group will hold a protest at Mumbai’s Shivaji Park on Friday (October 2). The protesters’ main demands include the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar and the filing of criminal charges against him.
CJP has also sought that the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) roll be frozen and that the process to appoint the Chief Election Commissioner be made transparent with civil society participation. After Mumbai, the group will hold protests in six other cities, concluding at Jantar Mantar in New Delhi by the end of October.
‘CEC is a traitor’
“Gyanesh Kumar is a traitor. He doesn’t deserve to be the CEC. He is a puppet of Amit Shah and Narendra Modi. There have been 13 crore deletions in the voters’ list since 2024. The gap between the NDA and INDIA bloc was a mere 2% (in the 2024 elections), whereas they got rid of 14% of the vote share. There is an illusion of democracy in the country, and no actual democracy,” Mr. Dipke said.
He added that since a large number of people were affected due to the deletions, many will hit the streets. “If Gyanesh Kumar doesn’t resign, they will seek Narendra Modi’s resignation,” he said, alleging that Mr. Kumar was winning elections for Mr. Modi.
Expressing apprehension about Electronic Voting Machines (EVMs), he alleged that all electronic machines can be hacked and demanded that elections be held using ballot papers.
Responding to Maharashtra Chief Minister Devendra Fadnavis’ statement about three days’ police custody for protesters, he said he did not mind three months’ custody either. “I want to tell Mr. Fadnavis, mi punha yein (‘I will come back,’ a reference to Mr. Fadnavis’s past statement claiming he would return to power).”
No permission for protest
Meanwhile, the Mumbai police have not given permission for the CJP protest. The Bombay High Court decides on petitions seeking permission to hold public events at Shivaji Park. The designated area for protests in the city is Azad Maidan. When asked if the group had approached the High Court to seek permission, Mr. Dipke said: “What will happen in the court? Taareekh pe taareekh (referring to prolonged court hearings).”
Responding to questions on why he did not choose to protest at Azad Maidan, he said: “We can protest anywhere. We want to protest at Shivaji Park only.”
‘SC equally guilty’
When asked why the group did not wait for the Supreme Court to hear the pending petitions about the problems with electoral rolls and the SIR, he accused the apex court of being equally guilty. “Which Supreme Court? The same court which did not allow people to vote in the West Bengal elections?” he asked.
Responding to allegations of being a B team of the Congress, Mr. Dipke said, “Sit together and decide whose B team we are. The Congress accuses us of being a B team of the RSS and BJP. The ruling party accuses us of being a B team of the Congress.”
IIT student death
Mr. Dipke was asked a question about reservation in education. While responding, he asked why nobody questioned management quota reservation. He said it was shameful that the parents of the IIT Bombay student who died by suicide had to sit on a protest to seek justice.
“Many students have died in IITs. Is there enough representation? There is not. People need to be made to feel that they belong there. How can you justify that a kid can die by suicide for cheating? How inhuman can you become? Children coming from tribal areas have to go through a lot to be at such places. That the parents continue to sit on a protest to seek justice for their child is shameful,” he said.

Netanyahu names ‘true hero’ Indian pilot who opened cockpit door after being stabbed on flight to Israel
Israel said Captain Smit Machchhar was stabbed repeatedly while trying to stop the deadly crash

The pilot who fought off his co-pilot who stabbed him during an attempted midair attack on a flight to Israel has been named as Captain Smit Machchhar.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu praised Cpt Machchhar, an Indian national, as a "true hero" for fighting back against the attacker and opening the cockpit door during the commercial flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv.
"My salute to the Indian pilot Captain Smit Machchhar for his extraordinary bravery," Netanyahu posted on X. "Despite being stabbed and seriously injured, he fought back, resisted, opened the cockpit door, and enabled passengers and crew to overpower the attacker."
The attack unfolded on Wednesday morning, roughly two and a half hours into Flydubai Flight FZ1073.
As the Boeing 737 crossed into Jordanian airspace, Machchhar’s co-pilot launched a knife attack inside the cockpit and attempted to sabotage the flight controls to crash the airliner, officials said. The aircraft plunged an extraordinary 14,000 feet in less than 30 seconds.
Despite bleeding heavily after sustaining multiple severe stab wounds, Israeli officials said Cpt Machchhar was able to hit the cockpit's door release mechanism before collapsing.
Several passengers then charged forward to breach the unlocked flight deck, joining crew members to physically restrain the attacker on the floor.
"My daughter heard screaming and saw a man with a knife put the pilot on the floor, with blood everywhere," said passenger Yasmin Abu Kasis. "The plane started to lose control, so all the people were screaming."
Meital, a passenger whose husband attempted to help, told Israel’s Channel 12: "There were stabbings and a lot of blood. My husband rushed to the front of the plane, and ... neutralised the terrorist."
Another passenger, Almog Itali, said an off-duty British pilot helped to rescue the plane and executed an emergency landing at Tabuk Airport in northeastern Saudi Arabia.
In a short translated clip on the BBC, Mr Itali said: “There were two pilots in the front, one stabbed the other, and there were two spare pilots who were supposed to operate the next flight.
“The relief pilots are European, one of them British, who entered (the cockpit) and pulled the aircraft up, pulled the yoke, stabilised the plane and landed us in Saudi Arabia.”
Local authorities arrested the suspect on the tarmac immediately after touchdown. Both pilots were then hospitalised in Tabuk, where the Indian Embassy in Saudi Arabia has since confirmed Machchhar underwent emergency surgery and is in stable condition.
Netanyahu added that Machchhar "saved the lives of 174 people, including Israeli citizens and other nationals," wishing him a full recovery.
Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz described the incident as an attempted “jihadist terrorist attack” and said the suspect intended to crash the plane with everyone on board.
In response, Netanyahu has ordered security services to immediately tighten screening protocols across all domestic and international carriers entering Israeli airspace.
The 174 passengers were later flown from Tabuk to Ben Gurion Airport on a replacement aircraft sent by Flydubai, where they were reunited with emotional family members late Wednesday evening.
The Israeli prime minister personally met with several of the returning passengers on the tarmac at Ben Gurion, praising their courage and thanking them for intervening.
Flydubai has confirmed that formal investigations into the attacker's underlying motives remain ongoing.

Suspected Ebola case at Montreal hospital turns out to be a false alarm
Hospital has lifted emergency isolation protocols
A Montreal hospital has lifted emergency isolation measures after a suspected Ebola case was determined to be a false alarm, officials said.
The female patient arrived at the Centre hospitalier de l'Université de Montréal (CHUM) late Thursday afternoon exhibiting signs of the deadly disease.
Earlier in the day, Irène Marcheterre, a spokesperson for the CHUM, said that as soon as the suspicious symptoms were identified, the hospital immediately enacted its required isolation protocols.
She said all necessary safety measures were put in place, and insisted there was no risk to the public.
Just before 8 p.m., another spokesperson, Ellen Caracas, told CBC News that the patient tested negative for Ebola and emergency protocols were lifted.
The suspected case came amid an ongoing and deadly Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo, where thousands have died in recent months.
Marcheterre could not confirm whether the patient had recently travelled from the region, stating she did not know the woman's travel history.
